title: Everybody Wants to F*ck Me review – Taron Egerton is hounded in sharp-toothed dating nightmare | Toronto film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: It’s Get Out meets the viral Shitty Media Men list in this hugely entertaining mix of dark comedy and stalker thriller with a brilliant alternating turn from Taron Egerton
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: It’s Get Out meets the viral Shitty Media Men list in this hugely entertaining mix of dark comedy and stalker thriller with a brilliant alternating turn from Taron Egerton
Content: Taron Egerton in Everybody Wants to Fuck Me.Photograph: Jaap BuitendijkView image in fullscreenTaron Egerton in Everybody Wants to Fuck Me.Photograph: Jaap BuitendijkFirst look reviewToronto film festival 2026ReviewEverybody Wants to F*ck Me review – Taron Egerton is hounded in sharp-toothed dating nightmareToronto film festival:It’s Get Out meets the viral Shitty Media Men list in this hugely entertaining mix of dark comedy and stalker thriller with a brilliant alternating turn from Taron EgertonBenjamin Leein TorontoSat 12 Sep 2026 11.27 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 11.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEveryone knows an Adam. He’s not like those other guys, the ones who won’t take no for an answer and speak lasciviously about women to their mates. He’s doing the work, listening to and uplifting female voices, working at an all-female gallery while being constantly aware of his cis white male privilege. He has a Mubi tote bag, reads Edna O’Brien’s Country Girl in Hackney cafes, has a poster of Cléo from 5 to 7 in his apartment and has even named his dog after his favourite Haim sister. He is … a nice guy.In first-time writer-director Jonathan Schey’s canny debut Everybody Wants to Fuck Me, Adam is also a fraud.Girl Group review – Rebel Wilson’s dreadful music comedy is a spice-free wannabeRead moreHe’s played byTaron Egerton, someone who has recently been finding his footing as an adult actor, whether as more conventional lead of Netflix’s excellent B-movie thriller Carry-On or as the less expected gonzo villain of Netflix’s mid B-movie thriller Apex. But freed from streaming shackles (he’s also led two Apple dramas, one of which I genuinely don’t think anyone knows exists), he’s able to show just how much more he can do in edgier, stranger territory and how far he’s willing to go without blinking. Turns out, pretty far.In a swiftly revealing cold open, we see Adam in a note-perfect meet-cute with Mia McKenna-Bruce’s unsuspecting Londoner. They dance to Troye Sivan (ally!), discuss their love for Before Sunset and, despite him not obviously pushing for it, they have sex back at his place. But the morning after, despite telling her he’s “obsessed” mid-thrust and despite making leaf art in her flat white, something is off. Maybe it’s the fact that she’s put her artisanal mug on the nightstand without a coaster or maybe it’s just because he’s in a “bojangled headspace” or maybe it’s because he does this all the time.His exhausted gay best friend Emma (Rooster’s Charly Clive, incredibly charming) accuses him of “romantic terrorism”, but rolling her eyes and gently jabbing him is part of their learned shtick as is her allowing him to cut their night out short when he spots an attractive woman at the theatre bar. Adam tries his luck with Sofia (Jessica Henwick), who sees through his performance, poking fun at his dating profile and his many, many matches left on read. But still, she seems interested and invites him back to her place …Something happens that night, the specifics of which we’re unsure of, like Adam. After a quick smoke, he’s knocked unconscious and he wakes to find Sofia gone. He chalks it up to yet another one-night stand but something has shifted not in him but in the world around him. Adam was never exactly struggling for female attention but there’s a new, more aggressive intensity to it with women staring at him on the tube and colleagues laughing a little too hard at his mediocre jokes. For a while, Adam makes the most of it, his door revolving that much more than usual but the sweetness begins to sour as he realises there’s something more sinister going on when even his dog Alana starts giving him the eye.There are elements here of last year’s Toronto breakout Obsession but we’re more firmly in the recently familiar, and increasingly exhausting, land of the “social thriller”, although wisely with more (genuinely funny) comedy than this often overly self-serious subgenre has entertained for a while. The post-Get Out surge has been far more miss than hit and while this is a smarter and sharper addition (a crude sell would be Get Out meets the viral Shitty Media Men list of 2017), it does still grapple with some recurring issues, especially as the last-act explanation rears its head. To Schey’s credit, he does a better job than most (the bar has been set low by the maddening stupidity of both Blink Twice and Don’t Worry Darling) and finds the right balance of serious to silly, but the film is reliant on a poorly thought through convenience that pushed me a little too far out. Schey also leans on a last-scene trope that ranks among my least favourite ways to end a movie, right next to a character asking another “what now?” as credits fade.But he mostly gets a lot right, both as writeranddirector, a not-to-be-sniffed-at achievement for a first-timer given how many tend to only convince while wearing one of those hats. The target here is so easy to so many of us (last year even saw aperformative male contestin Washington Square Park), but Schey works at making Adam a real person rather than a meme to be simply ridiculed. He doesn’t turn Adam into a full-throated bad guy but also manages to avoid softening who he really is, and even as we follow his descent right alongside him, Schey skirts falling back on uneasy “you can’t say anything any more!” frustration especially during a cleverly telling spiral speech (Adam complains how “exhausting” it is to be nice). So much is also down to Egerton, who delivers a fearless, full-on performance, scarily believable as both the guy who would politely andethicallyget you into bed and also the one who would coldly suggest you leave the morning after, and he shows himself to be a more specifically funny and understated comedy actor than he’s been given credit for.It comes from Margot Robbie’s LuckyChap production company, also behind the not dissimilar Promising Young Woman, but it rights so many of that film’s many wrongs, from an increase in emotional maturity to an improved aesthetic (this takes place in real, breathing, stylishly captured London, not a bright and tinny approximation of a 2000s Sundance indie) but most prominently in its willingness to bear and use its teeth to draw blood. If that film was a tease then this one isn’t scared to go all the way.Everybody Wants to Fuck Me is premiering at theToronto film festivaland will be released at a later dateExplore more on these topicsToronto film festival 2026First look reviewToronto film festivalTaron EgertonThrillersComedy filmsFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The moment I knew: I had planned to break up with him – then he snuck out of school to buy me hot chips | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: Maleah Pearce wanted to end her relationship with high school ‘bad boy’ Dylan before they grew too attached. Then one lunchtime, he brought her a surprise
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Maleah Pearce wanted to end her relationship with high school ‘bad boy’ Dylan before they grew too attached. Then one lunchtime, he brought her a surprise
Content: ‘I liked that he had a strong relationship with his mother … He also did a lot of pullups and had nice biceps’: Dylan and Maleah in their high school years.Composite: Supplied/Getty Images/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreen‘I liked that he had a strong relationship with his mother … He also did a lot of pullups and had nice biceps’: Dylan and Maleah in their high school years.Composite: Supplied/Getty Images/Guardian DesignThe moment I knewAustralian lifestyleThe moment I knew: I had planned to break up with him – then he snuck out of school to buy me hot chipsMaleah Pearcewanted to end her relationship with high school ‘bad boy’ Dylan before they grew too attached. Then one lunchtime, he brought her a surpriseFind more stories fromthe moment I knew seriesMaleah PearceSat 12 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 19.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDylan and I first started dating in high school when we were 16. He was a “bad boy” who got drunk at parties and occasionally spoke to other people with his fists.One night, I was sitting at my computer, chatting with friends on MSN and Facebook and Dylan’s name popped up. I enjoyed playing online checkers with people from school, so I invited him to a game. During the game we chatted online, which led to flirting. The winner got to choose what they wanted. I lost and what did Dylan ask for? To date me. We agreed to one date at the movies and to declare to the school we were boyfriend and girlfriend. I thought this was hilarious, though I planned to break up with him after a few days.The date went better than I thought – he offered to invite friends so that I wasn’t alone. He paid for my ticket, bought me Malteasers, and when I realised I’d left my glasses in the car, he ran back to the car park in skinny jeans and sandals to retrieve them.At school, I remember the first time he tried to touch me, on my lower back. When his hand made contact with my shirt I immediately told him he was not allowed to touch me without my permission. And he didn’t. I liked this about him and felt more comfortable around him.The moment I knew: I’d lost his number and was about to switch off my old phone for good – then a text pingedRead moreDays turned into weeks, and I still hadn’t broken up with Dylan. I liked that he had a strong relationship with his mother, worked two part-time jobs while at school, was eager to go to university and had great plans for his future. He also did a lot of pull-ups and had nice biceps.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsOn another date, we watched Toy Story 3 at the cinemas. Dylan pointed to the little girl character, Bonnie, and said, “That’s what our daughter would look like if we had one.” I was surprised that a teenage boy would think of this.He said he wanted a long-term relationship, someone he could be with for ever, and said he would like that with me. I wasn’t too sure about that yet. I had a lot of plans of my own. I wanted to go to university and go into scriptwriting or become a novelist – both difficult career paths. Dylan wanted to be an engineer. His future was very assured, while mine felt unknown. I decided to end the relationship before we grew too attached.Then one day at school, during lunchtime, I sat in a group with my friends and said I felt like some hot chips from KFC. Dylan overheard, and snuck out of the school grounds and walked all the way to the shops. I remember him jumping back over the school fence in his school uniform, clutching a brown paper KFC bag. I had no idea he was going to do it and was very surprised when he brought it to me – grinning, red-faced, hair a mess. He was put in detention. Dylan lost an afternoon, but he won my heart. And the chips were delicious.View image in fullscreen‘His way of saying “I love you” is by asking, “This weekend, should we buy some more books?”’: author Maleah Pearce and her husband, Dylan.Photograph: SuppliedFrom then on, this teenage boy would do anything for me. He drove me anywhere I wanted to go, stopped going to parties, never drank alcohol again and went to therapy to deal with his reckless spirit. I never asked him to do these things, but he said he did them for me. Although he did continue to ditch school and bring me KFC – which was traitorous, since he was doing weekend shifts at Red Rooster.At 18, when we were at uni, Dylan and I moved in together. In our early 20s, we married. In 2020, our little girl was born – we named her Bonnie.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDylan is so supportive of me. When I told him that I was going to work on becoming an author, the next day he renovated our spare room to become my office and surprised me with my dream computer. His way of saying “I love you” is by asking, “This weekend, should we buy some more books?” and “Do you want me to read what you’ve written today?”And of course, on date nights, Dylan and I always go out for KFC.Maleah Pearce writes under the pen name Penny Sunday.Kill To Loveby Penny Sunday is available now through Hachette Australia (AU$24.99)Tell us the moment you knewShare your experienceShare your love storyDo you have a romantic realisation you'd like to share? title: Naomi Klein: ‘Extreme wealth has a deranging effect. It turns you into a supremacist’ | Society books | The Guardian
description: She’s tackled neoliberalism and the digital world, now the writer and activist is taking on tech billionaires. She explains how the super-rich are capitalising on climate and financial chaos in pursuit of power
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: She’s tackled neoliberalism and the digital world, now the writer and activist is taking on tech billionaires. She explains how the super-rich are capitalising on climate and financial chaos in pursuit of power
Content: Naomi Klein.Photograph: Tanya GoehringView image in fullscreenNaomi Klein.Photograph: Tanya GoehringSociety booksInterviewNaomi Klein: ‘Extreme wealth has a deranging effect. It turns you into a supremacist’Zoe WilliamsShe’s tackled neoliberalism and the digital world, now the writer and activist is taking on tech billionaires. She explainshow the super-rich are capitalising on climate and financial chaos in pursuit of powerSat 12 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNaomi Klein’s new book starts on a mountaintop with two “faithful men gathering an audience to share their vision”. It’s a vision of a paradise city, gated at every entrance, no need for weapons there, everyone in it rich. One of the men has tears in his eyes as he describes its beauty. The opening scene of End Times Fascism, co-written with Astra Taylor, is not a metaphor, however. The men are Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. The year is 2026, the mountain is Davos. The paradise city will be calledNew Gaza.The World Economic Forum get-together inDavos, Switzerland, has always had a twin purpose – to provide a platform for the super-rich to describe all the good they are doing on poverty and climate, and to give us a glimpse into their enviable lives. This year what we witnessed was, quite brazenly, the world’s richest men gathering to discuss the real estate possibilities of a mass grave.At that same Davos, Donald Trump announced hisBoard of Peacefor the reconstruction of Gaza – it has delivered nothing substantial in the seven months since, but more significantly, Klein says, “we’re being hit with so many extraordinary events that it’s hard to hold on to what a big deal it is: they have announced a privatised United Nations”.“I think we understand that wealth compounds, right? Certainly rich people understand that wealth compounds,” Klein continues, speaking to me from her peaceful, roomy study in British Columbia. “But I don’t feel like we spend a lot of time really thinking about the implications of what it means for that much wealth to be compounded, and what that does psychologically. Part of the new shamelessness we’re seeing is just what happens when this amount of financial, mediagenic, technological and military weaponry is concentrated in the hands of this very small, unaccountable group of people. They stop trying to seduce us in any way.”Klein looks calm and curious as she delivers this message. She has a ready laugh. But then, she had the same unruffled, buoyant delivery when I interviewed her on stage in Manchester for Doppelgänger, her 2023 book in which she described how the digital world is destroying our connection to reality, and one another. In 1999, when her breakthrough work No Logo was published, she seemed exhilaratingly certain, at 29, that neoliberalism was bringing harm that we couldn’t yet even see the extent of, and nonetheless appeared centred and happy in the world. Somehow she manages to maintain this attitude, even though the news she delivers is always so convincingly, unbelievably bad.End Times Fascism describes the world we’re in, where the components of authoritarianism are modelled everywhere you look: anarcho-libertarian economics in Argentina, the destruction of a free press in Russia, the erosion of democratic institutions in Hungary (until Viktor Orbán was deposed), “anti-immigrant neofascism” in Italy, the weaponisation of trans identity by Jair Bolsonaro in Brazil, Islamophobia in Modi’s India. But this is fascism with a difference. Its proponents are actively willing an apocalypse, or a wave of interconnected apocalypses brought forth by climate change and financial chaos, to hasten us towards a post-democratic world in which only a rich few survive to prosper.double quotation markThese are trends I’ve been following for a long time, the privatised enclave born of shock, of disaster, I saw when I was reporting from IraqThis book started as anarticle in the Guardian, “which went totally viral,” Klein says. “Astra and I knew there was a lot more reporting to do, but on a personal level, did we want to spend the next year in the minds of these people, in these cultures? Then Astra said, ‘I’m down the rabbit hole, I’m gonna be listening to these guys anyway. So I may as well feel like I’m doing something about it.’ This is the reason it’s the first book I’ve co-written. When you go to dark, scary places, it’s nice to bring a friend.” Astra Taylor is also a writer, activist and documentary maker, and founded theDebt Collective, a fascinating experiment in building structured, quasi-unionised solidarity around personal debt, with the long term goals of abolishing student tuition fees, nationalising healthcare and building tenant power.In the book, Klein and Taylor introduce us to the religious fundamentalists, Christian Zionists and Christian Nationalists in the US, readying themselves for the second coming. Describing a “bunkered state”, the authors connect climate-related disasters, a rabid anti-immigrant standing army in the form of ICE and a politics built on false promises and misinformation to depict a febrile, riven society that doesn’t know what to believe. But the truly terrifying bit is the bridging section, on tech billionaires. The super-rich have apocalypse fantasies of their own, built not on faith or ideology but on a calm and rational evaluation of how best to maintain their position; they would genuinely rather reign in hell than share in heaven. And they have all the money to make sure they get there.“These are trends I’ve been following for a long time,” Klein says. “The privatised enclave born of shock, of disaster, I saw when I was reporting from Iraq. There’s the image of the Green Zone, this Emerald City run by the US in the middle of Baghdad, built by Halliburton and all of these private contractors, with the power to appoint a viceroy. In the final parts of The Shock Doctrine [2007], I talk about how these contractors migrated [from Iraq] to Hurricane Katrina, and the idea that these climate disasters are their next growth frontier. Reporters started calling New Orleans ‘Baghdad on the Bayou’. The gang’s all here, there’s Halliburton, there’s Bechtel, there’s Blackwater.”But, and she cannot stress this enough, as useful as it is to know the recent history of these trends, you should not take comfort from the idea that you’ve seen it all before. “I have found the image of a spiral really useful, in terms of how to make sense of the fact that our era is both familiar and different,” Klein says. “The thing about a spiral is that you’re going round, but you’re not going to the same place. If the spiral is pointing down, it’s deeper, it’s tighter, it’s carrying more velocity, it’s carrying more force, it’s carrying more heat, it’s carrying more violence.” The image is at once poetic and extremely sobering. She proffers a brief morale boost, like someone handing you a slice of orange on your way into a war zone. “You can flip a spiral – it goes outwards, it’s the spiral of the universe.”At the moment we’re in now, when crises and disasters hit so frequently that we’re in a constant state of disorientation and shock, the status quo isn’t static, it’s always getting worse. “There’s this impulse to read history,” Klein says. “We’ve seen it again and again. After 9/11, people were suddenly reading history books about Afghanistan and Iraq, Chomsky, trying to find their bearings. We saw it again during the pandemic, people were reading about the plagues of the past. But there’s a trap in believing that everything has happened before, that there is not a compounding effect of history. After Donald Trump was re-elected, I’ll be honest with you, Shock Doctrine sales went crazy. People were saying, ‘It’s exactly like you said,’ and I was thinking, ‘I don’t think it is’.”double quotation markMusk’s satellites  are crawling through the sky, and he wants more. Who said he could? Who gave him that right?’The neoliberal age – for brevity let’s call it the period between the end of the cold war and Covid – was “capitalism lying on the couch in its underwear, going ‘what are you gonna do, leave me?’ In the cold war, a little competition went a long way – after the collapse of the Soviet Union, that competition is lost, capitalism stopped trying.” But there was a vulnerability to being super-rich in those days, because whether you’d come by your wealth through privatisation politics in the US or Europe, or by hastier, more kleptocratic means in ex-communist states, it was plainly public wealth that you’d captured. “So they would stage these seduction rituals, whether it was at Davos or Aspen, or atTed, or theClinton Global Initiative. They’d say, ‘We are going to cure the sick, and we are going to fund your schools in this new and exciting way, don’t worry about us. Don’t be afraid of our wealth. This is actually a new way of redistributing for the public good.’”I distinctly remember that world: huge conferences like the Skoll foundation awards, where journalists would be wined and dined while watching immensely rich people hand out £20,000 prizes to grassroots clean water initiatives in Kenya. To be fair, in the era before and directly after the financial crash, there were plenty of dissenting voices about capitalist benevolence solving intractable problems like inequality. Many people, Klein at their vanguard, pointed out that it smelled like a scam. But while we were having that discussion, the wealth agenda moved on.In the run-up to the 2024 presidential election, at the Faena Hotel in Miami, Peter Thiel hosted panel discussions titled “the enemy”, naming sustainable development goals, “precautionary principles” and “social responsibility” as those foes, rounded off with an “apocalypse ball”-themed fancy dress party . Some of the costumes, Klein and Taylor write, were “a doctor of eugenics’’; a “Haitian chef with a bloodied cat toy hanging out of his apron [a reference to the Springfield immigrant pet‑eating hoax, which spread in 2024, repeated by both Trump and JD Vance]; a couple wearing pagers as a ha-ha reference to Israel’s murderous attack in Lebanon.”View image in fullscreenNaomi Klein and Astra Taylor.Photograph: naomiklein.substack.comThiel has been explicitly anti-democracy for years, writing in 2009, “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.” But other tech billionaires have had a complete volte face. “Jeff Bezos renamed a stadium in Seattle the Climate Pledge Arena, and gave out Earth prizes,” Klein points out. Elon Musk invested in electric cars and once saw himself as a saviour figure. “Any time anyone was in trouble, Musk would rush in to save them, ‘I shall save Puerto Rico’, ‘I shall save the children stuck down the mine’. It’s fun to be a superhero, right? But if you’re going to be a superhero, you should be worshipped. And people stopped worshiping them.” Now, the climate pledges are gone, replaced by a performed nihilism around averting climate crisis, coupled with a determination to build ever more data centres. “We’re not dealing with stupid people who don’t understand climate change,” Klein says. “We’re dealing with people who know very clearly what it means to wire together35 gas turbines in Memphis.” (It means gargantuan energy and water use, as well as the destruction of air and sound quality in the vicinity, all for Musk to power Grok, hisintermittently Nazi large language model.)The speed with which previously Democrat-leaning billionaires fell in behind Trump in 2024 was jaw-dropping. “I don’t think that Mark Zuckerberg’s phase of seeming to care deeply about democracy and climate change was real,” Klein says. “He reincarnates as whatever is good for his business. Figures like Thiel and Musk, where there is real ideology there, are easier to understand than figures like Bezos and Zuckerberg, where it really does feel like there’s notherethere, they’re just uninteresting guys that ended up massively rich.” She’s passingly interested in what combination of events created these men, many of whom were forged in the dotcom boom, when they were worshipped as gods, pictured on the cover of Time magazine in gold thrones. There’s an element of ego rage, that we just aren’t grateful enough. Ultimately, though, “we end the book concluding that wealth has its own deranging effects. It almost inevitably turns you into a supremacist because humans are creatures of story and you need a story to rationalise, why you? Why do you have so much in a time of so much want and need? And the only possible story that’s available is that there’s something about you that justifies it.”There’s a new goading quality to the talking points of the super-rich – explicit eugenicism and Islamophobia, raw delight in the prospect of AI wiping out our jobs. It almost feels as though they’re daring us to rebel, just so that they can prove that rebellion is fruitless.On that, though, Klein would disagree. It is not beyond our collective means to build a wealth disarmament movement, or a tech disarmament movement. She points to the Pearson brothers, KeShaun and Justin, fighting Musk’s Colossus 2 data centre in Memphis: “the way they so consciously root their struggle in the history of the civil rights movement, and the environmental justice movement in Memphis, going back to the formerly enslaved people who built Boxtown. This is where MLK was murdered, assassinated after marching with the sanitation workers in Memphis.” KeShaun Pearson leads Memphis Community Against Pollution, which has had major wins against oil pipelines, the industrial release of carcinogenic chemicals, and is now mobilising against data centres. Justin is running for Congress.In End Times Fascism, Klein and Taylor raise Walter Benjamin’s concept “jetztzeit”, literally “now time”, a moment so pregnant with the spirit, the urgency of revolution that it marshals the energy of all movements that went before it. Again, it’s poetic, but it’s also literal, observable. If we want to oppose this new fascist strain, we really have to get a move on. “I don’t tend to use this language, I try to be measured, but I think I’ve earned the right to escalate,” she says. “The moment we’re in, people are really mad and however mad you are, it’s not enough. Because there is something so profound about no longer believing in the future, about seeing no value in our shared home, in the natural world. They’re traitors to creation.”Klein doesn’t want for reasons to fight. “I’ve made a choice to live very close to nature in a pretty wild part of British Columbia,” she says. “On a dark night, it’s a blanket of stars. And now we see so many of what I call Elon’s space bugs [Starlink satellites] just crawling through the sky. He wants to increase that a hundredfold. Who said he could? Who gave him that right? That’s a place where I find my anger. I get really angry about the stars. I get really angry about the orcas. I get really angry about Gaza. Other people will find their anger somewhere else. We have to find our places of deepest love and fight like hell.”End Times Fascism by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor is published by Allen Lane on15 September.To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: From black-clad agitators to an appeal for ‘Tommo’s Mum’: an unsettling week with the Patriot Platform | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: A militaristic operation with features of influencer culture, the new anti-migrant movement seems to show a shift in tactics and rhetoric
Author: Amelia Gentleman
Headline: A militaristic operation with features of influencer culture, the new anti-migrant movement seems to show a shift in tactics and rhetoric
Content: From top left, a National Front demonstration, Oswald Mosley and his blackshirts, EDL supporters, Unite the Kingdom protesters, Stephen Yaxley-Lennon (Tommy Robinson); in the foreground, Daniel Thomas and Patriot Platform protesters.Composite: Guardian Design/SSPL/Getty Images/PA/Alamy/AP/AFP/EPAView image in fullscreenFrom top left, a National Front demonstration, Oswald Mosley and his blackshirts, EDL supporters, Unite the Kingdom protesters, Stephen Yaxley-Lennon (Tommy Robinson); in the foreground, Daniel Thomas and Patriot Platform protesters.Composite: Guardian Design/SSPL/Getty Images/PA/Alamy/AP/AFP/EPAThe Saturday readImmigration and asylumFrom black-clad agitators to an appeal for ‘Tommo’s Mum’: an unsettling week with the Patriot PlatformA militaristic operation with features of influencer culture, the new anti-migrant movement seems to show a shift in tactics and rhetoricAmelia GentlemanSat 12 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 01.01 EDTShareShortly after 7am last Saturday in the English coastal town of Dover, livestreamed footage distributed by Britain’s newest anti-migrant movement showed dozens of men in paramilitary outfits jumping out from the backs of vehicles, their faces covered beneath balaclavas, their hands in black gloves.Within an hour, hundreds more masked agitators, dressed head to toe in black, some wearing silver crosses around their necks, were marching through the town’s streets, clapping and chanting “Stop the boats” and “Christ is king”, blockading the busy port for hours.Anti-immigration protests have become a familiar sight in Britain over the past five years, with demonstrators expressing anger at successive governments’ inability to stop people arriving in small dinghies from France, across the Channel. But last weekend’s launch of the new Patriot Platform movement appeared to mark a significant shift both in rhetoric and tactics, disrupting once again the shifting ecosystem of the British far right.A disciplined, well-organised and militaristic operation was unleashed. The new movement also displayed features of online influencer culture, with manosphere undertones, led by people who seem skilled at swiftly pulling together flashmobs of protesters and highly adept at exploiting social media’s algorithms to attract attention to their cause and fundraise. Most unnerving was the masked appearance of protesters, and the intertwining of Christian chanting with anti-migrant sentiment.Footage of the weekend’s disruption posted on the YouTube page of the movement’s leader, Daniel Thomas, who calls himself Danny Tommo, has had, in total, more than a million views, with visitors to the site invited to pay a £4.99 monthly fee to subscribe to his channel and join the community of so-called patriots.“We’re doing this under Christianity. We’re doing this with Christian British and English men. We’re not doing this with thugs,” Thomas, 37, tells his viewers.But most politicians, even on the hard right, expressed instant scepticism. Reform UK’s leader, Nigel Farage, said the display was “disgusting”. “Nobody, at any political protest, whether they’re on the left or right, should be wearing balaclavas. It is wrong, it’s horrible,” he said.Concerned that police forces had revealed themselves to be unprepared, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said on Thursday that the government expected police officers in future to make “full use” of new powers allowing them to ban face coverings at protests.Academics and analysts of the far right have spent the week trying to assess whether the new grouping has staying power and whether Thomas is himself sufficiently disciplined to unite a splintered anti-immigrant right.View image in fullscreenDaniel Thomas arriving outside Associated Newspapers on Wednesday.Photograph: Carl Court/Getty Images“Is Danny Tommo a threat or a clown?” the anti-racist organisation Searchlight asked this week, before concluding: “A bit of both.”Joe Mulhall, the director of research at Hope Not Hate, the anti-fascist organisation, who has been charting the movement’s growth over the summer, described last weekend’s protests as “an alarming development”, which could prove dangerous if protesters continued to target boats carrying asylum seekers. He said the rhetoric, the optics and the movement’s recruitment strategy all represented a shift. “It’s much more vigilante in style, and organised in a more clandestine way,” he said.In the decades since Oswald Mosley launched the British Union of Fascists, with its blackshirted followers, Britain has seen an evolution of different far-right movements, their fortunes rising and falling. The National Front in the 1970s was followed by the British National party in the 1980s and 90s. The English Defence League, Britain First and Patriotic Alternative have had time in the headlines before receding in prominence. The secretive, militant neo-Nazi movement National Action, whose followers also appeared in masks and balaclavas, emerged in 2013, before it was banned as a terrorist organisation in 2016.View image in fullscreenOswald Mosley speaking at a rally in Leeds in 1936.Photograph: Fox Photos/Getty ImagesTo many, Thomas is just the latest iteration of that tendency, but an effective one at a febrile moment. Thomas, who previously ran a roofing firm and enjoys cage fighting and boxing in his spare time, has worked as a bodyguard to the UK’s leading far-right activist, Tommy Robinson (real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon). The father of five has spent two years in prison for attempted kidnapping. After being released, Thomas said: “I repented; I gave my life to Jesus.” On social media he describes himself as “dedicated to defending my family and homeland, trusting in Jesus Christ, Our Saviour”.The week began triumphantly for his agitators, with blanket media coverage both of Saturday’s visually startling protest and a second demonstration on Sunday in Portsmouth, another major port on the south coast. Late that evening and in the early hours of Monday morning, Thomas was knee-deep in the chilly seawater, attempting to prevent the landing of a boat thought to be carrying about 120 asylum seekers. He quickly rallied more masked protesters to try to stop coaches from taking the arrivals to an immigration processing centre.As a supporter brought phone chargers and other supplies by canoe to protesters in the water, he shouted at police and volunteers with the Royal National Lifeboat Institution: “I need these migrants to go home.” Uneasily watchable as it was, the four-hour livestreamed recording of events that night has had more than 700,000 views.The police initially described the Dover demonstration as “spontaneous”. But in fact, throughout the heatwaves of the summer, Thomas had been travelling across Britain, pulling together volunteers from small localised anti-migrant protest groups into his new umbrella movement. In clips posted to Instagram, Facebook, YouTube and X, he charted his progress towards building a network of men, who would, he claimed, become a “mass resistance group”, and would spark a “shockwave around the country” and send “shivers down the spines of those that have put this upon us”. He filmed new recruits, wearing black, lined up outside a village church and on village greens, describing them as “working-class men, bricklayers, roofers and carpenters”.The protesters’ media coup will have made awkward viewing for Reform politicians, coinciding with their party’s annual conference, which proved fractious amid lingering questions around overseas funding.The movement has no manifesto; its website offers vague outlines of intent, claiming that its followers are patriots who refuse “to stand by while Britain is dismantled”. Thomas has set out some of his views in short clips recorded on his phone, sitting in the driving seat of a stationary car. “For too long we’ve been walking down roads and waving flags and thinking this is somehow going to save us,” he says in one. “Migrants are having a detrimental effect on the safety of our women and children.”By Wednesday, Thomas’s self-declared claims to be making the country safer for all Britain’s daughters, sisters and mothers had veered unexpectedly into a more idiosyncratic campaign: one to protect his own mother, and secure new housing for her, amid a row over whether an article in the Daily Mail had made it possible to identify where she lived. That afternoon, Thomas brought dozens of masked men in black shorts and hoodies to the newspaper’s central London headquarters, livestreaming himself threatening that unless the newspaper organised his mother a new home within 48 hours, he would be back again with a larger contingent of men.Later he made an online appeal for donations to help his mother move house, because she was living in “a state of absolute fear”. “It would be right for the country to rally together and help her in this time of need,” he wrote on an online fundraiser, headed: “Help Danny Tommo’s Mum Relocate: a fresh start after unfair media harassment.” By Friday afternoon more than £62,000 had been raised.Some online commentators said they were sympathetic to his broader aims, but were irritated by this personal fundraising drive, condemning it as grifting. Even among supporters, Thomas’s leadership style is not to everyone’s taste.Over the past two years, Tommy Robinson has attempted to make his anti-immigration movement mainstream, explicitly calling on supporters not to attend rallies wearing face coverings, in an attempt to secure wider support. Details of his events are circulated on open Facebook groups, and often publicised weeks in advance, with police notified. Women are free to protest alongside men.Thomas appears to be trying something new. Mulhall said: “This is less about attracting mass numbers, and more about them saying: ‘We’re going to take things into our own hands.’ They want small committed numbers of people willing to take direct action.” Success was not guaranteed, he added, noting that an attempt to launch similar action on the beaches of northern France earlier this year, branded Operation Overlord (a reference to the second world war allied D-day landings), had failed, resulting in Thomas being banned from returning to France by the French authorities, who said: “Violent and hate-inciting tactics have no place in our territory.”Thomas has said that he wants to bring discipline to the protest movement, aims to avoid arrests and talks of having lawyers at the end of the phone. “We have clear rules, no shouting, no alcohol, no flag waving, no drugs,” he says (although the Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary reported damage to their vehicles and some injuries on Sunday night).Several researchers have noted the movement’s success at spreading its message through social media. Thomas’s claims that the British way of life is under threat as a result of immigration offered “a strong sense of purpose, belonging and orientation to those anxious about their future”, said Beatriz Lopes Buarque, a fellow in AI trust and security at the University of Manchester. “Racist conspiracy theories are profitable to tech companies and, consequently, there is little incentive on their part to reduce their amplification,” she added, noting that politicians needed to “raise awareness of the nexus between harmful conspiracy theories and algorithmic amplification”.View image in fullscreenProtesters in Dover.Photograph: Ay_audits/YoutubeDarja Wischerath, a research assistant at the University of Bath, who specialises in studying online and offline mobilisation of the far right, said Thomas displayed a celebrity influencer’s skill at uploading bits of content on to numerous social media sites throughout the day to keep followers engaged, building a community of like-minded people. There were manosphere undertones to some of the content, with the “misogynistic suggestion that women are helpless people need[ing] to be protected”, she said.Footage distributed by Thomas suggests activists have been drilled over the summer to respond in unison to his questions, like troops responding to a sergeant major. “Are we here to hurt the police?” Thomas asks lines of black-clad men in a clip of the Daily Mail protest. “No,” the lines of men shout back. “Are we here to stand up for our country?” The men respond: “Yes!” “Are we here to stand up for our women?” he asks. The men reply: “Yes!” Thomas concludes by bellowing “Amen!” at his volunteers, who shout back: “Amen!”Thomas was a tank driver with the King’s Royal Hussars, but was discharged on medical grounds before seeing active service.The movement’s regular references to Christ have triggered dismay within the Church of England. Thomas has posted videos of himself attending church, holding a prayer book. It is not clear where he attends church, but he tells followers: “When we go to church every Sunday, we go to church as a unit.” People donating to his fundraising pages can opt instead to press a button notifying organisers that they will pray for the cause rather than giving money.Over the past few years, Christian anti-migrant protesters have begun to position themselves against the inclusive, pro-refugee position of the established Church of England. Madeleine Pennington, the head of research with the thinktank Theos, where analysts are currently finalising a project on the rise of Christian nationalism in the UK, said research in 2013 had found little trace of the phenomenon in Britain, but said there had been a “step-change” in the past few years.“There are many Christians who are very concerned about a framing of Christianity that they don’t recognise as their own,” she said, adding that the bulk of the marchers’ rhetoric appeared focused on anti-immigration issues rather than religion.The bishop of Kirkstall, Arun Arora, who is the co-lead for racial justice in the Church of England, said the display of the cross on protest marches was not the cross of Christ “but rather a fashion accessory utilised by opportunists”.This week, Thomas was branded “an idiot” by the man he and two co-conspirators tried to kidnap at knifepoint in 2016. The trio had wrongly accused their victim of stealing £10,000 of drugs from them. Thomas pleaded guilty to attempted kidnapping and was jailed for two years; a judge condemned all three men for their “stupidity”. Thomas is due in court again in October, accused of going into a restricted zone in Dover earlier this year, and of threatening behaviour.There is some uncertainty about whether he can maintain momentum and continue to rally units of protesters. But Thomas has described the Dover protest as a “dummy run” and local politicians remain uneasy.Tony Vaughan, Labour MP in the neighbouring Folkestone and Hythe constituency, said he was concerned by the group’s “significant online coordination” that had allowed it to bring people intoKent“at very short notice and under the radar”. Police needed to “be alert to this tactic and have the intelligence and resources to respond effectively”, he said, to prevent further “intimidation and disruption”.

title: Deepfakes are wrecking influencers’ credibility, one fake ad at a time | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Influencers aren’t just battling competitors for brand deals. They’re now battling AI versions of themselves
Author: Arielle Pardes
Headline: Influencers aren’t just battling competitors for brand deals. They’re now battling AI versions of themselves
Content: ‘It’s so violating. [They look] just like me, but the upside-down version.’Illustration: Guardian Design/TiktokView image in fullscreen‘It’s so violating. [They look] just like me, but the upside-down version.’Illustration: Guardian Design/TiktokGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.ReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)Deepfakes are wrecking influencers’ credibility, one fake ad at a timeInfluencers aren’t just battling competitors for brand deals. They’re now battling AI versions of themselvesSupported byAbout this contentArielle PardesSat 12 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarlier this year, Emily Schuman, the creator of the lifestyle blog Cupcakes and Cashmere, saw a photo of herself she didn’t recognize onInstagram. In a sponsored ad, Schuman, who has more than 500,000 Instagram followers, is holding up a vial of GLP-1 drugs, advertising the telehealth company Gala. There was just one problem: Schuman had never heard of Gala and had nothing to do with the ad.The ad was based on a digitally altered version of a selfie Schuman had taken in her car and posted on Instagram years earlier. Once her followers got wind, they flooded her inbox with questions about the sponsorship as it didn’t seem consistent with Schuman’s personal brand. Soon after, Schuman discovered this was just the beginning. There was also an Instagram post where an AI version of her with darker hair appears to apply foundation to promote a makeup brand called Meroda Cosmetics, andTikTokposts with generated images of her promoting the blood testing company Superpower.“It’s so violating,” she said. The videos and images look “just like me, but the upside down version”.Neither Gala nor Meroda responded to requests for comment. Superpower CEO Max Marchione said the TikTok post wasn’t a real ad, but instead came from a scammer his company later reported. “Whilst scamming isn’t new, AI has made this much worse,” he said.As generative AI makes it easier to create text, code and media, it has also supercharged the creation of deepfakes, the synthetic photos and videos that can be nearly indistinguishable from reality. Influencers are some of the easiest people to impersonate due to the sheer amount of videos and images AI can learn from. The vulnerability represents a new workplace threat: influencers aren’t just competing for brand deals with other creators, but also fighting to preserve the credibility of their own likeness – the very asset that generates their income.“Their brand is their business,” said Alice Marwick, the director of research at the Data & Society Research Institute, who published a recent paper on the rise of AI impersonation scams. “If their brand takes a hit, so does everything in their business life.”On social media, impersonation schemes run a large spectrum, from deepfaked Elon Musk promoting a fraudulent cryptocurrency, to brands quietly scraping an influencer’s image to manufacture ads. Global consumers may have lost as much as $3.7bn due to deepfake scams in 2026, according toan investigationfrom the VPN-maker Surfshark’s research team. The investigation found that social media impersonations on social media accounted for about half of all losses.Easy targets for deepfakesCelebrities and influencers are often the easiest to impersonate because they “have hundreds of hours of footage and thousands of pictures of them online. So you can feed that into a model and produce a fairly convincing deepfake,” said Marwick. Taylor Swift, Oprah Winfrey, Kim Kardashian, Gwyneth Paltrow and Tom Hanks have all been deepfaked by AI to promote various products online.But big celebrities aren’t alone. On Instagram, beauty influencer Arielle Lorre was deepfaked to promote a skincare brand. Fashion creator Jessi Caparella discovered altered images of herself on Pinterest redirecting traffic to affiliate clothing links. And deepfaked videos of OnlyFans creator Elaina St James were used to trick fans into sending money to fraudulent accounts. While the financial impact of these impersonation schemes is hard to pinpoint, creators say that deepfakes dilute their value, cost them the trust of their followers, and can be time-consuming to fight: even when one deepfake post is reported and removed, another one pops up in its place.With AI, “impersonation is much easier and much more convincing … [so] scams can be operated at a much larger scale,” said Marwick. “It’s often really believable. And with every new frontier model, they get better and better.”One reason for the rise of deepfakes may be a growing use of AI-generated marketing content in general. AI-generated or “virtual” influencers accounted for $1.37bn, or about 4% of all brand spending in 2026, according toresearchfrom marketing consultancy Digital Applied. Virtual influencers may not have the same authenticity as real people, but they are much cheaper, always available, and infinitely customizable, which makes them attractive for some brand campaigns.While the ad industry has always blurred the line between real and fake with airbrushing, CGI and other digital editing tools, the rise of AI has allowed brands to generate content from nothing with minimal production costs. And for some brands, that means crossing the line into deepfakes.Influencers are doing whatever they can to fight the issue. Molly Tranchin, a fashion influencer known as FashionVeggie with more than 500,000 followers on Instagram, recently filed alawsuitagainst the underwear brand Eby. According to the lawsuit, Tranchin had a contract to create three marketing videos for Eby in exchange for a fee. Eby was entitled to one round of “reasonable edits” for Tranchin to revise. The lawsuit claims that instead of posting the videos Tranchin submitted – in which she posed “modestly covering her chest and breasts with her arms” – the brand instead posted a deepfake video of Tranchin in a different pose, “exposing her breasts and nipples through one of Eby’s sheer bras”.Tranchin has since dropped the lawsuit over a lack of jurisdiction and plans to refile it in a different court, according to court documents filed last month.Eby spokesperson Clara Spahr said the company couldn’t comment on the pending litigation but will address the claims through the legal process.The fight for their likenessTranchin, whose lawsuit is ongoing, has the benefit of knowing exactly who to hold accountable for the deepfakes. Other creators are not as lucky.When Schuman discovered the deepfaked ads using her likeness, she and her manager immediately reported them toMeta. She said many of her followers, who brought these ads to her attention, also reported them. But it took weeks of badgering before Meta removed the GLP-1 ad. The makeup ad still remains in circulation on Instagram, despite many attempts from Schuman to get it taken down.Both Meta and TikTok explicitly prohibit using artificial intelligence or digital manipulation to replicate a person’s identity. But the reality is that these platforms’ personalization algorithms may inadvertently grease the wheels for these schemes.Meta, for example, allows advertisers to use hyper-targeted audience slicing, meaning bad actors can quietly launch fraudulent ads, create new accounts if one gets flagged, and scale their reach rapidly. In response to complaints about rampant scams on its platforms, Meta introducednew toolsthis year, including stronger advertiser verification policies and an AI detection tool to prevent “celeb-bait”, or the impersonation of celebrities. But experts say these tools do not go far enough, and that the company lacks incentive to clean up its own ad ecosystem. Meta did not respond to multiple requests for comment.“The reality is that platforms make a lot of money off scams,” Marwick said.Meta made about $16bn from ads promoting scams or banned goods, accounting for about 10% of its revenue in 2024, according to a2025 investigationfrom Reuters. That investigation also quoted an internal presentation from Meta’s safety team, which estimated that its platforms were “involved in a third of all successful scams in the US”.Not only do deepfakes hurt brand deals for individual influencers, but they also challenge the entire influencer marketing ecosystem. They disrupt the already delicate premise that a real person trusts a product or brand, and therefore their followers should do the same.Schuman said she is deciding whether or not she needs to retain legal counsel to help her fight off the deepfakes as they keep popping up. Besides reporting the offending posts and threatening legal action, influencers don’t have much recourse.“That’s money and time lost,” Schuman said about hiring a lawyer. But the alternative is a hit to her reputation. “So it’s a lose-lose from all ways of looking at it.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ReworkedSocial mediaMetaTikTokInstagramDigital mediaDeepfakefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Christopher Harborne matches £36m Reform donation of Ben Delo | Party funding | The Guardian
description: Party leader, Nigel Farage, ‘humbled’ by contributions from billionaires as Harborne addresses ‘media speculation’
Author: Geraldine McKelvie
Headline: Party leader, Nigel Farage, ‘humbled’ by contributions from billionaires as Harborne addresses ‘media speculation’
Content: From  left, Christopher Harborne, Nigel Farage and Ben Delo.Photograph: LPN/Getty Images/The Ben Delo FoundationView image in fullscreenFrom  left, Christopher Harborne, Nigel Farage and Ben Delo.Photograph: LPN/Getty Images/The Ben Delo FoundationParty fundingChristopher Harborne matches £36m Reform donation of Ben DeloParty leader, Nigel Farage, ‘humbled’ by contributions from billionaires as Harborne addresses ‘media speculation’Analysis: donations of £72m make Reform’s prospects both rosier and riskierGeraldine McKelvieSat 12 Sep 2026 11.09 EDTFirst published on Sat 12 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe cryptocurrency tycoon Christopher Harborne has given £36m to Reform UK, matching a donationfrom fellow billionaire Ben Delo.The pledges mean Reform has received a cash injection of £72m in just 24 hours. They are jointly the largest donations made to a UK political party and have intensified calls for restrictions on money received from individual donors.Reform’s leader,Nigel Farage, said he was “honoured and humbled” by the payments, which come as the party is facing intense scrutiny regarding its funding. Reform said it planned to use the money to hire about 400 campaign managers in target constituencies and was now on an “election footing”.The Metropolitan police is conductingan inquiry into Reform’s financesand Farage is facing a parliamentary standards investigation into a £5m gift from Harborne, made before he was first elected an MP in 2024. Reform UK and Farage have denied any wrongdoing.Harborne’s donation was announced on Saturday afternoon. The Guardian understands the money has already been received by Reform.Bridget Phillipson, the chair of the Labour party, said that Farage couldn’t “buy his way out of the sleaze and scandal he and Reform UK are drowning in – or the multiple police investigations that are ongoing into Reform’s dodgy finances”.View image in fullscreenNigel Farage on stage at Reform’s annual conference earlier this month.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPARachel Millward, the deputy leader of the Green party in England and Wales, accused the prime minister, Andy Burnham, of “flip flopping”on a cap on domestic donations. Burnham, who previously appeared supportive of a cap, has faced lobbying from trade unions who fear restrictions would inhibit their ability to donate to the Labour party.The Labour MP Stella Creasy tabled an amendment to the representation of the people bill, which is progressing through parliament and has its second reading in the Lords on Monday.Creasy proposed an annual cap of £100,000 on most domestic donations. Although it attracted the support of 60 MPs from various parties, it was not put to a vote.“The Labour party urgently needs to find a spine and support a tight cap on donations from individuals,” Millward said.Duncan Hames, ofTransparency International UK, said the donations made “an irrefutable case” for a cap, adding: “At this rate just two people could end up buying our democracy before the next election.”The campaign groupSpotlight on Corruptionsaid the donations could have a “huge and damaging impact” and accused the government of “ignoring the very high risk of the Americanisation of our politics”.Farage said that Delo and Harborne “know that we are the only party that can turn the country around and win the next general election – thanks to their generosity, we are now able to fight that election on a level playing field”.Harborne said: “There will be a lot of media speculation regarding this donation. So what do I expect in return for my donations? Nothing. No peerage, no policy change, just a party that is ready for government.“I have already accumulated enough wealth for the rest of my life. I am committed to putting that to work for Britain and humanity as a whole. I want the same as everyone else in Britain: for my children and grandchildren to have the chance to live happy and productive lives here and be rewarded for their hard work.“At the next general election, people will have to vote for the party that they think will best get that done and I’m making a donation very clearly to the party that I believe will do so.”Harborne is a citizen of the UK and Thailand, while Delo recently moved back to Britain from Hong Kong. As part of the new legislation, donations to political parties from Britons living abroad or those who have returned to the country within the past 12 months will be capped at £100,000 a year, with the rules backdated to March.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe protest group Climate Resistance have launched a poster campaign questioning Harborne’s links to Farage.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersThe Guardian asked Reform exactly how long each has been on the electoral roll. A spokesperson said: “All donations toReform UKcomply strictly with Electoral Commission rules and UK law. Both men are British citizens who are fully entitled to support political change in their own country, despite the establishment’s desperate attempts to silence opposition.”Their donations have amplified concerns about the influence of “mega donors” on British politics.Margaret Hodge, a Labour peer and former chair of the House of Commons public accounts committee, said she was “gobsmacked” to hear of Harborne’s donation and said it “reinforces the urgency of us dealing with the issue”. Hodge, who favours a cap, said there was now a “real danger” that British politics could be “captured by rich individuals”.“There has been a reluctance on Labour’s side to confront this danger because of the trade unions,” she said. “This highlights what a lot of us have been saying – you have to tackle the issue. We can’t leave it alone. Self-interest shouldn’t dominate.”From black-clad agitators to an appeal for ‘Tommo’s Mum’: an unsettling week with the Patriot PlatformRead moreMany senior Labour figures, including Hodge, believe union funds could be classified as a series of individual donations from members.“Union members could tick a box saying, ‘I wish to contribute [to the Labour party]’, so it becomes an individual donation, rather than a union [donation],” Hodge said, adding that she believed this would “strengthen democracy” and challenge the power of union leaders.However, this proposal is likely to be condemned by opposition parties and transparency campaigners.Shaun Bowler, who runs the campaign group Wake Up GB, has proposed financing political parties through a government funded civic voucher, in which voters could choose to allocate a small sum to the party of their choice.“The unions funded the Labour party to compete with Conservative funding,” he said. “If you take funding away from the Conservatives and everyone else, it’s a level playing field.”Explore more on these topicsParty fundingReform UKNigel FarageChristopher HarborneAndy BurnhamBridget PhillipsonnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We must slow the pace’: CEO of Anthropic calls for an AI slowdown | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: In a social media post, Dario Amodei proposed a plan including third-party evaluations of AI systems
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: In a social media post, Dario Amodei proposed a plan including third-party evaluations of AI systems
Content: Dario Amodei said that AI development, if left unchecked, ‘could outrun our ability to understand and control’ it.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/ReutersView image in fullscreenDario Amodei said that AI development, if left unchecked, ‘could outrun our ability to understand and control’ it.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)‘We must slow the pace’: CEO of Anthropic calls for an AI slowdownIn a social media post, Dario Amodei proposed a plan including third-party evaluations of AI systemsEdward HelmoreSat 12 Sep 2026 11.46 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 16.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe CEO of the artificial intelligence companyAnthropicissued a new appeal on Saturday for theAIindustry to “slow down” and offered a three-part plan for doing so, saying that his company would “unilaterally” commit to the first of the steps.In apost on social media,Dario Amodei shared a link to an essay titled We Must Pace the Frontier in which he laid out how Anthropic would provide “third-party evaluators with permanent, employee-level access to our systems, so that they can verify adherence to our safety measures, report on incidents, and assess models’ alignment during training”.The move comes after a former Anthropic researcher warned on Wednesday that AI could precipitate human extinction by 2030. Researcher Jacob Coxon said in a series ofpoststhat he had quit his job because Anthropic and his previous employer, OpenAI, were ignoring or mishandling their response to the threat AI posed.“Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon wrote. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade … No other human activity poses this level of danger.”Anthropic researchers say AI could cause human extinction by 2030Read moreAn Anthropic spokesperson saidin a statement to the Guardianthat the company had “always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks” and it was building “models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry”.“I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,”Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI,postedon social media. “Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same. We’ll have more to share soon.”Other tech figures echoed this, including Elon Musk, whosimply posted, “Dario is right.” The OpenAI researcher Aidan McLaughlin alsocalledthe post “excellent” and said he agreed “with basically every word”.Earlier this year, Amodeipublished a lengthy essaytitled The Adolescence of Technology that addressed some of fears surrounding the accelerating technology.In his latest essay, he said that “carefully wielded, AI can be the latest in a long line of technological miracles that have uplifted and ennobled humanity.“But like many technologies before it, AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious … A race to the bottom, spurred by commercial incentives, can make these risks more acute,” he wrote.But, Amodei continued, “over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence – not just investing in risk prevention, but pacing the rate of capabilities advancement so that risk prevention has time to keep up.“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” he added in bold type.Amodei also wrote that over the summer he’d seen AI “advancing drastically faster”, a dynamic called recursive self-improvement.“Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all,” he said.The executive also addressed the recent Hugging Face incident, in which a swarm of AI agents created by OpenAI acted as a “fanatically devoted collectiveconducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAmodei wrote that simply dismissing the Hugging Face incursions because theOpenAIswarms appeared to have no malicious intent was not sufficient.“It’s easy to dismiss this incident because no one was hurt and the economic damage was minimal, but in my opinion, a swarm that possessed greater capabilities but a similar level of misalignment could have caused catastrophic damage,” he wrote.Anthropic details bad actors’ efforts to misuse its AI for bioweaponsRead moreClément Delangue, the CEO of Hugging Face,wrote in responseto Amodei’s Saturday letter that “it’s now clear that alignment is critical and won’t be solved behind the closed doors of a handful of frontier labs”. Delangue said Hugging Face had asked to be part of Anthropic’s “embedded evaluators” program.He added: “Let’s make AI safer by making it more transparent!”The three-step plan Amodei proposes includes building AI “at a balanced rate that aims to ensure its safety” by “ensuring companies take adequate time to align and safeguard their models, and for third party evaluators to confirm this”.The second step he proposes is to require industry-wide coordination, and the third is to ensure global coordination. “The steps do not need to be taken strictly in order, and some of them may be much harder to achieve than others,” he wrote.Amodei said he continues “to believe that AI can enormously improve the quality of human life”. But he warned that “the measures I propose to advance the frontier at a safe pace will not be easy. But I believe we owe it to humanity to try.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)AnthropicOpenAIElon MuskSam AltmanComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: IDF soldier filmed shooting Palestinian in leg amid West Bank settler standoff | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Incident is latest to raise questions over Israel’s ability or willingness to stop violent settlers in occupied territory
Author: Lorenzo Tondo
Headline: Incident is latest to raise questions over Israel’s ability or willingness to stop violent settlers in occupied territory
Content: A still from a video that shows a Palestinian man being shot in the leg.Photograph: Video Obtained by Reuters/ReutersView image in fullscreenA still from a video that shows a Palestinian man being shot in the leg.Photograph: Video Obtained by Reuters/ReutersWest BankIDF soldier filmed shooting Palestinian in leg amid West Bank settler standoffIncident is latest to raise questions over Israel’s ability or willingness to stop violent settlers in occupied territoryLorenzo Tondoin JerusalemSat 12 Sep 2026 09.44 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 11.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Israeli soldier has shot a Palestinian man, wounding him in the leg, as settlers confronted villagers by grazing livestock on Palestinian-owned land in the town of Faqqua in the occupiedWest Bank.Witnesses said a group of settlers had entered the area with their livestock, prompting residents to try to stop them. Israeli forces then intervened and, according to men at the scene, opened fire at residents. One of them shot Qassem Hussam, a Palestinian man in his mid-30s, wounding him in the leg.1:15Israeli forces shoot Palestinian man in the leg in West Bank village – videoReached by the Guardian, the IDF confirmed it had received a report of the incident and that the person who fired was one of its soldiers.“Earlier today [Saturday], a report was received regarding friction between Israeli civilians and Palestinians near the area of Faqqua,” the IDF said. “An IDF force that was at the scene fired into the air and toward a Palestinian.”Mohammed al-Sheikh, 34, who was standing next to Hussam, told the Guardian the confrontation began when villagers encountered Israeli settlers grazing livestock on Palestinian-owned land.“Then the Israeli soldiers came,” al-Sheikh said. “They started shooting. One soldier shot Hussam and he fell to the ground. We immediately went to help him and move him away. We couldn’t get an ambulance to the area, so we took him to hospital in a private car.”Hussam was taken to hospital in a light-to-moderate condition, according to thePalestineRed Crescent.The Israeli military said the incident was being reviewed by commanders and that its findings would be forwarded to the relevant authorities for examination. The IDF added that the military was investigating the soldier who shot the Palestinian man,apparently in breach of army protocol, according to the Times of Israel.Video of the incident shows a group of Israeli soldiers and settlers confronting unarmed Palestinian men before shots are fired.The incident is the latest to raise questions over the Israeli government’s ability or willingness to curb violent settlers in the occupied West Bank, where attacks have continued to increase.On 8 September, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, said he would “not stand by” as horrific suffering continued, writing in the Guardian that for too long the UK had been hesitant to act,“fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel”.Ed Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary, said the government would now take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety, and announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements.The dramatic shift in the UK’s position came after a summer of intense diplomacy against a backdrop of rising settler violence in the West Bank, which led 12 countries, including France and Canada, to announce sanctions.After Miliband described violent Jewish settler activity in the occupied West Bank as “ethnic cleansing” carried out with the tacit backing of the government of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, announced retaliatory measuresincluding the closure of the consulate and entry bans on several MPs.It marked the latest stage in a rapidly worsening dispute between the two countries, with diplomatic relations at their lowest point in years, even as violence in the West Bank has continued.Israeli forces also carried out raids across Jenin governorate on Saturday, arresting six people and injuring a 14-year-old boy, who suffered a broken hand, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa. Soldiers also raided several villages around Jenin, while forces entered at least five towns in Bethlehem governorate and set up a checkpoint at Za’atara.East of Ramallah, Israeli settlers attacked the outskirts of Burqa, throwing stones at homes and vehicles.On 4 September,two Palestinian teenagers were shot deadin al-Mughayyir after settlers entered the village under police and military escort and took dozens of sheep from a Palestinian home, residents and Israeli activists said.The victims were Khalil Abu Alia, 16, and Omar al-Nassan, 19. Three other pupils from their 470-strong school had already been killed by Israeli soldiers and settlers this year.According to the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), more than 1,111 Palestinians, including at least 243 children, have been killed in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since 7 October 2023.Explore more on these topicsWest BankIsraelPalestineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Portsmouth experiences second weekend of anti-immigration protests | Far right | The Guardian
description: Rightwing activists faced a heavy police presence and counter-demonstrations to their march against small boat crossings
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Rightwing activists faced a heavy police presence and counter-demonstrations to their march against small boat crossings
Content: 1:02Anti-migrant rally and counter-protesters face off in Portsmouth – videoFar rightPortsmouth experiences second weekend of anti-immigration protestsRightwing activists faced a heavy police presence and counter-demonstrations  to their march against small boat crossingsSammy GecsoylerandRaphael BoydSat 12 Sep 2026 13.41 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 15.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo men and a teenage boy have been arrested inPortsmouthat a far-right protest against immigration.Far-right activists have gathered in Portsmouth for a second weekend after a small boat with 140 people seeking asylum on board was intercepted last Sunday while heading towards the city.They were greeted by counter-protesters as police warned they would not tolerate incitement of fear or violence.From black-clad agitators to an appeal for ‘Tommo’s Mum’: an unsettling week with the Patriot PlatformRead moreOne of the arrested, a 76-year-old man from Southampton, was detained on suspicion of concealing his identity at the Portsmouth protest. Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary had warned that protesters wearing face coverings could be arrested under powers in the Crime and Policing Act.A 33-year-old man from Portsmouth was also arrested on suspicion of obstructing a highway and a 16-year-old boy, also from Portsmouth, was arrested on suspicion of violent disorder in relation to scenes last Sunday.View image in fullscreenProtesters gather for a counter-demonstration in Portsmouth on Saturday.Photograph: James Veysey/ShutterstockDonna Jones, the police and crime commissioner for Hampshire and Isle of Wight, said that they “thankfully didn’t see repeated scenes of Sunday night with assaults on police officers and criminal damage to police vehicles and people’s property” and that “with the exception of a few people, it was peaceful and conducted in accordance with the new law calling for their faces to be uncovered”.Jones added: “The people of Portsmouth deserve to go about their business without fear and disruption.“While some may think it was arbitrary to use the new power directing people to remove face coverings, the police ensured it was implemented equally and impartially for everyone involved.“I will ensure this power is used proportionately in the future for both sides of the spectrum of protesters.”View image in fullscreenDemonstrators at an anti-immigration march in Portsmouth on Saturday.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAIn Portsmouth city centre, there was a large police presence where demonstrators assembled to march on Saturday.Some protesters held union flags while some wearing Portsmouth patriot branded clothing gathered outside All Saints Church on Commercial Road.A man with a megaphone got the crowd chanting “stop the boats”. He said the protest was against “illegal men invading the shores”.In the neighbouring car park, demonstrators holding Stand Up to Racism (SUTR) andRefugeesWelcome banners gathered. Signs included: “RNLI are heroes, no one is illegal” and “stop pretending your racism is patriotism”.Hundreds of people also gathered inGlasgowfor an anti-immigration rally and associated counter-protest.View image in fullscreenThe Pink Ladies event in Glasgow. The event passed off peacefully amid a heavy police presence and segregation of opposing protesters.Photograph: Iain Masterton/Alamy Live NewsThe Pink Ladies movement organised their event at Glasgow Green, prompting opposing groups, including SUTR, to arrange a counter-protest.The two groups were contained in separate areas on the eastern side of the park, with the People’s Palace and a heavy police presence between them.Ch Supt Stevie Dolan warned of a “strong response” if there was any violence after flashpoints at a previous protest in the same park in July.MSPs Alison Thewliss, a Scottish government minister, and Iris Duane were at the SUTR rally, with the Scottish Trades Union Congress general secretary Roz Foyer.View image in fullscreenPolice officers contain counter-protesters against a Pink Ladies rally beside Glasgow’s People’s Palace.Photograph: Steve Welsh/PAProminent figures on the Scottish right, such as Reform UK’s deputy leader in Scotland, Thomas Kerr, and the Reform councillor Audrey Dempsey, attended the Pink Ladies event.Saturday’s protests came after hundreds of far-right activists descended on Portsmouth last Sunday after a small boat crossing the Channel approached the city. The demonstrators tried to stop those onboard from being processed.Hampshire police said: “We will support those who want to express their views peacefully and lawfully, but we will not tolerate those whose only aim is to create fear and incite violence.”The opposing groups were allocated specific locations at which they could gather under protest conditions. Failure to comply with conditions could lead to arrest, police said. The anti-immigration protest marched to Guildhall Square and the counter-protest followed later on the same route.View image in fullscreenLifejackets at Eastney abandoned by people seeking asylum who made the crossing from France on 6 September.Photograph: Ollie Thompson/Solent News & Photo Agency/Solent NewsThe incident with the small boat last Sunday was thought to be the first time such a large vessel containing asylum seekers had been brought to Portsmouth and the first time that a significant group of anti-migrant protesters had tried to block newly arrived asylum seekers from being processed.Small boat crossings have fallen by more than 40% compared with the same period last year.
