Whilethe Home Office has disrupted the smugglers’ business model, their methods appear to have evolved by launching boats – such as the one that arrived last Sunday – from different parts of the French coast much farther from the UK, making the crossings more dangerous.Most small boat arrivals are rescued by Border Force and RNLI vessels on the English side of the Channel and brought ashore at Dover. RNLI volunteers and staff have faced abuse from protesters over their rescue work bringing some small boat migrants ashore.The first man charged over last weekend’s anti-migrant demonstration in Portsmouth appeared in court on Saturday.View image in fullscreenPolice officers at Eastney beach, Portsmouth, where hundreds of protesters gathered to meet a small boat arriving from France.Photograph: PADel Leon Somerville, 42, of Paulsgrove in Portsmouth, appeared before the city’s magistrates court charged with violent disorder and assaulting a police constable in the execution of their duty.Assistant chief constable Tony Rowlinson said Somerville’s arrest was the “first of what we fully anticipate to be a number of arrests” and hoped it would send a “clear warning” to those planning future disruption and disorder.The government condemned whatit described as the “thuggish behaviour” of the protesterslast Sunday. “We condemn the intimidating and thuggish behaviour we are seeing tonight,” a government spokesperson said. “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder.”Number of UK anti-migrant vigilante groups surges in last 18 monthsRead moreThe home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, met police on Thursday for reassurance they are ready to move quickly in dealing with “far-right groups” seeking to intimidate communities after last weekend’s events in Dover and Portsmouth. Official vehicles were damaged in Portsmouth anda small number of officers were injured, police said. In Dover,crowds of masked men blocked road access to the portin scenes that were condemned by politicians of all parties.Mahmood said: “These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents.“This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons.”Explore more on these topicsFar rightPortsmouthProtestImmigration and asylumRefugeesGlasgownewsShareReuse this content

title: Donald Trump says he would ‘love’ to see united Ireland | Ireland | The Guardian
description: US president says on visit to republic that unification will happen eventually so ‘may as well happen now’
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: US president says on visit to republic that unification will happen eventually so ‘may as well happen now’
Content: 1:35Protesters against Trump’s visit to Ireland react to ‘united Ireland’ comments – videoIrelandDonald Trump says he would ‘love’ to see united IrelandUS president says on visit to republic that unification will happen eventually so ‘may as well happen now’Rory CarrollIreland correspondentSat 12 Sep 2026 12.05 EDTFirst published on Sat 12 Sep 2026 09.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has said he would “love” to see a united Ireland and that it “may as well happen now”.The US president appeared to endorse the push for constitutional change on the island at the start of a two-day visit to Ireland on Saturday. The unexpected intervention prompted a swift rebuttal from the UK government and Northern Ireland’s unionist leaders.“I don’t want ⁠to cause any problems, ​but ‌I will ‌tell you, I’d love ‌to see it unified,” Trump told reporters at joint press conference with the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, in Dublin. “I think it would be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. You know what? The way I look at it, it’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.”The unification of NorthernIrelandwith the republic of Ireland would be “fantastic”, Trump said. “The UK will have something to say about it, obviously. But I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?”View image in fullscreenMicheál Martin welcomes Donald Trump to Farmleigh House, in Dublin, during his trip to the Republic of Ireland.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAThe intervention jolted his hosts and came two weeks after Andy Burnham saida referendum on unification was “off the table”, which angered Sinn Féin and other Irish nationalists.Speaking later on Saturday, Trump acknowledged that his comments on unification, made in response to a reporter’s question, would be controversial. “No matter what you say or how you say it, there’s no good answer,” he said. “I gave a nice answer, I think. We’ll worry about it tomorrow.” Unification, he added, would be a “very cool thing”.A Downing Street spokesperson said the prime minister still believed there was not the required support for unification to trigger a referendum, as set out in the Good Friday agreement.Gavin Robinson, the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) leader, said Northern Ireland’s constitutional future would be decided by its people, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington.“Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom because that is the settled democratic will of its people. I am confident Northern Ireland will continue to choose the UK and the security it offers. As unionists we are not interested in the destruction of our country by joining with the Irish republic.”View image in fullscreenSpectators watch as Air Force One flies Trump over the Irish Open in Doonbeg, County Clare.Photograph: Damien Eagers/PAColum Eastwood, an MP and former leader of the Social Democratic and Labour party (SDLP), and frequent critic of Trump, posted a clip of the president’s remarks on social media and wrote: “Always liked him.”The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, said: “President Trump is shooting from the hip as usual, just like he did with Greenland and Canada becoming the 51st state. This sort of loose talk about the future of democratic countries is deeply unhelpful and creates unnecessary tension.”Trump’s comments strayed from predecessors who sought to keep the White House neutral on Ireland’s constitutional future, but the off-the-cuff nature of the remarks suggested there was no change in US policy.Trump’s unofficial visit is centred on golf – he flew on Saturday afternoon to his resort in Doonbeg, County Clare, which is hosting the Irish Open – but started with a courtesy call in Dublin to Áras an Uachtaráin, the official residence and workplace ofthe Irish president, Catherine Connolly.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump and Catherine Connolly at her presidential residence in Phoenix Park, Dublin.Photograph: Tony Maxwell/PABefore her election to the ceremonial post last year,Connolly called Trump a bully and criticised his policiesin Gaza and Iran. Their brief encounter, behind closed doors, appeared to go smoothly despite a coded critique of White House policies.Connolly said in a statement afterwards that she “conveyed the strong view of the Irish people that the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted” and stressed the importance of the United Nations – an organisation Trump has disparaged. Trump said they had a wide-ranging discussion, including about energy and water, and that Connolly was “terrific”.Trump held a separate meeting with Martin at the Phoenix Park, where he told the press that Iran would seek peace after the US midterm elections and repeated his claim that his war had prevented Tehran obtaining a nuclear weapon.Asked about protests against his visit – a large crowd was gathering in central Dublin, 5 miles away, as well as at Doonbeg – the president said he had not seen any protests.View image in fullscreenDemonstrators protesting against Trump’s visit in Dublin.Photograph: Natalia Campos/ReutersAddressing guests as at the US ambassador’s residence, Trump assailed US Democrats as extremists and criticised Europe’s approach to immigration.He lauded US-Irish relations but reiterated a complaint about the American pharma giants in Ireland. “You took all our medical companies, we’ve got to get a couple of them back. You fleeced us but that’s OK.”Thousands of protesters marched through central Dublin and held a rally outside parliament. Speakers accused Trump of facilitating genocide in Gaza and led chants of “Donald Trump, can you hear? We don’t want you here.”View image in fullscreenA protest banner at a rally against Donald Trump in Dublin mocks his renaming of the Gulf of Mexico.Photograph: Rory Carroll/The GuardianOthers in the crowd accused the president of misogyny, sexual assault, racism and xenophobia. “Donald Trump is utterly immoral and he’s wrecking the world,” said Anne McGuinness, 70, who held a banner that said “unwelcome”.Emily Hamilton, whose daughter held a banner saying “Get rid of the evil orange”, said the Irish government should have shunned him. “We can’t stop him going to Doonbeg but we should not be welcoming him.”Mick Brennan, 70, said he and his wife Helen do not normally attend protests but made an exception for the US president. “We can’t stand that Trump fella, from his toes to his nose.”View image in fullscreenHelen and Mick Brennan hold a banner in Dublin to protest Donald Trump’s visit to Ireland.Photograph: Rory Carroll/The GuardianA smaller protest was held at Doonbeg. Trump is to stay overnight at his resort and present the Irish Open trophy to the winner on Sunday before returning to Washington.Explore more on these topicsIrelandDonald TrumpNorthern Irish politicsEuropeUS foreign policyNorthern IrelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Woman Unknown wins Venice film festival as NAZA takes special jury prize | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: May el-Toukhy becomes eighth female director to take Golden Lion as Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love and Guardian-produced exposé of Israel’s Gaza killings also awarded
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: May el-Toukhy becomes eighth female director to take Golden Lion as Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love and Guardian-produced exposé of Israel’s Gaza killings also awarded
Content: Mathilde Arcel holds the Volpi Cup for best actress beside her Woman Unknown director, May el-Toukhy, who won the Golden Lion for best film.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersView image in fullscreenMathilde Arcel holds the Volpi Cup for best actress beside her Woman Unknown director, May el-Toukhy, who won the Golden Lion for best film.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersVenice film festivalWoman Unknown wins Venice film festival as NAZA takes special jury prizeMay el-Toukhy becomes eighth female director to take Golden Lion as Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love and Guardian-produced exposé of Israel’s Gaza killings also awardedBold and bravura choices as Venice celebrates A Woman Unknown, Possible Love – and NAZAPhilip OltermannEuropean culture editorSat 12 Sep 2026 17.17 EDTFirst published on Sat 12 Sep 2026 16.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMay el-Toukhy’s Woman Unknown has scooped the Golden Lion at theVenice film festival, at an awards ceremony that also saw the Gaza documentary NAZA win the jury prize.Set in the immediate aftermath of Danish liberation from Nazi occupation, the Egyptian-Danish director’s film tells the story of a young housemaid, Marie (Mathilde Arcel), who is about to marry her widowed employer but anxious about him discovering a shameful secret in her past: during the war, Marie had an intimate relationship with a German soldier.The Guardian’s film critic hailed Woman Unknown as“elegantly appointed” in his review, likening it to Alfred Hitchcock’s Rebecca.Arcel also won the festival’s best actress prize, the Volpi Cup, which puzzled some critics: usually,Venicedoesn’t award more than one prize to a film. Speaking to the press after the ceremony, the jury president, Maggie Gyllenhaal, said they were able to make an exception because the jury’s vote for the Danish actor was unanimous. “She is going to blow our socks off,” she said.View image in fullscreenMaggie Gyllenhaal (left), president of the 2026 Venice jury, and the festival’s president, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, hand the Golden Lion to May el-Toukhy.Photograph: Yara Nardi/ReutersIn an emotional acceptance speech, El-Toukhy thanked Gyllenhaal for addressing the underrepresentation of female film-makers at the start of the festival. Woman Unknown was the only film in competition to be solely directed by a woman.“This film has been incredibly challenging to make financially, logistically, emotionally,” El-Toukhy said. “And what kept me going was the urgent need to illuminate the unknown women of our common history, to make them known. And especially tonight, I feel like I succeeded in doing just that.”View image in fullscreenLee Chang-dong (right) is presented with the grand jury prize for Possible Love by veteran Hong Kong film-maker and jury member Johnnie To.Photograph: Scott A Garfitt/APThe runner-up grand jury prize went to the Korean directorLee Chang-dong’s Possible Love, a simmering tale of an unhappy married couple befriended by a documentary maker and her wealthy husband, which drew rave reviews.The special jury prize, Venice’s equivalent of a bronze medal, went toYuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary NAZA, about Israel’s AI-powered mass killing of civilians in Gaza.The film, which was produced by the Guardian, is based on testimony from24 Israeli military insiders who are interviewed anonymouslyat night on rooftops in Tel Aviv. It takes its title from an acronym used by the intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza.View image in fullscreenNAZA directors Rachel Szor, left, and Yuval Abraham with the special jury award.Photograph: Yara Nardi/Reuters“It’s honestly not very easy to stand here, thinking of all the Israeli politicians and journalists who are now attacking this film and denying it without even seeing it,” Abraham said when accepting his prize. “So much is being done not to look at reality.”The day after NAZA’s premiere, the Israeli military “categorically denied” the allegations made in the film.‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligenceRead moreThe Russian director Ilya Khrzhanovsky won the Silver Lion for best director forthe visually stunning DAU, a biopic of the Nobel prize-winning quantum physicist Lev Landau, who was pressured into working on the Soviet Union’s nuclear weapons programme.The inclusion of Khrzhanovsky’s film in the Venice lineup wascriticised by the Ukrainian governmentin the run-up to the festival, over its lead actor Teodor Currentzis’s refusal to condemn the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and for having received funding from a Russian businessman who was later sanctioned by the US and Ukraine.View image in fullscreenIlya Khrzhanovsky with his Silver Lion best director award for DAU.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersDAU was filmed in Kharkiv between 2008 and 2011, before the start of the conflict. At a press conference on the Lido, Khrzhanovsky said: “The only thing I can wish for is peace and success for the Ukrainian government to succeed in the best possible way, to save the country and to win this war.”John Malkovich took home the Volpi Cup for best actor, for his role as an erratic veteran CIA agent whose cancer diagnosis leads him to question the morality of his profession, inMartin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe 72-year-old US actor was not present in Venice and accepted his award via a video link. “I am humbled to be chosen for this award, which has been given to so many wonderful actors over the past 83 iterations of the Venice film festival,” Malkovich said.Full list of winnersGolden Lion for best film: Woman Unknown, directed by May el-ToukhyGrand jury prize: Possible Love, directed by Lee Chang-dongSilver Lion for best director: Ilya Khrzhanovsky for DAUSpecial jury prize: NAZA, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel SzorBest screenplay: Un bon petit soldat (A Good Little Soldier), Stéphane Brizé, Coralie Amédéo, Olivier GorceVolpi Cup for best actress: Mathilde Arcel in Woman UnknownVolpi Cup for best actor:John Malkovichin Wild Horse NineMarcello Mastroianni award for best young actor: Malou Khebizi in15/18 A Place to HealArmani Beauty audience award: Eu contez (I Matter), directed by Alina ȘerbanLuigi De Laurentiis award for debut film: La maison du vent (House of the Wind), directed by Auguste Bernard Kouemo YanghuExplore more on these topicsVenice film festivalGazaNAZAJohn MalkovichFestivalsWorld cinemaAwards and prizesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Céline Dion performs first live show in more than six years | Céline Dion | The Guardian
description: The singer’s triumphant return to the stage comes after health problems forced her to take a lengthy break
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: The singer’s triumphant return to the stage comes after health problems forced her to take a lengthy break
Content: Céline Dion wept as she begun her 26-show residency in Paris on Saturday.Photograph: Aurélien Morissard/APView image in fullscreenCéline Dion wept as she begun her 26-show residency in Paris on Saturday.Photograph: Aurélien Morissard/APCéline DionCéline Dion performs first live show in more than six yearsThe singer’s triumphant return to the stage comes after health problems forced her to take a lengthy breakRaphael BoydSat 12 Sep 2026 18.50 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 19.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCéline Dion wept on stage in Paris as she performed herfirst live show in more than six yearsafter taking an extended break to deal with her health.Addressing the sold-out crowd on Saturday, a visibly emotional Dion told them that it was “amazing we are all together”.She added: “I made a promise. I made a promise to come back and to be back on stage. Here I am singing for you, and singing for me. Thank you so very much for your support, your patience. I am everything I am because you love me.”View image in fullscreenFans queue up outside the Plenitude Arena in Nanterre, Paris.Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPAShe last performed a full set in 2020 as part of her Courage Tour, but was unable to continue with a planned 2022 North American leg after beingdiagnosed with stiff person syndrome(SPS) in 2022.The singer, who is scheduled to perform a residency at the Plenitude Arena inParisbetween 12 September 2026 and 29 May 2027, told fans that she “made a promise to come back”.SPS is a rare autoimmune neurological disorder that often causes muscle stiffness and painful spasms which vary in severity, caused by the body mistakenly attacking healthy nerve cells. There is no known cure for the condition.After her diagnosis, Dion stepped away from the spotlight and had only briefly performed three times since: at a virtual performance at a charity event for healthcare workers during the Covid pandemic in 2020, at the opening ceremony of the2024 summer Olympics in Paris, where she sang the Édith Piaf song Hymne à l’amour, and at the conclusion of fashion designer Elie Saab’s show in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, later that same year.View image in fullscreenDion thanked her fans for their patience and support as she addressed the sold-out crowd.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersThe performance in Paris is the first of 26 shows Dion is slated to perform at the arena, having increased from an initial 10 due to high demand for tickets. Dion first announced her comeback on 30 March, her birthday, with all the tickets for the shows – estimated to be about 1,170,00 – selling out within a few hours of going on sale. More than 9 million fans reportedly tried to buy them.Dion is expected to perform many of her most popular songs, including her Oscar and Grammy-winning ballad My Heart Will Go On, as well as hits in English and her native French, including It’s All Coming Back to Me Now, The Power of Love and Pour que tu m’aimes encore.Explore more on these topicsCéline DionParisFrancenewsShareReuse this content

title: Michael Barrymore becomes unlikely TikTok star with nearly 5m followers | Television | The Guardian
description: Former primetime TV host films himself eating dog biscuits, doing ‘munchie runs’ and addressing pool death case
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Former primetime TV host films himself eating dog biscuits, doing ‘munchie runs’ and addressing pool death case
Content: Michael Barrymore eating a Colin the Caterpillar cake, dog treats and a custard cream cake.Photograph: themichaelbarrymoreView image in fullscreenMichael Barrymore eating a Colin the Caterpillar cake, dog treats and a custard cream cake.Photograph: themichaelbarrymoreTelevisionMichael Barrymore becomes unlikely TikTok star with nearly 5m followersFormer primetime TV host films himself eating dog biscuits, doing ‘munchie runs’ and addressing pool death caseMichael SavageMedia editorSat 12 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFilming from the driver’s seat of his car, with his pet whippet, Lara, in the background, Michael Barrymore shows an array of dog treats he has collected to test to the camera. There’s a twist, though: it won’t be the dog doing the testing.In a series of quick edits, the fallen star of primetime 1990s televisiongrimaces his way through cheese biscuits and pork sausages. The lamb spaghetti is particularly challenging, though he claims to quite like the chicken sausage slices.Allow TikTok content?This article includes content provided byTikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueThe dog treat video is part of a steady stream of content being produced by Barrymore on his TikTok account, where the 74-year-old has become an unlikely hit. The platform is usedmost heavily by the under-30s, many of whom would have no memory of his former career as one of Britain’s leading light entertainers.Particularly popular are Barrymore’s “munchie runs” to supermarkets, sweet shops and takeaways, where he snacks his way through an alarming array of treats, energy drinks and fast food.It is all a long way from his ITV heyday hosting Strike It Lucky and Barrymore, a career he abruptly lost in 2001 afterthe death of Stuart Lubbock, a 31-year-old father of two who diedshortly after being found unconscious in Barrymore’s swimming pool.Despite investigations and several arrests, no one has ever been charged in relation to Lubbock’s death. The case remains unresolved. Barrymore has always denied any involvement, but his TV career did not recover.Allow TikTok content?This article includes content provided byTikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueHowever,TikTokand its all-powerful algorithm have allowed him to build a vast new audience over the past four years. He is on course to amass close to 5m followers by the end of 2026.More than 6m have watched him scoffa trending pistachio nut cakeafter driving across the south-west, where he now lives, to find one. In another viral hit, hedevours an M&S Colin the Caterpillar cake with his bare hands.His success has become a case study in the media’s digital revolution, which is causing angst among traditional broadcasters. It has allowed Barrymore to bypass TV gatekeepers who shunned him after Lubbock’s death.“Barrymore reflects an interesting aspect of modern online celebrity culture whereby you can become popular, or in his case regain popularity, even if you do not appear on mainstream TV,” said Scott Bryan, the TV critic and chronicler.“Twenty years ago, appearing on TV was essential, and it was the end of his career when ITV dropped him. These days, those who don’t think he should be in the public eye simply don’t follow him on social media.”Professional short-form video editors have noted there is more to Barrymore’s TikTok success than his snacking antics. His videos often adopt trending music or memes and his output is prolific – both crucial ingredients to feeding the algorithm.A social media expert at a major British media company said: “I would be shocked if he’s doing this entirely on his own. He feels like he’s got support.”In an email exchange, Barrymore confirmed he had his “own social media expert” but not a team.Barrymore did attempt a more traditional comeback route after Lubbock’s death, with appearances onCelebrityBig Brother in 2006 and Dancing on Ice in 2019. Yet the outings did not revive his TV career.According to calculations based on his public view counts, Barrymore’s TikTok and YouTube channels are providing him with an income, though not one comparable to his former earnings as the de facto face of light evening entertainment.“I have always done what I do for the love of it,” Barrymore said. “I certainly do make a living from social media, which is increasing substantially year by year.”Much of his content simply follows him around his daily activities, usually cooking, snacking or travelling. He delights in being recognised by cashiers pricing up his latest haul of treats. Some shop workers havecomplained about being filmed by him via his smart glasses.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMatt Navarra, a social media consultant, said: “Barrymore is simultaneously evidence that everything about the media has changed and almost nothing about entertainment has changed.“His whole career was built around spontaneity, comic timing, talking to ordinary people, reacting quickly and creating chaotic moments. Those are fantastic short-form video creator skills.“We haven’t really got rid of gatekeepers. We’ve swapped human gatekeepers for algorithmic ones.”While it may appear to open up a comeback avenue for other 90s stars who have fallen out of favour, it is not so easy in practice. Fellow entertainer Jim Davidson’s Ustreme channel is also on TikTok but does not have Barrymore’s reach.Barrymore said: “The majority of the followers are from today’s generation and don’t know me from television – this isn’t what I ‘think’, this is facts coming from the analytics of TikTok and YouTube.”The domestic banality of his videos contributes to their success. Holly Beddingfield, a creative strategist and founder of the Capsule pop culture newsletter, said: “We increasingly see gen Z audiences push back against perfection in favour of authenticity.“It makes sense, then, that someone like Michael would resonate. It’s similar to the success of [British social media personality]Big John– he is just a guy who people see as a sort of funny uncle or dad.”Even on TikTok, however, Barrymore cannot escape discussion of Lubbock’s death. He has repeatedly addressed the case in videos, taking issue with various claims circulating online.Barrymore has insisted his social media success meant he would now not go back to broadcast TV.“It would be like taking a step backwards,” he said. “It would, I think, struggle to get the 20m to 30m views I currently get a week.”Meanwhile, Essex police continue to appeal for information from those who attended the party at Barrymore’s house on the night of Lubbock’s death.“Nine people were at that party,” said a spokesperson. “We know that not everyone was responsible for what happened, but someone was. Anyone with information about Stuart’s death can always contact us, whether directly or anonymously through Crimestoppers.”Explore more on these topicsTelevisionCelebritySocial mediaTikTokDigital mediaEntertainment TVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Elena Rybakina beats Aryna Sabalenka to seal dramatic US Open title triumph   | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Elena Rybakina battled to a 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 victory over Aryna Sabalenka to succeed her rival as the US Open champion
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Elena Rybakina battled to a 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 victory over Aryna Sabalenka to succeed her rival as the US Open champion
Content: Elena Rybakina shows off the trophy in New York after beating rival Aryna SabalenkaPhotograph: Robert Deutsch/Imagn Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenElena Rybakina shows off the trophy in New York after beating rival Aryna SabalenkaPhotograph: Robert Deutsch/Imagn Images/ReutersUS Open Tennis 2026Elena Rybakina beats Aryna Sabalenka to seal dramatic US Open title triumphRybakina wins 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 despite first-serve problemsOvercomes top seed and two-time defending championTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsSat 12 Sep 2026 19.02 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 21.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEven after she had won grand slam titles and conquered all surfaces, Elena Rybakina has always been considered lesser than the greatest players of her era. She has long been one of the most devastating shotmakers in the world, but there were always a couple more consistent and mentally tougher players above her.She leaves New York, finally, as the undisputed best tennis player on the planet, the new standard bearer of the women’s game, after following up her snatching of the No 1 ranking fromAryna Sabalenkaby succeeding her as the US Open champion. As she has done throughout this unforgettable week, the Kazakhstani showed her toughness in another spectacular tussle with her great rival, nervelessly closing out a 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 victory over Sabalenka, the top seed and two-time defending champion.Elena Rybakina beats Aryna Sabalenka to win US Open for first time – as it happenedRead moreBefore the final, Rybakina had not always played her best tennis this year in New York, but the past two weeks stand as the greatest mental performance of her career. She has had to overcome an achilles injury that sidelined her for a week before the tournament and left her uncertain if she would even compete. There was also the immense pressure of trying to clinch the world No 1 ranking. Then four consecutive grand slam or Olympic champions laid in wait for her during the second week of the tournament. She cleared every hurdle without hesitation.Her trials throughout the past fortnight imbued her with the confidence to play such a composed match against her biggest rival to close out the tournament. Here, the 27-year-old began the match with her serve, the most important shot in her arsenal, completely misfiring, yet she still showed off the breadth of her game by completely overpowering Sabalenka from the baseline. When the Belarusian fought her way back into the match and forced a final set, Rybakina was unfazed. She saved her best serving for the most important stretch, flitting through her service games early in set three and putting pressure on Sabalenka to keep up. Sabalenka, like so many players over the past year, simply could not.View image in fullscreenElena Rybakina struggled to make first serves in the opening set but otherwise her game was in good shape.Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPARybakina has become known and loved for her understated reactions to such monumental achievements, but after shouting in jubilation following her semi-final win over Coco Gauff, here she triumphantly raised both hands into the air upon firing down her 12th ace of the match to seal the victory. It meant everything. “It’s still so difficult to process what happened,” she said. “Too much achievements these few weeks. I’m super happy, very proud of all the work. Yeah, it’s just amazing. Difficult to find words, but super happy.”In addition to taking Sabalenka’s No 1 ranking, Rybakina has now also taken the status as the best hard-court player in the world. She now holds the three biggest hard-court titles: the Australian Open, the US Open and the WTA Finals. She joins figures such as Lindsay Davenport, Jennifer Capriati, Ash Barty, Angelique Kerber and Virginia Wade as three-time grand slam champions. Having previously won Wimbledon in 2022 and the 2026 Australian Open, Rybakina is suddenly a French Open away from completing the career grand slam.Sabalenka’s run to the final was an impressive feat considering how disastrous her past few months have been on the tour, but there was no consoling her after this defeat. Although she showed good sportsmanship in all of her interactions with Rybakina, including initiating a warm hug at the net, Sabalenka tossed her racket and then slumped into a seat in her courtside player box. When a cameraperson approached her, they were quickly told to “fuck off”.View image in fullscreenAryna Sabalenka had lost the No 1 ranking and now her US Open title to Elena Rybakina.Photograph: Eduardo Muñoz/ReutersSabalenka has reached eight consecutive grand slam finals on hard courts, an astounding feat, but any competitor in her shoes would be upset by the number of titles she has been able to win from those positions. Sabalenka is now 4-6 in grand slam finals and just hasn’t been able to produce her best tennis when it matters most. Most painfully of all, her opportunity to three-peat at the US Open has come and gone: “It’s really tough to control your emotions when you lose in the final of the grand slam and when you were trying to go for three-peat,” Sabalenka said of her on-court emotions. “So I just wanted to let it go, because if I would hold it inside, right now or here or there on the court, I wouldn’t be able to say a word or I would just go not really nice over there. So I just wanted to let all of that aggression and disappointment go outside.”This was a historic encounter. Since the Australian Open became a hard court tournament in 1988, this is just the second time that the same two players contested both finals in the same year. It is also the third time that the top two players in the world have competed in a grand slam final with the ranking switching hands. No matter the terrain or stakes, though, these two champions inspire a high level of tennis from each other. Their three major finals have each produced dramatic, high quality three-set matches.However, for a long time Sabalenka was clearly the superior player in this rivalry, even if Rybakina could beat her on any given day. This year the terms of engagement have truly shifted with Rybakina winning their last two grand slam finals in addition to defeating Sabalenka in the championship match of the WTA Finals. It is now up to Sabalenka to return to the practice court and figure out a way past the new leader of her sport.Afterwards, as Sabalenka discussed the end of her reign at No 1, she was informed that her time on top of the WTA rankings had lasted for 99 consecutive weeks, the sixth longest consecutive run at No 1 in history: “Well, that’s amazing. Let’s see if Elena can beat me in that,” she said, laughing. Then she added: “If she continues to play like that? Then, yeah, I’m in trouble.”Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisTennisUS sportsAryna SabalenkanewsShareReuse this content

title: From socialist student to Trump proxy: the 25-year rise of Venezuela’s Delcy Rodríguez | Delcy Rodríguez | The Guardian
description: Those who have encountered the interim president paint her in starkly different ways, but all agree she is likely to remain in power
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Those who have encountered the interim president paint her in starkly different ways, but all agree she is likely to remain in power
Content: Eight months after the capture of Nicolás Maduro, Delcy Rodríguez is still in power – despite leading a country many now consider a US protectorate.Photograph: Leonardo Fernández Viloria/ReutersView image in fullscreenEight months after the capture of Nicolás Maduro, Delcy Rodríguez is still in power – despite leading a country many now consider a US protectorate.Photograph: Leonardo Fernández Viloria/ReutersDelcy RodríguezProfileFrom socialist student to Trump proxy: the 25-year rise of Venezuela’s Delcy RodríguezThose who have encountered the interim president paint her in starkly different ways, but all agree she is likely to remain in powerTom PhillipsLatin America correspondentSat 12 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was April 2002 andDelcy Rodríguezwas a woman on a mission.Venezuela’s then president, Hugo Chávez, had been temporarily toppled by a bungled coup and Rodríguez, a junior diplomat who had been studying at Birkbeck, University of London, decided to act.Rodríguez, then 32, set about trying to convince two reporters from the BBC programme Newsnight to accompany her to Venezuela’s capital to tell the world about what had happened.“She desperately wanted to get the story of Chávez and the coup out there on a big platform,”says one of those journalists, Meirion Jones, who engaged Rodríguez as their fixer and flew to Caracas with her.As the trio travelled around the South American city trying to land an interview with Chávez – who by then had reclaimed the presidency after being briefly detained – Jones had no inkling that his Venezuelan field producer and interpreter might one day become president herself.“She looked like she was still a student really … it was just impossible to imagine at that point that she would become president of Venezuela,” Jones says.Yet that is precisely what Rodríguez, now 57, has become, albeit in extraordinary circumstances precipitated by Donald Trump’s decision to abduct Chávez’s authoritarian heir, Nicolás Maduro.When US special forces snatched the unpopular Maduro on 3 January this year, he was widely expected to be replaced with María Corina Machado, the Nobel-winning opposition leader whose movement beat him in the stolen 2024 election.View image in fullscreenMany expected the opposition leader and Nobel laureate María Corina Machado to replace Nicolás Maduro.Photograph: Heiko Junge/EPAInstead, Trump discarded Machado and backed Maduro’s vice-president, Rodríguez, who became Venezuela’s interim leader two days after the downfall of her boss.Eight months later, Rodríguez is still in power – despite leading a country many now consider a US protectorate – and looks likely to remain there for the foreseeable future, with scant sign of fresh presidential elections being called.“We are very happy with the president-elect that we have right now,”Trump saidof the un-elected Rodríguez after announcing what he called“the biggest oil deal in world history”.Imdat Oner, a former Turkish diplomat in Caracas, believes the deal has strengthened Rodríguez and dealt a big blow to those hoping for democratic change. “Delcy is winning … I see Delcy Rodríguez staying in the presidency for at least four or five more years,” he says.The Delcy Rodríguez that Jones flew with to Caracas more than two decades ago was a well-connected but politically insignificant figure known fundamentally because of her father.Jorge Antonio Rodríguez was a Marxist activist who died in police custody in 1976, when his daughter was seven, reputedly after being tortured while detained over the kidnapping of a US businessman.“All the Chavistas knew who her father had been – but they didn’t really know who she was,” says Jones, who is now a freelance investigative journalist. “[Butduring our time in Caracas]she’d made herself known to all these people … and I think by the end of the trip she was starting to think: ‘Maybe there is an opening for me in politics in Venezuela.’”Soon after, Rodríguez returned to Venezuela, landing jobs with its state oil company, PDVSA, and foreign ministry. By 2006, she had become Chávez’s chief of staff, although she fell out of favour after clashing with Venezuela’s then ambassador to Russia during a visit to Moscow.View image in fullscreenDelcy Rodríguez became Nicolás Maduro’s vice-president in June 2018.Photograph: Luis Robayo/AFP/Getty ImagesThat row interrupted Rodríguez’s rise but she was rehabilitated by Maduro when he became president after Chávez’s 2013 death. In the years that followed, as her country nosedived into hunger and authoritarianism, Rodríguez enjoyed a rapid ascent.She served as foreign minister before taking charge of the country’s economy as petroleum minister, finance minister and Maduro’s vice-president. Her brother, a psychiatrist turned politician, Jorge Rodríguez, established himself as the head of the national assembly.After Maduro’s capture, the siblings formed a powerful triumvirate, alongside the feared interior minister, Diosdado Cabello.“Delcy is not Delcy. Delcy’s Delcy and her brother. They do everything in tandem … they don’t do anything without each other’s approval or consent,” says Andrés Izarra, Chávez’s communication minister who went into exile after falling out with Maduro.View image in fullscreenOne former Chávez minister says Delcy Rodríguez and her national assembly president brother, Jorge, do everything in tandem.Photograph: Lucas Aguayo/AFP/Getty ImagesThose who have encountered Rodríguez during her unlikely 25-year rise, from being a leftwing student in the UK to the pinnacle of power in Venezuela, paint her in dramatically different ways.Admirers describe a pragmatic, witty and intelligent workaholic who they credit with helping Venezuela escape years of hyperinflation and believe can fulfil promises to revive the country’s decaying oil industry and economy.“Venezuela under Delcy is going to have the best possible kind of technocratic care – and that’s what is needed right now … she’s going to get that oil moving,” says Greg Palast, the other journalist who flew to Caracas with Rodríguez for the BBC in 2002.Palast believes Venezuela is “way better off” under Rodríguez than the incompetent Maduro, calling her a clever strategist who plays politics “on a four-dimensional chessboard”.Detractors paint Rodríguez as a belligerent, power-hungry chameleon whose political leanings can change on a dime and who, as a key member of Maduro’s regime, was herself responsible for Venezuela’s slide into poverty and dictatorship.“They’re evil, they are crazy and they are smart … they’re evil geniuses,” a prominent opposition politician, who asked not to be named, says of the Rodríguez siblings.Izarra says his former friend is “very machiavellian” and has a taste for luxury.Tom Shannon, a retired US diplomat who has worked with Venezuela since the 1990s, describes the multilingual Rodríguez as a “very smart, very articulate, very determined” and profoundly ideological person.View image in fullscreenTom Shannon believes Delcy Rodríguez’s objective in her partnership with the US is political survival and making sure the right do not return to power.Photograph: Paul J Richards/AFP/Getty ImagesShannon recalls being “intercepted” by Rodríguez – then foreign minister – after flying to Caracas to meet Maduro during Barack Obama’s second term.Their conversation was wide-ranging. “But I remember very distinctly, at one point I raised the issue of human rights – our interest in especially seeing the release of certain people from prison,” Shannon says.“She … turned to me, with a look almost of contempt, not for me, but for the subject I was raising and she said: ‘You might not know my story, but my father was a revolutionary member of an armed revolutionary movement in Venezuela who was arrested [and] tortured during interrogation and killed by the Venezuelan security services when I was a girl.’“And she said: ‘This interrogation and the killing of my father took place during a time when, from your point of view, Venezuela was a democratic country governed by the rule of law. But I can tell you, the security services weren’t.”Shannon adds: “It was very striking … it was evident to me that she saw her father as kind of a revolutionary north star, kind of a martyr point of reference – and I believe that’s still the case.”He thinks Rodríguez’s objective in her new partnership with Washington is political survival “and to make sure that a revanchist, conservative, elitist, democratic opposition does not return to power”.View image in fullscreenDelcy Rodríguez with the US energy secretary, Chris Wright, during the signing of an oil agreement in Caracas on 2 September.Photograph: Juan Barreto/AFP/Getty ImagesSpeaking in the White House, Trump heaped praise on his unlikely Venezuelan partner. “Delcy is doing a very, very good job – very highly respected,” he told reporters.Trump claimed Venezuela had only just escaped a “very nasty” regime and was not ready for elections. “You know, it’s very new. We took them out of a dictatorship, and we’re getting along great with the government,” he said.Such comments will have been music to Rodríguez’s ears. “Delcy wants to survive,” says Oner. “And she knows that if she gives enough to theTrump administration, the Trump administration will allow her to stay in power.”Explore more on these topicsDelcy RodríguezVenezuelaAmericasUS foreign policyTrump administrationOilprofilesShareReuse this content

title: I survived a stroke during an ocean swim. Here’s what I’ve learned about fear | Stroke | The Guardian
description: After his stroke in rough surf, Graham Russell embarked on an unexpected journey into fear. Three lessons helped him return to the joy of the ocean
Author: Graham Russell
Headline: After his stroke in rough surf, Graham Russell embarked on an unexpected journey into fear. Three lessons helped him return to the joy of the ocean
Content: ‘I assumed I already knew what fear felt like – I had surfed in rough conditions before, saved lives in the ocean and pursued plenty of adventure in my early years – but this was different’: Graham Russell.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I assumed I already knew what fear felt like – I had surfed in rough conditions before, saved lives in the ocean and pursued plenty of adventure in my early years – but this was different’: Graham Russell.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianStrokeI survived a stroke during an ocean swim. Here’s what I’ve learned about fearAfter his stroke in rough surf, Graham Russell embarked on an unexpected journey into fear. Three lessons helped him return to the joy of the oceanGraham RussellSat 12 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 16.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLooking out over the ocean, I would watch the waves sparkling in the sunlight as they grew and spilled into a burst of froth. It was a fun way to relax, to breathe deep and enjoy an awesome display of energy. But lately it had become exhausting.In winter last year I tore the lining of an artery in my neck during a rough ocean swim off the Central Coast of New South Wales. Itcaused a strokewhile I was in the water, which saw me scrambling back to shore where a surfer noticed me and sounded the alarm. Six months later, the injury had healed, and my motor functions were all back to normal. But as I prepared for a dip in calm conditions on a sunny day in January, I paused. An unexpected journey into fear began.Standing on the sand, a thousand scenarios would play out in my mind: how big was that wave? Was it powerful enough to injure me? Where would the currents take me? Would I be safe?View image in fullscreenDistant storms create waves, which coalesce to form swells whose power emerges much later. Fear seemed to behave similarly.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianI assumed I already knew what fear felt like – I had surfed in rough conditions before, saved lives in the ocean and pursued plenty of adventure in my early years – but this was different. This was fear in the total absence of any bravado or exhilaration or reward. It did not feel like a physical challenge to surmount, it felt simply like my energy would disappear and I would sink beneath the waves.I would stand on the shore for an age, scrunching up my eyes against the morning sun and scrutinising the conditions for so long that my face would start to ache.The scales tippedIt started as a straightforward fear of being fearful. In the days after I left the emergency department, my thoughts revolved around: what if I saw the beach where it happened and freaked? Would I take fright the moment the chill water hit my skin? What if the sound of a crashing wave sent me back to that day? I was scared to even turn my neck to breathe when swimming freestyle. Thankfully, it turned out I loved the ocean just as before. The real fear came later. It came embedded inside fatigue.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsThe neurologist advised me it could take six months for post-stroke fatigue to ease. That felt like a long time. I was impatient to be out there, doing everything I did before, maybe doing it better. Pushing, pushing, pushing. I cannot express how keen I was to get back to work, to pull my bootcamp boxing gloves on again, to get stronger. But each time I tried, I was getting weaker. The scales eventually tipped: the next time I looked at a rough ocean, I felt exhausted.View image in fullscreenI needed to learn to go out when I thought I couldn’t. But how could I do that safely?Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianDistant storms create waves, which coalesce over time and distance to form swells whose power emerges much later. Fear seemed to behave in a similar way. I had survived the initial peril, I still enjoyed the water, and I assumed healing was a linear process. I was totally wrong.As the exhaustion built, the window for when it felt OK to go into the ocean became smaller. Over time, these narrowing criteria created a space for fear to flourish. I created more obstacles, asked myself more questions, and dived in less and less.My fitness dimmed, my sense of heaviness grew, the ocean became strange to me.Three lessonsI learned three lessons as I crawled my way out of this heaviness. It was in coming to terms with this strangeness, and being determined to regain the familiarity and joy of the ocean that I had to learn patience – not with others, but myself. I realised that the post-disaster euphoria of survival is just that: a fleeting moment. I also learned to build my resilience, becoming comfortable in the presence of fear. I scrutinised it like I had scrutinised the waves. I sat next to it, like a passenger on a train. I didn’t rail at God for exposing me to fear, I asked for help to fix the issues in my life and keep moving forward.That’s where the third and most crucial lesson came in: relationship. Dealing with trauma often involves talking about it, sharing it, being honest and asking for help. The best light to shine on a trouble comes from multiple angles, from those around you who care. For men, and perhaps particularly for fathers, it is not always easy to tell your family you don’t know what’s going on and that you’re scared your life will never be the same again.View image in fullscreenI spoke to another mate who had suffered a surfing accident; he told me his recovery involved asking someone to paddle out for a surf with him.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianThat many fathers view their role as the provider, the one who evokes stability and protection, is well known. For me there was added poignancy – one of my teenage daughters had been diagnosed with cancer two months earlier. I was needed more than ever. How profoundly selfish it would be if I took a wrong step and left my wife to deal with this alone. This year was either going to break us or bond us.It was such an astonishingly terrible situation that we did what any family would do: we laughed. Suddenly, a comedy during a family movie night had never seemed so funny. Gallows humour echoed through my mind, and our home.However, the kindness and the curse of this closeness was that I didn’t need to ask for help. My family already knew the score. I hadn’t really needed to make such a plea, beyond the privacy of my own prayers. I was out of practice.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI had a stroke during an ocean swim. Most people passed by unaware. One didn’tRead moreRather than getting professional guidance, help arrived through conversations with those around me, often friends from my surf club. It was counselling via community.A fellow volunteer surf lifesaver and good friend, who was watching me agonising over the ocean conditions one day, told me recovery was vastly more about the mental game than anything physical. He was right. I needed to learn to go out when I thought I couldn’t. But how could I do that safely?I then spoke to another mate who had suffered a surfing accident that saw him floating face down in the water with a fractured neck, unable to move or breathe until help arrived. He told me his recovery involved asking someone to paddle out for a surf alongside him.It was patrol season and the conditions were big. I was desperate to get out there, and equally petrified of what might happen. I took a leap and asked a fellow surf lifesaver if he would join me in swimming out. I needed some backup, I admitted to him. It felt like a huge question to ask, like everyone on the beach would turn to look at me. He turned to look at me. His expression suggested it was the simplest request and said: “Sure.”Returning to the waterPulling on the swim fins once more and navigating the shore dump brought unhappy memories. Swimming out, my brain was screaming at me to head back. My head spun as it switched between examining each approaching wave and current, while keeping my friend in sight.My heart was pounding but my brain was learning in the background. Doing this ocean thing had been my passion, remember? I reached the sand again and felt a sense of euphoria. I turned around and looked out over the waves. I saw them through a different lens. They didn’t look scary at all.The second time I headed out, the panic eased slightly.View image in fullscreenTwelve months on, and the sense of exhausting struggle has dissipated.Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The GuardianThese three lessons – learning patience, building resilience and embracing relationships – became an iterative practice, fine-tuned each time they were needed. I did not move through them and then discard them. They were on repeat, sometimes used every day.A year after the stroke, my neurologist gave me the all-clear. My risk was back to the same baseline as any other person.I embarked on a long-held desire: to train to become a surf lifesaving jetski operator. Each weekend, during rescue scenarios designed to induce stress, I could see my confidence growing as I got the hang of to this new tool. The jetski felt akin to the lessons I had learned over the past year. It was allowing me to do things I couldn’t do before. The more I used it, the more it became a natural part of me.Twelve months on, and the sense of exhausting struggle has dissipated. The events of that day last year had given me membership of a community of people. Those who had faced life-threatening trauma and had survived. It had not made me special, but it did change the conversations I would go on to have with a wide range of people who, in countless different scenarios, either could have died themselves, or knew someone who had. I move through life now in a different way.Graham Russell is Guardian Australia’s deputy international editorExplore more on these topicsStrokeDeath and dyingHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tove Lo: ‘The rumour I hear the most is that I’m either pregnant or in rehab. I want both of those to not be true’ | Music | The Guardian
description: The Swedish electro-pop singer-songwriter on eloping to Vegas, checking cupboards for murderers and her spooky party trick
Author: Emma Joyce
Headline: The Swedish electro-pop singer-songwriter on eloping to Vegas, checking cupboards for murderers and her spooky party trick
Content: Swedish singer-songwriter Tove Lo: ‘I would be a lynx, the Nordic wildcat. It’s what Lo means in Swedish.’Photograph: Charlie DenisView image in fullscreenSwedish singer-songwriter Tove Lo: ‘I would be a lynx, the Nordic wildcat. It’s what Lo means in Swedish.’Photograph: Charlie Denis10 Chaotic QuestionsMusicTove Lo: ‘The rumour I hear the most is that I’m either pregnant or in rehab. I want both of those to not be true’The Swedish electro-pop singer-songwriter on eloping to Vegas, checking cupboards for murderers and her spooky party trickEmma JoyceSat 12 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 20.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat’s been your most memorable interaction with a fan?The one that comes to mind is a fan in Austin who I met on one of my first tours there. He ran up to me and said, “SIGN MY ARM!” I signed his arm and then when he came back to the show the next night he had it tattooed – there was plastic over it. I remember saying, “I would have done a better job if I knew you were going to get it tattooed.” Then we took a picture of us, with me pointing at the tattoo.Luke McGregor: ‘I don’t like Pokémon. It really feels like animal cruelty to me’Read moreThe next year when I was playing at Austin City Limits, the sound broke down and I was talking to the crowd for quite a while, and I saw him – he had a T-shirt on with the photo of me and him pointing at his tattoo. He’d made a T-shirt for me as well, so he threw it up on stage … I still have that T-shirt in my closet.Is there a rumour you’ve heard or read about yourself that you wish were true?The one that pops up the most is that I’m either pregnant or that I’ve gone to rehab, so right now I want both of those tonotbe true.What’s the most impulsive thing you’ve ever done?Probably get married. We eloped to Vegas and took a group of our closest friends with us and had a party weekend. We went to the Little White Chapel and just did it, I think within two weeks of us talking about getting married.Your latest single is called DNH, meaning “drunk and horny”. When was the last time you were drunk and horny?Last weekend. I was at this party in downtown LA called Midnight Lovers – they throw parties in an outside venue under a bridge – and a DJ that I love called Azzecca did a really great set. We were dancing, hanging out and then went back to my friend’s house for an after party. We got in the hot tub when we got home. It was a very typical LA night for me and my crew. It was fun and sexy.What’s the first thing you do when you get to a hotel?If it’s late, I check under the bed and in all the closets and the bathroom to make sure that no one’s in there ready to murder me – and then I will pour a drink and take a bath.If you could be any animal, what would you be?I would be a lynx, the Nordic wildcat. It’s what Lo means in Swedish. It’s the animal that I’ve always gone back to, my favourite animal since I was kid[shows a tattoo of a lynx on her hand].How many lynx tattoos do you have?I have this one right here ofSunshine Kitty[the name of her fourth album] with Super Ted. The rest of my tattoos are hearts, bunnies, vaginas and aliens.What’s the most chaotic thing that’s happened to you on stage?Trash hits! Why a wave of hedonistic, feral female pop stars are rejecting respectabilityRead moreHaving food poisoning and needing to run off stage to puke. I was playing a festival in Bali and I got sick like five minutes before. I was thinking, I’ve done the initial spew so I probably have an hour until I need to puke again, so let’s go! I got through the whole set, ran off to spew, ran on again and did the last two songs. Afterwards I was like, “Get me to bed.”Would you rather die at the bottom of the ocean or out in space?Out in space. I don’t know why. Maybe because it feels like I’ll be floating and slowly suffocating, whereas drowning for some reason feels really painful. I think I will just be mesmerised that I’m even out there.Do you believe in extraterrestrial life?I do. I don’t know if we have yet figured out their shape or form. But I don’t think that we’re the only ones out there. I think there’s already proof that we’re not, we just haven’t found anything that we can communicate with.Do you have a party trick?I’ve kind of stopped doing it but I can go down into a bridge pose from standing, then walk like the girl fromThe Exorcist. But if I’m a little too drunk and I fail and land flat on my head, it gets dramatic. If I’m walking down a hallway and I can hear someone coming, I go into the Exorcist pose and start walking at them. It looks pretty impressive and spooky.Tove Lo’s album Estrus is out on 18 September. The Estrus tour is coming to Brisbane, Melbourne, Sydney and Perth, 1-7 March 2027Explore more on these topicsMusic10 Chaotic QuestionsElectronic musicPop and rockSwedenLos AngelesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I said, if you want to fire me, just fire me. And so he did’: my showdown with Donald Trump | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: What’s it like to be shown the door by the US president? A former national security adviser, an Apprentice contestant and more share their stories
Author: Kate Lloyd
Headline: What’s it like to be shown the door by the US president? A former national security adviser, an Apprentice contestant and more share their stories
Content: ‘Trump is the ideal politician for this moment: he’s all personality, he understands how to trigger you, he knows the power of his own mythology’: Gene Folkes, Apprentice contestant.Photograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Trump is the ideal politician for this moment: he’s all personality, he understands how to trigger you, he knows the power of his own mythology’: Gene Folkes, Apprentice contestant.Photograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty ImagesDonald Trump‘I said, if you want to fire me, just fire me. And so he did’: my showdown with Donald TrumpWhat’s it like to be shown the door by the US president? A former national security adviser, an Apprentice contestant and more share their storiesPlus:The truth about my 11 days in the White House, by Anthony ScaramucciAs told toKate Lloyd,Julian BorgerandDavid SmithSat 12 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 08.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGene Folkes, 62, based in Manhattan, was a contestant onseason 10 of The Apprentice, which aired in 2010. A formerairforce recruiter until 1991, he retrained as an investment banker, then launched his own business before appearing on the reality show. He was fired by Trumpin episode 5. He now runs the technology consulting firmOshunXand hosts apodcast,Folkes Unfettered.I didn’t audition to be onThe Apprentice. I received the call out of the blue: “Would you be interested in doing this show?” I didn’t know a lot about it. However, like any young business person, you look for people who you consider titans. There’s this mythology around Trump. He was one of the people I wanted to emulate.View image in fullscreenGene Folkes met Trump on The Apprentice: ‘You can really get drawn into all things Donald.’Photograph: Christopher Lane/The GuardianThe first morning, wardrobe comes into your room at 3.30am. You meet the other contestants for the first time, then within an hour you’re on your first task. You learn really quickly that you’re playing a game and the rules can change at any moment.The first time we met, Trump was outside his building on Wall Street. He is an imposing figure. When he walks into a place he owns the room and there’s not a lot of air for anyone else to breathe. I thought, “OK, he’s presenting as exactly who I believed him to be.” There was a sense of admiration and aspiration. It was only when you dug deeper that you realised the emperor had no clothes.In the corporate world, there are certain things you just don’t do without consequences. And they were so natural for him. The first time we met him in the boardroom, Trump asked us if we thought the women were attractive. He would make these innuendoes – things that were sort of hard to pin down – but you felt kind of icky afterwards.The first round was split men v women. I put myself forward to be the project manager for the men’s team. Task one was to design a modern office space. We won that task, and my prize was a one-on-one with Trump. His desk in Trump Tower was rather small and somewhat messy. Initially, I felt he knows how to connect with people. There was charisma, there was charm; he evokes a certain amount of confidence. You can really get drawn into all things Donald, but as I sat back and started really listening to him, I thought, “Oh, I don’t think this is the person that I have tried to model myself after.”I didn’t feel empathy from him: I was more product than person. I think about it a lot now, because I believe that anyone who wants to lead a nation has to have a certain amount of empathy. If you don’t, then how can you relate to someone who’s a single mom or dad who’s struggling to put food on the table?A producer told me the series was mine to lose. The week I got fired, I didn’t feel like it was coming. We had to put on a fashion show for Rockport. When you’re an air force recruiter, like I had been, all you do is publicly speak, so my project manager selected me to be master of ceremonies. I wear glasses. In that episode I decided to wear my contacts. They weren’t bifocals, and I remember saying, “I need to go back and get my glasses.” We never got to it. We got on to the test and I couldn’t read a freaking thing on the script.When we went to the boardroom and we lost, they brought in three of us. Trump really took me off guard. The narrative shifted from, “Hey, I couldn’t see, and I wasn’t going to admit that I couldn’t see, because I didn’t want to start making excuses”, to one where I became illiterate: I couldn’t read; I couldn’t speak. It was very coded language that I was familiar with. It dawned on me: oh my God, he is framing me as a dumb person of colour. I’m sitting here with a degree in finance and he’s talking to me like I’m a moron. At that point I pushed back and said, “No one gets to talk about my speaking abilities. I don’t know what the bleep you’re talking about, but that’s not me.”double quotation markI did not feel anger. I felt relief. At that point you realise you’re playing in a system that’s riggedView image in fullscreenFolkes on The Apprentice in 2010.Photograph: YouTube/NBCHis face was red. He was visibly angry. One of the things he did when pushed back on was escalate. It was like he didn’t hear anything you said. He was animated but in a controlled way. He was playing to camera. He knew the audience was salivating for his line.I finally said, “You know what? If you want to fire me, just fire me.” And so he did.I did not feel anger. I felt relief. At that point you realise you’re playing in a system that’s rigged. And the person in power controls the narrative, controls the outcome. This was a game, but my real-life consequences were: what is my life going to look like after the programme, for my relationships, business dealings, opportunities?When I watched the series, I got on the phone with NBC to say, “Holy crap, that’s where you guys want to go with that? That I was uneducated, ignorant?” There was no sense of empathy or compassion from the network or him.Afterwards I did not want to leave the house. I could not get out of bed some mornings. I really became almost a recluse for three months. It took me years to get comfortable talking about it. I was depressed.When I got a hold of myself, I began to do what I normally do: I started fighting. I wrote a blog where I gave my opinion on Trump considering running for the presidency. NBC asked me to take it down, which I refused to do.I remember someone saying to me, “You’re hurting the Trump brand, you’re hurting the NBC brand and you’re hurting the Apprentice brand”, and I remember saying, “But you’re hurting the Gene Folkes brand, and I didn’t sign off for this crap.”In the 15 years since I was on The Apprentice, media, entertainment, politics and news have started converging. Trump is the ideal politician for this moment: he’s all personality, he understands how to trigger you, he knows the power of his own mythology.When I served in the military, there were certain leaders you would follow to death. You knew they loved and cared about you. They were able to manage their emotions. They realised that the goal of the team outweighed their individual personality. Trump is the opposite. He’s all personality; there is no team.Good leaders want to be challenged. And what I learned from The Apprentice, and what I’m seeing now in politics, is consistent: don’t challenge him.As told to Kate LloydNBC declined to comment.View image in fullscreenJohn Bolton, former national security adviser.Photograph: Stephen Voss/The Guardian‘Trump isn’t disciplined by anything, and so most of what I did was struggle to keep the train on the track’John Bolton, 77, based in Washington DC, is anattorneyandformer ambassador to the United Nationswho wasnationalsecurityadviserfrom2018 until 2019, under Trump. His exit from government wasannounced by the president over Twitteron10 September2019: “I informed John Bolton last night that his services are no longer needed at the White House. I disagreed strongly with many of his suggestions, as did others in theadministration, and therefore I asked John for his resignation, which was given to me this morning.” Bolton says things played out differently.For me, there was no one straw that broke the camel’s back, and I think that’s true in many resignation situations. It was an accumulation of factors. I had had a resignation letter drafted, and kept one copy in my desk drawer in the office and one copy at home, knowing I could print it out whenever I needed to.It was basically a one-sentence resignation, which was the way I wanted to do it. And it finally came to that in September 2019.The last conversation really was on 9 September. He was complaining about this and complaining about that, having heard, obviously from people inside the administration, of something I had done that they didn’t like. And I said to him, “Well, look, if you feel that way, I’ll resign.” And he was leaving the Oval Office to go and give a speech. [Trump told Bolton they would talk about his resignation offer the following morning.]I went back to my office and I just thought, I am going to resign; I’m not going to talk to him. So I did a few other things that evening and then I went home, and came in early the next morning. There were a couple of meetings I wanted to finish up, particularly the freeing up of the security assistance to Ukraine. I got that done and I gave the letter to my secretary and said, “I’m going home. I’ll call you when I’m there.” I wanted to get out of the blast zone. So I told her to hand it to Trump’s secretary and then be prepared that she would probably be leaving soon thereafter.The only mistake I made was that I should have tweeted right then that I had resigned, because when Trump saw it he went through the roof. I did get one tweet out saying I had resigned, and then they closed my Twitter account. I had to fight later to get it back.I believe in pre-emptive strikes, and I had failed to follow my own advice. I should have fired first, but I was pursuing old-fashioned norms.I tell this story in my book: before the Singapore meeting with Kim Jong-un, the first in the series on the North Korean nuclear programme, there was a chance that Trump was going to cancel, which I thought was exactly the right thing to do. I thought the whole thing was going to be a terrible waste of time. He was going off to a dinner, I think, with state governors, and as he was leaving, I said, “We can send out something saying we’re not coming if you want to do that.” And he said, “Let me think about it.” He said, “When I was dating, I always liked to be the one to break up with the girl. I never wanted the girl to break up with me.”double quotation markIt really is an aberration in American politics – I’d say almost in world history – to have somebody who performs the way he doesView image in fullscreenBolton with Trump in February 2019.Photograph: Leah Millis/ReutersI didn’t keep that much stuff in the White House office. A lot of things – pre-government files of clippings and things – I thought my secretary would be able to walk out with because they clearly weren’t government property. But we had to fight over that, too. There were several other of my staff who were also let go within 24, 48 hours. Some of their stuff was taken as well.I don’t think I get called naive very often. I thought I knew what I was getting into, largely because I thought that the weight of the decisions Trump would have to make in the national security area, the gravity of the responsibility, would discipline him. It turned out I was completely wrong about that. Trump isn’t disciplined by anything, and so most of what I did in my 17 months was struggle to keep the train on the track. Things like long-range planning? Forget it. By and large, there just wasn’t time to do it.I firmly believed that Trump would be no different from his predecessors. And, to me, it just exemplifies that it really is an aberration in American politics – I’d say almost in world history – to have somebody who performs the way he does. People would just ignore the [national security council policymaking] process and go directly to Trump. It was the phenomenon of the last person in the room gets his attention.There was this occasion when the Iranians shot down an American drone over the Persian Gulf, in what we believed was international airspace. We sized up what we were going to do, came up with retaliation, the president ordered it, then literally as planes were in the air, he changed his mind. So that leads people to say, why are we doing this? Why do we even bother?Look, everybody’s got an ego. Politicians notoriously have bigger egos than most. But I’ve never seen a politician where the ego wasn’t subsumed to at least some extent by bigger considerations. With him, it’s not subsumed by anything. That was part of the mistake I made. I just had never seen a personality like that before.As told toJulian BorgerView image in fullscreenRebecca Kelly Slaughter, former commissioner of the FTC.Photograph: Stephen Voss/The Guardian‘I was at the school drama club when I had an email from somebody I had never heard of before. “Message from the president.” I thought, well, that can’t be good’Rebecca Kelly Slaughter,45,lives in Maryland. ADemocrat, she was appointed to theFederal Trade Commission(FTC), anindependent agency of the US government, byDonald Trump in 2018. The FTC’s work includes fighting illegal business practices, safeguarding online privacy and promoting competition to keep prices down for consumers.Slaughter wasfired last yearand fought a protracted legal battle, arguing that Trump did not have the right to remove an agency commissioner without cause. This culminated inthe supreme court caseTrump v Slaughter,whichdecided in favourof the president’s at-will removal power, overturning a91-year-oldprecedent.It was an incredible privilege and honour to work for the FTC.In the time I was there we blocked the largest grocery store merger in history, which would have raised grocery prices even further. We sued big tech platforms for violating children’s privacy, for subscription traps that charged people more money than they should have been paying. We investigated things like the price of insulin and the role of pharmacy benefit managers in keeping drug prices unnaturally high.Right after the inauguration in January 2025,the president removed commissionersat a different independent board, the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board. But he didn’t fire me or my colleague, commissioner Alvaro Bedoya. We went through a period from mid-January through mid-March thinking, is he going to fire us today? He didn’t fire us today. Does that mean he’s not going to fire us? We don’t know.We decided early on that we couldn’t and wouldn’t operate in a way that was inconsistent with our oaths of office or our principles in order to avoid getting fired. We were just going to do the jobswe had as well as we could, and we couldn’t control how the president was going to react.On 18 March 2025, I worked a full day in the office then went to our local public elementary school, where I was volunteering in the evenings with the drama club production of Beauty and the Beast. I was the parent lead for this production. But, much more importantly, my second kid was playing Belle. She was in fifth grade. This was the culmination of all of her hopes and dreams in her 10-year-old life.double quotation markI feel a lot of anger on behalf of institutions of government, of public servants throughout the governmentView image in fullscreenSlaughter in 2018, when she started working for Trump.Photograph: FTCI was sitting outside the dusty elementary school gym, children were running around pretending to be plates and spoons, inviting my daughter to come be their guest, and I checked my work phone and I had an email from somebody I had never heard of before. I can’t remember what it was titled – “Message from the president” or something like that.I thought, well, that can’t be good. I opened it, and it was a very long email, purportedly on behalf of the president, clearly not written by the president – many legal citations, no words in caps – the culmination of which was, your continued service on the FTC is inconsistent with my priorities, therefore you are terminated effective immediately.I took a deep breath and saidsome expletives in my head. I looked at the other parent volunteers sitting next to me and said, “I think I might have just gotten fired. Is it OK if I step outside to deal with this?” They said, “No, go home, go take care of what you need to do.” I said, “Oh no, I am not leaving Beauty and the Beast.”The rest of that evening is a blur in my mind. I talked to my husband, who was in California. I talked to my staff. I talked to a million reporters. We hastily organised a press conference that I participated in from the parking lot, holding a phone in front of my face, under the floodlights with a brick background behind me.I didn’t want my daughter to hear about this from other parents or other kids.I pulled her aside after they got through the run-through and said, “I have to tell you something. It’s going to sound scary but we are going to be OK and I don’t want you to be worried about it.” She said, “OK, what?” I said, “I got fired this evening.”I could see her little face well up. She said, “Are you going to have to stop working on the show?” I said, “No, I’m not going to let that happen”, and she said, “OK.” That was the key information she needed.
