You can try to take my job but you cannot take drama club from me.Alvaro [who was also fired] and I knew pretty quickly that we wanted to challenge our dismissals in court, because if we failed to do so it would be like acceding to this blatant violation of the law and destruction of these institutions, but the timing and structure of doing that were all questions we had to sort through.I was doing that until about midnight when my doorbell rang, which I thought was odd. I went to the door and there was a pizza delivery guy there. I said, “I didn’t order any pizza.” He showed me an order form with my name, my personal email address, my cellphone number, my home address. I said, “Well, I didn’t order it and I’m not gonna pay for it, so, sorry.”I called my husband and I was, like, this weird thing happened. Isn’t that funny? He goes, “No, it is not funny. That’s a thing that online trolls do to people, especially people who the president doesn’t like, in order to scare them.” I didn’t like that I was home with my four kids in the middle of the night when this happened. I talked to Alvaro, who also got a pizza. His take was, thank God, I’m starving, I haven’t eaten all evening!I don’t feel angry on my own behalf. It is very much not about me.I don’t feel any personal animus. I do feel a lot of anger on behalf of institutions of government, of public servants throughout the government. I have a lot of anger for those reasons.Donald Trump doesn’t think about me at all. I don’t think he knew that he fired me; I don’t have any evidence he actually knew and was involved in it. The president cares a lot about a ballroom and gold plating the White House and building monuments to himself. I don’t think he’s thinking about conservative legal theory. I also don’t think he is thinking about the American people.Last summer, in my interregnum period, I knew that I needed a project, so I signed up for the New York City marathon and ran it for charity. I had never run a marathon and I always thought it was impossible, and it felt like a metaphor for the professional experience I was going through. It was hard. It didn’t go as well as I had hoped or trained for, but I finished anyway. And that was also the metaphor for me: we do the hard things because they’re the right things to do, and that is the reward – even if it doesn’t turn out exactly the way you envision.View image in fullscreenBarbara Res, former executive VP of the Trump Organization.Photograph: Christopher Lane/The Guardian‘He didn’t have the courage to be the one to fire people. He didn’t want to face people’Barbara Res,76, based in New Jersey, met Donald Trump in 1978, when she was working as anassistant superintendentfor the contractorHRH, building theGrand Hyatthotel in New York.Two years later, he hired her tolead construction on Trump Tower. She eventually becamesenior vice-presidentandexecutive vice-presidentof theTrump Organization. She quit after a final stint as a consultant, when the redevelopment of the Ambassador hotel site in Los Angeles fell apart amid a prolonged condemnation battle with the Los Angeles school district and a collapsing real-estate market. Res says a last‑minute change in leadership, made by Trump against her advice, undermined negotiations that she believed could have allowed the project to finish with a small profit. She haswritten two booksabout her experiences over those years. Sheretrained as a lawyerand is now semi-retired.I worked for Donald for close to 18 years. I left on friendly terms. If I saw him at a function, we’d nod to each other.But in 2016 I wrote an op-ed in the New York Daily News about my experiences with him. He came out blazing guns against me at rallies and on Twitter. He released emails I had written to him five years earlier when I was looking for a job. A tabloid newspaper wrote that he had “got rid” of me and that I had begged him for a job. Both lies. His supporterstweeted thingsabout me like “glad Trump fired her”. I wasn’t fired.I’d impressed him when I was working for HRH. In meetings the project managers and superintendents would talk about different problems on the job, and the architect would often blame the contractor or the subcontractors. I’d say, “That’s bullshit.” He loved that.At a meeting at his apartment, Donald asked me to be in charge of the construction of Trump Tower. I remember it was in a nice building on Fifth Avenue. Everything inside was white: the carpet, the upholstery, the walls, the ceiling. Donald went through a spiel about what he was building. I was to be the last word on site, he said. “You’ll be like a Donna Trump.” He offered me almost twice the salary I was getting.double quotation markWe were able to keep him somewhat under control. Nobody does that nowI liked being there. Trump Tower was a big deal and I had the best crew in the world. There were times when Donald was actually like a human being. We used to go into his office and sit and talk. He’d tell jokes. He was pretty funny. Now, I’m not saying he was a nice guy. Not at all. Any time anyone really disagreed with him, he would yell at them. He always needed someone to blame. If he screamed at me in front of the team it didn’t matter, because they were all getting screamed at. If he’d screamed at me in front of an architect or an investor, I would have walked out the door.When he wanted to do something that we thought was wrong or illegal, you couldn’t just say that. He couldn’t handle it. So we found ways of working around it – making him think that a substitute idea we’d come up with was his. I used to put him in a good mood by saying, “Hey Donald, did you see Ivana this morning? What an incredible outfit she’s wearing. She’s so gorgeous.” We were able to keep him somewhat under control. Nobody does that now.I was offered a partnership elsewhere and left. Donald threw a massive party for me. He got me a Cartier bracelet, signed, “Towers of thanks, love Donald.” A few years later, I got back in touch with him for some advice and he hired me again, this time to be in charge of all construction, then construction and development, for the Trump Organization.When I went back in 1987, he was surrounded by yes‑sayers. His bookTrump: The Art of the Dealabsolutely changed him in terms of his picture of himself. Even though he always said he was the smartest, now he thought he was a real big-time player. Everybody knew everything about him: how great he was, how brilliant he was.View image in fullscreenRes and Trump c1999.Photograph: Courtesy of Barbara ResThe second time I left was around 1990, when I was running Trump’s big West Side project on the riverfront. Neighbourhood groups and some big-name opponents – including Christopher Reeve – were fighting it hard. And a friend of Donald’s came to him and said, “You’ve got to meet with these people, and you’ve got to make a deal with them.” He wanted to build 14m sq ft. He made a deal to build just7.5m. In that deal, the opposition group put their person in charge of the project. They wanted a semi‑famous lawyer who worked in development and didn’t have construction experience. I quit primarily because they brought in this other person.I told Donald I had to leave. My son has to have surgery, I said. The surgerywasa big deal, but I wouldn’t quit over that. I told him it to soften the blow.I stayed on as a consultant on two other projects. One of those was the Ambassador hotel. One of our partners was going under. He wanted to be in charge of everything. My assistant and I told Donald this would blow up the project, which it eventually did. Donald allowed him to take over against our advice. Afterwards, at a big meeting with the realtor and the partners, Donald came down on me. I told him, “I told you not to let this guy get involved.”He started screaming. His face was contorting. That was the only time he’d ever done that in front of external people. I was enraged. I looked at him and I said, “You know, Donald, there are medicines that can help you control that.”He got crazy about that.After the people left, I went back up to Donald’s office and said, “Look, I can’t do this, I’m leaving.” And he said, “Why?” I didn’t say, “Because you made a fool out of me in front of the partners.” I said, “I’m looking after my son, I’m still having problems” – which was not true. “They’re just going to start school now, and I think I really should find something that won’t take me to California every week.”Donald talked about running for president when I was at the Trump Organization. I thought at the time that he was a very good manager, given the right people, and that he could be a decent president. I didn’t know then that he had zero knowledge of government.The Apprentice thing I’ve always thought of as a big joke. In my experience, he didn’t have the courage to be the one to fire people. He didn’t want to face people. He didn’t want to look bad. If someone was going to get fired, he wasn’t doing it.In my case, we had a woman who was working on some lobbying efforts we were doing. She had gotten pregnant. He found out and said, “Fire her.” I said, “You can’t, that’s against the law.” He got angry at me. “Fire her now!” I did it. It was terrible. I told her I would support her if she wanted to go after him because I knew that it was illegal to fire her.Here’s another story I remember: when we needed an apartment manager at Trump Tower, he found a guy and hired him to work under me. He was terrible.  We didn’t like him; he had a bad attitude. I told Donald, “We’re going to fire him.” He said, “Go ahead.” We fired him, and he went across the street to where Donald’s office was at the time. Donald was convinced by him. He told us, “Give him another chance.” And that happened twice. It took three times to fire this guy.I think all the firing he has done in government shows a big shift in his attitude. But he has to blame someone. And how do you prove someone is at fault better than firing them? Even if they didn’t do anything wrong.As told to Kate LloydTower of Lies: What My Eighteen Years of Working With Donald Trump Reveals About Him by Barbara Res (Graymalkin Media, £14.99) is available now.The Trump Organization did not respond to a request to comment.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS politicsJohn BoltonThe ApprenticefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jamaican delegation defends legal route of petition to King Charles for slavery reparations | Reparations and reparative justice | The Guardian
description: Petition to king, who remains Jamaica’s head of state, is formally lodged in landmark visit to UK by officials
Author: Natricia Duncan
Headline: Petition to king, who remains Jamaica’s head of state, is formally lodged in landmark visit to UK by officials
Content: Olivia Grange, Jamaica’s culture minister, has led a delegation to the UK to petition King Charles.Photograph: Jess Hurd/PAView image in fullscreenOlivia Grange, Jamaica’s culture minister, has led a delegation to the UK to petition King Charles.Photograph: Jess Hurd/PACotton Capital: ongoing seriesReparations and reparative justiceJamaican delegation defends legal route of petition to King Charles for slavery reparationsPetition to king, who remains Jamaica’s head of state, is formally lodged in landmark visit to UK by officialsNatricia DuncanCaribbean correspondentSat 12 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTShareA palpable surge of emotion swept through Brixton’s New Park Road Baptist church as the packed congregation rose to sing Bob Marley’s Redemption Song.The service on Sunday marked the anniversary ofthe 1781 Zong massacre, when more than 100 enslaved Africans were thrown overboard so the ship’s owners could claim insurance for “lost cargo”.Jamaica’s plea to the king: use your authority to ensure colonial slavery is examined | Olivia GrangeRead moreAndthe song– a lament for the horrors of transatlantic slavery and a tribute to the resilience of those who fought for freedom – set the tone for a landmark visit to the UK by Jamaican officials to petition King Charles over reparations for slavery.The petition,backed by leaders of other Caribbean nations, asks the monarch to request legal advice from the privy council, the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries.It asks Charles, who is still Jamaica’s head of state, to seek guidance on three questions: whether the forced transport of Africans toJamaicawas lawful; whether it constituted a crime against humanity; and whether Britain is under an obligation to provide restitution for slavery and its enduring consequences.Led by the culture minister,Olivia Grange, the Jamaican delegation included lawyers and members of the country’s national council on reparations.The delegationmet diaspora communities, UK politicians, church leaders and institutions – including the British Museum, from which Jamaica is seeking the return of artefacts.Grange also held talks with the UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, though sources say these were not focused on reparations.View image in fullscreenOlivia Grange, Jamaica’s culture minister, took part in a service at a Brixton church during her delegation’s visit to London.Photograph: Alberto Pezzali/APJamaica’s petition has ignited a fierce debate about the legality of transatlantic slavery and political implications. The former privy council member Lord Sumption dismissed the legal strategy as “nonsense” and argued that the issue was “not a question of law at all” but one of morals and politics. Jamaican experts have defended the legality of the petition.Speaking at a briefing for UK parliamentarians, Edward Fitzgerald KC insisted Jamaica was acting in accordance with a little‑used mechanism in theJudicial Committee Act 1833which allows the king to refer questions of “legal or constitutional nature” to the privy council when they cannot be resolved through ordinary courts.Harj Narulla, a member of the UK team of counsels, told the Guardian it was an “obvious jurisdictional route”.“It was quite clear you can’t do a judicial review, for example, of some government decision … The issue is with the state itself, with the United Kingdom, which is the state responsible for slavery in Jamaica,” he said.Ulele Burnham, another member of the UK legal team, added: “The petition argues that the atrocities, theforced uprooting, the violent subjugation for profit was of course immoral, everyone knows that. But the petition’s very focus is to show that it was also clearly inconsistent with the law of the time. Non-Europeans did not suddenly become human when slavery ended. They always were. And even in those days, humans had some rights in English and international law.”In Jamaica, though the pursuit of reparations is supported by the two main parties, members of the opposition People’s National party raised concerns that the delegation had not managed to secure a meeting with the king. Grange said a meeting with Charles“was not part of the plan”.“Before we came toLondon, we had consulted with both the Palace and the privy council to confirm the correct legal process for filing the petition. Both confirmed the correct process was to file it by post and email, which is what we did,” she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |MonthlySign up toCotton CapitalStarting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenBell Ribeiro-Addy, the MP for Clapham and Brixton Hill in London, said the Jamaicans were ‘enacting their rights under English law’.Photograph: Bell Ribeiro-AddyThe Labour MP Bell Ribeiro‑Addy, the chair of the all‑party parliamentary group for Afrikan Reparations, said Jamaica was well within its rights to petition the monarch. “Due to colonialism, which obviously initially had its root in enslavement, there are certain responsibilities that [the UK] has. We don’t get the privilege of still having Jamaica as part of the realm … without them also in turn having the right to petition King Charles. They are enacting their rights under English law and they have the right to ask those questions,” she said.In December 2024, Jamaica’s government tabled a bill in parliamentto remove the king as the country’s head of state. The bill has not progressed to becoming a law.Pointing to recent global momentum – including 123 nationsvoting for a UN resolutiondescribing chattel slavery as the gravest crime against humanity – Ribeiro‑Addy said it was time for Britain to confront its past and the decisions that continue to shape the present.She described headlines quoting huge reparation figures (which were not mentioned in the Jamaican petition) as a distraction. “What seems to happen a lot when we talk about reparations is people want to distract people with figures,” she said. “They divorce themselves from the reality of what we are talking about. No one is saying that reparative justice will never include any sort of payment. But that is never the starting point. And we have to remember that this country refuses to even apologise. This country refuses to do the things that it can do, which don’t cost any money at all.“The enslavement of peoples of African descent … meant that anybody who was not white was considered less than … almost being classified as not quite human. And that is a serious issue. If we are ever going to challenge racism properly, we have to get down to its very root.”As the delegation lodged the petition on Monday, a spokesperson for the prime minister, Andy Burnham, reiterated the British government’s long‑held position that “the UK does not and will not pay reparations”.Ribeiro‑Addy said it would be an insult to African andCaribbeancountries if Britain refuses to discuss reparations at the upcoming Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua, which the king is scheduled to attend.“We’re meant to no longer be a group of countries under an empire. We were meant to be a group of countries with a shared history and who are treated as equals,” she said. “The idea that all of the countries bar one want to have a discussion and so the discussion is stopped has to be wrong … if we do things like that, I think we will soon see the crumbling of the Commonwealth. And that would be a huge shame.”Explore more on these topicsReparations and reparative justiceCotton Capital: ongoing seriesSlaveryJamaicaKing Charles IIIColonialismBritish MuseumLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Last Seen to Angine de Poitrine: the week in rave reviews | Culture | The Guardian
description: Patrick Brammall and Maxine Peake star in a propulsive new drama, and the microtonal polka-dotted alien duo return to the live stage. Here’s the pick of the week’s culture, taken from the Guardian’s best-rated reviews
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Patrick Brammall and Maxine Peake star in a propulsive new drama, and the microtonal polka-dotted alien duo return to the live stage. Here’s the pick of the week’s culture, taken from the Guardian’s best-rated reviews
Content: Maxine Peake and Brendan Cowell in Last Seen.Photograph: Ben King/Apple TV.View image in fullscreenMaxine Peake and Brendan Cowell in Last Seen.Photograph: Ben King/Apple TV.The week in reviewsCultureLast Seen to Angine de Poitrine: the week in rave reviewsPatrick Brammall and Maxine Peake star in a propulsive new drama, and the microtonal polka-dotted alien duo return to the live stage. This is riveting television, and one of the standout shows of the year.”Luke BuckmasterRead the full reviewPick of the restColin from AccountsBBC iPlayer; available nowView image in fullscreenColin from Accounts.Photograph: BBC/CBS Studios/Easy Tiger Productions/Foxtel Management/Create NSW/Lisa TomasettiSummed up in a sentenceThe final season of the charming hit Aussie romcom picks up three years after Ashley rejected Gordon’s humiliating proposal.What our reviewer said“Colin from Accounts has been like a ray of sunshine in the schedules. I hope it turns out to be a happy one at least.”Rachel AroestiRead the full reviewBritain’s Forgotten GirlsBBC iPlayer; available nowSummed up in a sentenceAn infuriating look at how victims of grooming gangs in the UK have been repeatedly failed by authorities.What our reviewer said“The details are few and horrifying. Your mind can hardly take it in.”Lucy ManganRead the full reviewTommy Robinson: Where’s the Money Gone?Channel 4; available nowSummed up in a sentenceMatt Shea investigates a number of allegations about the co-founder of the English Defence League’s finances – and puts big questions to him.What our reviewer said“Has Shea landed an unanswerable haymaker? Not quite. Would any evidence of impropriety cause the flow of money from the faithful to dry up? Probably not. But this programme asks a lot of the right awkward questions.”Jack SealeRead the full reviewYou may have missed …RecklessITV1; available nowView image in fullscreenTasma Walton and Hunter Page-Lochard in Reckless.Photograph: ITVSummed up in a sentenceNeil Forsyth’s excellent Leith-set dark comedy drama Guilt relocates to Fremantle, Perth, where a brother and sister accidentally kill someone.What our reviewer said“Reckless is a fantastic, fun ride grounded by a realistically fractious, but at heart loving, relationship between the siblings, the light but piercing commentary on the wider racial and socioeconomic dynamics at work in Australia, and a cast of credible, however idiosyncratic, characters whose size makes the tonal consistency all the more wildly impressive.”Lucy ManganRead the full reviewFilmIf you only watch one, make it …Everybody Digs Bill EvansIn cinemas nowView image in fullscreenEverybody Digs Bill Evans.Photograph: Cowtown Pictures Limited Hot PropertySummed up in a sentenceGrant Gee’s film delves into the creative and personal torment of the great American jazz pianist – with a terrific supporting Bill Pullman turn as his cantankerous father.What our reviewer said“It’s a film about music; particularly, about what remains when a musician cannot play and is left to consider the terrible sacrifices made, without conscious consent, to this all-consuming vocation that creates family pain and jealousy almost as a toxic byproduct.”Peter BradshawRead the full reviewPick of the restOasis: Don’t Look Back in AngerIn cinemas nowView image in fullscreenOasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger.Photograph: Harriet TK Bols/PASummed up in a sentenceThe Gallagher brothers’ mammoth comeback concerts are given the full fan-worship treatment, but it’s impossible to begrudge the euphoria they have created.What our reviewer said“We see again the Oasis congregation engaging in colossal Dionysian events of mass joy – but of course, the poignancy of time passing and the irresistible narrative of the brothers’ public reconciliation give a new layer of emotion to the songs.”Peter BradshawRead the full reviewFurther reading‘Would they fight or hug?’ The Oasis comeback film’s makers on shooting fans, vicars, police – and the GallaghersBetter Go Mad in the WildIn cinemas nowSummed up in a sentenceDirector Miro Remo journeys deep into the Czech countryside to find two brothers living an isolated life filled with quixotic ideas in this surreal documentary.What our reviewer said“There is copious wisdom regarding family, nature, interdependency and love in this rowdy, rapturous and brilliant film.”Phil HoadRead the full reviewLa Femme InfideleIn cinemas nowSummed up in a sentenceClaude Chabrol’s eerie 1969 domestic thriller charts a complex marriage in which a husband suspects his wife is cheating on him.What our reviewer said“It does not in fact look like a classic noir thriller in the style of Chabrol’s hero Hitchcock, which is how it is often described, but more like something by Buñuel: an elaborate absurdist joke at the expense of the French bourgeoisie, a ballet of repression and fear.”Peter BradshawRead the full reviewNow streamingCall My Agent! events.What our reviewer said“Writers Fanny Herrero, Lison Daniel and Violaine Bellet, along with director Émilie Noblet, skilfully open the tap and let the stream of industry-insider jokes flow at an fast.”Read the full reviewThe Castle by Jon RonsonReviewed by Anthony CumminsSummed up in a sentenceThe journalist goes down the rabbit hole of modern masculinity.What our reviewer said“Ronson makes title: From Practical Magic 2 to Saturday Night Live UK: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead | Culture | The Guardian
description: Bullock and Kidman try to put a second spell on you in the fantasy comedy sequel, while the topical sketch show returns after a well-regarded debut
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Bullock and Kidman try to put a second spell on you in the fantasy comedy sequel, while the topical sketch show returns after a well-regarded debut
Content: Every witch way … Nicole Kidman as Gillian Owens in Practical Magic 2.Photograph: Jaap Buitendijk/© 2026 Warner Bros. Ent. All Rights ReservedView image in fullscreenEvery witch way … Nicole Kidman as Gillian Owens in Practical Magic 2.Photograph: Jaap Buitendijk/© 2026 Warner Bros. Ent. All Rights ReservedGoing out, staying inCultureFrom Practical Magic 2 to Saturday Night Live UK: your complete entertainment guide to the week aheadBullock and Kidman try to put a second spell on you in the fantasy comedy sequel, while the topical sketch show returns after a well-regarded debutSat 12 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleContents1Going out: Cinema2Going out: Gigs3Going out: Art4Going out: Stage5Staying in: Streaming6Staying in: Games7Staying in: Albums8Staying in: Brain foodView image in fullscreenGoing out:CinemaPractical Magic 2Out nowThe beloved fantasy romance from the 1990s returns with Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman reprising their roles as the Owens sisters. The story picks up 25 years later, with more family secrets and curses in the offing, plus a trip to the UK. Sure to be spellbinding stuff.Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore?Out 18 September for one night onlyCaptured during their 2025 tour, this music documentary blends footage from the live shows with archive material and new narration from Jarvis Cocker, to trace the band’s rise from outsider status in Sheffield to global fame, via megahits such as Common People and lesser-known fan favourites. Directed by Garth Jennings.PressureOut nowAndrew Scott heads up an all-star cast in a drama exploring the second world war from a slightly quirky angle: the weather forecast. Don’t laugh: it was a crucial piece of the puzzle in the 72 hours leading up to D-day, with Britain’s chief meteorological officer James Stagg unexpectedly finding himself the man of the moment.Everybody Digs Bill EvansOut nowA winner at the Berlin festival, Grant Gee’s biopic explores the aftermath of the death of bass player Scott LaFaro, and the impact the tragedy has on jazz pianist Bill Evans, who is torn between New York and suburbia as he attempts to navigate his profound grief. Starring Anders Danielsen Lie, Bill Pullman and Laurie Metcalf.Catherine BrayGoing out:GigsView image in fullscreenLast days of disco … Saint Etienne call it quits.Saint EtienneBirmingham,12 September; Manchester,15 September; Bristol,16 September; London,18 September; tour continues to 26 SeptemberThe beloved indie dance-pop trio head out on their final tour after more than 30 years. So expect songs such as the bangersome Glad from last year’s album International to rub shoulders with their 90s classics.Michael CraggCBSO/YamadaSymphony Hall, Birmingham,17 SeptemberThe dynamic Japanese conductor has embarked on one of classical music’s great endurance tests: a complete cycle of Gustav Mahler’s symphonies. Symphony No 2 promises to be a truly monumental season-opener – and also marks the CBSO Chorus’s 1,000th performance.Flora WillsonChris CheekLondon,15 September; Leeds,16 September; Aberdeen,17 September; Cambridge,18 SeptemberThe album Dear Paul by this versatile saxophonist was dedicated to Paul Motian, his old employer and one of jazz’s most creative percussionists. These gigs with fine Swiss drummer Florian Arbenz, a true Motian inheritor, will confirm just why.John FordhamWu LyfDublin,15 September; London,17 September; Brighton,18 SeptemberReleased in April, A Wave That Will Never Break marked the return of the enigmatic Manchester experimentalists after their 2012 split. It luxuriates in what they call “heavy pop” so remember your earplugs.MCGoing out:ArtView image in fullscreenIt’s grate … a work by Laura Porter from her exhibition Holding.Photograph: Courtesy of Laura PorterLaura PorterIrving Gallery, Oxford,to 10 OctoberThis north Devon-based artist is seriously into recycling, taking discarded old clothes, breaking them down and turning them into a mouldable, papier mache-style pulp and twisting them into wobbly geometric shapes.Liz LarnerCamdenArtCentre, London,to 17 JanuaryIt’s the debut UK institutional show by this influential American sculptor and ceramicist, filled with rocky, prehistoric-looking references to cosmic matter, ancient mythology and the grizzly politics of resource extraction.Gabriel OrozcoWhite Cube Bermondsey, London,16 Septemberto 8 NovemberMexico’s leading conceptualist returns to London for another show of minimal, ephemeral geometric installation work, this time dealing with the idea that objects can act as historical records.Celebrating Julia Carter Preston, CeramicistVarious venues, Liverpool,to 28 FebruaryLiverpool is rolling out the red carpet for home-town ceramics hero Julia Carter Preston (1926-2012) with five galleries across the city hosting displays of her work at the same time, including shows at the Bluecoat and Walker Art Gallery.Eddy FrankelGoing out:StageView image in fullscreenGeneration gain … Phil Wang.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianPhil WangStockton,12 September; Leeds,13 September; Tunbridge Wells,16 September; Northampton,17 September; Guildford,18 September; touring to 23 MayThanks to hit podcasts, presenting gigs and film cameos, a small cohort of millennial standups have finally ascended to the mainstream comedy firmament. Foremost among them is 36-year-old Wang, who returns to muse on ageing and his generation in new show Uh Oh.Rachel AroestiJasmin Vardimon: LullabyJV Home, Ashford,18& 19 September; touring to 13 FebruaryThe work that got choreographer Jasmin Vardimon noticed 23 years ago was a dance-theatre piece called Lullaby, set on a hospital ward. Two decades later, she’s revisiting and reinventing it for today’s world.Lyndsey WinshipGolden BoyAlmeida theatre, London, to 31 OctoberDirector Sam Yates has assembled a knockout cast for his revival of Clifford Odets’s classic American play. Josh O’Connor stars as a gifted violinist, drawn into the brutal world of professional boxing in depression-era New York.Miriam GillinsonTill The Stars Come DownNottingham Playhouse, to 26 SeptemberBeth Steel’s heartfelt and exquisitely observed comedy was an Olivier-nominated smash in the West End. It’s set in Mansfield, where a family gather for a wedding.MGskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStaying in:StreamingView image in fullscreenSure shot … Maria Sten in Neagley.Photograph: Amazon Prime VideoNeagleyPrime Video,16 SeptemberThe Alan Ritchson-led TV adaptation of Lee Child’s Jack Reacher novels has been a huge hit with critics and viewers, making a spin-off a no-brainer. This new series revolves around Maria Sten’s titular protege and private investigator.Saturday Night Live UKSky One & Now,12 September, 10pmA new prime minister means plenty of fresh material for the British iteration of the US sketch behemoth, but let’s hope the show doesn’t change too drastically: series one’s subtle edginess and stubborn idiosyncrasy was a recipe for surprising, naysayer-silencing success.ApocalypseChannel 4,13 September, 9pmChannel 4 be Channel 4-ing with its latest discomfiting social experiment. A group of civilians are left in an abandoned town to test how they cope with the kind of end-of-civilisation situation (no running water, no heating, no electricity) that could in reality be merely a couple of cyber-attacks away.Monster: The Lizzie Borden StoryNetflix,17 SeptemberRyan Murphy and Ian Brennan’s queasily contentious anthology series has previously dramatised the lives of some of America’s most notorious killers. This time round, however, the focus is on a more ambiguous figure in Borden, who was ultimately acquitted of the 1892 murders of her father and stepmother.RAStaying in:GamesView image in fullscreenSlash and burn … Wolverine.Illustration: Sony Interactive EntertainmentMarvel’s WolverinePS5;out15 SeptemberThe creators of the brilliant Marvel’s Spider-Man games take on an altogether more brutal hero in this pummelling slash-’em-up. Evil billionaire Bolivar Trask is kidnapping mutants and only you and your claws can stop him.Fire Emblem: Fortune’s WeaveNintendo Switch 2;out17 SeptemberIn the vast, fantastical Dagdan empire, warriors gather to fight in a tournament where the winner is granted one wish – but dark forces are gathering on the horizon and the fate of young contender Cai is in your hands. Expect an epic narrative adventure with fiendish tactical combat.Keith StuartStaying in:AlbumsView image in fullscreenA certain romance … Bloc Party.Photograph: Charlie PryorBloc Party – Anatomy of a Brief RomanceOut nowFollowing a further lineup reshuffle in 2023 – new bassist Harry Deacon makes his debut here – art-rockers Bloc Party return with their seventh album. Produced by Trevor Horn, songs such as Love Bombs and Coming on Strong are full of frontman Kele Okereke’s tightly wound energy.This Is Lorelei – The Singer in My BandOut nowAs one half of art-rock misfits Water from Your Eyes, Nate Amos, AKA This Is Lorelei, often deals in shape-shifting abstraction. On The Singer in My Band, however, he swaps that for twangy guitar riffs, crumpled Elliott Smith-esque singalongs and a surprising amount of sunshine.Standing on the Corner – IIOut nowFormed in Brooklyn more than a decade ago, Standing on the Corner, who have previously worked with Solange, are a multidisciplinary collective led by Gio Escobar. On the frazzled II they blend psychedelia, rock, no-wave rap, R&B and post-hardcore into a heavy sonic soup.Sylvan Esso – Ow ∞Out nowHaving built their own studio, the American electropop duo of Amelia Randall Meath and Nick Sanborn set about improvising, writing five to 10 songs a day. The result is this obscurely titled fifth album, which features the pogoing Hot Slob and the blown-out bop Sledge.MCStaying in:Brain foodView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Bob HolmesAcross the HorizonPodcastMusician Bob Holmes hosts this soothing series analysing the world of ambient country music. He and his guests, including guitarist Hayden Pedigo, discuss how Americana can conjure imaginative worlds.RobWordsYouTubeYouTuber and linguist RobWords produces fascinating video essays on the many quirks of the English language. Highlights include the hidden logic behind typographical symbols, the literal meanings of body parts and sarcastic punctuation.People Fixing the World: The Pictures That Help and HealBBC World Service,15 September, 8.06amJournalist Myra Anubi’s documentary on the creatives producing visual aids for disabled people is a hopeful insight into how technology can be harnessed for good. She hears from one app user who believes they saved his life.Ammar KaliaExplore more on these topicsCultureGoing out, staying inDanceTheatreTelevisionArtGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Guimarães and Saka fire Arsenal to win at Sunderland after Raya spot-kick save | Premier League | The Guardian
description: A stoppage-time penalty from Bukayo Saka sealed Arsenal’s 2-0 victory against Sunderland, who missed a spot-kick to take the lead in the second half
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: A stoppage-time penalty from Bukayo Saka sealed Arsenal’s 2-0 victory against Sunderland, who missed a spot-kick to take the lead in the second half
Content: Bruno Guimarães shows his delight after giving Arsenal the lead in the second half.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAView image in fullscreenBruno Guimarães shows his delight after giving Arsenal the lead in the second half.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAPremier LeagueGuimarães and Saka fire Arsenal to win at Sunderland after Raya spot-kick saveLouise Taylorat the Stadium of LightSat 12 Sep 2026 17.14 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 19.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the final whistle blew Bruno Guimarães wore a mischievous smile, Enzo Le Fée was a study in dejection and Arsenal’s immaculate start to the season remained unblemished.Sunderland 0-2 Arsenal: Guimarães and Saka sink Black Cats in Premier League – liveRead moreTwo minutes after David Raya had rather majestically saved Le Fée’s second-half penalty, Guimarães delighted his new north London public and plenty of old friends in Newcastle by sending a shot curving past Robin Roefs from the edge of the area.Mikel Arteta’s champions were en route to another win in a campaign that has now produced six victories in six games in all competitions, including the Community Shield. No one, though, should be deceived by the emphasis lent to the scoreline by Bukayo Saka’s stoppage-time penalty; this was most definitely the toughest test this term for Arsenal.IfSunderlandcan keep playing like this, Régis Le Bris and his players should have real cause for optimism – even if they could have done without Reinildo’s late sending-off for felling Saka when conceding that penalty and collecting a second yellow card.His penalty miss aside,chapeauxoff to Le Fee, who has deservedly made Zinedine Zidane’s provisional France squad for the forthcoming Nations League matches. Sunderland’s attacking playmaker knew another good performance here could only enhance his chances of moving from longlist to shortlist and he did not take long to draw a foul and win a dangerous free-kick.View image in fullscreenPlayers tussle in the Sunderland penalty area during a even first half.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersArsenal’s former captain Granit Xhaka delighted in curling the meanest of dead balls in Dan Ballard’s direction but the home central defender, a one-time Gunners youth captain, could not quite connect.There had been a similar reprieve for Le Bris’s rearguard when Saka failed to make the most of Declan Rice’s fine early delivery. Yet, bar a Gabriel Magalhães shot from distance that whizzed just wide of Roefs’s goal, a Kai Havertz shot on the turn saved smartly and a low 20-yard effort that Le Fée dragged fractionally wide of an upright, that was pretty much it in terms of first-half goalmouth action.Mikel Arteta’s side were taking their time to establish a settled passing rhythm. If Sunderland’s superb organisation hardly assisted the visiting cause, Arsenal looked a little fazed whenever the outstanding Nordi Mukiele – surely another candidate for the France squad – advanced from right-back.Ezri Konsa, meanwhile, did not appear to be either relishing or winning his extremely physical contest with Le Bris’s ever-combative centre-forward, Brian Brobbey. If a packed Stadium of Light enjoyed that little subplot, the roof was nearly lifted off by the roar of approval that greeted Reinildo’s full-blooded early challenge on Martin Ødegaard.View image in fullscreenMikel Arteta is booked by John Brooks for leaving his technical area.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersOne constant was Arteta’s excursions outside his technical area and eventually the referee, John Brooks, responded by jogging over to the touchline and waving a yellow card in the Arsenal manager’s face. While that booking was hardly unmerited, it seemed a shame that Brooks turned a blind eye to some persistent shirt-pulling from both sides at corners.With the match even at the interval, Arteta replaced Myles Lewis-Skelly and the hobbling Ben White with Guimarães and Jurriën Timber. The Brazilian’s past as Newcastle’s captain ensured Guimarães’s every touch was booed, while Sunderland started the new half strongly, with Brobbey continuing to bully Konsa.A penalty area encounter with Ballard at a throw proved no more welcome and when Konsa grappled the defender to the ground, Brooks – much to Arteta’s chagrin – had no hesitation in pointing to the spot.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenBruno Guimarães, who had been jeered by Sunderland fans for being a former Newcastle player, taunts them after scoring.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersLe Fée attempted to squeeze his kick just inside an upright but Raya, excellent throughout, guessed correctly and tipped the ball quite brilliantly on to the woodwork. Talk about a sliding-doors moment. Two minutes later and very much against the run of play, Arsenal broke from another Sunderland throw and Guimarães did the rest.Mikel Arteta says penalty given to Sunderland ‘unacceptable at this level’Read moreWith no option but to take risks, Le Bris switched to 4-4-2 and also introduced Malick Fofana, newly signed from Lyon, and he quickly created chaos in Arsenal’s box.Although it took Roefs, who saved superbly from Saka, and Ballard, responsible for a vital header off the line, to keep Le Bris’s side in the game, while Timber had a headed “goal” disallowed for offside, Arteta had reason to look slightly nervous as Mukiele volleyed Le Fée’s corner over the bar.By now Xhaka, booked for sliding into Guimarães, was enjoying himself in midfield and from one of his corners Mukiele again went close.A comeback beckoned but Saka had different ideas as Arsenal issued a reminder that they will not surrender their title lightly.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueSunderlandArsenalmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Flying Kurt-Lee Arendse helps South Africa clinch New Zealand series  | Rugby union | The Guardian
description: Kurt-Lee Arendse scored the key fifth of six tries as South Africa beat New Zealand 47-28 in Baltimore to win the Greatest Rivalry series 3-1
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Kurt-Lee Arendse scored the key fifth of six tries as South Africa beat New Zealand 47-28 in Baltimore to win the Greatest Rivalry series 3-1
Content: South Africa's Kurt-Lee Arendse scores the key fifth try against the All Blacks in Baltimore.Photograph: Stephanie Scarbrough/APView image in fullscreenSouth Africa's Kurt-Lee Arendse scores the key fifth try against the All Blacks in Baltimore.Photograph: Stephanie Scarbrough/APRugby unionFlying Kurt-Lee Arendse helps South Africa clinch New Zealand series4th Test: South Africa 43-28 New ZealandDe Allende scores early in each half in BaltimoreAgence France-PresseSat 12 Sep 2026 19.32 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 19.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSouth Africa thrashed New Zealand 43-28 to complete a 3-1 victory in Baltimore in the fourth and final match of the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry Test series. The Springboks, who led the series 2-1 after the opening three Tests in South Africa, produced a devastating second-half display at the M+T Bank Stadium to seal victory.Tries from Damian de Allende, Morne van den Berg, Malcolm Marx, Pieter-Steph du Toit, Kurt-Lee Arendse and Cameron Hanekom clinched a deserved win for the Springboks in front of a capacity 71,000 crowd.South Africa v New Zealand: fourth and final rugby union Test – liveRead moreNew Zealand’s tries came from the recalled captain, Codie Taylor, plus Will Jordan, Ethan Blackadder and Beauden Barrett, but the All Blacks were always chasing the South Africans in a fast-paced game.There was controversy in the first half when play was held up for more than eight minutes after a failure in communication equipment between the match officials. But that interruption had no impact on the outcome as South Africa’s total dominance at the breakdown, setpiece and aerial battle proved decisive.New Zealand threatened a comeback, getting to within eight points at 29-21, but Arendse gathered a loose ball and ran from deep in his own half, side-stepped a couple of defenders and scampered away.View image in fullscreenSouth Africa players celebrate their victory.Photograph: Stephanie Scarbrough/APThe Springbok captain, Siya Kolisi, paid tribute to South Africa’s coach, Rassie Erasmus, after the victory. “He knows how to get us up, and when he speaks to us he reminds us where we come from, the country that we come from,” Kolisi said.“The players who are in the group who are not playing. We do it for them. The guys that are injured, the guys that couldn’t make the tour, and also for the people of South Africa.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNew Zealand’s Taylor, meanwhile, had few complaints with the defeat. “We talk a lot about moments throughout the week when we review our Test matches and South Africa just stacked a few more moments against us over the last couple of games,” the veteran hooker said. “Full credit to them – they’re a great side and they’ve proven why they’re world champions.”Taylor, though, said New Zealand would take positives from the series defeat as they build towards the 2027 Rugby World Cup. “It’s a good stepping stone,” he said. “We’re at an interesting place at the moment as a rugby nation. We’ve fallen short in this series but I can assure you and everyone back home that we’re working hard.”Explore more on these topicsRugby unionSouth Africa rugby teamNew Zealand rugby union teammatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Tottenham waiting for first league goal of season after draw against Everton | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Everton missed big chances in the second half of the 0-0 draw against Spurs, who are now without a win in four Premier League games
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Everton missed big chances in the second half of the 0-0 draw against Spurs, who are now without a win in four Premier League games
Content: Mateus Fernandes holds off the challenge of the Everton defender Vitalii Mykolenko.Photograph: David Cliff/EPAView image in fullscreenMateus Fernandes holds off the challenge of the Everton defender Vitalii Mykolenko.Photograph: David Cliff/EPAPremier LeagueTottenham waiting for first league goal of season after draw against EvertonDavid Hytnerat Tottenham Hotspur StadiumSat 12 Sep 2026 14.47 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 16.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs it too early for a Tottenham crisis? To which the answer is surely that it is never too early for a Tottenham crisis. After fourPremier Leaguegames, they have yet to score. This kind of run has never happened in their history at the beginning of a league season.At least they mustered a couple of shots on target this time, having failed to do so last weekend in the0-0 draw at Nottingham Forest. The first – from Mateus Fernandes – at the start of the second half was greeted by ironic cheers from the South Stand. It has certainly not been what the club expected when they spent £300m on overhauling the squad in the summer.De Zerbi says Spurs have ‘mental block’ after wait for league win continuesRead moreSpurs were anxious, they lacked certainties – apart from the one about how they were never going to score. They were fortunate thatEverton, who remain defiantly unbeaten, did not do so at the other end. David Moyes’s team had big chances in the second half through Thierno Barry, Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall and the former Spurs winger, Brennan Johnson. Everton defended superbly, albeit they were helped by Tottenham’s bluntness, and were full value for the draw. They probably deserved to win.Spurs have won only one league game at home this year – in do-or-die circumstances against Everton on the final day of last season. Going back to November 2024, their record in the competition here reads: P35 W5 D10 L20. As Everton savoured the result with their fans at full time, the Spurs crowd turned to a familiar soundtrack: a burst of booing.It was difficult not to remember the game here last season whenSpurs won 1-0 to stay up. Defeat and they would have been relegated. It was an extraordinarily nervy occasion for them, all the way to the last knockings of stoppage time. The pessimistic edge about the home support has not gone away. Far from it. You could hear it before kick-off. ‘Good luck? Yeah, we’ll need it.’ That sort of thing. A major part of the mission was to try to tear down the psychological barriers. They failed.There was hope, too. It always bubbles somewhere in the background. And Spurs did start well, pressing on to the front foot, moving the ball quickly. Rodrigo Bentancur imposed himself. Savio was a ball of pace and tricks. There was a statistic beforehand that rated Tottenham as the worst team in the league for the quality of chances created. What could they do with their possession against an Everton defence that knows how to stifle? It was the question that pounded.Everton travelled with confidence after good results in their opening fixtures. Their squad is alarmingly thin. But they have enough at this point of the season and the fallout from that disastrous transfer deadline day appears to have bonded the squad. Everton were the second worst team on the chance quality index but they were always likely to be measured by how well they defended.View image in fullscreenJordan Pickford makes a save from Lucas Bergvall.Photograph: David Cliff/EPASpurs pushed for the first half of the first period, albeit the pickings in front of goal were slim. Jan Paul van Hecke banged a half volley high from a tight angle at the far post after an Andy Robertson free-kick and that would go down as their only chance of the opening 45 minutes. There was a stumble from Fernandes inside the area after a nice ball up through the lines from Van Hecke which summed things up for them. The anxiety transmitted itself to the crowd and bounced back.James Garner worked Antonin Kinsky with a free-kick at the end of the first half, which went down as the first shot on target. When Fernandes mustered his from distance in the 47th minute, it was met with that sarcasm.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEverton were more proactive after the restart. They fed off the Spurs nerves. They threatened to get in behind. Tyrique George did beat Archie Gray, who stood in for the injured Pedro Porro at right-back; Roberto De Zerbi was also without Destiny Udogie through injury at left-back. George’s cross picked out Barry at the far post and his header hit Kinsky before flying off target. The goalkeeper knew little about it. George also had a blast that hit Bentancur.Tottenham came to be undermined by terrible errors on the ball. There were so many passes that were woefully off target, including one from Kinsky that he sent straight to Dewsbury-Hall on the edge of his area. Kinsky made amends with a smart block. Dewsbury-Hall cursed the passing up of a golden opportunity.Everton were the likelier team to score. Spurs battled the internal demons. There were cross words between some of their players, Omar Marmoush overtaken by frustration at one point. Johnson blew his chance on 75 minutes, lifting high after a Dewsbury-Hall tee-up.Spurs had one flicker at the very end after Jordan Pickford sent a poor clearance straight to James Maddison, who had come on as a substitute. Spurs moved it to another replacement, Lucas Bergvall, and his low drive worked Pickford. It was a comfortable save. Everton were exactly that.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueTottenham HotspurEvertonmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Keely Hodgkinson has to settle for silver as Audrey Werro takes Ultimate gold | Athletics | The Guardian
description: Audrey Werro won the 800m and the $150,000 prize, 0.38 ahead of Keely Hodgkinson, at the Ultimate Championships in Budapest
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Audrey Werro won the 800m and the $150,000 prize, 0.38 ahead of Keely Hodgkinson, at the Ultimate Championships in Budapest
Content: Keely Hodgkinson (left) overtakes Femke Broeders-Bol (centre) but Audrey Werro (right) takes gold in the women's 800m at the Ultimate Championships.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenKeely Hodgkinson (left) overtakes Femke Broeders-Bol (centre) but Audrey Werro (right) takes gold in the women's 800m at the Ultimate Championships.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAAthleticsKeely Hodgkinson has to settle for silver as Audrey Werro takes Ultimate goldSwiss wins $150,000 with dominant display in 800mGeorgia Hunter Bell second to Kazimierska in 1500mSean Inglein BudapestSat 12 Sep 2026 16.50 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 19.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis season has witnessed an extraordinary arms race between three of the greatest female 800m runners in history. But, as so often over the summer months, it concluded with the sight of Audrey Werro going nuclear.There were some in the press seats who wondered whether the brilliant 22-year-old Swiss might be tired and vulnerable, whether Britain’s Olympic champion,Keely Hodgkinson, or the fast-rising Dutch star Femke Broeders-Bol could take advantage. But at these Ultimate Championships in Budapest, Werro proved again she was 2026’s ultimate performer as she took the $150,000 first prize with another dominant display.Brave new world: Ultimate Championship brings glowing javelins and $10m prize fund to track and fieldRead moreWerro’s formula is simple but devastatingly effective. Run the first 200m in a shade over 27sec to take the lead, control the race like a puppet master, and then apply the squeeze in the last 300m. As things stand, no one has an answer.She applied it perfectly here, to win in 1min 55.88sec, with Hodgkinson second in 1:56.26 and Broeders-Bol a further half a second back in third.Werro’s statistics during the outdoor season are extraordinary. Sincelosing to Hodgkinson at the world indoor championships, Werro has won all 14 events she has entered, run four of the 10 fastest times in history, and tookgold at the European championships. Indeed, the only time she has failed to cross the line first was when she was tripped up in the semi-finals in Birmingham.After this latest win she described her season as “really crazy” and suggested she would use her first prize to improve her training. God help her rivals if that is truly the case.The scary thing for Hodgkinson and Broeders-Bol? Werro is 22, and only started full-time training this year after finishing her studies. Jarmila Kratochvilova’s 43-year-old world record is already within striking distance. Would anyone be surprised if she found the 0.43 needed to topple it in 2027?However, it would be foolish to write off Hodgkinson, who confirmed that she had torn a hamstring during the European championships, which meant she was unable to do the speed work needed to compete with Werro.“I think, on the outside, people might think I’d be disappointed with that, but I’m actually quite proud of how I approached that,” said Hodgkinson. “I didn’t even know I was going to be here. It was very much touch and go. I was really going at it with rehab.“It’s been a bit of a frustrating season, but I think overall I’ve finished second in the world, and I can’t really be too hard on myself with that,” she added. “And congrats to Audrey, as well. Incredible season, absolutely incredible, dominant. Yeah, I look forward to racing her again next season.”That comment was a measure of Hodgkinson’s class after a frustrating year, which started with a world indoor 800m record and a world indoor title. But she has not been able to show the same form after badly scarring her knees in a fall in Eugene in July, and then tearing her hamstring last month.“I felt good,” said Hodgkinson. “I think with the injury I had to prepare a bit like Tokyo last year. I had to just take my foot off speed and focus more on strength.”Earlier in the evening Hodgkinson’s training partner Georgia Hunter Bell also finished second behind Klaudia Kazimierska after a thrilling 1500m.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen Kazimierska kicked for home with 200m remaining, Hunter Bell was the only athlete to immediately respond. It led to a thrilling duel along the final straight, with the Pole having just enough to win in 3:57.55, with Hunter Bell 0.15sec back in second.It left Hunter Bell $75,000 richer and she was delighted with her performance, after what she felt was a flat display in the Diamond League final last weekend. “I thought it was a great race,” she said. “I’m really happy with that. I felt really comfortable the whole race. I chose to go on the rail because last week I ran 15 extra meters by running wide, and that really took the sting out of my kick at the end.”View image in fullscreenGeorgia Hunter Bell, (left) congratulatesKlaudia Kazimierska, after winning the women’s 1500m final.Photograph: Dénes Erdős/APWhen it comes to the cash, Hunter Bell has certainly earned it this year, having won gold at the world indoors, Commonwealth Games and European championships. “I mean, the money is interesting,” she said. “I’m not really thinking about that in the home straight. I’m just thinking about trying to get to the line first.“But I’ve run 20 races this year. I’ve shown up to absolutely everything that I can, and done myself proud. I had 14 wins, three out of four majors won, one runner-up. I’m not going to sniff at 75k.”One of the performances of the night came in the women’s 100m as the world champion, Melissa Jefferson-Wooden, ran a scorching 10.62sec to take victory. It was the fastest time in the world this year, too quick for the Olympic 100m gold medallist, Julien Alfred, who was second in 10.74, with another US star, Sha’Carri Richardson, third in 10.76. Britain’s Amy Hunt was last in 11.09.Explore more on these topicsAthleticsKeely HodgkinsonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Joe Root makes most of no-ball luck as England win despite Pakistan scare | England v Pakistan 2026 | The Guardian
description: England fell to two for two but beat Pakistan by eight wickets for a series whitewash, with Joe Root unbeaten on 62 after he chopped on a no-ball on 23
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: England fell to two for two but beat Pakistan by eight wickets for a series whitewash, with Joe Root unbeaten on 62 after he chopped on a no-ball on 23
Content: Joe Root hits a four off Pakistan's Mohammad Imran.Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenJoe Root hits a four off Pakistan's Mohammad Imran.Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/ReutersEngland v Pakistan 2026Joe Root makes most of no-ball luck as England win despite Pakistan scareEngland lose two wickets in first over but take series 3-0Root, reprieved on 23, finishes with unbeaten 62Ali Martinat EdgbastonSat 12 Sep 2026 08.28 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 16.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a run chase that began in alarming fashion for England as Mohammad Abbas hitched up his strides, glided in to the crease and sent Ben Duckett and Emilio Gay trudging back to the pavilion at either end of a magical first over.Pakistan’s players suddenly believed, their supporters inside Edgbaston likewise. After Razaullah’s firework display with the bat the previous evening, it was hard not to wonder whether their penchant for the unexpected – that seemingly innate ability to flip the script from nowhere – was rearing its head once more.England beat Pakistan after early scare: third men’s cricket Test, day four – liveRead moreBut, albeit with a couple more heart-in-mouth moments, England had enough about them to reel in their target of 130 to complete an eight-wicket victory and their first series clean sweep for two years.Joe Root, 62 not out, and Jordan Cox unbeaten on 59, finished things off by 1.07pm.“We had a little bit of pushback yesterday, which was, in a strange way, quite a good thing for the group,” said Root, in a nod to Razaullah’s incendiary 81. “But for us to come through it and be so convincing in the way that we’ve finished the series off, and throughout the whole three games really, has been really pleasing.”View image in fullscreenPakistan’s Mohammad Abbas appeals successfully for lbw to dismiss England’s Emilio Gay.Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/ReutersRoot had walked out at the end of the first over with the scorecard in disarray at two for two. Abbas had nicked off Duckett first ball to continue a rather sorry Test match for England’s opener, and then pinned Gay lbw for a duck that dented some of the credit built up by the left-hander’s 60 in the first innings.Alongside Cox, whose start to Test cricket has been an assured one, Root immediately got down to business, batting on leg stump in an attempt to minimise the threat of lbw, and the scorecard soon started to tick over. On a pitch with no demons by this stage, all it needed was a couple of calm heads.Razaullah was unable to roll over his personal momentum after being handed the new ball – an early hand injury did not help – while no frontline spinner meant Abbas, bowling with the wicketkeeper stood up, was the only way that Babar Azam could make things claustrophobic out in the middle. There were two more chances created along the way and neither came to fruition.The first came when Root was on 20 and an expansive cover-drive cannoned into his leg-stump. Mohammad Ali was haring off in celebration, only to turn around and see the umpire’s arm outstretched for a front foot no-ball, his 17th such offence in this series, but the first to rob him of a wicket.View image in fullscreenJoe Root’s stump goes flying but he would be saved.Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/ReutersEngland would have been 36 for three and Root’s response was emphatic, drilling Ali through the covers for four. Abbas then saw an edge off Root’s bat fly between first and second slip on 34 without either man going for it – much to his disgust.The pressure eased, as this thinned-out, day-four crowd essentially watched a 90-minute net, a couple of tidy half-centuries, and the winning runs coming off a mis-field. Root has resumed the England captaincy with a pretty comfortable 3-0 series victory while knowing that tougher challenges are to come.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEngland in better shape after ‘coming through chaos’ of a torrid summer, says Joe RootRead moreFor Pakistan it was a chance to finally breathe after a helter-skelter tour that sawseven players sent home at 2-0 down, a head coach removed, and a cast of new faces for this third Test. For Razaullah, just 21, it may be the start of something special, even if it was not enough to secure the player of the match award.That instead went to Dan Lawrence, who made 65 with the bat, picked up a couple of wickets with his slightly eccentric off-spin, and two catches that included a one-handed blinder to remove Shan Masood, Pakistan’s top-scorer in their resurgent second innings. Lawrence made three half-centuries in the series and has seven in his career to date. The key now is to bank that first hundred.View image in fullscreenMohammad Ali reacts to bowling Joe Root before the delivery is ruled a no-ball.Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/Reuters“If I keep playing the way that I am, I’m sure that three figures will come,” said Lawrence, whose frustration at getting out on day two was palpable. “I’m desperate to get multiple hundreds for England. Contributing in all three games has really helped my confidence. Hopefully I get the nod to carry on playing.”With 21 wickets at just shy of nine runs apiece, Ollie Robinson was England’s player of the series. For Pakistan it was Abbas, another master of the wobble seam. The 36-year-old probed to the very end, an island of calm in what at times has been a maelstrom of a tour for the visitors.Explore more on these topicsEngland v Pakistan 2026England cricket teamPakistan cricket teamCricketJoe Rootmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Solheim Cup: Hull and Woad flop for Europe as Kupcho pulls USA level | Solheim Cup | The Guardian
description: USA win three fourballs matches to make score 8-8 against Europe and leave the Solheim Cup finely poised heading into the final day
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: USA win three fourballs matches to make score 8-8 against Europe and leave the Solheim Cup finely poised heading into the final day
Content: Charley Hull (left) has struggled for Europe, who are level at 8-8 with USA in the Solheim Cup.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APView image in fullscreenCharley Hull (left) has struggled for Europe, who are level at 8-8 with USA in the Solheim Cup.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APSolheim CupSolheim Cup: Hull and Woad flop for Europe as Kupcho pulls USA levelScores level at 8-8 after dramatic day twoAnna Nordqvist pairing of star duo fails to pay offEwan Murrayat Bernardus GolfSat 12 Sep 2026 14.25 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 17.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has been the great anomaly of this Solheim Cup. Europe keeping perfect pace with the United States is an impressive achievement even without factoring in the meagre points contribution from Charley Hull and Lottie Woad. European hopes of reclaiming thetrophy lost to the United States two years agosurely depend heavily on their star turns finding singles form.The heroics of Jennifer Kupcho in fading light dashed Europe’s ambitions of taking a lead. It is 8-8 as things stand. A 12-match shootout remains.Solheim Cup golf 2026: Europe take charge against USA after day two foursomes – liveRead moreAnna Nordqvist’s deployment of Hull and Woad as a pairing on Saturday morning has to be considered odd. The duo had claimed half a point from two previous outings. Hull does not look particularly suited to foursomes. Woad is aSolheim Cupdebutant. Nordqvist, it appeared, focused heavily on the status of both players inside the world’s top 10. The tactic backfired; Alison Lee and Lauren Coughlin thumped the English pair, 6&5. Undeterred, Nordqvist sent Hull and Woad back out. This time it was Yealimi Noh and Andrea Lee who emerged victorious.“I don’t think people understand these are the best players in the world,” said Nordqvist when asked whether Saturday afternoon selection was wise. “I think they played [against] the strongest pairings in each session. Lottie herself made six birdies yesterday in the afternoon. So they’re playing solid and I wouldn’t be surprised if we get a little bit of blue on that board this afternoon.”View image in fullscreenA 90-foot birdie from Jennifer Kupcho (left) at the 17th hole pulled her and Lindy Duncan (right) level.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APThe Swede’s hopes proved in vain. Troubles on the greens undermined the performance of Hull and Woad as the Americans prevailed on the final green. The Europeans gave the regular impression they would rather be elsewhere. A high point came on the 17th, where Woad’s brave putt from 15ft kept the match alive. At the final tee, Hull pulled a fairway wood into water.Nordqvist’s decision-making created history, with Hull and Woad the first to play four sessions together in the same Solheim Cup. Nordqvist’s faith has failed to find reward. In fairness, in Noh the Europeans in question faced the player of this event. She has been exceptional.Hull and Woad said they knew they would play every session, which raises questions over how nimble their captain is. “It was pretty frustrating,” said Hull of the fourball loss. Woad added: “It doesn’t matter who wins the points. I would happily lose my matches if we win.”This is indeed a team business. After back-to-back tied sessions, Europe forged ahead on Saturday morning. The superb Maja Stark and Linn Grant saw off Allisen Corpuz and the world No 1, Nelly Korda. Angela Stanford, the US captain, stood down Korda after lunch.View image in fullscreenThe world No 1 Nelly Korda did not compete in the afternoon fourballs.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APLeona Maguire and Esther Henseleit enjoyed a successful reunion as they defeated the US pair of Kupcho and Rose Zhang. The European rookies Mimi Rhodes and Nastasia Nadaud were again outstanding as they claimed a point from Auston Kim and Andrea Lee. Alison Lee and Coughlin returned the sole US reward of the foursomes.Coughlin will be the only US player to feature in all five sessions. Stanford explained that was not determined before the event. Coughlin and Megan Khang tasted fourball defeat to Stark and Grant. “Maja played out of her mind,” Coughlin said.Noh and Andrea Lee confirmed victory over Hull and Woad on the last green. Kim and Zhang were 3&2 winners over Maguire and Nadaud. In seeking to tie the fourball session, Europe needed Carlota Ciganda and Céline Boutier to hold off Kupcho and Lindy Duncan.Europe were two up after 14. A three from Duncan on the 15th narrowed the deficit, but the Europeans looked like they would do enough to cling on. Enter Kupcho, who converted in extraordinary circumstances from 90ft and off the green at the 17th. She followed it up with a birdie from 30ft at the last. From moments like these, Solheim Cups are won. No wonder Ciganda and Boutier looked distraught.A background cause for concern for the US arrived from Angel Yin. The 27-year-old had been a serious doubt to feature due to illness that significantly disrupted her season. That Yin did not play on Saturday was no great shock, but the sight of her pounding balls for a lengthy time on the driving range as competitive action unfolded elsewhere implied she is struggling for form.Yin and the US need six points from the 12 remaining to hold on to the trophy. Six and a half is the European requirement. Momentum is suddenly with the visitors.Explore more on these topicsSolheim CupUS sportsGolfnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ben Shelton faces date with destiny against Zverev in US Open final | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: World No 4 will become the first Black American man to win the singles title at Flushing Meadow since Arthur Ashe if he can beat Zverez for the first time
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: World No 4 will become the first Black American man to win the singles title at Flushing Meadow since Arthur Ashe if he can beat Zverez for the first time
Content: Ben Shelton has defeated Carlos Alcaraz and Frances Tiafoe on the way to the US Open final.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAView image in fullscreenBen Shelton has defeated Carlos Alcaraz and Frances Tiafoe on the way to the US Open final.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAUS Open Tennis 2026Ben Shelton faces date with destiny against Zverev in US Open finalWorld No 4 will become the first Black American man to win the singles title at Flushing Meadow since Arthur Ashe if he can beat German for the first timeTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowSat 12 Sep 2026 15.32 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs Ben Shelton lapped up the explosion of joy and adoration from a full Arthur Ashe Stadium after reaching a grand slam final for the first time, one of his first thoughts was of his paternal grandmother, Regina, who died this year. Shelton credited his grandmother with ensuring that his father, Bryan, made it as a top professional, becoming one of a small group of Black men on the tour. “My dad lost his mom earlier this year and she’s the reason he was able to play tennis,” he said. “Without her, there’s no Ben Shelton standing here today. So this one is for her.”Shelton stands on the verge of history. On Sunday, he will attempt to become the first Black American man to win the US Open singles title since Arthur Ashe in 1968, a feat he will attempt inside the stadium named after Ashe. Shelton would also be the first Black man to win any grand slam singles title since Yannick Noah at Roland Garros in 1983, and the third overall. He is also aiming to become the first American man to win a major singles title since Andy Roddick won the US Open in 2003.Five-set tennis is under attack. Killing it would be a colossal unforced error | Andrew LawrenceRead moreThe final step, however, will be the most difficult. Tennis is a game of match-ups and Shelton has had an especially difficult time against Alexander Zverev,the Roland Garros championand the top seed in the absence of Jannik Sinner. After winning the first set they played, at Cincinnati in 2024, Shelton has lost 10 sets in a row to Zverev, compiling a 0-5 record against the German on hard courts, grass and clay.Zverev is well suited for left-handed opponents due to the strength of his two-handed backhand, which allows him to counter the effects of their swinging serve out wide from the left advantage side as well as their crosscourt forehand from the same position.There are plenty of reasons, however, for Shelton to be hopeful that things will be different in New York. He will remind himself of the fact that they have never faced each other in a grand slam tournament, where the American so often elevates his game, and particularly that the theme of this tournament has been breaking new ground in difficult match-ups.“Problem-solving has been the name of the game here,” he said. “I was 0-1 against Stef [Stefanos Tsitsipas], 0-3 against Carlos [Alcaraz], Foe [Frances Tiafoe] beat me the last time we played on this court. It’s been a lot of uphill battle, so I think I’m fully ready for the challenge to problem-solve.”His father and coach, Bryan, stressed how well his son, who is 7-2 in finals, competes with a title on the line: “He’s got an amazing record on Sundays. Don’t want to jinx him here, but if you look at his record throughout his career, he’s played well on Sundays.View image in fullscreenBen Shelton has failed to beat Alexander Zverev in their previous five meetings.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPA“So that’s where he wants to be. He feels like he’s going to play his best tennis at the end of the week, or end of the two weeks. So glad he has a chance at the US Open.”One of the most striking aspects of Shelton’s emergence has been his relentless improvement. His path took him through the college route where he started as an unremarkable prospect. When he first emerged on the ATP Tour, the strengths he showed with his enormous serve, athleticism and the variation he could play with were counterbalanced by glaring weaknesses in his backhand, return and consistency from the baseline. They were all still present on his explosive first full season on the tour in 2023, which he began with a run to the quarter-finals of the Australian Open on his first trip outside the United States. He reached the semi-finals of the US Open that year, yet despite progressing only one round further this year, Shelton is a different player now.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe has made such drastic improvements to his backhand, return of serve and consistency, which is what has allowed him to perform at such a high level during this tournament.Against Alcaraz, he returned well and was the far more stable player from the baseline. In hiswin over Tiafoe, he saved one of the best backhand days of his career for one of the biggest matches.“I still feel so many categories that I think I have a long way to go, but I’ve made improvements and changes in some of the most important categories to be able to compete at the top,” he said. “Return of serve, stability from the baseline, even my serve, the way that I go about putting together my service games has improved, and my ability to focus for long periods of time are all areas that have come together and have helped me play at the level I’m playing. But the pursuit and hunger to get better, to find ways that I can improve, it’s just a part of who I am and something that will never change.”Late on Friday night, as Shelton left the court and only just began to digest his achievement, a smile spread widely across his father’s face. “To do it here at the US Open and be playing on the final day, this kid, it’s kind of surreal,” he said. “I didn’t think he was going to even get into this sport and then to be where he’s at right now, I mean, it’s just hard to believe, hard to believe and just super, super grateful.”Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisTennisAlexander ZverevUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Frustrated Liverpool lack any spark as Fulham claim deserved first point | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Liverpool struggled to create any chances as they were held to a 0-0 Premier League draw with Fulham at Anfield
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Liverpool struggled to create any chances as they were held to a 0-0 Premier League draw with Fulham at Anfield
Content: Bernd Leno makes a save to keep Fulham’s clean sheet intact at Anfield.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenBernd Leno makes a save to keep Fulham’s clean sheet intact at Anfield.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAPremier LeagueFrustrated Liverpool lack any spark as Fulham claim deserved first pointAndy Hunterat AnfieldSat 12 Sep 2026 12.06 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 16.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleÁlvaro Arbeloa was often the obstacle to Andoni Iraola’s international ambitions back in the days when both were vying for a right-back role with Spain. On his return to Anfield, and under the watchful eye of former manager Rafael Benítez, Arbeloa thwarted Iraola once again to claim his firstPremier Leaguepoint as Fulham head coach against an ineffective Liverpool.Fulham belied their lowly position and run of three league defeats to take a merited point from a Liverpool team that was a pale imitation of the one thatbeat Atlético Madridin the Champions League on Wednesday. Iraola fielded a front four that cost almost £400m but the most impressive forward on display was the Fulham academy graduate Josh King. The draw was Liverpool’s third in four league games under their new head coach and the seventh in 12 Premier League matches at Anfield in 2026.
