Progress can be painfully slow at times.Hull stun Chelsea with Mohamed Belloumi double before João Pedro rescues a pointRead more“It is the first game we’ve had problems creating chances and making the difference offensively,” Iraola said. “It is easy for me to say the players were tired (after Atlético). There was a lack of freshness and, we cannot hide it, it was the worst turnaround in terms of 60-70 hours. But this is going to happen in the season and we have to adapt. Sometimes you need a set play or a moment of brilliance to win these kind of games but we were not as good offensively as other games.”Liverpool were sluggish and sloppy – Florian Wirtz and Kostas Tsimikas put simple passes straight out of play in the first half, setting the tone for a disjointed performance – while Fulham bypassed the central midfield pairing of Dominik Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch repeatedly. The visitors’ confidence and composure on the ball, along with their defensive organisation, was hugely impressive considering the start to the season under the former Real Madrid interim coach andLiverpooldefender. With more conviction in front of goal, Arbeloa’s side could have capitalised on Liverpool’s malaise.Bradley Barcola created an early, difficult chance for Alexander Isak that the striker swept wide of the far post. Victor Muñoz went closer still with a glancing header from a Szoboszlai corner. Bernd Leno, theFulhamgoalkeeper, reacted superbly to claw the ball away. But that was the sum total of Liverpool’s first-half enterprise.Fulham were gifted a glorious opportunity when Alisson played a ridiculous pass to Gravenberch, who was under pressure from Sander Berge. Berge’s challenge fell to King, who was sent flying by the Liverpool goalkeeper but the referee, Thomas Bramall, played a good advantage as Gonzalo García received the loose ball. García had time to pick his spot but Jérémy Jacquet blocked his shot in front of the goalline.View image in fullscreenJérémy Jacquet clears the ball off the line to deny Fulham the lead.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAThe visitors prospered down their left and Oscar Bobb missed another good opening when, unmarked and 18 yards out, he miscontrolled Alex Iwobi’s pinpoint delivery. Jacquet came to Liverpool’s rescue once again seconds later when preventing García breaking through with an excellent challenge.Liverpool were deserving of a few home truths during the break – chiefly, you would have been lambasted for this last season under Arne Slot – and performed with more intensity in the second half. But not with any more threat. The introductions of Cody Gakpo, Alexis Mac Allister and Milos Kerkez brought modest improvement but Fulham continued to contain the hosts comfortably. The new signing David Affengruber had a fine debut and Calvin Bassey was commanding against Isak.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe visitors remained dangerous on the counterattack and Alisson pushed away a King effort that was heading for the top corner. King’s replacement, Rodrigo Muniz, let a decent chance run away from him inside the area and the substitute Kevin dragged a shot wide from 18 yards. Isak finally escaped Bassey’s attentions in stoppage time but his flicked header from a Szoboszlai corner sailed wide.Arbeloa said: “When you are not winning games it’s not so easy for your players to believe in your ideas. But they believe in the way we have been working and I showed them the things that we were doing so well. We were more balanced and controlled the transitions well. I’m happy with the point but more with the performance of my players and the character, the personality and the ambition they showed in this stadium.”Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueLiverpoolFulhammatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: European football: Dortmund win again but Freiburg top after Gladbach rout | European club football | The Guardian
description: Borussia Dortmund beat Paderborn 3-0 but Freiburg topped the Bundesliga on goal difference after thumping Borussia Mönchengladbach 5-0
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Borussia Dortmund beat Paderborn 3-0 but Freiburg topped the Bundesliga on goal difference after thumping Borussia Mönchengladbach 5-0
Content: The ball hits the back of the net for Felix Nmecha’s second goal as Borussia Dortmund beat Paderborn 3-0.Photograph: Christopher Neundorf/EPAView image in fullscreenThe ball hits the back of the net for Felix Nmecha’s second goal as Borussia Dortmund beat Paderborn 3-0.Photograph: Christopher Neundorf/EPAEuropean club footballEuropean football: Dortmund win again but Freiburg top after Gladbach routMilan come from behind in 2-2 draw with LazioKylian Mbappé strikes twice as Real Madrid cruiseAgence France-PresseSat 12 Sep 2026 17.17 EDTFirst published on Sat 12 Sep 2026 13.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFelix Nmecha scored twice and Fábio Silva grabbed another asBorussia Dortmundwon 3-0 at home to promotedPaderbornto continue their perfect start in the Bundesliga. Dortmund’s win made it three from three in the league this campaign, their best start in 11 seasons, dating back to Thomas Tuchel’s time.Starting up front alongside Serhou Guirassy for the first time this season, Silva converted a clever pass from the Guinean to give the hosts the lead after five minutes. Guirassy had two goals disallowed for offside in the first half but Dortmund were rarely troubled by the toothless visitors, who are yet to score since returning to the top flight.Nmecha came off the bench to score twice, wrapping up victory for the hosts with a stunning late bicycle kick.Dortmund captain Nico Schlotterbeck made his first appearance since picking up an ankle injury at the World Cup and told Sky Germany he kept his comeback under wraps. “We just hadn’t communicated that much yet because I didn’t want to,” Schlotterbeck said, adding “I missed it terribly. It was a serious injury but I’m glad to be back now.”Freiburgthumped a poorBorussia Mönchengladbach5-0 at home to climb to the top. Yannik Engelhardt and Igor Matanovic netted twice each and Maximilian Eggestein added a late fifth as the hosts sent Gladbach, who finished with 10 men, to the foot of the table.View image in fullscreenFreiburg’s Matthias Ginter (centre) congratulates Igor Matanovic on the opening goal against Borussia Mönchengladbach.Photograph: Philipp von Ditfurth/DPA/APA 2-2 home draw withBayer LeverkusenendedAugsburg’s short stint as leaders. Augsburg were top after the last matchday for the first time in their history but were held by Leverkusen despite a double from Michael Gregoritsch.Eintracht Frankfurtwon their first match of the campaign with a 3-1 victory at neighbouringMainz, with Can Uzun’s double either side of a Jonathan Burkardt goal. Frankfurt’s goalkeeper Noah Atubolu kept his remarkable penalty-saving record alive when he stopped a first-half effort from Nadiem Amiri. Atubolu’s save was his sixth in a row, extending his own Bundesliga record.West Ham loanee Niclas Füllkrug kept his excellent run of form since returning to the Bundesliga going, scoring the equaliser forWerder Bremenin a 1-1 draw atCologne. Thijs Dallinga missed a penalty after eight minutes but teammate Linton Maina put Cologne ahead moments later.Füllkrug’s goal came in the 69th minute and is his third in four games since returning to Germany. He only found the net three times in 29 matches for West Ham and scored just once in 20 games on loan atMilanlast season.Elsewhere,Hoffenheimwon 2-1 at home againstStuttgartthanks to a double from Adam Hlozek. On Sunday,Bayern Munichtravel to promotedElversberg– who have a 100% record – whileRB LeipzighostHamburg.In Spain, Kylian Mbappé scored twice ⁠asRealMadridenjoyed a 4-1 victory overRayo Vallecano⁠in La Liga ⁠at ​the Santiago Bernabéu. Goals from Álvaro Carreras and Jude ⁠Bellingham made the result comfortable for José Mourinho’s side.View image in fullscreenKylian Mbappé celebrates scoring Real’s fourth against Rayo Vallecano.Photograph: Manu Fernández/APA 14th-minute ⁠penalty from Mbappé was followed three minutes ​later by ‌a simple finish ‌from Carreras, with Mbappé turned provider ‌this time. A relaxed Real found little resistance from Rayo thereafter and, 11 minutes before half time, Vinícius Júnior raced down the left to set up ‌Bellingham for a neat finish into the corner.Six minutes into the ​second half, Sergio Camello pulled a goal back for Rayo following sloppyReal Madridplay. Despite whistles from the ⁠home crowd, Real kept Rayo at ​bay, ​before closing out the ​game with a 90th-minute goal ​from ‌Mbappé.The result ​moved ​Real on to 12 points, level with leadersBarcelona, who have a game in hand. Barça are atLevanteon Sunday afternoon.Alavésmissed the chance to go top overnight with a 2-1 defeat atRacing Santander.In Italy, Diego Moreira scored twice asMilancame from two goals down to hold early season Serie A pacesettersLazio2-2 in Rome on Saturday. Moreira came off the bench at half-time and hauled Milan level after Matteo Cancellieri and Tijjani Noslin had given the hosts the lead at the interval.Despite losing their 100% record having started the season with three wins, Gennaro Gattuso’s side move to the top of the table. Ruben Amorim’s Milan are fourth on eight points, after also drawing last weekend at Juventus.View image in fullscreenMilan’s Diego Moreira celebrates scoring in his side’s 2-2 draw with Lazio.Photograph: Riccardo Antimiani/EPACancellieri opened his account for the campaign after 10 minutes when he connected with a Mattia Zaccagni cross. A dominant Lazio had good chances to pull further clear before Noslin doubled their lead after 39 minutes with a close-range finish.Amorim attempted to stem the tide by making three substitutions at half-time, bringing on playmaker Christian Pulisic and Moreira. His changes bore fruit after 65 minutes as Moreira volleyed home to halve the deficit. Less than two minutes later, the former Strasbourg player equalised with a fierce strike from outside the box, but neither side could find a late winner.Atalantaslumped to a 2-1 defeat at home toCagliari, with Sead Kolasinac handling the ball in the box to concede a second-half penalty that gave the visitors the win.Cagliaritook the lead in the 19th ⁠minute when 19-year-old forward Paul Mendy rattled in the opener off the underside of the crossbar, ​but Gianluca Scamacca levelled for the home side ​four minutes before the break.Mendy had the ​ball in the net again early in the second half only for the goal to be ruled out ​for a narrow offside, but ‌they took the lead ​again after Kolasinac was penalised, ​Daniel Maldini firing home from the spot to secure the three points.The result moved Cagliari up to fourth in the table with nine points from their four games, whileAtalantaare in ninth spot on six points. Earlier, hostsGenoa, who have yet to win this season, were held 1-1 by newly promotedFrosinone, who have seven points.ChampionsInterhostUdineseon Monday, withRomaheading toTorinoandComoat home toParma. Inter and Roma have both won each of their first three matches.Explore more on these topicsEuropean club footballBundesligaLa LigaRacing SantanderAlavesBorussia DortmundPaderbornnewsShareReuse this content

title: Call it the Miliband doctrine. Let’s hope the new Israeli settlement boycott is just the start | Steve Bloomfield | The Guardian
description: This week’s bold move suggests that Britain will once again have an ‘ethical dimension’ to its foreign policy. That’s good for the world, says former Observer international editor Steve Bloomfield
Author: Steve Bloomfield
Headline: This week’s bold move suggests that Britain will once again have an ‘ethical dimension’ to its foreign policy. That’s good for the world, says former Observer international editor Steve Bloomfield
Content: Illustration: Nate Kitch/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Nate Kitch/The GuardianOpinionEd MilibandCall it the Miliband doctrine. Let’s hope the new Israeli settlement boycott is just the startSteve BloomfieldThis week’s move suggests that, even in the age of Trump, Britain will once again have an ‘ethical dimension’ to its foreign policy. That’s good for the worldSat 12 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 09.29 EDTShareAlmost 30 years ago, the Labour titanRobin Cookannounced his arrival at the Foreign Office by laying out what would become described as an“ethical foreign policy”. The UK, he said, “must support the demands of other peoples for the democratic rights on which we insist for ourselves”. Human rights would be “at the heart of our foreign policy”.In the 25 years since Cook was demoted, Britain has had a further 14 foreign secretaries – including seven in the past six years – few of whom can claim to have placed progressive ideals at the heart of their actions.Ed Miliband’s speech on Tuesdayoutlining the UK’s decision to impose economic sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank – and unveiling the international coalition he has built to support it – suggests that Cook may finally have a successor.Describing what is happening in theWest Bankas “ethnic cleansing” carried out by “settler terrorists”, Miliband used language that Palestinians have longed to hear from a British foreign secretary. Vital, too, was his official recognition that the occupation of the West Bank is “unlawful”.Britain was not acting alone. Miliband and diplomats at the Foreign Office have carefully formed a 12-nation coalition, including France and Canada, that spoke with one voice. A cautious European Union, partly blocked by a handful of Benjamin Netanyahu allies, could not have taken such action; while US membership of the G7 – regardless of Donald Trump – would have always made that avenue impossible too.The consequences of the sanctions forIsraelcould be profound, although much will depend on the implementation. The most far-reaching proposal announced by Miliband was the targeting of those who “finance … illegal settlements”. That could mean every single Israeli bank. For those banks it will pose a crucial question: do you want to do business with the settlements or the UK? It could pose a question for Israeli citizens too: do you want your credit card to work in the settlements or when you’re on holiday in London?Ahead of elections at the end of next month there is growing awareness in Israel of the lack of western allies the country can now rely upon. Supportis ebbing away in the US too. More Americansnow sympathise with the Palestinians than the Israelis,while more than half now back a Palestinian state.Even centrist Democrats are beginning to suggest the US position could change. In the wake of Miliband’s announcement, Hillary Clinton, the former secretary of state, on Thursday called for a“crackdown on settler violence”and said the US should “take a very tough position” if Netanyahu is re-elected.Beyond Israel, the past few days have shown that Britain now has a government that understands that the world has changed since Trump’s re-election. Since the second world war, the US has been Britain’s most important diplomatic partner. For many of those in Whitehall, adjusting to the realisation that Washington is no longer the first phone call when trying to come up with a diplomatic solution has not been straightforward.It is enormously promising that the Foreign Office could not only pull together a strong coalition but also lead it. This time the phone calls to Washington came at the end, once the policy had been agreed –Andy Burnhambriefing Trump, and Miliband talking through the details with his secretary of state, Marco Rubio.Alongside the E3 of Britain, France and Germany, which has taken the lead on forming a rival western policy on Ukraine, it is clear we’re moving into a new era of ad hoc diplomatic groups that may be just as effective as their more formal predecessors.Traditional alliances, from the G7 to Nato, are falling apart – destroyed from the inside by a US president who is opposed to multilateralism, liberal democracy and the rule of law. For the first year of Trump’s second term in office, the “rest of the west” was inert: some leaders simply refused to believe that the US was no longer an ally, while others fully understood the challenge but hadn’t worked out how to meet it.But since the start of 2026, the debate has been over, thanks to the publication of Trump’s incendiary national security strategy and his relentless desire to annex Greenland, threatening a Nato ally with invasion. AsMark Carney laid out in Davos, there has been a “rupture” in the international rules-based order and it is vital that the middle powers come together.The big question for Burnham and Miliband is whether they can build on this start and turn Britain into a progressive international force. How they deal with three key issues will be indicative. The easiest – but most expensive – will be aid. Both have expressed a desire to reverse Keir Starmer’s 40% cut to the international aid and development budget, a decision that managed to be both immoral and self-defeating. If this can be done, the UK may regain some of the soft power it so carelessly threw away.They will face a bigger challenge in Ukraine, where the E3-led “coalition of the willing” has so far had little impact on the only two men who count, Trump and the Russian president, Vladimir Putin. While the US president so far appears unwilling to waste any political capital in saving Netanyahu, he seems more disposed to come to the aid of his counterpart in Moscow.Finally, there is another war that Miliband should be striving to end: the long-running conflict in Sudan. Just as with Israel, it will involve standing up to a close ally in the Middle East, in this case the United Arab Emirates (UAE). For the past few years, the UAE has been funding and arming the Rapid Support Forces, a militia group that now controls large swathes of the country and has been accused by a UN report of committing atrocities that bear the“hallmarks of genocide”.The bravery that the government has displayed on Israel has been, so far, sadly missing on Sudan. The UK has consistently failed to criticise the UAE, merely urging nameless “external actors” to stop“supplying, funding and fuelling the war”. Another coalition of the willing exists here, too, the E4+, which includes France, Germany and Norway. But they need to move beyond statements expressing “deep concern” if anything is going to change.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThese ad hoc alliances may not last. By next spring, Emmanuel Macron will no longer be in the Élysée palace, possibly replaced by a far-right president. Friedrich Merz is fighting for his political survival in Germany too, where again the biggest threat is a far-right party aligned with Trump. It is vital that Miliband makes use of these alliances while he can.Placing values at the heart of foreign policy is fraught with political risk. Within days of Cook’s speech in May 1997, it emerged that the UK was planning to sell more Hawk jets to an Indonesian regime that was attacking its own civilians in East Timor. “Ethical foreign policy” became a joke, rather than a doctrine.But it’s worth noting that Cook didn’t actually use the phrase he was credited with. Instead he said the UK’s foreign policy “must have an ethical dimension”, a caveat that showed an understanding that human rights cannot always trump realpolitik.During his four years in office, that ethical dimension could be seen in the banning of landmines, an annual human rights report and the Nato-led military action to stop ethnic cleansing in Kosovo.Miliband, too, is no wide-eyed idealist. There were those who would have wanted him to go further – for instance, by declaring that there has been a genocide inGaza. He has also come to the conclusion that however dangerous Trump is, the UK must be careful about how – and when – it stands up to him.But the past few days have shown that foreign policy with an ethical dimension is not only possible but can make a difference. There will be many people around the world, from Gaza to Darfur, who hope it continues.Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer and a previous winner of the Orwell prizeDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsEd MilibandOpinionEthical foreign policyForeign policyIsraelWest BankGazaMiddle East and north AfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: Why is Trump’s $5,000 offer to voters ‘like a woman’? Ask Fox News | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Host Jesse Watters says Trump’s offer to Americans if Republicans retain Congress is ‘an enticement’, not a bribe
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Host Jesse Watters says Trump’s offer to Americans if Republicans retain Congress is ‘an enticement’, not a bribe
Content: ‘The president himself, meanwhile, doesn’t seem keen to elaborate on his cunning plan to win friends and influence voters.’Photograph: Callaghan O’Hare/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The president himself, meanwhile, doesn’t seem keen to elaborate on his cunning plan to win friends and influence voters.’Photograph: Callaghan O’Hare/ReutersOpinionDonald TrumpWhy is Trump’s $5,000 offer to voters ‘like a woman’? Ask Fox NewsArwa MahdawiHost Jesse Watters says Trump’s offer to Americans if Republicans retain Congress is ‘an enticement’, not a bribeSat 12 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTShareIthink I finally understand why Fox News pays Jesse Watters the big bucks. The network star, famous for hot takeslikemen shouldn’t “eat soup in public”, has an incredible talent for inserting misogyny into absolutely any news story.Take, for example, Donald Trump’s ludicrousannouncementon Wednesday night that he will give every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the US Congress in November’s midterm election. That’s a story about apparent bribery, right? A story about fiscal recklessness and empty promises. A story about how the president, whose popularity is plummeting, is so out of ideas that he’s resorted (yet again) to dangling cash in front of voters.Actually, says Watters, it’s none of the above; it’s just Trump behaving like a woman.“That $5,000 check, Dana, that’s not a bribe,” Watters told Fox anchor Dana Perino onThursday. “We’re calling it an enticement … It’s like a woman. Sometimes a woman can entice you, OK? Maybe – it doesn’t mean you’re going home with her, but it keeps you interested. It keeps you intrigued and wanting more. That’s what this is about.”Perhaps the Fox News host isn’t completely wrong. After all, I am a woman and I am about to entice you tolook upthe story about how Watters courted his much younger second wife. It’s very intriguing.But back to thisdefinitely-not-a-bribe$5,000 payment which the president calls a Trump “dividend”. I wouldn’t start spending it now, if I were you. The president, like his right-hand manElon Musk, has a habit of making grandiose promises he doesn’t keep. Remember theDoge dividendsfloated last February? Those haven’t materialized. Nor have the tariff dividends that Trump made so much noise about. “People that are against Tariffs are FOOLS!” Trump said in aTruth Socialpost last year. “We are taking in Trillions of Dollars and … A dividend of at least $2000 a person (not including high income people!) will be paid to everyone.” Almost a year after that post, nobody has received a tariff dividend. However, ithas been estimatedby the Joint Economic Committee – Minority that the average American family will pay more than $2,500 in tariff costs this year.I feel pretty confident saying there is a 0.00001% chance that anyone is going to get a $5,000 Republican celebration check. But let’s just play along for a minute and pretend that Trump isn’t afabulist. Let’s pretend that the president is a serious man who makes thoughtful policy proposals, rather than an opportunist who says whatever inane thing happens to pop into his brain in the moment. Isn’t it a bit reckless to be giving all this money away, a total that exceeds $1tn, when the US national debtrecently surpassed$40tn for the first time? As Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, said in a statement, that debt “doesn’t exist solely on the government’s ledgers”, it is shouldered by everyone. “The more we borrow, the more we exacerbate inflation, squeeze out other priorities in the budget, and leave ourselves vulnerable to emergencies at home and turmoil abroad.”Don’t worry about all that, says the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick. “It’s not tax money,” Lutnick told NBC News onThursday. The Trump administration is going to earn that money from various moneymaking endeavours like the Trump Platinum Card, which allows wealthy people to pay up to $5m to extend their US visas. JD Vance, meanwhile, has suggested that the money might come from US tariff revenues, even though economists have pointed out the $125bn in tariff revenues wouldn’t come close tocovering the costs.The president himself, meanwhile, doesn’t seem keen to elaborate on his cunning plan to win friends and influence voters. When the ABC reporter Rachel Scott asked him about the rationale behind the $5,000 checks on Thursday night, he said it was a reward to Americans for putting up with Joe Biden. After Scott tried to ask a follow-up question, Trumplunged at herand said: “Your network … you’re the worst.” Which is very on-brand for the president. He can’t seem to handle being asked tough questions by anyone, but gets particularly nasty when those questions areposed by a woman.While Trump doesn’t want to get into the details of his dividend, the proposal reflects how the president is looking at some very unconventional ways to sway the midterms. He may not end up issuing people celebration checks, but he has alreadygutted election security programsand attempted to limit voting access. The real story here isn’t $5,000 cheques, it’s the fact that America’s self-styled king seems intent on meddling with the election, and no meaningful checks and balances are stopping him.Ectopic pregnancy deaths in the US have nearly doubledA ProPublica analysis found almost 200 women died after an ectopic pregnancy from 2020 to 2025. That’s compared to about 100 in the previous six years. To nobody’s surprise, mortality is worse in states with strict abortion bans. “While they cautioned that abortion bans alone can’t explain the national rise, maternal health experts said any examination of the spike should include the documented delays in care caused by the laws, including for ectopic pregnancies,”ProPublica notes.Sudanese refugees are being forced into sex workSudan’s civil war, which started in 2023, has created the world’s worst displacement crisis. Now, many of the women who fled to Egypt arebeing sexually exploited.What’s happened to Pete Hegseth’s testosterone screening guidance?The Pentagon published a guidance document on 2 September outlining a new mandatory testosterone screening process to create a “High-T military”. However, the very next day it was withdrawn from the public domain forreasons that remain unclear.Maybe someone in the Pentagon came to their senses.Secret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealedNaza, ahighly-fetednew film from the Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, reveals the secret systems used in mass killings of civilians in Gaza. “Several interviewees worked in a secret intelligence unit that reports directly to the office of Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu,”the Guardian writes. “[O]ne said their mission was to ‘thwart peace’.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhy does the hard right shrug off domestic abusers in their midst?The short answer is because they are misogynists who cynically weaponize women’s rights to advance their agenda. But do readZoe Williams, who has a longer and more eloquent answer, following on from the attack on a female protester at theReform UK conference.The Republican convention showed an image of Hasan Piker in his underwearThey seem to think showing photos of a buff podcaster in his underwear demonstrates that the left are scary “radicals”.The rise of hairy young womenPhoebe Bridgers’unshaven legsat her Venice film festival debut sparked a flurry of headlines. But,says Leah Harper, Bridgers’ “au naturel look may signal that attitudes are changing – particularly among younger generations”.Emma Bonino, feminist Italian politician, dies aged 78Boninogot involved in politics after she had an abortion (then illegal) at age 26 and said she decided that “never, never, never again should anyone have to suffer this humiliation”. She handed herself in to the police as an act of protest, leading a campaign to eventually legalize abortion in 1978.Princess Diana’s ‘revenge dress’ is going up for auctionDiana famously wore the fitted black dress on the same night that Charles admitted to his infidelity on TV in 1994. It will be auctionedoff in December.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionFox NewsUS midterm elections 2026FoxcommentShareReuse this content

title: Bayeux tapestrymania has gripped Britain. But what does it say about our own age of war and upheaval?  | Charlotte Higgins | The Guardian
description: The tapestry is drawing crowds to the British Museum – and each person who sees it will draw a different meaning from this epic, vivid artwork, says the Guardian’s chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins
Author: Charlotte Higgins
Headline: The tapestry is drawing crowds to the British Museum – and each person who sees it will draw a different meaning from this epic, vivid artwork, says the Guardian’s chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins
Content: Bayeux tapestry-themed merchandise at the British Museum in London, September 2026.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenBayeux tapestry-themed merchandise at the British Museum in London, September 2026.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersOpinionBayeux tapestryBayeux tapestrymania has gripped Britain. But what does it say about our own age of war and upheaval?Charlotte HigginsThe tapestry is drawing crowds to the British Museum – and each person who sees it will draw a different meaning from this epic, vivid artworkSat 12 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 12.50 EDTShareIhave seen theBayeux tapestryfour times since childhood, and loved it on each viewing, for the sheer miracle of its survival and the glorious vividness of its detail. But the fourth time, earlier this week, was different – how could it not be?Tapestrymania has taken hold in London. The textile has been proffered as a diplomatic symbol, the occasion for crowned heads and presidents to mingle and speechify. And, assuming you agree that it was embroidered in England by Englishwomen’s hands (since many scholars argue it waslikely stitched in Canterburyrather than Bayeux, Normandy – the tapestry’s home),it is charged with the potency of return, rather than simply of arrival.If you want to see the Bayeux tapestryat the British Museum, be alert for the next ticket release in October, be resigned to sitting in along digital queueand be ready to hand over £33. Or, perhaps more realistically, be prepared for disappointment. Viewing times are restricted to protect its delicate fibres from damage, so they can’t simply be extended beyond normal hours. Demand will outstrip supply.We see celebrated artworks through the lens of our own historical moment, our own biography. Encountering the tapestry again this week, in a time of war, it seemed impossible to observe the violence of the battles it depicts without a cold dread: the decapitated trunks, the horses clashing and tumbling, the looters stripping the killed of their arms and armour. But what really struck me was how legible the artwork is. Across nearly 1,000 years, its narrative clarity is such that, in its temporary gallery, you barely need to glance up at the British Museum’s animated interpretation. All it asks of you is to look, and the story will lay itself out generously before you.The Bayeux tapestry: a stupefying, thrilling, horrifying masterpiece that shakes the earthRead moreView image in fullscreenPeople queueing to see the Bayeux tapestry at the British Museum in London, 10 September 2026.Photograph: James Manning/PAAs a child, on a school trip to Bayeux, I was encouraged to see the tapestry as a cartoon strip. That makes sense, of course, to a child, and cartoonists of recent times have often used the tapestry to riff on.In his coverfor the post D-day, 15 July 1944 edition of the New Yorker, Rea Irvin lovingly parodied the tapestry, putting “George Rex” on his throne instead ofEdward the Confessorand depicting landing vessels stuffed with GIs, rather than wooden ships filled with Norman troops. It was irresistible in its neat reversal: Normandy invaded from England rather than vice versa.Now, though, I’d rather see it as a visual poem. An epic of conquest. In the wake of that other recent cultural sensation,Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, you do not need to be a classics nerd like me (and Mary Beard and I will make apodcaston the tapestry through a classical lens soon) to spot the resonances with ancient epic. The voyaging, the misadventures, the landing on an unfamiliar shore to be met by hostile inhabitants – and then the battle.One of the most satisfying elements of the tapestry is its pacing, which also has the feel of epic. The relatively slow buildup, with the scenes of Harold and his English setting out across the sea with falcons on their wrists, and tunics pulled up as they wade out to their boats. The drama of Harold’s capture in northernFrance, his retrieval by William of Normandy, and Harold’s rescue of men sinking into the quicksand at Mont Saint-Michel. The fateful (but unspecified) oath Harold swears to William. The death of Edward back in Westminster, his weeping wife and Harold’s acclamation as king of England. Finally, the clash of armies and Harold’s death.View image in fullscreenA detail of the 70m-long Bayeux tapestry, September 2026.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersBut – also like an ancient epic – it has its moments of strangeness and humour. The main scenes on the textile are bordered by images of fantastic beasts, but also scenes of everyday life – of people ploughing and scattering seed. A reminder of existences that grind on despite the machinations of kings. It reminds me of how imagery works in ancient epic, where similes do a comparable job of pulling the reader out of the main action into a world of nature and ordinary people doing ordinary things.Above all, the tapestry resonates with theAeneid, the origin myth of the Roman empire by the poet Virgil (who died in 19BC), the story of which would certainly have been available to the learned elites of 11th-century northern Europe. Like the Aeneid, the tapestry offers adventures at sea, a decisive battle, a new ruler, all heralded by the arrival of a comet signifying a great reversal. Even the feasting scene – William and his men devouring skewers of meat before the battle – has an epic feel.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is, then, an English epic: an origin myth for Norman power in England, a story that everyone, or nearly everyone, educated in the UK knows: 1066, Harold with an arrow in his eye, William the Conqueror. Like the Aeneid, it has surface-level propaganda stitched into it. Quite likely commissioned by William’s half-brother, Odo, in the 1070s, its business is to show viewers the inevitability of the crown’s acquisition by this new Norman king. And, since it began to be part of the British imagination from its rediscovery in the 18th century, it has been so successful at imparting that narrative that hardly anyone hasheard of Edgar Ætheling, the figure who had a stronger claim on the English throne than either Harold or William, and is completely absent from the tapestry.But there is another reason for its extraordinary modern persistence than its sheer narrative force, economy and clarity. Despite its “official” status, an object created at the behest of conquering Normans, it is an incredibly open, and surprisingly even-handed, work of art. It has none of the posturing that blatant propaganda contains. Harold and William are portrayed as equals, with Harold accorded significant moments of valour and virtue – it is far from puffing up William solely as a new but better Julius Caesar who managed to conquer England, unlike Caesar, as his biographer, William of Poitiers, had it. The Latin text of the tapestry is clear but laconic. When we are told that “Harold swears an oath to William”, we are not told the nature of this oath (to support William in his claim to Edward’s crown? But who knows).The textile is an object whose story is completed by its viewer, which is why it is such a rich and generative artefact. Sometimes that “completion” has been for ill:the Nazissaw it strongly in relation to theories of racial superiority, fascinated by the Normans’ Nordic origins.And what now? TheBayeux tapestry, back (perhaps!) in England after as much as (perhaps!) 900 years, is just beginning a period of intense and excited scrutiny by a thrilled public. What will be read into those ancient threads? What will we take from it? Whatever emerges, it will almost certainly reveal more about us, now, in the 21st century, than the time in which it was made. The narrative of the tapestry is wonderfully clear. But the story it is telling us is ours to compose.Charlotte Higgins is the Guardian’s chief culture writerExplore more on these topicsBayeux tapestryOpinionBritish MuseumArtFranceEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: Comedians should not be hot | Amy Annette | The Guardian
description: People making a living from being funny should be exempt from the beauty rules the rest of society plays by, says comedian Amy Annette
Author: Amy Annette
Headline: People making a living from being funny should be exempt from the beauty rules the rest of society plays by, says comedian Amy Annette
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onComedyThe hill I will die on: Comedians should not be hotAmy AnnettePeople making a living from being funny should be exempt from the beauty rules the rest of society plays bySat 12 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 06.12 EDTShareIt’s a fact that being funny is an evolutionary trait, developed by the unattractive to entice the very good-looking to mate with them. Yes, that is a fact, and no I won’t look it up. And therefore it is not OK for attractive people to also be funny. And I don’t think that I’m going too far when I say that comedians being hot is a crime against nature.I use the word “hot” intentionally. Beauty is ineffable. It can be found anywhere and in anyone. Hotness is different. It’s playing the game of society’s beauty norms and winning. Although, by spendinganytime playing, you have lost (like golf). I’m not ugly, but I’ll never be hot. I simply don’t have it in me. The effort! The commitment! The other day I went to a wedding and thought to myself: “I really like this couple, maybe I’ll shave above the knee.” A hot person would have probably already been professionally hairless, and, if not would have booked in a wax ASAP.Many US comedians these days are celebrity-level hot. Hot by normal people standards, not just by comedy’s traditionally low bar. I think I know why. If you are a woman with any visibility, there will inevitably be a response online to your looks. If you are in any way not meeting normative beauty standards, it will be pointed out to you. A lot. If you can attain hotness, you may think that you become more bulletproof – that you will be judged on your jokes and not your looks. That’s what I think has happened with comedians such as Nikki Glaser, whodid an incredible job of hostingthe Golden Globes, but did so looking as polished as any A-list actor.It wasn’t always like this. I grew up looking up to Wanda Sykes, Rosie O’Donnell, Dawn French and Jo Brand. Now to be clear, these are attractive people –no onewore a velvet tabard dress/top in the early 00s like Dawn French, and no one ever will – but they weren’t trying to be hot. They talked about beauty standards and they often addressed how they differed from the norms, but they never felt the need to meet them.Of course, when I say “hot comedians”, really I mean “hot female comedians” – because there is obviously more pressure on women to be hot. There is still room for the schlubby, basketball-shorted Adam Sandler everyman comedian. But for the new generations of comedians, it seems that similar pressures are now affecting men.Matt Rife angrily refuted claimshe’d had plastic surgery recently, claiming that he just can’t help being gorgeous. “If anything,” he said, “as a comedian, it actually made shit harder.” I agree, if by “shit harder” he means “much, much easier”.No good can come of this new standard. I’m not saying all comedians need to be ugly, but I am worried we’re getting to a point where all comedians need to be hot. Please. No. Think of us, the happily hairy thighed, and let us be as non-hot as we like.Amy Annette is a comedianskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsComedyThe hill I will die onWomencommentShareReuse this content

title: Jeremy Thomas, British producer of The Last Emperor and Sexy Beast, dies aged 77 | Film industry | The Guardian
description: An outstanding figure in the UK film industry, Thomas was noted for collaborations with directors including Bernardo Bertolucci and David Cronenberg
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: An outstanding figure in the UK film industry, Thomas was noted for collaborations with directors including Bernardo Bertolucci and David Cronenberg
Content: Jeremy Thomas was the acclaimed producer behind a string of commercial and critical hits.Photograph: Anoush AbrarView image in fullscreenJeremy Thomas was the acclaimed producer behind a string of commercial and critical hits.Photograph: Anoush AbrarFilm industryJeremy Thomas, British producer of The Last Emperor and Sexy Beast, dies aged 77An outstanding figure in the UK film industry, Thomas was noted for collaborations with directors including Bernardo Bertolucci and David CronenbergAndrew PulverSat 12 Sep 2026 10.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 15.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJeremy Thomas, the distinguished British producer of films including Sexy Beast, High-Rise and the multi-Oscar-winning The Last Emperor, has died aged 77.A representative for Thomas said he died on Friday “peacefully, at his country home in Oxfordshire, surrounded by his family and loved ones”.Thomas, who started producing feature films in the early 1970s, was known for forging strong creative relationships with acclaimed auteurs, producing a string of films directed by the likes of Nicolas Roeg, David Cronenberg andBernardo Bertolucci.Jeremy Thomas: producer was cross between a kindly Cambridge don and the movie world’s cool uncleRead moreThe Last Emperor, directed by Bertolucci, was an early triumph for Thomas, winning nine Oscars including best picture. He went on to become a major figure in the British film-making establishment, including a spell as chair of the British Film Institute and winning a Bafta for outstanding British contribution to cinema.Thomas was held in universally high esteem by the rest of the film industry. Fellow producer Stephen Woolley told the Guardian: “He was a huge inspiration and a massively undervalued genius and necessary rebel in our industry. He sided with the subversives and movie anarchists and we loved him dearly. Jeremy showed with his first movie success The Shout that boundaries were there to be ignored or broken, and that movies are an international and all-embracing experience. Myself and my producing partner Elizabeth Karlsen look up to his guiding star still moving across the galaxy and inspiring film-makers from all nations and genders with his extraordinary body of stellar work.” Mike Downey, producer and former chair of the European film academy said: “Jeremy Thomas was one of the most significant producers of world cinema in the world. The list of the giants of cinema that he curated, encouraged, selflessly supported and believed in, often when others wouldn’t take the risk, was a tribute to his belief in film as an art above all else. Jeremy’s legacy is incalculable and he has left an indelible mark on cinema history.” Trainspotting producer Andrew Macdonaldsaid in a statement to Variety: “He was a hero for me. A rebel with taste.” Luca Guadagnino, director of A Bigger Splash and Queer said: “The canon of his work is unmatched, and some of the greatest movies of the past 50 years have been produced by him. And the level of the partnerships that he established in his career is incredible, from Nagisa Oshima to Bernardo Bertolucci.”Born in 1949, Thomas’s father, Ralph, was a prolific film director whose work included the popular Doctor in the House series starring Dirk Bogarde, and his uncle Gerald Thomas directed all 30 of the Carry On films. Thomas started out as an assistant editor, working on the Jimmy Cliff thriller The Harder They Come and Ken Loach’s Family Life, before gaining his first producer credit on Mad Dog Morgan in 1976, with Dennis Hopper as the 19th-century Australian outlaw of the title.Thomas was quickly into his stride, making Bad Timing, Insignificance and Eureka with Roeg, The Shout with Jerzy Skolimowski and Merry Christmas, Mr Lawrence with the Japanese master director Nagisa Oshima. The success of The Last Emperor, which Thomas had to finance independently, consolidated his status as a leading figure in British cinema, and he subsequently concentrated on prestige projects including The Sheltering Sky and Little Buddha (both with Bertolucci) and Naked Lunch (with Cronenberg).Thomas then suggested to Cronenberg he should direct JG Ballard’s Crash, and theresulting film was enormously controversial, resulting in local authority bans in several areas in the UK. Following this, Thomas’s films included riskier propositions, such as Sexy Beast, directed by Jonathan Glazer, an adaptation of Alexander Trocchi’s Young Adam, by David Mackenzie, and Terry Gilliam’s bizarre corpse comedy Tideland. Later highlights were Jim Jarmusch’s vampire fantasy Only Lovers Left Alive, another Ballard adaptation, High-Rise, directed by Ben Wheatley, and Tale of Tales and Dogman from the Italian director Matteo Garrone.In 2019 Thomas wasthe subject of a documentary by Mark Cousins, who accompanied him on his car drive from the UK to the Cannes film festival for another Garrone film, Pinocchio; it screened there in 2021. Thomas also directed one film himself: All the Little Animals, starring Christian Bale, which was released in 1999. His most recent film, Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo, directed by Takashi Miike, is due to premiere at the Toronto film festival on Monday.Explore more on these topicsFilm industryBFIKen LoachBernardo BertolucciFilm adaptationsDavid CronenbergnewsShareReuse this content

title: Revealed: the university courses students regret – and those they don’t | Higher education | The Guardian
description: We looked at graduates’ satisfaction levels after leaving university – and while most were happy, up to a third wish they’d picked a different subject
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: We looked at graduates’ satisfaction levels after leaving university – and while most were happy, up to a third wish they’d picked a different subject
Content: The majority of graduates feel that they made the right choice.Photograph: David Schaffer/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe majority of graduates feel that they made the right choice.Photograph: David Schaffer/Getty ImagesUniversity Guide 2027Higher educationRevealed: the university courses students regret – and those they don’tWe looked at graduates’ satisfaction levels after leaving university – and while most were happy, up to a third wish they’d picked a different subjectRichard AdamsSat 12 Sep 2026 06.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGloomy headlines might claim that a degree is less worthwhile than it once was, but one sliver of good news is that the most recent graduates don’t regret their time on campus.When those who graduated in the summer of 2024 were surveyed 15 months later, more than eight out of 10 said they would still go to university ahead of any other option, despite a media drumbeat of pessimism about graduate jobs and increasing levels of student debt.Matt Hiely-Rayner, an analyst who compiles the Guardian’s University Guide, says the new data supplied by the Higher Education Statistics Agency, was positive news. “Very few students say they would do something different than go to university – only about 20% of graduates say they would do something completely different.“And the proportion who are happy with the provider they selected has stayed strong and has actually gone up slightly this year, suggesting that people were more satisfied with their choice.”Table of best and worst subjects rated after graduationTable of happiness of graduates ranked by institutionBut fewer of the recent graduates appeared to be happy with their choice of subject, with just 70% saying they would stick with their original subject.“Even that is relatively good, there hasn’t been a collapse, which is interesting because we’ve seen positive outcomes around graduate jobs continue to come down faster than in previous years,” says Hiely-Rayner. “So with hindsight, 15 months after graduation, students are more likely to regret their subject choice than they are going to university at all or which institution they went to.”According to the latest data, the University of Bath’s graduates were happiest with their choice of institution, leaping above its rivals at Oxbridge and the Russell Group of research universities. The top five universities clustered around 90% of their graduates saying they remain happy with their choice, with just 0.8 of a percentage point separating Bath at the top from Oxford in fifth place.But that happiness doesn’t extend to subject choices – with dissatisfaction visible even among most highly selective professional courses that offer well-paid graduate careers.Fifteen months after graduation, fewer dentists, vets and paramedics than in the previous year said they would choose the same course, while architecture and computer science have fallen out of the top 10 in terms of course satisfaction.The fall in computer science may be linked to the wayAI has replaced entry-level jobs, as well as early career employment opportunities not being as abundant as they once were. Four years ago, 66% of computer science students went on to graduate-level employment but the latest figures show just 56% did so.AI may also be harming the career prospects of graduates who studied animation and game design, who are now among the least enthusiastic about their career choices. Fewer than two out of three animation and game design graduates would choose the same course again, putting it in the same league as journalism, marketing and PR graduates for highest levels of regret.The latest data also highlighted a surprising fall in satisfaction in economics, which regularly tops league tables for graduate pay and has seen a surge in interest among A-level students and university applicants.This may reflect the fact that not all economics courses are created equal, says Hiely-Rayner. “Economics has always been quite a secure one [in terms of graduate jobs]. It seems like a safe bet, but the proportion who are getting a job varies by institution.”Explore more on these topicsHigher educationUniversity Guide 2027StudentsUniversitiesEmployabilityUniversity excellenceUniversity teachingYoung peoplefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Nashville airport board unanimously approves name change to honor Dolly Parton | Nashville | The Guardian
description: The city’s mayor and Tennessee’s governor threw their support behind the name change last month
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: The city’s mayor and Tennessee’s governor threw their support behind the name change last month
Content: The Nashville international airport will soon be renamed after the beloved singer-songwriter and philanthropist.Photograph: George Walker IV/APView image in fullscreenThe Nashville international airport will soon be renamed after the beloved singer-songwriter and philanthropist.Photograph: George Walker IV/APNashvilleNashville airport board unanimously approves name change to honor Dolly PartonThe city’s mayor and Tennessee’s governor threw their support behind the name change last monthEdward HelmoreSat 12 Sep 2026 09.40 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 09.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheNashvilleairport is to be renamed afterDolly Parton, a board of commissioners voted on Friday, in tribute to the Smoky Mountain singer who is estimated to bring $1.8bn each year toTennesseethrough her Dollywood theme park.The decision ensures that Parton, who died last month at 80 years old, will be memorialized with her name on an airport, although the renaming process will take time to complete.In her lifetime, Parton did not think the idea, which came about last year, would come to fruition.Tennessee to wear Dolly Parton tribute on helmets during 2026 college football seasonRead more“I think that’s probably more of a joke than anything,”Parton told the Tennessean. “I mean, it does sound like a lot of fun to say: ‘Your flight is departin’ from Nashville’s D Parton.’”The move to rename gained traction last month when the Nashville mayor, Freddie O’Connell, and theTennesseegovernor, Bill Lee, threw their support behind the name change.“Dolly Parton’s extraordinary life is forever woven into the fabric of our state,” Leesaid in a statement, recognizing what he called her “Volunteer spirit”.“It is fitting thatNashvilleinternational airport would bear the name of our state’s favorite daughter and greet travelers with the enduring legacy of Dolly’s music, generosity, faith and kindness,” Lee added.After the airport’s commissioners voted in favor of the change, Lee said it was an “important step to honor her remarkable legacy” as “Dolly has always helped the world fall in love with Tennessee”.The name change is likely to be pricey since it will require new signage across the entire 4,500-acre (1,700-hectare) property, and updates to an airport monuments, merchandise, shuttle buses, uniforms, business cards, legal contracts and leases.Although the new airport name in her honor has not been decided,Tennessean columnist Alejandro Ramos argued last monththat the case for the change “is larger than music” because of her contributions to the state of Tennessee and to international literacy through her Imagination Library charity.“Parton’s songs helped make Tennessee recognizable around the world. But her deepest legacy may be what she did with the success that followed. She accumulated the kind of fame, wealth and influence few people ever experience. Then she repeatedly turned those resources outward,” Ramos wrote.The Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authoritysaid in a statement: “While a final name has not yet been determined, we are working closely with the appropriate parties to thoughtfully determine how Dolly Parton’s name and legacy will be incorporated”.Explore more on these topicsNashvilleDolly PartonTennesseenewsShareReuse this content

title: Mississippi police say more arrests to come in death of woman found hanging from tree | Mississippi | The Guardian
description: Officials still investigating death of Tasia Fortune, a Black woman, a day after man’s arrest in relation to killing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Officials still investigating death of Tasia Fortune, a Black woman, a day after man’s arrest in relation to killing
Content: Christy Spivey poses with a portrait of her late daughter, Tasia Fortune, on 8 September in Marion, Kentucky.Photograph: George Walker IV/APView image in fullscreenChristy Spivey poses with a portrait of her late daughter, Tasia Fortune, on 8 September in Marion, Kentucky.Photograph: George Walker IV/APMississippiMississippi police say more arrests to come in death of woman found hanging from treeOfficials still investigating death of Tasia Fortune, a Black woman, a day after man’s arrest in relation to killingAssociated PressSat 12 Sep 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMississippipolice said on Saturday they were still investigating the death of Tasia Fortune, a Black woman found hanging from a tree last month, a day after aman was arrestedin connection with the killing.Loved ones also painted a picture of Fortune as a mother, athlete and woman of faith who they hoped would not solely be remembered for her horrific death.Police sought and found Jarques Ratliff, 51, who is Black, and arrested him when they encountered him walking on the street, authorities said on Friday. Jackson’s police chief, RaShall Brackney, also said on Friday that additional arrests are expected in the case. Ratliff should appear in Jackson municipal court no later than Monday morning, said André de Gruy, Mississippi’s state defender.Brackney said Ratliff had an “association” with Fortune but would not elaborate on their relationship. She said police arrested Ratliff on a homicide charge and called that “an important development” in the investigation.“But it is not the conclusion. This case remains active, and additional arrests will be pending as our investigators continue to follow the evidence wherever it leads,” Brackney said on Friday. “We understand that this case has received media attention from across the globe, and across this community.”The state medical examiner’s office determined on Thursday evening that the death was a homicide, Brackney said, allowing police to execute the warrants they already had on hand.Police did not respond to calls and messages from the Associated Press on Saturday about potential updates to the investigation beyond confirming it was still going on.Ratliff also did not appear in Hinds county jail records on Saturday. It couldn’t immediately be determined if he had a lawyer, and a message was left for the public defender’s office. If represented by a public defender, it would be the Hinds county public defender, de Gruy said.Man arrested over death of Mississippi woman found hanging from a treeRead moreChristy Spivey, Fortune’s mother, said on Friday after police told her of the arrest: “I just started crying and told them, ‘Thank you, thank you, thank you.’”Spivey said police did not share a motive or whether DNA led them to the arrest. Spivey said she did not know the man who had been arrested, but she was asking her daughter’s friends if they knew him. Spivey described the family as “in disbelief” and “shock”.“We still don’t have a lot of answers,” Spivey said.Police discovered Fortune’s body hanging in the backyard of an abandoned home in Jackson on 3 August.Spivey said she was certain that her daughter, 29, would not have killed herself.“Absolutely not. Even if she could climb that tree, no, no, she would never, ever, ever,” Spivey said.An obituary about Fortune posted on the website of Tucker funeral home in Central City, Kentucky, in August stated that Fortune’s “path was not always easy, and there were highs and lows”. It also stated that she skipped her junior year of high school, was a star cross-country runner, and had a strong faith in God. Services were held last month inKentucky.“She leaves behind a powerful legacy of resilience, rooted deeply in her unwavering faith. Even in her darkest hours, she never stopped believing in her Savior,” the obituary stated.Fortune was also the mother of four children, but she rarely saw two of them, Spivey said. The last time Spivey saw her daughter was in late July for a planned family reunion in Kentucky that was canceled, but her daughter came to see her anyway.“When she was there, there was this pull, like a spiritual pull to her. I needed her. I guess God knew that was going to be it,” Spivey said.Spivey said she and Fortune’s father faced racism and violence as a mixed-race couple in Crittenden county, Kentucky, before Fortune was born.Fortune was taken from her parents and placed in foster care as a child. During her high school years, she moved around among group homes and eventually ran away to Mississippi. The obituary stated that she had lived in Jackson for 10 years.Spivey wasn’t sure where Fortune was living at the time of her death but said her daughter had been struggling with homelessness in recent years. Fortune had two sisters and was close with them. The father of one of her children was verbally and physically abusive to Fortune, Spivey said.Before she died, Fortune had talked about starting a cleaning business and was trying to get her life in order.“Say her name. Keep it going,” Spivey said. “Because I’m not going to stop until I get answers.”Explore more on these topicsMississippiUS crimeUS policingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Heatwaves hit the Sunday roast: why the RHS says cauliflower is off the menu | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Charity urges gardeners in England to swap thirsty brassicas for drought-tolerant crops
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Charity urges gardeners in England to swap thirsty brassicas for drought-tolerant crops
Content: Cauliflowers as they should be. The Royal Horticultural Society said the vegetables get easily stressed and fail to form a good head  in high temperatures.Photograph: Thanasis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCauliflowers as they should be. The Royal Horticultural Society said the vegetables get easily stressed and fail to form a good head  in high temperatures.Photograph: Thanasis/Getty ImagesClimate crisisHeatwaves hit the Sunday roast: why the RHS says cauliflower is off the menuCharity urges gardeners in England to swap thirsty brassicas for drought-tolerant cropsHelena HortonSat 12 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThey are an integral part of the British Sunday roast – but cauliflowers are now going to be off the menu, according to the Royal Horticultural Society.England’s climate has changed so much that the RHS is now recommending that gardeners exclude the brassicas from their vegetable patches.The UK is expecting a poor harvest of most brassicas, such as broccoli, cauliflower and cabbages, owing to the drought, with farmers saying this year could be one of the worst on record.This summer was theUK’s hottest on record, according to provisional Met Office data. In England, temperatures peaked at 38.1C (100.1F) at Kew Gardens in London on 13 August, and June had already been confirmed as the country’shottest since records began in 1884.Scientists have said these heatwaves are only possible because of the climate crisis, predominantly caused by burning of fossil fuels.The RHS says home gardeners should stop growing cauliflower because of the change to the climate, adding many of its horticulturalists had stopped a long time before as planting cauliflowers had been so unsuccessful.The charity said cauliflowers and their close relative capabrese were thirsty and easily stressed in high temperatures, in which they fail to form a decent head. It recommends gardeners also reconsider planting other vegetables in the brassica family such as cabbages and brussels sprouts.View image in fullscreenCauliflower cheese may soon no longer feature in the British roast dinner.Photograph: Felicity Cloake/The GuardianGuy Barter, the RHS’s chief horticulturist, said: “Cauliflowers and their brassica cousins have been the hardest hit of those commonly found in domestic veg patches, and with summers likely to follow recent patterns, swapping them out for an equally as flavourful and nutritious alternative will save on all-important watering and provide a better guarantee of a good harvest.“There’s no doubt that we’re set to see tomatoes continue as the most popular summer vegetable, but with the likes of Asian loofah and okra cropping up more at mealtimes. Hopefully with recent rains we will see winter crops, carrots, leeks and brussels sprouts, make a recovery this year.”Horticulturalists in the charity’s gardens said they had been experimenting with alternatives to cauliflower.Simone Bratt, who tends the kitchen gardens at RHS Bridgewater, said she had not grown cauliflower for “a few years”. Growth had been “very hit and miss with the extremes of weather and we would only grow them as a late crop”, she said.“We tried a spring sowing again this year, but the heat really won. They bolted before we even got them in the ground. They simply haven’t been able to cope with the severity of the conditions, and need a lot of water and cool conditions.”Bratt added that purple sprouting broccoli was a good swap for cauliflower. “They also should cope much better as a ‘cut and come’ crop, rather than waiting for a single full head of calabrese or cauliflower.”View image in fullscreenGardeners will have to start rethinking what to plant.Photograph: Karen Robinson/The ObserverThe gardening charity said its members said the heat this year had allowed tomatoes and peppers to thrive outdoors, and that melon and watermelon could now be grown outside in some parts of the country, and where their watering needs could be met.Some gardeners have swapped from cauliflower to kale, as some kale is perennial, with deeper roots, so can better survive droughts.Gardeners have been able to grow cucumbers and sweet potatoes outside successfully, said Liz Mooney, a horticulturist on the edibles team at RHS Garden Wisley, in Surrey. She added she had not grown cauliflower this year, focusing instead on “warmth-loving crops”.Cat Hood, a horticulturist at RHS Hyde Hall in Chelmsford, Essex, said she had been experimenting with a range of warmer-climate vegetables, including chillies and okra.“We’ve had some really strong results from a number of crops this year,” she said. “Chillies, peppers and aubergines have all performed well in the outdoor beds, and we’ve had an amazing crop of loofah in the glasshouse. The okra have also done well, as have tortarello and carosello, the Italian heirloom cucumber-melons. A real surprise has been the yard-long beans, which have given us the best crop I’ve seen since I’ve been here, which I assume is because of the heat.”Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisVegetablesDroughtGardensExtreme heatEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We can see into the other room’: insurers face surge in subsidence claims | Insurance industry | The Guardian
description: Stressed UK homeowners tell of cracks opening up in the walls around them after two record-hot summers
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Stressed UK homeowners tell of cracks opening up in the walls around them after two record-hot summers
Content: A crack in Melissa's 1901 home in Walthamstow, north London, is big enough to hold a pencil.View image in fullscreenA crack in Melissa's 1901 home in Walthamstow, north London, is big enough to hold a pencil.Insurance industry‘We can see into the other room’: insurers face surge in subsidence claimsStressed UK homeowners tell of cracks opening up in the walls around them after two record-hot summersJulia KolleweSat 12 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“We’ve got one wall with an absolutely huge diagonal crack, through which we can see through to the other room; you could easily put your fingers in it and chunks of plaster are falling off,” says Henry Biggs, 49, from Stroud inGloucestershire.He and his partner started noticing cracks in their family home in June 2025, a few months after buying it, and filed an insurance claim for subsidence that was accepted by their insurer, Admiral, in the spring. Monitoring devices were only recently fitted, about a year after they first submitted the claim, and they have no idea when the damage might start to be repaired.They are among a growing number of UK homeowners who face subsidence after tworecord-hot summers. August was the joint-hottest month ever recorded around the world. Signs of subsidence include widening and lengthening diagonal cracks, typically around window and door frames, as well as sloping floors, and sticking doors and windows.Millions of homes are at risk of subsidencebecause of the worsening climate crisis, the British Geological Survey has warned. Under its worst-case scenario, 11% of UK homes could be at risk of subsidence by 2070, more than 4.2 million houses.Ashotter, drier summersand warmer, wetter winters become more frequent, the ground under houses can shrink and drag down a property’s foundations. Older properties with shallow foundations are more at risk, and those built on clay-rich soils. The most vulnerable areas include London, Essex, Kent and a tranche of land from Oxford up to the Wash on England’s east coast, according to scientists.Insurers have experienced a rise in claims for subsidence in recent months. Hastings says it hadrecord subsidence claims in August, up 140% on last August. So far in 2026, its claims are up by 30% year on year. Axa, one of the biggest home insurers, has talked of a “surge year” for subsidence, and Aviva is reviewing its reserves and pricing models.View image in fullscreenHenry Biggs says there are cracks throughout his house, door lintels have dropped and some doors won’t close.Photograph: Robin PhilpotDuring this year’s heatwaves the damage at Biggs’s house, which was built in 1970, worsened progressively. “There are cracks now throughout the house, diagonal cracks around almost every window, windows are getting harder to open and close, and the door lintels have dropped, so we have doors now that won’t close,” he says. “In the main part of the house, the kitchen, dining room, the hallway, the floor is dropping and cracking because it’s just falling away in the middle.”He adds: “It’s quite upsetting when you’ve just bought your first home, and we can’t even decorate at the moment.” The couple have hired their own loss assessor as subsidence claims tend to be complex and lengthy, often lasting several years.The average subsidence claim in the UK hit arecord £20,000between April and June, more than £2,000 higher than a year earlier, according to the Association of British Insurers (ABI). Insurers paid out £72m for domestic subsidence claims, compared with £60m in the same period last year.Timothy Farewell, a geospatial environmental data scientist, whose company MapleSky advises 20 insurers, as well as water companies, on ground movement, says: “We have seen widespread drying of soils across the UK in 2018, 2022, 2025 and 2026 leading to an uptick in the number of cracking houses, bursting water mains and failing roads.”It is all about “differential movement”, he says. “You can imagine if your house, road or pipe is built across two different soil types, with one soil more shrinkable than the other, then this differential movement is when you get significant problems, with one part moving more than the other. And differential movement could also happen when you have a tree on one side of the house that is drying out (and shrinking) the soil more on one side of the house than the other.”As old water pipes are more vulnerable than houses to ground movement, summer failures on the water network can indicate that the subsidence risk is increasing in that region. While fewer houses are built on peat-rich soils, movement in these soils has a considerable impact on rural roads and pipe networks, Farewell adds.Shaune Worrall, the deputy head of insurance of the BritishInsuranceBrokers’ Association, has warned of a “double surge” of claims, as many subsidence claims from last year are still being processed.graph showing Eastern England’s soils hit record dryness in summer 2026As well as environmental conditions, modern housing layouts can affect the risk, he says. Open-plan extensions, larger kitchens and interconnected living areas can mean that extensive structural repairs are needed.Subsidence excess is usually much higher than for other perils, and a figure of more than £1,000 has become common. This sum could rise to £10,000 for a property that has had subsidence in the past, despite underpinning works.Melissa, who works in the arts and has two children, says she and her husband “reluctantly” lodged an insurance claim for subsidence last month. While the cause of the extensive cracks in their 1901 home in Walthamstow, northLondon, is still to be determined, the couple felt they had no choice.“When we came back from holiday towards the end of August, our cracks had got a lot worse, in a short period of time. In some parts, wider than 1cm that you can fit a pencil in. Our front door was also sticking such that we could barely open or close it.”Structural engineers have still not been round to look at the damage, with long delays due to the general surge in insurance claims. Repair schedules will also be affected, with insurers stating months before remediation. Melissa says she has been warned that even if it turns out not to be subsidence, once a subsidence claim is lodged, “that will potentially affect your ability to get future insurance with other providers and will likely drive up your premiums”.View image in fullscreenA crack at Rachel Hogarth Smith’s late Victorian/Edwardian houseSeveral homeowners told the Guardian that they might not make an insurance claim for subsidence because they worry about rising premiums, or not being able to get insurance cover in future.Rachel Hogarth Smith, 58, a recently retired headteacher, says she has been “quite stressed” about subsidence at her late Victorian/Edwardian house. She has held off from making an insurance claim after her insurer warned her about the potential repercussions. She has been advised by a structural engineer to wait until the spring before doing any repair work, while an olive tree near the house should be removed because it sucks moisture from the ground, exacerbating the situation.“I’m now not opening any of the windows in the bay window because they’re sticking a bit and I don’t want to be in a position where I can’t get them closed again,” she says. “There’s a small gap between the skirting board and the floorboards underneath the bay so you can see daylight in between them.” If the subsidence remedial works end up costing a lot more than hoped, she may file an insurance claim after all.Modern homes are considered less vulnerable, but Richard Smith, the head of standards, innovation and research at the National House Building Council, says it is reviewing whether changes should be made to its standards.Subsidence claims can be costly and complex, but underpinning or other remedial work should resolve the issues.Sarah Dodd, founder of the law firm Tree Law, says: “In around 25 years working with tree-related subsidence cases [that led to legal disputes], I can recall fewer than 10 cases where significant subsidence has recurred following underpinning.”Explore more on these topicsInsurance industryPropertyExtreme weatherInsuranceLondonGloucestershirefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Beyond the heatwave: what it really takes for climate warnings to cut through in the UK | Extreme heat | The Guardian
description: As trust in institutions wavers, experts say local, collective action is more effective in driving change
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As trust in institutions wavers, experts say local, collective action is more effective in driving change
Content: More than a third of Britons feel that the Labour government has done a ‘bad job’ on climate issues since taking office in 2024.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMore than a third of Britons feel that the Labour government has done a ‘bad job’ on climate issues since taking office in 2024.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesExtreme heatAnalysisBeyond the heatwave: what it really takes for climate warnings to cut through in the UKNatalie WintAs trust in institutions wavers, experts say local, collective action is more effective in driving changeSat 12 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 12.38 EDTShareWildfires, excess deaths, hosepipe bans, school closures: this summer many British people have experienced the often devastating effects of the climate crisis in ways they had not before. In that sense, policymakers and climate experts have a unique opportunity to engage with the public about what needs to happen to better prepare the country for the years ahead. But as trust in institutions wavers – and yellowed, drought-stricken grass begins to recover – can the messaging cut through?This week,reflecting on a summer as “hot as hell”, the UN’s head of climate, Simon Stiell, said: “Climate is sometimes seen as a partisan issue, as territory in the culture wars. That is palpably false.”He said: “Climate cuts across the core concerns of voters, whatever their politics: [affecting] family health, community safety and economic stability; affordable food and available water; jobs, business costs and household bills.”In policy terms, there are two ways to lessen the impact: climate mitigation and climate adaptation. Mitigation involves reducing the emissions causing global heating, while adaptation is about responding to its impacts. For climate experts and policymakers, the distinction is important.But recentresearchconducted by Climate Outreach, a charity specialising in climate communication research, found that people in the UK do not generally divide climate action into these two categories. “People talk about them interchangeably,” said Chris Pollard, a senior researcher at Climate Outreach. Only about half of those in the study understood the term “climate adaptation”.However, the mixed response to thegovernment-issued “severe alert”to wildfire risk in mid-August highlighted the need for clearer communication on both.
