title: Julia Donaldson: ‘Am I the Gruffalo Granny? Not really. I’m the mouse’ | Julia Donaldson | The Guardian
description: As she introduces the latest member of her Gruffalo family, Julia Donaldson talks about storytelling, loss and the worries that come with being Britain’s all-time bestselling author
Author: Joanna Moorhead
Headline: As she introduces the latest member of her Gruffalo family, Julia Donaldson talks about storytelling, loss and the worries that come with being Britain’s all-time bestselling author
Content: Julia Donaldson, shot on location at Raffles London at The OWO.Photograph: Suki Dhanda/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJulia Donaldson, shot on location at Raffles London at The OWO.Photograph: Suki Dhanda/The GuardianJulia DonaldsonInterviewJulia Donaldson: ‘Am I the Gruffalo Granny? Not really. I’m the mouse’Joanna MoorheadAs she introduces the latest member of her Gruffalo family, Julia Donaldson talks about storytelling, loss and the worries that come with being Britain’s all-time bestselling authorSat 12 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 16.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1999 a journalist asked a then-unknown author to share her millennium wish. The author, who was 51 years old and had published only one book before, said she hoped her new one, out that year, would become a classic. “But then straight away I said: ‘Only joking!’ Because I didn’t want to sound full of myself, and I certainly didn’t think the wish would come true,” she remembers today.That author is Julia Donaldson; the book she published in 1999 was The Gruffalo; and, as you hardly need telling, her wish did indeed come true. And how. Since its publication, more than 18.2m copies of The Gruffalo and its sequel have sold worldwide. The Gruffalo’s Child was published in 2004, and together these tales of the terrible creature with terrible claws, and terrible teeth in his terrible jaws, have helped Donaldson to sell more than 50m books in the UK. In 2025 she was named the country’s bestselling author – across all genres, children’s and adult’s – since records began.Now the Gruffalo is making what Donaldson – who was made a dame in June – confirms will be his final outing. Gruffalo Granny, out this week, extends the protagonist’s family back a generation. In the new book, the Gruffalo and his daughter are awaiting a visit from Granny Gruffalo. The mouse, who played a pivotal role in the first and second books, is again centre stage; and longtime characters owl, fox and snake are all part of the action too.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: © Julia Donaldson and Axel SchefflerWhen we meet in a swish hotel in central London, I’m struck by the similarities between Donaldson and her new character. Her hair, like the Gruffalo Granny’s fur, is grey; in Donaldson’s case, it’s a neat bob, curled under at the ends. She is wearing a blue floral dress and navy shoes, and when she smiles her eyes twinkle; but I suspect that, like the Gruffalo Granny, she has prickles that reveal themselves when needed. What’s more, she has nine grandchildren, aged between five and 16. So is she the Gruffalo Granny?“Not really,” she says. “I’m the mouse.” The new book, she says, is a celebration of storytelling. “The mouse tells stories, then the Gruffalo’s child tells the stories to the granny, and the granny is going to read them back again. So there are three storytellers in the book – everyone apart from the Gruffalo.”The inspiration for the book – without plot-spoiling, though presumably there aren’t many under-sevens reading this – is Shahrazad from The Arabian Nights, who saves her life by never finishing her stories. “I had that idea and couldn’t think at first what the stories were going to be – and then I thought, why not use my own stories? It won’t be so much work for Axel [Scheffler, the Gruffalo’s illustrator] because he’s already done those pictures.” So the new book is a celebration of many of Donaldson’s earlier works. “It works well because a lot of the people who read this book will already have read the ones I refer to – Room on the Broom, Monkey Puzzle, and The Snail and the Whale. They’ve all been made into films, and they’re quite well known.”“Quite well known” is an under­statement: Donaldson isn’t just a children’s author, she’sthechildren’s author. Seeking out a book for my two-year-old grandson from Gatwick south terminal’s WH Smith a few days ago, I noticed every single book on offer in the picture book section of the small airport shop was by her. Is she concerned that, despite being a global champion of children’s literature, she has crowded out potential competitors – not to mention new talent? “I worry that some other author will stab me in the night,” she jokes. But yes, she is worried. “That’s why I have a project for the National Year of Reading [to compile] a list of recommendations of picture books not by me.” The project is still under wraps; an announcement is expected by the end of the year.double quotation mark‘Adult authors aren’t asked all the time why libraries are important. But children’s writers are seen as educators’Does the new book connect with what the former current children’s laureate, Frank Cottrell-Boyce (Donaldson held the post in 2011-13), has said about the power of storytelling in a digital age? “Yes, but that follows naturally from my plot line,” she says. “I wasn’t trying to remedy the situation – to be didactic.” The Gruffalo prickles hove into view: she is irked by what she sees as the media position that it is the responsibility of children’s authors to have views on issues to do with children and reading. “An adult author isn’t asked all the time about why libraries are important.” (Donaldson has, to be fair, done plenty of campaigning to keep libraries open.) It sometimes feels to Donaldson that we’ve “gone back to Victorian times … [Children’s authors] are seen as educators.”The new Gruffalo book highlights the role of a grandparent; so what kind of grandmother is Donaldson? “I teach them the card games that my grandmother used to teach me,” she says. “I do jigsaws with them, I play with them, and I read with them. I’m not so keen on changing nappies or doing the school run. ” Her grand­children also provide ideas: a new book, now being illustrated, is called Baby Grandpa. “That’s because my youngest grandchild is called Malcolm. When he was born my husband, Malcolm, was over the moon, and they asked the next one up, Rita, who was only 18 months, to do a video saying ‘Baby Malcolm’, but instead of that she said ‘Baby Grandpa’. And that’s such a good title for a book: I’ve written it in prose – about a grandpa and a baby with the same name.” Baby Malcolm, she says, “will probably be about seven when it comes out”.Sadly, Grandpa Malcolm didn’t live to see the book published: a consultant paediatrician based for much of his career in Glasgow, he died in 2024, aged 75. Losing him has been tough – “the fabric of your life totally changes” – but she had already faced tragedy with the death of their son Hamish, who had schizoaffective disorder and took his own life in 2003, aged 25. She doesn’t want to say much about it, she says, “but the thing is it wasn’t just the loss of a child, it was all the other things we faced because of what he was like – it was very hard times before he died”. His death was “devastating”, but living through the aftermath has helped her cope with losing Malcolm. “I know he’d be very proud of not just me but the boys [their other sons are Alastair and Jerry], who now play the guitars on the shows which he would have done.”View image in fullscreenIllustration undefined: Copyright Julia Donaldson and Axel Scheffler - Macmillan Children’s BooksAh, the shows: look online and you’ll find charming videos of Julia and Malcolm taking part in theatre performances and recording sessions,singing songsabout the Gruffalo and her other stories. Family members joined in, including her sons, grandchildren and her great-nieceLola Young, now one of the UK’s most successful singer-songwriters, whose 2024 single Messy reached No 1 in six countries and has been streamed more than a billion times. “Some people have said she’s a nepo baby but that’s ridiculous,” says Donaldson. “I’m as nepotistic as anyone. If I could have pulled any strings I would have done. But there’s no relationship whatsoever between the world of rock and pop music and the world of children’s books.” Donaldson lives in Sussex these days, and when Young played in Brighton she was in the audience. “I’m very proud of her,” she says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMusicality and family are the keys to Donaldson’s life and career: she and Malcolm kept on doing what they most enjoyed, alongside two illustrious careers. As students they had busked their way round Europe together; and growing older and becoming successful in other fields seemed no reason to stop. For Donaldson – who grew up in a musical family, with a mother who sang in a choir and a father who played the cello – it has brought balance into her life as a writer. Writing, she says, is “private and creative”; performing, along with book signings, gives her opportunities to meet people. “The variety is what I like.”As well as being a grandmother herself, she surely also drew on her memories of her own grandmother, who lived on one floor of the family house in Hampstead where she grew up with her parents and sister (another aunt and uncle had another floor). It was “like Milly-Molly-Mandy,” she says (in Joyce Lankester Brisley’s stories, three generations inhabit the same cottage); and her own grandmother bought her collections of fairytales – Hans Christian Andersen, retellings of Chaucer, myths – that she still has today. “I was heartbroken when she died. I was 16.”Julia and Malcolm met while studying at the University of Bristol, and went on to spend most of their married life living near Glasgow. Scots is one of the 119 languages and dialects into which The Gruffalo has been translated (Latin is another).Gruffalo Granny might be the end of the series, but it’s certainly not the end of Donaldson’s working life. She turns 78 next week, and her next book, Winifred Duck, will be out early next year with Scholastic. “It’s based on the true story of how a cargo of bath toys fell off a ship. They were carried around the world, and have helped oceanographers understand currents and tides.”Several others, including Baby Grandpa, are in the pipeline. “Every now and then you get an idea for another one, so it seems to keep ticking over.” And she’s lucky enough to know that, if she ever did stop writing, “I’ve still got the royalties coming in.” But she sees no reason to stop: “I can go on doing what I do as long as I’m fit enough, as long as I haven’t lost my marbles.” You get the sense of someone who, despite having been through tough times, is grateful for where she now finds herself. To borrow her own analogy, and in the words of the final page of the original Gruffalo book, she is the mouse who found a nut, and the nut is good.Gruffalo Granny is published by Macmillan (£14.99). title: Apocalypse: this end-of-days survival show is an absolute slam dunk  | Television | The Guardian
description: Geeks, toffs and biceps go to war in a wild survival experiment that answers that eternal question: if society collapsed, could you cope? This is going to be huge!
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: Geeks, toffs and biceps go to war in a wild survival experiment that answers that eternal question: if society collapsed, could you cope? This is going to be huge!
Content: Bertie looking at Scott in Apocalypse.Photograph: channel 4View image in fullscreenBertie looking at Scott in Apocalypse.Photograph: channel 4The watcherTelevisionApocalypse: this end-of-days survival show is an absolute slam dunkGeeks, toffs and biceps go to war in a wild survival experiment that answers that eternal question: if society collapsed, could you cope? This is going to be huge!Rhik SamadderSat 12 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHave you ever wondered how Cormac McCarthy’s wasteland novelThe Roadcould be made into a reality show? No? Well someone who works in TV has, so here we are. Who knows if they experienced a follow-up thought: that the instinct to package the end of the world as entertainment might be the most dystopian aspect of the whole enterprise, but hey. Apocalypse (Sunday 13 September, 9pm, Channel 4) launches this week, and people are buzzing!It’s a slam dunk for a show, because we’ve all run the thought experiment. If society collapsed, how would you get food and find shelter? Would you hunker down or forge alliances? To what depravities might you stoop without the rule of law? Apocalypse puts this empty talk to the test. Seven strangers are dropped at the edge of an abandoned town. They have no access to phones, light, electricity or infrastructure. They do have access to boarded-up supermarkets, desolate buildings, broken vehicles. How soon until they eat each other?I’d have loved to see this done with ordinary Joes off the street, like the first series of Big Brother. But we live in a different time, and so each of the volunteers is a “type”. There is inevitably a content creator, a Paralympian, a theatre director and an event emcee, who sounds plummier than nana’s crumble. There is useful testosterone to be found in the form of a diesel mechanic, and a square-bodied Australian hunter with a Crocodile Dundee accent thicker than his biceps. (I think he’s a cattle farmer, though it’s possible he works in Kettle Pharma.)Naturally, tensions spill over. When the team find live chickens near an abandoned trailer and a can of Spam, they become hysterical with joy. Crocodile Dundee, despairing of their sweetshop mentality, rations everyone to a quarter of a tomato a day. The geeks start muttering about a revolt. Starving and fractious, one positive is at least they’re not alone. On the downside, they’re not alone. Within hours of the contestants realising they are not the only team in the town, tribalism starts to do its thing.When the Spam is stolen, a full-scale battle is declared, and teams tool up with baseball bats. Resource scarcity does this. Some contestants go three or four days without eating. Even before things get that bad, anxiety is abnormally high. “It’s been 45 minutes, and tanks are running low,” gasps Kiera, a psychologist and self-identified princess. She is attempting to prise the boards off a food mart within one hour of arriving in the town, and I’ve never related to anything harder.The showHuntedhad us all imagining how we would go on the lam, evading the attention of the surveillance state. Apocalypse picks up the baton, imagining a world with no state whatsoever. It’s an omnipresent dread, thanks to climate crisis, global instability and AI-induced job despair. There have been countless wilderness survival shows, but none in an urban setting. This feels close to home.Here’s my hot take: I reckon most people think that when the apocalypse comes, they will secretly be good at it. They imagine finding high ground, teaming up with a doctor, foraging nuts from Tesco. Maybe they’ll repopulate the Earth with Dannii Minogue or something. Pure fantasy. As one mate cruelly framed my chances: “Your glasses will break on the first day, and then you’ll be screwed.” Joke’s on him; I never thought I’d be good. I panic when my phone drops to 4G. If the end of days comes, I will simply vomit and turn to the wall, well before my spectacles betray me.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionApocalypse will probably be huge. I found watching it depressing, because the mirror it holds up is not a flattering one. Loudmouths take charge, people steal and lie, dehumanise each other, thirst for violence. I’m sure the production has guardrails against how far they’ll go, and what they’ll show – I know the chickens’ chances don’t look good – but that’s not even the point. It’s a bleak view of us, the only certainty being that human nature will out. Maybe we’re all selfish when we’re lying in a hole in the ground. Cormac McCarthy would dig it.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe watcherReality TVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: surprise smash hit show Saturday Night Live UK is back! | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Jeff Goldblum is the first guest host and new faces join the comedy cast. Plus, another magnificent farewell to the Proms! Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Jeff Goldblum is the first guest host and new faces join the comedy cast. Plus, another magnificent farewell to the Proms! Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: New faces … Freddie Meredith joins Saturday Night Live UK.Photograph: Sky UK/Eva PentelView image in fullscreenNew faces … Freddie Meredith joins Saturday Night Live UK.Photograph: Sky UK/Eva PentelTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: surprise smash hit show Saturday Night Live UK is back!Jeff Goldblum is the first guest host and new faces join the comedy cast. Plus, another magnificent farewell to the Proms! Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Priya Elan,Jack Seale,Graeme VirtueandEllen E JonesSat 12 Sep 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 01.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSaturday Night Live UK10pm, Sky OneEarlier this year, pretty much everybody expected this US late-night import to fail. But it turned out to be such a hoot (mostly thanks to Jack Shep’s golden Princess Diana impression) that its return is a welcome relief to autumn nights. The comedy names that made it such a success are back – along with newbie Freddie Meredith – and they’re joined by the first celebrity host, Jeff Goldblum.HRLast Night of the Proms7.10pm, BBC TwoThe biggest night of the Proms and a bittersweet end to the season. Katie Derham and Nick Mohammed host the classical bonanza, ranging from Bernstein’s dazzling Overture to Candide to Holst’s buoyant Jupiter and hits from Guys and Dolls. As per tradition, Land of Hope and Glory et al marks the big end and can be seen on BBC One from 9pm.HRThe Celebrity Inner Circle8.15pm, BBC OneWith Britain’s Got Talent not returning until next year, Amanda Holden’s reign of Saturday night telly continues with season two of this QI-meets-The Traitors quiz show. Six contestants including a standup and a “retired granny” are paired with celebrities, as they outsmart each other until one of them goes home with £18k.Priya ElanThe Box8.15pm, ITV1Gary Lineker’s bafflingly contrived celebrity gameshow continues, randomly. After a witless debating task at the Oxford Union, Brighton beach at least offers the appearance of physical peril as the contestants swim in the murky sea. But if you can identify the point of any of what’s going on, you ought to win a cash prize.Jack SealeBeck9pm, BBC FourAnother chewy case for venerable cop Martin Beck (Peter Haber) and the Stockholm homicide squad. Their attempts to solve the gang-related murder of a 17-year-old girl are disrupted by a shotgun-wielding vigilante with street justice on his mind.Graeme VirtueChaka Khan: Radio 2 in the Park 202610pm, BBC TwoYou can catch highlights of the vintage pop festival at 9pm, featuring Lulu, Texas and Emeli Sandé. Then stick around for this full set from the queen of funk, Chaka Khan, with all the hits to sing along to, from Ain’t Nobody to I Feel For You and, of course, I’m Every Woman.HRFilm choiceIn the Grey, out now, Prime VideoView image in fullscreenDirty work … In the Grey on Prime Video.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyThere’s a conspicuous absence of cockneys in this new action thriller – but otherwise it’s your typical Guy Ritchie joint, elevated by the presence of Jake Gyllenhaal as Bronco Beauregard, one half of a glorified, globe-trotting debt-collecting duo with Henry Cavill as his more reticent other half, Sid. Eiza González is on – effectively – Miss Moneypenny duties as Rachel Wild, a lawyer who employs Bronco and Sid to do her dirty work (ie all the cool stunts), on account of their absolute willingness to operate in the legal-moral grey zone of the title.Ellen E JonesThe History of Sound, 7.50am, 2.50pm, Sky Cinema PremiereFeted young actors Paul Mescal and Josh O’Connor have teamed up for this melancholy romance about music and missed connection. Mescal plays Lionel, a gifted musician who meets a more scholarly academic, David (O’Connor), while studying at the New England Conservatory of Music, in the midst of the first world war. Reunited after armistice, the two travel around rural Maine together, recording their folk music on the new-fangled “wax cylinders” and – ultimately, fleetingly – falling in love. Director Oliver Hermanus’s previous work includes Living, the Bill Nighy-starring re-imagining of Kurosawa’s 50s classic Ikiru, and this is a similar symphony of longing and decade-spanning desire.EEJThe Red Shoes, 9.50am, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenSpectacular sissonnes … The Red Shoes on BBC Two.Photograph: The Archers/AllstarIf you’ve never seen Powell and Pressburger’s 1948 meta-dance-thriller, you’ve never seen the colour red. It’s that serious. Loosely based on Hans Christian Andersen’s gruesome fairytale, it revolves round aspiring ballerina Victoria Page (a resplendent Moira Shearer) and her toxic relationship with the world-renowned impresario Boris Lermontov (Anton Walbrook). Boris forces her to choose between her art and her love for composer Julian Craster (Marius Goring). But the story is near-irrelevant when the cinematography and choreography are this spectacular.EEJLive sportSolheim Cup Golf, 6am, Sky Sports Main EventDay two of the women’s competition.Premiership Rugby: Harlequins v Northampton Saints, 4.30pm, TNT Sports 2At Twickenham Stoop.Athletics: The Ultimate Championships, 5pm, BBC TwoDay two, with the women’s javelin.Premier Leage Football: Tottenham v Everton, 5pm, Sky Sports Main EventFollowed by Sunderland v Arsenal at 6.30pm on TNT Sports 1.Tennis: US Open, 8pm, Sky Sports Main EventThe women’s final.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Extended reality takes visitors from the ruins of West Bank to 17th-century Amsterdam at Venice Immersive | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: From frivolous to serious, virtual nosy passersby to the impact of climate change, the groundbreaking festival draws to a close – but this year the exhibits live on
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: From frivolous to serious, virtual nosy passersby to the impact of climate change, the groundbreaking festival draws to a close – but this year the exhibits live on
Content: High hopes … Everest: The First Ascent, part of the XR section of Venice Immersive.Photograph: Courtesy Venice film festivalView image in fullscreenHigh hopes … Everest: The First Ascent, part of the XR section of Venice Immersive.Photograph: Courtesy Venice film festivalVenice film festivalExtended reality takes visitors from the ruins of West Bank to 17th-century Amsterdam at Venice ImmersiveFrom frivolous to serious, virtual nosy passersby to the impact of climate change, the groundbreaking festival draws to a close – but this year the exhibits live onXan Brooksin VeniceSat 12 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first installation one encounters on visiting Venice Immersive, the film festival’s reliably head-spinning showcase for new media, is a chest-high metal box fitted with an eyepiece and two speakers. On peering inside you see a view of yourself from about 20ft above. You see the other guests walking past, a couple of pigeons on the ground. When one of these passersby lingers at your side for just a moment too long, the obvious impulse is to glance up from the eyepiece in order to see what they want. It is at this point that the experience blooms into a Lynchian nightmare.The passerby is not real – or rather, he’s only real in the box. He wears a blue suit and speaks with a heavy French accent and tells a tale that would sit badly in polite company. He says that I must have too much time on my hands, to stand hunched over this eyepiece for several minutes on end. “Why do people keep looking inside this box?” he demands. “What is it that they hope to see? It is not reality.”The name of Celine Daemen’s fabulous installation – Nothing to See Here – is immediately belied by the presence of 67 further exhibits (the organisers refer to them as “experiences”) arranged cheek by jowl on a small dedicated island. But the creepy Frenchman’s contention should not be so lightly brushed aside. Venice Immersive’s projects run the gamut from the frivolous to the serious, the escapist to the harrowing. But is the island a backwater or a new-found land? Does it represent reality or different versions of a dream?View image in fullscreenIs this real? … a visitor experiences the VR project Eyes of Shame at Venice Immersive.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockIncredibly, Venice’s vision of an immersive, interactive new media future is now 10 years old. In that time it has bloomed from a small sideshow inside the big Mussolini-era casino to a thriving 10-day event out on the lagoon. Attendance figures have shown a year-on-year increase and this is borne out by the external, more visible markers of success. There used to be one boat ferrying punters to the island. This year there are two, crisscrossing and sometimes berthing side by side so that passengers are forced to access one boat via the deck of the other. The bank by the lagoon was once a blighted strip of parched grass. It’s now home to a thriving shantytown of street food vans and stalls. The merchants of Venice, as ever, tend to follow the money.If Venice Immersive’s story thus far has been one of exponential growth – in visitor numbers, in tech, in the sophistication of the stories being told – there must come a point when growth is arrested or slips back – and maybe this, too, counts as a measure of underlying good health. I’ve gushed at some length about this event in the past. Each successive selection has felt like a giant leap forward. But just as the headline film festival can only be as good as the quality of work it receives, that’s bound to apply to Venice Immersive as well. The programme is strong; much of the work is astounding. But it still feels a notch down on 2025’s golden vintage.While headsets – once the future – continue to dominate, there’s now a new kid in town in the form of the lightweight XR (extended reality) glasses. These are being showcased on several projects including Nevatars, an interactive kids’ animation co-created by Andy Serkis. The glasses are great and deserve better than Nevatars, which is shrill and simplistic and a little too obviously indebted to Pixar’s Inside Out. It stirs a memory of those rudimentary first years on the island, when the stories tended to lag some way behind the tech.View image in fullscreenNew kid in town … a visitor wears XR glasses at Venice Immersive.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockSpace is at a premium on the island of Lazzaretto Vecchio, which presents a challenge to the makers of the larger installations. The smart ones are those that lean into the difficulty, folding the room like origami and making a bonus of confinement. Misa Haru’s Tomori uses the space brilliantly, opening sly peepholes on the virtual wall that indirectly invite the user to bop their head against the real one. Better still is Yuqi Zhang and Shixin Tao’s The Pigeon Ring, in which a fraught family drama is often glimpsed through half-open doors and closed windows. At one point, kneeling on the floor, we are made to peer into a television screen that shows an alternative parallel living room to the one we are in.Is this reality? It is at least grappling with it – and usually with more heart and vigour than most of the films in competition. Rory Mitchell and Nonny De La Pena’s Out of the Ashes provides a moving eyewitness account of the 2025 LA wildfires, complete with 3D reconstructions of the homes and neighbourhoods that were lost. Around the corner, Barthélemy Antoine-Loeff and Hugo Arcier’s The White Saboteur dares the viewer to direct their gaze at sections of a degraded polar landscape. Each time one does, the ice proceeds to melt and break down. I try not to look, but it is human nature to do so (just look at Lot’s wife). And this, I come away thinking, is the reason we all may be screwed.After a visit to Raj’in (We Shall Return) a 360-degree documentary about displaced communities in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, I sit down with its directors, Keren Manor and Faiz Abu Rmeleh. They made their film to bear witness, they explain, and record the on-the-ground realities of widespread settler violence. But the 360-degree footage also helps to digitally preserve a community that is fast being erased. “Since we started filming in the middle of 2023,” they say, “most of these places don’t even exist any more.”View image in fullscreenDelightful … Amsterdam 1652: The Hands of the City.Illustration: Made with Google AIWhat becomes of these works when they have all left the island? It’s the crashing in-built irony of Venice Immersive: the fact that these inclusive, interactive, often communal experiences remain out of reach to the average punter. That’s finally changing, say the event’s organisers, with an explosion of location-based exhibition spaces that can accommodate scores of people – especially in Asia, where the market is booming. When it comes to the smaller pieces, the XR glasses throw a lifeline. They look like chunky shades but provide full surround sound and vision.Many of the larger installations already have a berth in museums. That’s the case for Smithsonian Starstruck, a wafting journey through the cosmos. Also for Amsterdam 1652: The Hands of the City, a delightful historical tour of the old streets and docks that is the centrepiece exhibit of the ENTR VR Museum in the Netherlands. Museums may even be an option for Solwata, a portrait of flooded communities in the Solomon Islands that boasts powerful wraparound visuals and a voiceover by Mark Ruffalo.“To be frank, the exclusivity of the medium does annoy me,” says Felix Gaedtke, who created Solwata alongside Gayatri Parameswaran. “I want to be able to show it to as many people as possible. But with this the challenge is to find the right target audience.” Solwata, Gaedtke explains, is primarily an advocacy tool. It’s already been shown to members of the World Bank in Washington. In November he’ll be taking it to the UN Climate Change Conference in Turkey. “That might be a case of quality over quantity. It’s not showing it to thousands of people but maybe to a hundred who can make a real difference.”Where will the next decade take us? Nobody knows; they’re still tinkering with the map. How fast will we get there? Again, not a clue. But if one measures the success of a section by the entertainment value of the work, Venice Immersive has proved itself the equal of its cousins in traditional cinema. It’s groundbreaking, sometimes galvanising, playful and enraging. It’s telling fresh stories in new forms and invites the visitor to pitch in. Nothing to see here: just 68 illuminating windows on the world.Explore more on these topicsVenice film festivalFestivalsVirtual realityInstallationDigital artAugmented realityfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Scottish Ballet: Emergence review – riveting visions of gods and insects | Dance | The Guardian
description: The world premiere of Julia Cheng’s Entress and a bold return for Crystal Pite’s Emergence both explore collective power
Author: Róisín O'Brien
Headline: The world premiere of Julia Cheng’s Entress and a bold return for Crystal Pite’s Emergence both explore collective power
Content: Sensorial force … Rishan Benjamin (left) and Kayla-Maree Tarantolo in Entress.Photograph: Andy RossView image in fullscreenSensorial force … Rishan Benjamin (left) and Kayla-Maree Tarantolo in Entress.Photograph: Andy RossGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.DanceReviewScottish Ballet: Emergence review – riveting visions of gods and insectsTheatre Royal, GlasgowThe premiere of Julia Cheng’s Entress and a bold return for Crystal Pite’s Emergence both explore collective powerRóisín O'BrienSat 12 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is a significant moment for a choreographer to create work for a large ballet company for the first time. This is the thread that joins these two Scottish Ballet performances: the world premiere of Entress by Julia Cheng and a restaging of Crystal Pite’s Emergence, choreographed for the National Ballet of Canada in 2009 and first performed by Scottish Balletat the Edinburgh international festival in 2016.Coming from a varied dance background that includes hip-hop andwaacking, Cheng received Olivier nominations for her choreography for Cabaret and Fiddler on the Roof. She brings an assured patience to the myth-like Entress (from an old Scottish word meaning “right to enter”); scenes exploring groupthink, purging and transformation are allowed time to develop.Yann Seabra’s smartly designed set comprises a scratched black floor that rises halfway up the stage and a floating white sheet that hangs from the ceiling, a soft, open chrysalis. Nüwa (Rishan Benjamin), the Chinese goddess who created humanity, hovers aloft on the raised platform edge, distant from the darkly clad, crouched ensemble.View image in fullscreenA soft, open chrysalis … Julia Cheng’s Entress, designed by Yann Seabra.Photograph: Andy RossStanding alone is the nameless protagonist, the compellingly emotive Kayla-Maree Tarantolo. A pariah figure, she pulses and rebels against her group, who fly past and through her in scenes of increasing strain. Cheng is less focused on the dancers’ technique (though it’s there in nimble partnering and complex hand-patterns), and more on the sensorial force their collective impression makes.Under a capacious score by Isobel Waller-Bridge, flitting between tinkling keys and brooding strings, percussionist Beibei Wang brings momentum and palpable sonic texture. There’s a visual simplicity to the overall arc of Entress, even if the specific events of the story are sometimes hazy. Nonetheless, it’s an absorbing vision from Cheng.View image in fullscreenComplex machinations … Emergence by Crystal Pite.Photograph: Andy RossSeeing the dancers for Emergence creep through a large black eyelet at the back of the stage is a rare instance when a contemporary dance viewer can get genuinely giddy. Pite’s ability to craft physical complexity without losing thematic substance is unmatched.In this scuttling, twitching ballet, we see a mostly segregated hive; the female dancers dominate on their pointe shoes, whispering counts as their wooden blocks deliberately pound the dancefloor, adding to the cacophony of insect-like sounds in Owen Belton’s score. The men, each with black ink traced down their arms, hunch down then fearlessly slide across the floor in elastic contortions. There’s an order here – a frenzied, alien, and deathly beautiful order – but its complex machinations gleefully resist easy interpretation. It’s a bold entry from near the beginning of this choreographer’s astounding oeuvre.AtTheatre Royal, Glasgow, until 12 September. title: ‘I could get laid every night of the week!’: punk icon Legs McNeil on booze, benders and dating Sinéad O’Connor | Punk | The Guardian
description: As he releases a tell-all book, the Punk magazine founder and self-described ‘fuck-up’ holds forth on 1970s excess, the American roots of punk and why the Beatles are ‘stupid’
Author: Jim Farber
Headline: As he releases a tell-all book, the Punk magazine founder and self-described ‘fuck-up’ holds forth on 1970s excess, the American roots of punk and why the Beatles are ‘stupid’
Content: Legs McNeil, flanked by Richard Hell and Andy Warhol at Warhol's Factory, New York, 1976.Photograph: Roberta BayleyView image in fullscreenLegs McNeil, flanked by Richard Hell and Andy Warhol at Warhol's Factory, New York, 1976.Photograph: Roberta BayleyPunkInterview‘I could get laid every night of the week!’: punk icon Legs McNeil on booze, benders and dating Sinéad O’ConnorJim FarberAs he releases a tell-all book, the Punk magazine founder and self-described ‘fuck-up’ holds forth on 1970s excess, the American roots of punk and why the Beatles are ‘stupid’Sat 12 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 10.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLegs McNeil vividly remembers the reaction he got from the original CBGB bands in 1975 when they heard the name of the magazine he co-founded: Punk, the first publication ever dedicated to the form. “Absolutely noone wanted to be called a punk back then,” he said. “Not eventhe Ramones. Johnny Ramone demanded that we cross out every reference to punk in an article about them.”Flash forward a few years and, “suddenlyeverybodywanted to be called a punk!” McNeil said. “The Ramones started running around telling everyone, ‘you know, we were the first punk band!’”No doubt McNeil had something to do with that. After all, his affinity for the punk attitude and ethos ran so deep, he received billing in the magazine as its “resident punk”. As an illustration-heavy publication that was driven by the zany art of the magazine’s co-creator John Holmstrom, each issue presented McNeil as a consummately sly and seedy cartoon character, instantly transforming him into a real-life answer to Mad Magazine’s mascot of snark, Alfred E Neuman. “My only qualification was that I was this huge fuck-up,” McNeil said. “I was barely literate and I wasn’t much of a writer at the time. But I wasthat guy.”In a way, he still is. While the mission of this interview, which takes place at a diner in Brooklyn, is to delve into McNeil’s new memoir, titled Resident Punk: How I Smoked, Drank and Stumbled My Way Through the ’70sPunkScene (and Beyond), the opinions he spews today, at 70, are just as gleefully free of nuance as they were when he was the 20-year-old brat he channels in his prose. In a wide-ranging conversation (ie a rambling one), McNeil has this to say about the Beatles’ crowing achievement, Sgt Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band: “It’s a stupid record – except for that John Lennon song, A Day in the Life.”About Tom Verlaine, leader ofTelevision, one of the most vaunted bands to emerge from the club that launched punk, CBGB, he said, “He was full of shit, and he couldn’t sing.”On artists and academics: “You can flush ’em both down the toilet as far as I’m concerned.”On music criticism: “I hate it! Writing about music is not something that comes across on the page. I’d rather read about action and crime and war.”On the iconic rock critic Lester Bangs: “He smelled bad. And he started the worst band [Birdland] in the history of the world.”View image in fullscreenJoey Ramone and McNeil, 1978.Photograph: Tom HearnBut if McNeil’s sensibility has barely budged in the last five decades, his lifestyle has by miles. He left New York in 1998 when it became a place where “you couldn’t smoke anywhere”, eventually settling down in a town of 1,500 in Pennsylvania where he lives with his wife and dogs in a three-story brick farmhouse from 1870. “I moved to a place where I knew no one would ever ask me, “what were the Ramones really like?” he said. Helping to finance the move was the smash success of the book he co-wrote with Gillian McCain, Please Kill Me, the hilarious and definitive oral history of punk that has sold more than 2.5m copies worldwide since it was published in 1996. Its success floored him. “None of the bands we were writing about sold. Why would a book about them sell?” he said.His sole theory? “We put punk into a narrative that people could understand. Before that they really didn’t know what it was, or where it came from,” he said. “And we followed the story all the way through so that people thought, ‘Wow, this sounds like fun! We should have listened to this stuff the first time!”Of course, as a self-identified fuck-up, McNeil was no stranger to having his feelings and experiences ignored. In his book, he describes a childhood scarred by death, small-mindedness and his own hapless character. When he talks about that time now he sounds like a cross between a lost Ramones lyric and a scuttled Rodney Dangerfield routine. He was just three months old when his father died of stomach cancer at age 33. “My mother was pregnant with me the whole time he was dying,” McNeil said. “And I could never talk about my father because my mother would just start crying.”True to his contrary character, he considers not having a dad an advantage. “Everyone I knew kinda hated their father,” he said. “Every time I would cut through a Little League game there would be some father screaming at his kid, ‘pick up the goddam ball!” I thought, ‘thank God I don’t have that!’”View image in fullscreenMcNeil’s new book Resident Punk, out 15 September.Photograph: Courtesy of Simon & SchusterMoney was also an issue. (“We were the brokest people in Cheshire, Connecticut,” he said). He spent most of his childhood playing in a swamp near his house where he became friends with the local snakes, a pastime he found far more pleasurable than any group activity. “I HATED sports,” he said. “And I was really skinny, so everybody called me ‘faggot’.”Things didn’t go any better at home. “My mother and sister and brothers blamed me for everything,” he said. “And because most things actually were my fault, they were kinda right.”He was also relentlessly clumsy. (“I couldn’t open a box of cereal without getting it all over the floor.”) Part of that may have had to do with the fact that he was born with one leg shorter than the other, a circumstance that wound up serving as a metaphor for his entire worldview. “I was an asymmetric person living in a lopsided world,” he writes in the new book. “Nothing made any sense to me.”He was not able to get an operation to deal with his physical issues until he stopped growing in his mid-teens. “When I should have been out drinking and picking up chicks I was in a hospital,” he said. “I was in a full body cast and couldn’t walk for a year. I felt like I got hit by a train and I looked like a Picasso painting.”The operation proved a nightmare. “That doctor was a sadist,” he said. “They wanted me to get up out of bed after two weeks and I said, ‘I can’t. I’m going to pass out.’ So they gave me grape juice and I stood up and threw up and passed out. No one ever listened to me! So I started smoking in my room right next to the oxygen tank. I could have blown the whole place up, which I thought was kinda funny.”He found rare solace by checking out library books about history, folklore and war. But he would always lose them, along with seemingly everything else he came in contact with. “At the end of the school year I would go to the Lost and Found and every single thing in it was mine,” he said.View image in fullscreenMcNeil in 1976.Photograph: Tom HearnMcNeil finally stumbled into a kind of salvation when he ventured into New York City in 1975 with friends like Holmstrom where they happened upon the untamed brilliance blasting out of CBGB on the Bowery, the sleaziest downtown thoroughfare of the day. A born primitivist, he became obsessed with the stripped-to-the-bone guitar music of the Ramones. “They played these perfect two-and-a-half-minute pop songs,” he said. “To me, they were like the 1910 Fruitgum Company. It was bubble gum, which I loved!”Not only did he and the magazine champion the leading lights of CBGB, they also touted ones that never became famous, including the no wave outfit Steel Tips, whose frontman had a yen for exploding firecrackers under his armpits and an interest in playing venues like prisons and insane asylums. It was Holstrom’s idea to start a magazine to celebrate such folk. While the word punk had been used sporadically by various critics for at least five years, usually to describe garage rock, it hadn’t formalized into its own genre until the magazine came along. To underscore its ornery spirit, McNeil was given the nom-de-punk “Legs”. (Roderick is his real first name.) His primary motivation for going along was to get free beer and easy sex, which worked out great. “Girls recognized me from Holmstrom’s cartoons,” he said. “So, I could get laid every night of the week!”Along the way, he also developed creatively, conceiving key concepts for the magazine like an entire issue devoted to a punk noir story imagined as Italian fumetti comic strips. Barely two years into the magazine, the UK launched its own punk revolution – a far more successful one – igniting such a media frenzy that people everywhere began to think it all started in London instead of New York, an untruth that infuriates McNeil to this day. “Even my own mother called me and said, ‘punk started in England!’” he said. “You couldn’t win.”In retaliation, Punk Magazine continued to focus on the New York bands. In that pursuit, he became close with its emerging stars like Patti Smith – close enough, in fact, to question the stories they later sold to the public. When Smith published her universally admired book, Just Kids, McNeil found her dreamy presentation of her relationship with the gay photographer Robert Mapplethorpe a bit much. “While I don’t doubt that she loved him, to write all about the great romance they had was like, ‘oh, come on!’ And she won the National Book Award for that! Please Kill Me should have won the National Book Award!”At the height of the magazine, McNeil achieved his own kind of fame, earning the curious attention of literary stars like Norman Mailer and gawking features that presented him as a cross between a classic screw-up and a teen seer. At the same time, the magazine was a financial disaster, leading to its demise by 1979. McNeil went on to work for Spin Magazine, where he found his writing chops by penning stories like a cover piece onSinéad O’Connorat a time when she was barely known in America. In his book McNeil writes that, during the 80s, the super-hunky John F Kennedy Jr asked O’Connor for her phone number. She told him to “fuck off”, choosing instead to go out with McNeil. During their time together, he took her to a Harlem barbershop to fulfill her dream of getting a “tram line” haircut. “All the Black guys there were laughing at her,” he said. “No Irish bald woman had ever come in asking for that!”View image in fullscreenSid Vicious and McNeil, 1978.Photograph: Bob GruenAfter a spell at Spin, McNeil launched Nerve Magazine, serving as its editor-in-chief but the project died after six issues. “I was writing five- and ten-thousand-word stories right when the internet was starting up and making everything shorter and shorter,” he said.McNeil rallied big time with the 1996 publication of Please Kill Me. Originally, the book was just supposed to be an oral history on Dee Dee Ramone, but the tome’s co-author McCain realized “this story is so much bigger than that.” Its success made McNeil more famous than ever, which he detested. “People began staring at me,” he said. “I’m too self-conscious to be famous.”Leaving New York greatly eased that problem while doing no harm to his career. He went on to write an oral history of the porn industry and also co-authored, with McCain, a book called Dear Nobody: The True Diary of Mary Rose which captured the tortured words of a teenager who died at 17 after an epic struggle with cystic fibrosis, addiction and unraveling mental health. In the years since, McNeil had a total falling-out with Holmstrom. “He lies,” he said. “And when he did his book The Best of Punk, he cut out all my best stuff because he was so jealous that I became more famous than him!”Despite such slights, McNeil remains happy to have retained his reputation as punk’s original avatar. “I owe my whole career to that!” he said. “For a guy who was a total fuck-up somehow I ended up with a pretty enjoyable life.”Resident Punk: How I Smoke, Drank and Stumbled My Way Through the ’70s Punk Scene (and Beyond) by Legs McNeil with Crispin Kott is released on 15 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsPunkAutobiography and memoirBiography booksThe RamonesTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Eurovision made me realise that I was autistic at 34 | Eurovision | The Guardian
description: I had always dreamed of attending the song contest. But all that glitter brought on sensory overload – and I finally understood who I actually was
Author: Scott Bryan
Headline: I had always dreamed of attending the song contest. But all that glitter brought on sensory overload – and I finally understood who I actually was
Content: ‘Most of my youth had consisted of trying to work out how I could work at the contest if it ever ended up in the UK again.’Illustration: Martin O’NeillView image in fullscreen‘Most of my youth had consisted of trying to work out how I could work at the contest if it ever ended up in the UK again.’Illustration: Martin O’NeillMy cultural awakeningEurovisionEurovision made me realise that I was autistic at 34I had always dreamed of attending the song contest. But all that glitter brought on sensory overload – and I finally understood who I actually wasScott BryanSat 12 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheEurovisionsong contest meant a lot to me growing up. The eclectic performances. Terry Wogan’s despair. The yearly tradition of Greece giving “douze points” to Cyprus and Cyprus giving “douze points” to Greece.The hedonistic, unpredictable event playing out on my bedroom television couldn’t be further away from the idyllic yet conservative Dorset I grew up in. Most of my youth consisted of trying to work out how to perfectly align my future career so I could work at the contest if it ever ended up in the UK again, all while being confused by why my friends were not interested in my written analyses on each entrant.So you can imagine my delight when, 20 years later in 2023, Eurovision came to Liverpool. I was now a TV critic, and my job the week of the show consisted of writing detailed analyses on each entrant (fancy that). I was so excited that I turned up to collect my press accreditation at the Eurovision media centre before anyone else had even arrived.There is far more to Eurovision week than just Saturday’s grand final – it is a washing machine of noise and publicity. Think of it like a general election but with a glitter cannon thrown in. It started well enough. I attended rehearsals and even got a selfie with Andrew Lambrou, the Cypriot entrant with the huge arms.Yet as the week went on, and the Liverpool Arena was transformed into one of the biggest TV studios in the world, I started to feel a weird fuzz, like static electricity, throughout my body. It was not painful, but never comfortable. Before I knew it, I was in the men’s toilet, curled into a ball.It was the only place that I could decompress. I had nowhere else to go. I couldn’t go outside to Liverpool’s Pier Head because the English National Opera were playing Eurovision hits. I couldn’t go to the media centre because vloggers were cheering on their favourite by standing on their tables. I left the loo after feeling like my brain was caving in on itself, only to hear the booming voice of host Hannah Waddingham rehearsing in French.double quotation markI left the loo feeling like my brain was caving in, only to hear the booming voice of Hannah Waddingham rehearsing in FrenchThe fuzz caused some surreal moments. I remember taking a breath while sitting on the pavement,hoping I was alone, only to look up and see the then BBC director general popping out for a sandwich. At the grand final that Saturday, I watched the Finnish entrant Käärijä form a kind of human centipede with his fellow dancers, my body feeling like a church spire that had been struck by lightning.When I mentioned it – now quite dismissively – to a mate a few weeks later, he suggested I should look into an autism diagnosis, which I later received, at the age of 34. This late diagnosis gave me a wave of emotions, along with explanations for why I have found it hard to make eye contact with strangers at a queer club (as well as why I’ve Googled “how to flirt”, as if love had the same instructions as assembling furniture). I have gradually accepted that sensory overwhelm might be here to stay – unless I make adjustments and take some time out when it all gets a bit much.Yet I feel grateful for my autism, too. Many autistic people have a special interest as a way to self-regulate. Mine happens to be television (including Eurovision), a subject I have built my career around. I doubt I would have got this career without my encyclopedic knowledge of TV. And if nothing else, I am useful at a pub quiz.I find it ironic that, all my life, I thought it was my destiny to work at Eurovision, but when I finally got there I found it a bit much. Yet the event changed me just as much an adult as it had when I was a child. And while it’s possible thatI may have later stumbled my way into a diagnosis, if my realisation had happened anywhere other than at Eurovision, under all that glitter, it wouldn’t have been as much fun.Out Now: A Queer Journey Through Modern Televisionby Scott Bryan is published by Blink.Share your cultural awakeningsShare your experiencesYou can tell us how a cultural moment has prompted you to make a major life change by filling in the form below or emailing us on cultural.awakening@theguardian.com.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish.
