title: ‘I love a bit of mischief!’ Liza Tarbuck on why she’s swapping her Radio 2 mic for a potter’s wheel | Television | The Guardian
description: Her riotous weekly show had an army of devoted fans. Now Tarbuck has joined the ranks of star presenters leaving the BBC – and she’s getting her hands dirty
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: Her riotous weekly show had an army of devoted fans. Now Tarbuck has joined the ranks of star presenters leaving the BBC – and she’s getting her hands dirty
Content: ‘It’s the stuff of dreams!’ Liza Tarbuck doing her Radio 2 show.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreen‘It’s the stuff of dreams!’ Liza Tarbuck doing her Radio 2 show.Photograph: BBCTelevisionInterview‘I love a bit of mischief!’ Liza Tarbuck on why she’s swapping her Radio 2 mic for a potter’s wheelMichael HoganHer riotous weekly show had an army of devoted fans. Now Tarbuck has joined the ranks of star presenters leaving the BBC – and she’s getting her hands dirtySat 12 Sep 2026 04.22 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 16.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAtragedy. A national disaster. A loss to the cultural landscape that should be discussed in parliament. These were just a few listener reactions when Liza Tarbuck left herRadio 2show earlier this year. “I was bereft about it, too,” sighs Tarbuck. “I miss angsting over the playlist. I miss the texts and emails. For two hours every weekend, we were a proper gang.”Tarbuck hosted her Saturday evening show for 14 years, building it into the funniest show on British radio. Her riotous mix of freewheeling chat and hand-picked tunes (the music could span nine decadesin the same show) drew an audience of 2 million, and received more messages from listeners – 50 per minute – than any other programme on the station.Allow TikTok content?This article includes content provided byTikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueIt became a cult phenomenon thanks to its running jokes, hilarious crowd-sourced stories and Tarbuck’s anarchic links to the 7pm news bulletin (“Smell that fromage! We interrupt this fun to bring you some miserable news”). “I love a bit of mischief,” she chuckles. “It’s like nectar to me.”She called it “by appointment radio” and it was, attracting a loyal fanbase – including many fellow broadcasters. Regular listeners were dubbed “the hivemind” or “the murmuration”.The final edition aired in January but her departure wasn’t confirmed until March, when Tarbuck posted a heartfelt, hand-written farewell message on Instagram. “I think you’ve guessed,” she wrote. “Some fool left a door open and I sneaked out. A French exit. Together we made two hours of radio feel like a private members’ club. That’s the stuff of dreams. Thank you for letting me in, it’s been a privilege.” Many devotees were distraught. They still take to social media each Saturday to compare it to missing a friend.View image in fullscreenTarbuck as Siobhan in The Change.Photograph: Channel 4Mystery swirled around her departure. Over a video call overlooking her verdant London garden (“My top tip is pots with drip trays”), Tarbuck cheerfully shrugs this off. “Lots of people, very kindly, thought I was ill or my parents were ill, but that wasn’t the case,” she says. “I was at Radio 2 on and off for 36 years in total. I realised it was time to go. The messages I received were deeply moving.”She joined a talent exodus from the station in recent years, following the likes of Ken Bruce, Zoe Ball and Simon Mayo, as well as the late Paul O’Grady, out of the Broadcasting House door. “The talent leaving Radio 2 tells its own story,” she says. “It’s no wonder people get upset by it. Listeners have allowed us into their home, which is a precious thing and should never be taken for granted. That’s why the audience take it personally.”She laments the loss of such stalwart names and maverick talents. “TheBBCneeds high standards and a certain level of curation because it’s a world leader. Ever since we were all sat in front of Bill & Ben or Blue Peter, it was the place to be. But you can’t live off that reputation for ever. You have to keep it being the place to be. You do that by pushing the boundaries and not worrying about what commercial radio is doing. Let them do it. It doesn’t matter.”Fans retain hope for a triumphant return to the airwaves. “Maybe there will be a comeback in some form,” she says. “I genuinely don’t know. I couldn’t do a show that didn’t have music flowing through it, and the difficulty is how to pay the artists. But I’m figuring that out.” So the murmuration should keep the faith? “Always. We’re all still out here, flying in some line of formation.”View image in fullscreenTarbuck (right) with Emma Wray in Watching.Photograph: Cinematic/AlamyThe 61-year-old actor and broadcaster – daughter of comedian Jimmy – has enjoyed an eccentrically eclectic career. After making her name in long-running ITV sitcom Watching, she took the lead in Linda Green, Paul Abbott’s BBC comedy-drama. More recently, she appeared inBridget Christie’s menopause comedy The Change and played Anne Hathaway in Ben Elton’s Shakespeare sitcom Upstart Crow.She has presented everything from The Big Breakfast to Britain’s Top Dog. Tarbuck even won Taskmaster while wearing asurprisingly convincing false beard. “It was eight years ago but people still stop me to talk about the beard and the BMXing,” she laughs.Now she is returning to TV to present The Great Celebrity Pottery Throw Down. This fresh twist on Channel 4’s ceramic contest sees six celebrities roll up their sleeves, brave the wheel and battle the clay. Across five weeks, the contestants – comedians Lucy Beaumont, Richard Herring and Fatiha El-Ghorri, former footballer Paul Merson, actor Layton Williams and presenter Denise van Outen – make everything from raku animals to garden gnomes.View image in fullscreen‘It’s inspiring!’ … Tarbuck with judges Keith Brymer Jones and Rich Miller on The Great Celebrity Pottery Throw Down.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Channel 4In the process, they blossom under the expert eye of judges Keith Brymer Jones and Rich Miller. “Keith is fabulous,” says Tarbuck fondly. “A really good laugh. But trust me, Rich is the one slyly holding it all together. They’re both open-hearted and emotionally intelligent, which is a lovely quality in men of a certain age. That makes it a safe space and brings people’s barriers down. Celebrities aside – what a horrible label – they’re just humans. Keith said to me early on: ‘Just watch the clay work as therapy,’ and it really did.”El-Ghorri makes a cathartic cancer confession. Beaumont and Williams find pottery helps with their recent ADHD diagnoses. Merson plans to continue the hobby beyond the series because it helps him stay in the moment – which he needs as a recovering addict. He believes ceramics classes should be offered in rehab. “Mr Merson’s got a great slant on things,” says Tarbuck. “He’s a blokey bloke but he’s done so much work on himself. He’s great company and very intelligent. Although he’d hate me saying that.”Her favourite contestant, however, was Beaumont. “I just love Lucy, she’s so ‘other’,” laughs Tarbuck. “She has an unbelievable brain, but bless her, she had a nightmare. Every time she emerged from the drying room, her hair would be full of fine clay dust. She was furious but in a hilarious way.”There’s a dramatic droppage (“I was terrified that I’d break something but thankfully it wasn’t me”) and some trademark blubbing from Brymer Jones. “‘Keith the Weep’ set me off once,” admits Tarbuck. “Somebody really needed praise at that time and, seeing how it was received, that’s what made me go. It was tangibly moving.”Over the heartwarming series, these rookie potters display real progression. “Growth definitely happens,” nods Tarbuck. “It’s inspiring TV. I enjoy [sister show] The Great British Sewing Bee because I leave that programme thinking I can make a jacket. I have a go and end up with a wrap skirt. That’s happened three times.”She’s more of a ceramic collector than a maker herself, Tarbuck confesses, but she relishes crafting. “I’m quite handy. I paint. I garden. I’m into beading and mosaic. I think it comes from having an airy-fairy job where there’s nothing tangible at the end. As an antidote to acting and presenting, you make something you can put your hands on and go: ‘Look what I did today!’ It helps me stay sane and grounded.”It’s a treat to have Tarbuck back on our screens and she’s quietly plotting more projects. “I’ve got a good idea for a Time Team type of show. Roaming the British isles, having a dig around. History is entrancing. You’ve got to keep the creative possibilities bubbling. I do something nice and mundane like walking the dog [she has a Portuguese podengo called Ringo] and all sorts of ideas start percolating. All I can do is keep pushing them out there and some will stick.”Meanwhile, the murmuration should watch this space. “I’m interested in the immediacy of YouTube,” she says. “I don’t know much about Patreon but I’m assured that would be a good platform if I were to do a radio show. But it’s not just about radio – it’s about variety. You can sit and wait for an acting job to come in, but I don’t know how much good that does you. Sometimes you have to branch out and be brave. Why limit yourself?”The Great Celebrity Pottery Throw Down starts on 13 September on Channel 4Explore more on these topicsTelevisionRadio 2Channel 4The Great Pottery Throw DownBBCTelevision industryRadio industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tim Dowling: how not to interview eminent scientists – a control freak’s guide | Family | The Guardian
description: It was supposed to be a meeting between a great mind and mine. Instead, I was plunged into darkness and did some swearing
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: It was supposed to be a meeting between a great mind and mine. Instead, I was plunged into darkness and did some swearing
Content: Illustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianThe Tim Dowling columnFamilyTim Dowling: how not to interview eminent scientists – a control freak’s guideIt was supposed to be a meeting between a great mind and mine. Instead, I was plunged into darkness and did some swearingTim DowlingSat 12 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 12.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe transition to owning an electric car is in its final phase: our electricity supplier is set to install a smart meter in conjunction with a special tariff that will allow us to charge the car cheaply in the dead of night. After that, all I have to do is live long enough to see a return on my considerable investment.In the meantime – as sometimes happens in the course of my work – I need to interview some eminent scientists. In my experience eminent scientists are easy to reach – they tend to be attached to academic institutions that readily provide their contact details – and surprisingly willing to spend an hour explaining their work to a moron. But there is always a period – the long interval after I’ve emailed four or five, and before any of them have answered – that I begin to suspect a conspiracy of silence. What is it, I think, about my oily emails that they don’t like?When I go to bed that night, I still haven’t heard back from anybody. I wake at 7am and immediately check my phone: nothing.“Why are the scientists ignoring me?” I say.“What?” my wife says, looking up from her own phone.double quotation markI move my laptop to its optimal Zoom meeting angle, so my head is framed by bookshelves“Nothing,” I say. “A work thing.”“The smart meter man just texted to say he’s coming between 12 and 12.30,” she says. “Will you be in?”“Yes,” I say. “I will be here, trying to find five other scientists.”Four hours later I’m sitting in my office shed, composing another oily email, when my wife leans in the door.“I’m popping out,” she says. “Don’t forget about the man.”“What?” I say, “Yeah, no, fine.”I spend some time staring into space. When I look at my computer screen, I see a new email in my inbox, from an eminent scientist: he is happy to be interviewed, he says, but it needs to be in the next 45 minutes. I check the time difference: five hours. He is evidently up very early in an effort to accommodate me.Of course! I reply. I arrange a Zoom meeting in 30 minutes. I track down the notepad with my questions on it. I move my laptop to its optimal Zoom meeting angle, so my head is framed by bookshelves. I lay my phone on the desk to record the meeting, as a backup. I review the scientist’s biography on his institution’s website. Then I remember the meter guy. I ring my wife.Tim Dowling: my TV contract has run out – and so has my patienceRead more“Where are you?” I say.“Walking towards the front door,” she says.“Oh good,” I say. “So you’ll be here to let the man in?”“I’m here now,” she says.“Because it turns out I will be interviewing an eminent scientist at that time,” I say.“OK,” she says. “I’ll deal with it.”I adjust my chair. I check my questions again. I look toward the house in time to see a figure backlit by the open front door: the meter man arriving, exactly on time.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI enter the Zoom meeting space five minutes early, and centre my head on the screen. One minute before the scheduled start time, I begin recording on my phone. All the elements of my control-freakery are falling into place.Suddenly my desk lamp goes off. At the same time, my computer screen dims, and the picture of me freezes. The wifi signal is gone.double quotation markThe recording on my phone does not pick up my laboured breathing, or the thudding of my heartI have no memory of the next 30 seconds, but they are captured for posterity by the automated transcription service I use:Speaker 1: What is happening?Speaker 1: Oh my God, He’s turned off the electricity!Speaker 1: Holy shit! Um. Come on! What do I do?I stand up and run into the house, where I find a man in a polo shirt bearing the logo of my new electricity provider, with a length of cable in his hand.“Did you just turn off the electricity?” I say.“Yes,” he says.“For how long?” I yell.“About 40 minutes,” he says.“Fuck!” I scream. This is to be our only interaction.I run back to my office. After three further minutes of blind panic, I realise I can access the internet via my phone’s personal hotspot. I re-enter the Zoom meeting, where the eminent scientist is waiting patiently.The recording on my phone does not pick up my laboured breathing, or the thudding of my heart. All you can hear is my apology, followed by the hour-long interview, punctuated by the steady pinging of new emails arriving: all the other scientists, getting back to me.Explore more on these topicsFamilyThe Tim Dowling columnfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: Straw bales, tweed and a vintage Massey Ferguson – this is how farmers get married | Farming | The Guardian
description: Ravenstonedale, Cumbria: The wedding day of my son and his now wife – both farmers – was full of both emotion and tradition
Author: Andrea Meanwell
Headline: Ravenstonedale, Cumbria: The wedding day of my son and his now wife – both farmers – was full of both emotion and tradition
Content: Hector and groomsmen on a tractor on their way to the church.Photograph: Andrea MeanwellView image in fullscreenHector and groomsmen on a tractor on their way to the church.Photograph: Andrea MeanwellCountry diaryFarmingCountry diary: Straw bales, tweed and a vintage Massey Ferguson – this is how farmers get marriedRavenstonedale, Cumbria:The wedding day of my son and his now wife – both farmers – was full of both emotion and traditionAndrea MeanwellSat 12 Sep 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 03.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt felt as if autumn had arrived in the Howgills earlier this week, so it was a great relief that the wedding day dawned dry. I was up early checking the stock before helping the six groomsmen get their cufflinks and bow ties on in the farmhouse kitchen.Our middle son, Hector, was marrying Georgia from a farm in the nearby village of Ravenstonedale. The wedding was taking place in the village church, and the reception on her family’s farm.Hector is county chair ofCumbria Young Farmersand over 300 were invited to the evening reception. The organisation has been an invaluable social network for Georgia and Hector, and they both have leadership roles in their local groups.View image in fullscreenGeorgia and bridesmaids outside St Oswalds church.Photograph: Andrea MeanwellThe groomsmen were all dressed in tweed, and travelled from our farm to the village sitting on bales of straw in a trailer attached to a beautiful vintage Massey Ferguson tractor. Meanwhile, I drove behind with my hazards flashing and ribbons all over my Land Rover.It is still common for young farmers in our area to have a traditional church wedding and make sure that local traditions have been honoured. I had found a big old horseshoe in one of our barns and painted it to give to Georgia after the wedding for good luck.Another of the local customs is that children tie the gates of the churchyard closed with string, and won’t untie it until they are given money after the service, so we had bags of coins for Hector to throw to them. Outside the church, more young farmers were dressed in white show coats holding decorated hay forks to make an arch.Family and friends were gathered in the church. The 18th-centurySt Oswaldswas decked out in autumnal bloom; the church is unusual as the pews face the centre of the church, so when Georgia arrived with her dad we were all looking towards them as they walked along the aisle.It was a happy day, not a day for tears, but when I saw Georgia, and when my dad and oldest son, Oscar, surprised us by singing Stand By Me to the happy couple, I did get a lump in my throat.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsFarmingCountry diaryMarriageRural affairsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Meera Sodha’s vegetarian recipe for mushroom claypot rice | Vegetables | The Guardian
description: I’m taking a break to replenish my creative reserves. Until then, I leave you with this champion champignon number
Author: Meera Sodha
Headline: I’m taking a break to replenish my creative reserves. Until then, I leave you with this champion champignon number
Content: Meera Sodha’s mushroom claypot rice.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.View image in fullscreenMeera Sodha’s mushroom claypot rice.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.Meera Sodha recipesVegetablesMeera Sodha’s vegetarian recipe for mushroom claypot riceI’m taking a break to replenish my creative reserves. Until then, I leave you with this champion champignon numberMeera SodhaSat 12 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the nine years that I’ve been writing this column, I’ve had two babies,a breakdownand very little time away from writing a weekly recipe. I love this column, and creating recipes for you makes me feel like the luckiest duck alive, but I don’t believe that anyone can be endlessly creative without occasionally filling up their own cup. So, I’m taking six months out to travel, replenish and see what treasures I can find for us out there in the big wide world. Treasures such as this gentle claypot rice, which is based on the magical one atDongnae in Bristol. Until then, so long.Mushroom claypot riceYou’ll need a casserole pot with a tight-fitting lid. Weighing the stock will ensure just the right amount of liquid to rice, so use digital scales, if possible.Prep10 minSoak30 minCook1 hrServes4400g white short-grain rice, or sushi rice60g (4 tbsp) light soy sauce60g (4 tbsp) Shaoxing wine30g (2 tbsp) mirin15g white-wine vinegarFine sea salt400g mixed enoki, shiitake, king oyster and oyster mushrooms4 tbsp neutral oil– I use rapeseed2 tbsp toasted sesame oil10 spring onions(100g), whites and greens trimmed, finely sliced and washed1½cm x 1½cm piece fresh ginger, peeled and finely minced2 large garlic cloves, peeled and minced4 eggs(medium or large ones)Put the rice in a large bowl, cover with cold water, then swish with your hands until the water turns cloudy. Pour away the water, then repeat five more times, until the water is clear-ish. Leave the rice to soak in cold water for 30 minutes, then drain.Meanwhile, weigh out the soy sauce, Shaoxing wine, mirin and vinegar into a jug, add 380ml water and half a teaspoon of salt, and mix well.Tear the oyster mushrooms into 2cm-thick strips and chop the shiitake into ½cm-thick slices. Put three tablespoons of neutral oil in your widest frying pan on a medium to high heat. When bubbles form around a wooden spoon, add half the mixed mushrooms, or as many as will fit without (really) overlapping, and leave for three to four minutes without touching them. Turn over the mushrooms and cook for another three to four minutes, or until beautifully bronzed all over. Transfer the mushrooms to a plate, season with a big pinch of salt, then repeat with the remaining mushrooms; add a drizzle of more oil, if need be.Put the last tablespoon of neutral oil and the sesame oil in a casserole pot on a medium heat. When it’s hot, add the spring onions, ginger and garlic, and fry for two minutes, until the onions are Kermit-green and the garlic smells good. Add half the fried mushrooms, mix, then add the drained rice and mix again.Add the stock and bring to a boil. Scatter the remaining mushrooms evenly over the top and pop on the lid. Turn down to a simmer and leave the rice to cook for 15 minutes. Take off the heat and, with the lid on, leave to rest for 10 minutes.In the meantime, soft-boil the eggs (for a soft, slightly jammy egg, I cook medium eggs for six and a half minutes), then peel them.Divide the mushroom rice between four bowls, use the back of a spoon to make a dent in the middle of each portion and serve with two soft-boiled egg halves (or a raw egg yolk, to be stirred in before eating).Explore more on these topicsVegetablesMeera Sodha recipesFoodRiceEggsMain courseKorean food and drinkAutumn food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Blind date: ‘He probably thinks I hold a lot of strong opinions on frivolous matters’ | Dating | The Guardian
description: Joe, 27, works in advocacy at a charity, and meets Jade, 29, a PR account manager
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Joe, 27, works in advocacy at a charity, and meets Jade, 29, a PR account manager
Content:
Composite: Christian Sinibaldi and David LeveneView image in fullscreenComposite: Christian Sinibaldi and David LeveneBlind dateDatingBlind date: ‘He probably thinks I hold a lot of strong opinions on frivolous matters’Joe, 27, who works in advocacy at a charity, meets Jade, 29, a PR account managerSat 12 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJoe on JadeView image in fullscreenWhat were you hoping for?Human connection outside an algorithm – good conversation and a fun anecdote.First impressions?Jade was friendly and the conversation flowed easily from the get-go.What did you talk about?Favourite Doctor Who episodes (The Girl in the Fireplace, obviously). The joys of London in the summer. Favourite gig venues. The need for the transatlantic accent to return.Most awkward moment?A slight disagreement about whether the BT Tower is evil – I begged to differ.Good table manners?Impeccable from my end.Best thing about Jade?She has a clear sense of what she wants in life. And excellent chat.Would you introduce Jade to your friends?Sure thing.Q&AFancy a blind date?ShowBlind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two 
strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans 
to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we 
take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the
 UK) and online attheguardian.comevery Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you canread all about how we put it together here.What questions will I be asked?We
 ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of
 person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions 
cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.Can I choose who I match with?No,
 it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, 
preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely 
to be.Can I pick the photograph?No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.What personal details will appear?Your first name, job and age.How should I answer?Honestly
 but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that
 Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.Will I see the other person’s answers?No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.Will you find me The One?We’ll try! Marriage! Babies!Can I do it in my home town?Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.How to applyEmailblind.date@theguardian.comWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Describe Jade in three words.Open, enthusiastic, fun.What do you think Jade made of you?Probably too many gesticulations, but otherwise, hopefully, normal enough.Did you go on somewhere?No, she had an early flight, but we made a pretty good dent in the Guardian’s tab at the restaurant!And … did you kiss?No, merely a hug on the Mildmay line on the way home.If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be?It was a lovely evening, so no complaints here.Marks out of 10?8.Would you meet again?We have exchanged numbers!View image in fullscreenJoe and Jade on their dateJade on JoeView image in fullscreenWhat were you hoping for?To make a connection with someone and have a good story to tell our future pets.First impressions?Cute and well dressed.What did you talk about?Books. Family pets. Our favourite parks in London. The housing crisis. The constant yearning to be by the sea when you grew up by the coast. Debating whether it’s better to be a reality TV villain or completely erased from the final cut for being too boring.Most awkward moment?We got right into chatting and I wasn’t prepared when they came to take our order – so had to ask for extra time.Good table manners?He kept my water glass full and humoured my plan to say cheers with every new drink.Best thing about Joe?He was really fun to talk to. We were on the same wavelength on a lot of things, but it was also fun to discuss when we weren’t.Would you introduce Joe to your friends?I would.Describe Joe in three words.Intelligent, thoughtful, affable.What do you think Joe made of you?Probably that I’m very talkative and hold a lot of strong opinions on frivolous matters.Blind date: ‘She’s one of the easiest people to talk to that I’ve ever met’Read moreDid you go on somewhere?I had to catch an early flight the next morning, so we parted ways on the Overground.And … did you kiss?Just a hug goodbye.If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be?I would have enjoyed staying out a bit later – I doubt it would have made my 5am start the next day much harder.Marks out of 10?9.Would you meet again?Yeah! We’re in touch about planning our next outing.Joe and Jade ate attheBull& Last, London NW5. Fancy a blind date? title: Is university still worth it? What you need to know before committing  | Higher education | The Guardian
description: With AI, an unsettled jobs market and rising student costs, it’s crucial to make the most of your experience
Author: Sally Weale
Headline: With AI, an unsettled jobs market and rising student costs, it’s crucial to make the most of your experience
Content: A degree is costly in time and money, but the personal rewards can go beyond the merely financial.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA degree is costly in time and money, but the personal rewards can go beyond the merely financial.Composite: Getty ImagesUniversity Guide 2027Higher educationIs university still worth it? What you need to know before committingWith AI, an unsettled jobs market and rising student costs, it’s crucial to make the most of your experienceSally WealeSat 12 Sep 2026 02.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“To me it’s definitely still worth going to university – absolutely it is,” says Nick Hillman, chief executive of the Higher Education Policy Institute thinktank. “I’ll certainly be urging my children to go on to higher education,” he adds. “Relative to everything else, it’s still a very, very good bet.”Yet the national conversation around universities in recent months has been relentlessly negative. Rising tuition fees, spiralling studentdebtand thefinancial crisisgripping many institutions are more than enough to give pause to sixth-formers currently trying to decide whether it makes sense to go on to university.Reportsthat graduate job vacancies in the UK have sunk to their lowest level since tracking began a decade ago have only added to the gloom. Just 8,383 jobs for people leaving university were advertised in July, according to the recruitment website Adzuna, down 45% compared with the same point last year, amid fears that AI is wiping out many entry-level roles.So is university still the right choice? And how can undergraduates make the most of the experience and use it as a springboard to building a successful career?According to Hillman, the current state of the graduate labour market actually makes the case for going to university even stronger. “When the labour market is in a bad place, it’s not a logical response to say, ‘I’m going to get fewer qualifications.’ The more qualifications you have the more insulated you are.“Even if graduates are not doing as well as they did, people with no skills are doing much, much worse. And what are these alternatives that people are meant to be doing?Degree apprenticeshipsare wonderful, but they are incredibly hard to come by.“Of course people should absolutely go into higher education with their eyes wide open,” he says. “But you don’t only go to higher education for the job at the end. You go to higher education to mature as a person and very often to have the best years of your life. It is an expensive thing to do, but normally it turns out to be an investment and you get more than your money back.”Research published recently by the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) attracted a lot of attention when it estimated that as many asone in fourUK graduates can expect to be financially worse off as a result of going to university, especially those who take creative arts degrees.The other side of the equation however, according to IFS projections, is that the majority of those who go on to university will be £100,000 better off over their lifetime, while some graduates will see far greater returns for their investment if they study economics or medicine, for example.“There is risk involved and university does not pay off financially for everybody,” says Kate Ogden, senior research economist at the IFS. “But when you look at people who went to university in the recent past, it still looks like university is a good financial bet for most people.”Choice of course is a critical factor. “You might go and do a creative arts degree because you love art and you really enjoy those three years,” says Ogden. “It might not get you a much better job at the end of it. But it doesn’t mean you shouldn’t go and do an arts degree.”Hillman advises young people to listen to their heart as well as their head as they try to decide on their degree course. “They need to think what matters to them.” Once at university, he urges them to take full advantage of all opportunities available to them.double quotation markThe most important thing is to make sure you are living a varied life when you are there“The most important thing is to make sure you are living a varied life when you are there. So you’re not just doing your course work or spending every spare hour working in paid employment,” though he acknowledges that the cost of living crisis makes it essential for many undergraduates to work. “You want to come out of university a rounded individual,” he says.Young people considering going on to higher education may want to look at universities that are developing programmes to try to maximise employability among their graduates. TheUniversity of Manchester, for example, is promising work placementsto all undergraduates regardless of their degree, to better equip them for the challenges of the job market. “We want every student to have the opportunity to apply what they are learning before they graduate,” the university says. “That could mean a placement, short internship, live employer project, or work with a public or community organisation.”From this September, Sheffield Hallam University is guaranteeing its students a paidinternshipif they can’t find a job or are not engaged in further study 12 months after successfully completing their course. The university is also launching a campus recruitment agency, connecting students with part-time jobs, placement opportunities and graduate-level roles.View image in fullscreenFor careers such as teaching, a degree is essential.Photograph: Viktor Cvetkovic/Getty ImagesDan Hawes, co-founder of the Graduate Recruitment Bureau, is confident going to university can still open doors and launch careers, especially where a degree is essential such as law, medicine, engineering or teaching. “Not only that, but the university experience offers personal growth through building social confidence, life skills and friendships.“However, all degrees are not equal,” he warns, “so careful consideration must be given to the subject and the university chosen. Information is available to applicants on the employability rates by subject and institution.“The jobs market is tough at the moment with the economy in poor shape. We feel that while, in the short term, AI may displace some roles in sectors which are very process-driven, in three years’ time, students will be graduating with common knowledge of AI and therefore put a premium on their skillset.”Hawes thinks it’s imperative for students to make the most of their time at university in order to maximise their chances in the jobs market. “You should see day one at university as the start of your career,” he says. “While it may be unclear what you want to do when you leave university, you should think how you would like your CV to look by the end of your degree, work back from there and create a plan to hoard skills and learn new things. Research what skills employers value and speak with your tutors for guidance.”Lewis Wilson, 24, got a 2:1 in law from the University of Sussex, and when he last checked was almost £60,000 in debt. “It’s a lot of money,” he says, “but there’s no replacement for a higher education. I had the best time ever. I had a world-class education from professors who are at the top of their game.“But it’s way more than that – getting the chance to move away from home, live in a brand new city, make new friends and connections, and all of the extracurricular stuff as well.“There’s a million and one other things you get from going. Going to university was the best decision that I’ve ever made, and I think it will be anyone else’s too.”Wilson is now vice-president higher education (England) for the National Union ofStudents(NUS). His advice to those planning to go on to higher education? “Really throw yourself into uni life and take as many opportunities as you can, because it flies by. Oh, and read all the emails! I did not read my emails and I missed a lot of opportunities as a result.”Explore more on these topicsHigher educationUniversity Guide 2027Graduate careersStudent financeUniversitiesStudentsYoung peopleEmployabilityfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I love the boldness of modernism’: New York fashion week goes highbrow | New York fashion week | The Guardian
description: Georgia O’Keeffe inspires the latest Calvin Klein while Michael Kors feels indebted to Alexander Calder
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Georgia O’Keeffe inspires the latest Calvin Klein while Michael Kors feels indebted to Alexander Calder
Content: The Michael Kors show was held in the garden of New York’s Museum of Modern Art.Photograph: Julia D’Ambola/BFA.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Michael Kors show was held in the garden of New York’s Museum of Modern Art.Photograph: Julia D’Ambola/BFA.com/ShutterstockNew York fashion week‘I love the boldness of modernism’: New York fashion week goes highbrowGeorgia O’Keeffe inspires the latest Calvin Klein while Michael Kors feels indebted to Alexander CalderJess Cartner-Morleyin New YorkSat 12 Sep 2026 08.08 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCalvin Klein has taken a highbrow turn in the two years since Veronica Leoni took charge. The Italian designer, a philosophy graduate who was schooled in the chic design studios of Jil Sander and Celine, has shifted away from jeans, boxer shorts and logos, stripping the brand to its minimalist bones: slip dresses and simple coats, slim skirts and crisp T-shirts.Leoni called this the “discipline of removal”. Her muse this season was Georgia O’Keeffe, an artist who the brand’s namesake founder admired. Klein bought O’Keeffe’s painting Summer Days in 1983 for $1m, subsequently donating it to the Whitney Museum. A checked pattern taken from O’Keeffe’s distinctive capsule wardrobe of utilitarian chic appeared on this catwalk as a wrap coat, hardware-free with a fabric belt and no buttons.View image in fullscreenVeronica Leoni has talked of the ‘discipline of removal’ in new pared back designs for Calvin Klein.Photograph: Calvin KleinOne nod to pop culture was allowed: a model in a crepe-back satin ivory slip dress, her blond hair scraped back by a simple headband, called to mind the late Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy, the iconic Calvin Klein employee who was launched back into the fashion conversation byRyan Murphy’s Love Storyearlier this year.Over at the Michael Kors show staged in the sunny courtyard of the Museum of Modern Art, the first model was wearing glossy black disc earrings the size of potato crisps suspended from glinting stainless steel hooks. They looked like pieces from Alexander Calder’s huge mobile, Lobster Trap and Fish Tail, which hangs in the stairwell of the museum.View image in fullscreenA model shows off glossy black disc earrings, part of the new Michael Kors collection.Photograph: Michael KorsNo art heist had taken place, but Kors admitted to being indebted to Calder. This summer, the designer travelled with his husband to Paris, where a major Calder retrospective was held. “We were just in love! The magic of it,” Kors enthused at a preview before his show. Modernism became the theme for this latest collection.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMossy catwalks, mycelial designs and Monty Don: the growth of gardener styleRead moreAs well as the Calder-adjacent earrings, there was an evening dress carved with crescent-shaped edges at the shoulders in homage to Matisse’s cut-outs, and a pencil skirt zigzagged with black and white stripes which winked to Carmen Herrera. A ribbon of banana yellow floating from the hem of a black dress was giving Ellsworth Kelly.View image in fullscreen‘A ribbon of banana yellow’: some of the clothes on display at the Michael Kors show.Photograph: Julia D’Ambola/BFA.com/Shutterstock“I love the boldness of modernism and the optimism of it,” Kors said. After the bedazzled glamour of last season’s show, held in the Lincoln Center opera house, this collection leaned into a more artsy sensibility, with traditionally feminine colours swapped out for tobacco, black and moss green.Held onthe 25th anniversary of 9/11, the show was also “a remembrance”, Kors said, and a tribute to the resilience of the city. “We keep going. Everyone said that no one would ever want to live downtown again,” he recalled. “And now look at us.”Tory Burch has transformed her brand, once synonymous with logoed ballet flats and polished Upper East Side good taste, into one of the most directional names ofNew York fashion week.Her show was accompanied by the eerie, unsettling soundtrack from The Shining, because “it’s quite dystopian for all of us right now”, she said backstage. The clothes were a cheerful contrast, opening with a lavender silk dress accessorised with a boa of golden silk feathers.Jewel-toned pencil skirts, embellished cardigans and ballerina necklines had a midcentury sophistication. “I was thinking about how much people need to feel joy right now. We need to dream and escape, to find bright spots where we can, and that’s where this collection came from.”Explore more on these topicsNew York fashion weekGeorgia O'KeeffeNew YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Hide and chic: are clothes and apparel made from alternative leathers better for the environment?  | Sustainable fashion | The Guardian
description: Vegan leathers are complicated by questions of commercial viability and sustainability. How do they compare to traditional leather?
Author: Lucianne Tonti
Headline: Vegan leathers are complicated by questions of commercial viability and sustainability. How do they compare to traditional leather?
Content: The global production of raw hides used in traditional leather has increased over the last two decades from 10.5m tonnes in 2005 to 13.8m tonnes in 2024.Photograph: fstop123/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenThe global production of raw hides used in traditional leather has increased over the last two decades from 10.5m tonnes in 2005 to 13.8m tonnes in 2024.Photograph: fstop123/Getty Images/iStockphotoChange by degreesSustainable fashionHide and chic: are clothes and apparel made from alternative leathers better for the environment?Vegan leathers are complicated by questions of commercial viability and sustainability. How do they compare to traditional leather?Change by degreesoffers life hacks and sustainable living tips each Saturday to help reduce your household’s carbon footprintGot a question or tip for reducing household emissions? Email us atchangebydegrees@theguardian.comSupported byAbout this contentLucianne TontiFri 11 Sep 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn sustainable fashion, breathless promises about vegan leather have arrived thick and fast for over a decade. Innovations promise mushroom and cactus alternatives that look and feel like real leather – minus the negative associations with methane, deforestation, chemical pollution andanimal welfare.While these next-gen materials have absorbed billions of dollars in capital under an environmental banner, experts are concerned they remain a shiny distraction while the fashion industry’s emissions and reliance on fossil fuel-derived materials grows.“Apple leather, orange leather, pineapple leather, fruit salad leather. It’s like, seriously do we really have to call it leather?” the founder of Nature Matters, Dr Helen Crowley, says. She spent a decade leading nature and sustainable sourcing for the luxury conglomerate Kering. “I haven’t yet seen an alternative leather become an alternative, I’ve seen it just added to the portfolio. It’s about more variety and more stories to sell more stuff.”Don’t drain the budget: how to save on water heating costsRead moreAccording to Textile Exchange, global production of raw hides used in traditional leather – a co-product of the meat industry – has increased steadily over the last two decades from 10.5m tonnes in 2005 to 13.8m tonnes in 2024. It’s evidence that despite the time and money spent on new materials, and endless campaigns by animal rights activists, alternatives to leather have failed to slow growth in demand for real leather.Approximatelyhalf of all leather is used in footwear, 5 to 10% goes into apparel, 10 to 15% in home textiles, and the remainder is spread across other applications like leather goods (bags, wallets) and the automotive industry.Advancements in vegan leathers are complicated by the commercial viability of new materials and questions about whether or not they are actually better for the environment, since most rely on some amount of plastic. For those wanting a hide-free wardrobe, here’s what to know about alternative leathers.Difficulty bringing alternatives to marketIn the last few years, three of the most prominent leather alternatives have stopped being produced: Mylo which was made by Bolt Threads from mushroom mycelium, Piñatex which was made by Ananas Anam from pineapple leaves, and Mirum which was made by Natural Fiber Welding (NFW) from cork. A fourth, MycoWorks, who makes a lab grown mushroom leather called Reishi, narrowly escaped insolvency last year.Investors have poured over $1bn into these companies, but even such huge sums couldn’t help them overcome the barriers that continue to plague material innovators: price parity, brand adoption beyond capsule collections, questions over performance and reliance on binders and coatings made using fossil fuels.Death cleaning, downsizing and decluttering. How do we learn to live with less stuff?Read moreTo this end, shoes, bags and wallets made from plant-based and lab grown materials are rare. Guardian Australia contacted over a dozen innovators producing plant based or lab grown leathers, and only four – Desserto which uses cacti, Innovera from Modern Meadow which uses plant-based proteins, Nutico which uses cocoa and walnut waste, and Pliant which is made from bio-based rubber – could point us to products currently available to buy.The founder of consultancy Sustainabelle, Christine Goulay, who also worked in sustainable sourcing and innovation at Kering, says material innovation takes time. “If you look at [it] historically, most of them take 30, 40, 50 years to mainstream … I think we need to just readjust what we think should be happening and when.”Where the innovation standsAlternative leathers generally fall into four categories: plastic, plant-plastic hybrids, bio-based and lab-grown.Most vegan leather products that can be bought today fall into the first category:plastic. They are made from polyurethane (PU) and polyvinyl chloride (PVC) i.e. pleather. These are derived from fossil fuels, shed microplastic into the environment, cannot be repaired as effectively as real leather, smell and will hang around polluting landfill and the ocean.Many plant-derived alternatives consist of a vegetable-textile-plastic sandwich. These include materials like Desserto, Innovera and Nutico; Banofi which is made from unspecified plant fibres; and Grapeskin by Vegea which is made from wine waste. The amount of plastic varies in each material with some containing as little as 2% and others as much as 50%. Some use bioplastic derived from renewable resources. While many use food or agricultural waste, for those that don’t, effects associated with industrial farming for growing plant feedstocks, such as land use, fertilisers and pesticides, need to be considered. How these wear over time varies, but plastic coatings generally crack and flake when bent and subjected to friction.Then there are more advanced, plastic-free alternatives including Reishi from Mycoworks made from fungi, Alt-leather which also uses unspecified plant matter, TomTex which uses chitosan from mushrooms and shrimp shells, and Ephea which is made from mycelium (fungi).For a few years, scientists have been working on lab-cultivated leather using cells of animal origin to grow materials that mimic the properties of real leather (so these aren’t technically vegan). They include Oval by Pact which uses collagen derived from skincare and pharmaceutical waste, and Vitrolabs (bought by Faircraft last year), whose technology involves taking a small biopsy from a real cow.Real leather is a complex mix of collagen and protein fibres that make it inherently durable, flexible and repairable. When cared for properly,leather can be rehabilitatedand over time develops a patina that makes it one of the only materials that improves with age. Since shoes and bags made from leather are expensive, people are more inclined tocare for them, wear them for longer and keep them in circulation by donating or selling them. These properties are difficult to replicate in plastic or plant-based materials which tend to degrade and split and cannot be repaired.Environmental trade-offsAt the heart of the debate about which material is better for the environment are two issues: the fact that livestock is responsible for between12 – 19% of greenhouse gas emissionsglobally andongoing concernsthat the measurement tools used to determine environmental impact are weighted to favour synthetic materials.But as biodiversity loss ramps up, alongside global temperatures, rampant deforestation and the desertification of farmland, Crowley says we need to move beyond conversations about what materials mitigate harm and start investing in materials that are actively doing good – a metric plastic cannot compete on.“We have to start thinking in a very clear-sighted way, not faffing around to sell more stuff. We need things that deliver on climate and nature,” she says. “The current intensive, overproduction of meat and leather is bad. But if you compare it to regenerative farming, it’s a whole different story.”Regeneratively farmed materials – including wool and leather – can improve soil health, sequester carbon, increase biodiversity and restore water cycles, making landscapes more resilient to extreme weather events. “Let’s just get those cattle grazing in humane, healthy ways that help farmers, that help the land and help the animal,” she says. Process the hides using non-toxic chemicals and “you could have a beautiful natural leather product that creates net positive outcomes. Why don’t we replace bad leather with good leather?”Explore more on these topicsSustainable fashionChange by degreesEthical and green livingVeganismAnimal welfarefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kent is having a champagne moment: ‘English wine has gone from a joke to world-class’ | Wine holidays | The Guardian
description: French champagne house Taittinger is helping produce a premium fizz in the Garden of England – and now visitors can visit the beautiful winery and sample it
Author: Phoebe Taplin
Headline: French champagne house Taittinger is helping produce a premium fizz in the Garden of England – and now visitors can visit the beautiful winery and sample it
Content: The Domaine Evremond vineyard sits within an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, just outside Chilham in Kent.View image in fullscreenThe Domaine Evremond vineyard sits within an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, just outside Chilham in Kent.Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Wine holidaysKent is having a champagne moment: ‘English wine has gone from a joke to world-class’French champagne house Taittinger is helping produce a premium fizz in the Garden of England – and now visitors can visit the beautiful winery and sample itPhoebe TaplinSat 12 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe grapes are turning purple on tall green vines, which stretch down towards the distant flint-and-limestone tower of Chilham church. These rows of Pinot Meunier, destined for English sparkling wine, are 51% owned by French champagne house Taittinger. “England is now the most exciting wine region,” says host and sales executive Hilary Sharp as she leads me aroundDomaine Evremondvineyard, which opened its visitor centre last year to coincide with the launch of its first wine.In his 2023 bookVines in a Cold Climate, drinks writer Henry Jeffreys charts the rise of English wine “from a joke to world-class in 30 years”. The book opens with an alcohol-fuelled scene of vine-planting at Domaine Evremond in May 2017: unseasonably cold, rainy, muddy, with rambling anecdotes from anglophile Pierre-Emmanuel Taittinger about “English women encountered in his misspent youth”. The vineyard is named for the exiled French aristocratCharles de Saint-Évremond, a symbol of hedonistic Anglo-French cooperation. The bon vivant introduced champagne to England and party-loving Charles II made him governor of Duck Island in St James’s Park.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian GraphicsWe stroll past a Land Rover, parked up by a windbreak of crab apple trees. Harriet opens the back to reveal a tray of glasses with a chilled bottle ofDomaine Evremond’s Edition I, and we’re soon sipping creamy, citrussy fizz with a view of vines. It tastes great to me, but I’m no expert.Wine critic Jancis Robinson gave it a “distinguished” 16/20 and Jeffreys, in hisSubstack, Drinking Culture, describes “bright green apple fruit with a reassuring bass note of croissant and Marmite”. King Charles III toasted French president Emmanuel Macron with this wine at a state banquet last summer.double quotation markThe vineyard is named for the exiled French aristocrat Charles de Saint-Évremond, the bon vivant who introduced champagne to EnglandTaittinger’s vineyard director, Christelle Rinville, supervises the vines at Domaine Evremond, regularly taking Le Shuttle from Champagne and enthusing about flinty Kentish subsoils. One of the companies that dug through chalk to make the Channel tunnel excavated Evremond’s 25-metre-deep cellars, where 1.5 million bottles can stay cool around the UK’s first subterranean winery.View image in fullscreenDomaine Evremond’s new winery buildingAn elegant umbrella-shaded terrace outside the chalk-cliff walls of the winery has long rustic tables with vases of wildflowers. Visitors can sample the wine (£12.50 a glass, £55 a bottle) from Wednesday to Sunday and there areyear-round tours and tastings. Sitting here under blue skies, among banks of yarrow, knapweed, vetch and wild carrot scorched by the relentless sun, it doesn’t feel very English.Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent. The unirrigated vines (unlike many other crops) seem to be thriving, and the harvest will be up to three weeks early. Jeffreys writes: “Currently the climate in south-east England is similar to that of Champagne in the 1970s.” Optimal latitudes for wine are supposed to be 30 to 50 degrees, with Champagne at the northerly end of the range. Chilham sits at 51 degrees north.double quotation markAn orchard of plums is drooping under the weight of purple fruit. In the hedges, honey-scented wild clematis tangles with wine-dark blackberriesThe vineyard is ahalf-hour walk through fieldsfrom the village, with its cafes, pubs and railway station, where only the front four carriages fit next to the short platform. Bearded butter-yellow cobs of sweetcorn are bursting out of pale green husks beside the path. I loop back to Chilham throughPerry Wood. Just beyond the vines, I can see an old oasthouse through branches laden with rosy gala apples. The land was bought in 2015 from the fruit-growing Gaskain family, whose managing director, Mark Gaskain, oversees day-to-day operations in the vineyards as well as producing about 70 million apples a year.Further on, an orchard of plums is drooping under the weight of purple fruit and crates are stacked up ready for harvest. In the hedges, sprawling hops and honey-scented wild clematis tangle with reddening rosehips and sweet, wine-dark blackberries. Sparrows snack on early-ripened hawthorn under arching beech and sweet chestnut trees, ancient ivy-wreathed hedge maples and squirrel-haunted hazels. Huge clumps of mistletoe hang from towering poplars.View image in fullscreenChilham Castle’s gardens were landscaped by Capability Brown and now include a vineyard.Photograph: Goddard New Era/AlamyCottage gardens are heady with late summer roses, scented lavender, aromatic catnip. I wander past wisteria-clad walls and a row of mud-built house martin nests with late fledglings still cheeping under half-timbered eaves while gathering swallows twitter on the wires.Deputy church warden Lynda Twaite shows me round the flint-walledSt Mary’s, pointing out memorials and a battered old school table, graffitied by 18th-century kids. The pilgrim route to Canterbury runs through the lime- and yew-shadowed churchyard. Across the square, I peer through the gates at creeper-covered Jacobean Chilham Castle. Itsgardens, landscaped by Capability Brown, now include a new vineyard.double quotation markKent has 120 commercially-active vineyards, with last year’s harvest producing more than five million bottles.Before heading to theWoolpack Innfor the night, I take an evening stroll by the River Stour, with a view of weatherboarded Chilham Mill framed by willowherb and ripe elderberries. The river sparkles in the sun and turquoise damselflies hover among loosestrife and waterlilies.The Woolpack’s garden has a Mediterranean feel, with pink hydrangeas, agapanthus and a 600-year-old olive tree. The brick-walled bar has a curving window seat, weathered oak beams and is stuffed with prints and plants and quirky lighting. After a multimillion-pound renovation a couple of years ago, suites and bedrooms upstairs are named after Kentish vineyards, while the big rooms in Rose Cottage, across the lane, come with their own private gardens.View image in fullscreenThe Woolpack Inn’s ‘Woolly cheeseboard ’is served on a slice of tree trunk.Photograph: Phoebe Taplin/The GuardianI sit in the leafy shade with a “Woolly cheeseboard” on a slice of tree trunk. As much cheese-based installation as meal, its applewood-smoked and creamy goat are artfully arranged among crackers, olives, nuts, dried fruit, chutneys and tangy homemade pickles. To go with it, there are pints of Shepherd Neame’s toffee-appley Master Brew from down the road in Faversham, or glasses of the local cuvée at cellar door prices.The best UK vineyards to visit this summer – and what to drink at themRead moreDomaine Evremond helped found theWine Garden of England, a collaboration of Kent vineyards. August 2026 also saw the launch of a new tourism initiative, theKentish Wine Way, encouraging people to visit “England’s largest and most awarded wine region”. The county has 120 commercially active vineyards and more than 25% of Britain’s vines by area, with last year’s harvest producing more than five million bottles. From the train window next day, after hours of walking through wooded hills and burdened orchards, several vineyards roll past, glowing in the evening sunlight.Accommodation was provided bythe Woolpack Inn(doubles from£140 B&B) and some transport bySoutheastern(advance tickets from London St Pancras from £16 each way)Five more Kent vineyards to visitBalfour WineryView image in fullscreenBalfourproduced the first English wine to win a gold medal and a trophy at theInternational Wine Challengefor its 2004 Brut Rosé. Most days, you can pick up a map at the Cellar Door and wander free around the vineyards, orchards, wildflower meadows and ancient oakwoods – or book a range ofexperiences(from £15pp for a self-tutored tasting). There’s a freeshuttle busto Balfour from Marden train station Friday to Sunday (45 mins from London or Canterbury), andcar-free visitors get 20% offthe year-round tours and tastings.Biddenden VineyardsFive miles fromSissinghurst Castle Garden, the vineyard atBiddendenis the oldest in Kent. Drinks journalist Henry Jeffreys writes that the Barnes family are “apple growers who moved into grapes in 1969 when Joyce Barnes … heard a segment about English viticulture on Radio 4’s Woman’s Hour and decided to plant some vines”. You can still buy all kinds of fancy apple juice and cider here, as well as a range of experiences. Most run from May to September (from £15 for a self-guided tour and tasting flight) with a new behind-the-scenes production tour and tasting added this year for the colder months (£30).Chapel DownView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Tim WinterChapel Down, near Tenterden, is England’s largest wine producer, with bottles in numerous supermarkets, made using fruit from more than 700 acres of vineyards across south-east England. A half-hour taxi ride from Ashford International, it offers various tours and tastings, including a cheese and wine pairing (£70).Simpsons’ Wine EstateRuth and Charles Simpson started making wine in Languedoc in 2002 and, since 2012, in Kent, which they call “one of the most dynamic wine-producing regions of the world”.Bookable sessionsinclude tastings (from £25) on a glass-walled mezzanine floor in the winery with velvet sofas and an optional helter-skelter slide to get back down after sampling their still and sparkling wines.WestwellView image in fullscreenOn the edge of the Kent Downs,Westwellis close to Charing station and a short walk from the Pilgrims’ Way. The vineyard is known for its experimental approaches, including wild yeasts, small-scale production and cloudy, naturally sparklingPet Nats. Alongside regular tours, there are Friday pizza nights and seasonal supper clubs. Tour and tasting £28.Explore more on these topicsWine holidaysKent holidaysFood and drinkEngland holidaysUnited Kingdom holidaysShort breaksWeekend breaksfeaturesShareReuse this content

Author: Rosanna Greenstreet
Headline: The Hobbit and Fast & Furious actor on the joy of strawberry laces, hating that he’s so hard on himself, and his sneaky way of leaving a meeting
Content: Luke Evans: ‘Who would play me in the film of my life? Joe Locke.’Photograph: Lev Radin/AlamyView image in fullscreenLuke Evans: ‘Who would play me in the film of my life? Joe Locke.’Photograph: Lev Radin/AlamyThe Q&ALife and styleInterviewLuke Evans: ‘As a child I was in love with Harrison Ford as Indiana Jones’Rosanna GreenstreetThe Hobbit and Fast & Furious actor on the joy of strawberry laces, hating that he’s so hard on himself, and his sneaky way of leaving a meetingSat 12 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 10.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBorn in south Wales, Luke Evans, 47, left school at 16 and trained at London Studio Centre before appearing in various West End shows. His films include Clash of the Titans, the Fast & Furious franchise, The Hobbit trilogy and Beauty and the Beast. He has released two albums and amemoir, was Tony-nominated for his role in The Rocky Horror Show on Broadway, and stars in The Party, an ITV adaptation of Elizabeth Day’s novel. He lives in Lisbon with his partner.When were you happiest?I’m always happy.What is your greatest fear?Being old and lonely.Adele Parks: ‘If I could ​edit my pas​t, I’d be fitter younger – I​ would have been hotter’Read moreWhat is the trait you most deplore in yourself?Being hard on myself, saying negative things in my head that are not helpful.What is the trait you most deplore in others?Arrogance.Aside from a property, what’s the most expensive thing you’vebought?My business.BDXYis a clothing brand I started with my partner three years ago with no investment.Describe yourself in three wordsKind, inclusive and empathetic.What makes you unhappy?Arguments.What do you most dislike about your appearance?The wrinkles.If you could bring something extinct back to life, what would you choose?My great-aunt Lala, who I named my dog after. Lala was 94 when she died and I was seven. We saw her every Saturday and I’ve got tape recordings of me and her singing. I was the apple of her eye and she would have been thrilled being part of my journey.Who would play you in the film of your life?Joe Locke.Who is your celebrity crush?As a child, Harrison Ford in Indiana Jones. I was in love with him.Which book are you ashamed not to have read?The Hobbit!What was the last lieyou told?That I had a meeting to go to so that I could leave another meeting.What is your guiltiest pleasure?Strawberry laces.What does love feel like?It’s like a blanket I wrap around myself knowing that every mountain I have to climb, every problem I have to deal with, I will share with someone who will help me, and vice versa.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Always questioning how I looked and how people felt about me, and worrying about the wrong things.How often do you have sex?Weekly.What single thing would improve the quality of your life?Working less.What keeps you awake at night?Absolutely nothing.Would you rather have more sex, money or fame?Money.How would you like to be remembered?As a good person.Tell us a secretI’m a really good barber.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe Q&ACelebrityLuke EvansFast and FuriousThe Hobbit: An Unexpected JourneyThe Hobbit: The Battle of the Five ArmiesThe Hobbit: The Desolation of SmaugfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Burial of King Oyo takes place in Uganda as news anchor prepares for throne | Uganda | The Guardian
description: Royal guards carry casket through streets of Fort Portal amid row over appointment of Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Royal guards carry casket through streets of Fort Portal amid row over appointment of Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma
Content: Royal guards escort the body of the late King Oyo for his burial at the Karambi Royal Tombs, in Fort Portal.Photograph: Michael Muhati/ReutersView image in fullscreenRoyal guards escort the body of the late King Oyo for his burial at the Karambi Royal Tombs, in Fort Portal.Photograph: Michael Muhati/ReutersUgandaBurial of King Oyo takes place in Uganda as news anchor prepares for throneRoyal guards carry casket through streets of Fort Portal amid row over appointment of Edward Rukidi KijanangomaReuters in KampalaSat 12 Sep 2026 11.09 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 12.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUganda’s King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, long the world’s youngest monarch, has been buried among the tombs of his royal forebears as ⁠his Tooro kingdom looked to put ⁠a bitter succession battlebehind ​it.Oyo’s appointed successor, the news anchor Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, cast nine coffee berries into the grave at the Karambi Royal Tombs, marking the formal handover of power in the western Ugandan kingdom.Oyo made global headlines in 1995 when he took the throne at the age of three. Images of the toddler king wearing a crown and royal robes sparked curiosity and adoration around the world.View image in fullscreenKing Oyo of the Toro kingdom was for a long time the world’s youngest monarch.Photograph: Sipa/ShutterstockHe died last month at 34 ⁠in the United States, where he was receiving treatment for cancer.Uganda is led by an elected head of state but retains several kingdoms that pre-date the ​British colonial era and are regarded as bulwarks of traditional identity ‌and heritage.At a church service before ‌the burial, Oyo, who became a UN goodwill ambassador championing the fight against HIV and Aids, was eulogised as a reserved but jovial young man.“Although ‌he became king and carried responsibilities far beyond what most people ever experience, he never completely lost the young boy who loved to have fun,” said his sister, Ruth Komuntale.Royal guards clad in orange shawls then led the hearse carrying Oyo’s casket through the streets of the kingdom’s capital, Fort Portal, to the royal tombs, as thousands of mourners joined the procession on foot.The burial, which was held 31 years to the day after Oyo’s coronation, followed days of bickering within the notoriously fractious royal family.A committee consisting of members ‌of the royal clan announced on Wednesday it had chosen Oyo’s cousin, Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at state broadcaster UBC, as king.But the late king’s immediate family said his hitherto unknown son should succeed him, as called ​for in his will. Oyo never married and was not known to have any children until the kingdom’s prime minister said in the statement announcing his death that he had a son.View image in fullscreenUBC news anchor Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma.Photograph: UBC UgandaSupporters of Kijanangoma’s succession say Oyo’s family has not been able to produce basic information about the purported son.A source with knowledge of crisis talks over the matter said Ugandan authorities had successfully pushed through Kijanangoma’s succession on Friday. A government spokesperson could not be reached for comment.The archbishop of the ⁠Church of Uganda, Stephen Kaziimba Mugalu, called for unity.“Words spoken in grief can cause pain, division and conflict,” he ​told mourners. “It can even destroy the legacy ​of the king we are mourning.”Oyo himself took the throne after a protracted succession battle that finished in court.Secret son revelation ignites bitter succession dispute in Ugandan kingdomRead moreIn ​addition to his ceremonial responsibilities and campaigning ‌against HIV and Aids, ​Oyo cultivated close ties with former ​Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, whom he named a special adviser to the monarch. Gaddafi donated money towards refurbishment of the royal palace.The 56-year-old Kijanangoma, who maintained a low profile as the succession battle played out, has been described by fellow Ugandan journalists as quiet and humble.Besides the throne, the new king will inherit a considerable royal estate including swathes of land and sizeable cash payouts from the central government.Explore more on these topicsUgandaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Six Nigerians extradited to US over $6m online romance scam | FBI | The Guardian
description: Alleged members of Black Axe criminal network that swindled US women out of $6m flown from South Africa
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Alleged members of Black Axe criminal network that swindled US women out of $6m flown from South Africa
Content: FBI officials at the Cape Town international airport during the extradition process of suspected Black Axe members in South Africa on 11 September 2026.Photograph: Esa Alexander/ReutersView image in fullscreenFBI officials at the Cape Town international airport during the extradition process of suspected Black Axe members in South Africa on 11 September 2026.Photograph: Esa Alexander/ReutersFBISix Nigerians extradited to US over $6m online romance scamAlleged members of Black Axe criminal network that swindled US women out of $6m flown from South AfricaGuardian staff and Associated PressSat 12 Sep 2026 10.05 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 16.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSix Nigerian nationals linked to an organized criminal network that allegedly swindled American women out of more than $6m throughonline romance scamswere extradited to the United States on Friday.South Africanpolice confirmed they were to be extradited earlier on Friday, whilelocal newsin Africa confirmed that the Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation, known as the Hawks, facilitated their handover to officials from the US Federal Bureau of Investigation and Secret Service at Cape Town international airport, in collaboration with Interpol South Africa.The men, who were arrested in the South African city of Cape Town in 2021, face wire fraud and money laundering charges.They are accused of belonging to a criminal network known asthe Black Axe, which Interpol describes as being among criminal groups responsible for a significant share of the world’s cyber-enabled financial fraud, typically through romance, cryptocurrency and investment scams.According to South African police, the men are alleged to have targeted more than 100 women in the US, defrauding them of more than $6m through online romance or love scams.Among the alleged victims were pensioners and businesspeople who were reportedly targeted through sophisticated online relationships.“Through the coordination of Interpol South Africa, the six will today be transported from a correctional facility in Cape Town to Cape Town international airport, where they will be handed over to officials from theFBIand the United States Secret Service, who arrived in South Africa this morning,” said police spokesperson Katlego Mogale.A recent operation byInterpoltargeting west African organized crime groups led to the arrest of 58 people and the identification of 263 suspects linked to various criminal networks involved in similar crimes, the multinational police body said last month.The operation aimed to disrupt money laundering, identify high-value targets, seize assets, and support arrests and prosecution.InSouth Africa, authorities raided seven locations in the city of Johannesburg linked to a syndicate that ran romance and investment scams targeting retirees in English-speaking countries.In that operation in South Africa, police arrested 39 people, seized $2.67m and froze more than 250 bank accounts, Interpol said.Explore more on these topicsFBISouth AfricaNigeriaCybercrimeScamsInternetUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Xi Jinping gets red carpet at Brics summit amid thaw in India-China relations | India | The Guardian
description: Chinese president’s arrival in Delhi seen as step towards reconciliation after deadly 2020 military clash
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: Chinese president’s arrival in Delhi seen as step towards reconciliation after deadly 2020 military clash
Content: Xi Jinping, right, is visiting India for the first time in seven years to attend the Brics summit.Photograph: Indian ministry of foreign affairs/EPAView image in fullscreenXi Jinping, right, is visiting India for the first time in seven years to attend the Brics summit.Photograph: Indian ministry of foreign affairs/EPAIndiaXi Jinping gets red carpet at Brics summit amid thaw in India-China relationsChinese president’s arrival in Delhi seen as step towards reconciliation after deadly 2020 military clashOliver HolmesSat 12 Sep 2026 08.39 EDTFirst published on Sat 12 Sep 2026 06.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Chinese president,Xi Jinping, has received a red-carpet welcome in India for a summit of Brics developing nations, as regional rivals Beijing and Delhi make a public display of thawing relations while quietly competing to lead at a time of shaky US global dominance.As Xi stepped off the plane, he was walked past an honour guard of Indian soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses. Later on Saturday, he was due to attend a gala dinner for the two-day summit.The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, and Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, had already been welcomed by the Indian prime minister,Narendra Modi, who is hosting one of the group’s most closely watched gatherings since its inception.The summit marks Xi’s first visit to India in seven years and is seen as the biggest step towards reconciliation after adeadly 2020 military clashalong the disputed Himalayan border, in which ‌20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers were killed.Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giantshave been warming recently, with flights and high-level contacts gradually being restored. China was “willing” to work with India to properly manage differences and be “good neighbours and friends”, China’s foreign ministry said on Friday.Leaders and diplomats have been convening in India for the annual gathering of the Brics grouping, named after five of its earliest members – Brazil, Russia, India,Chinaand South Africa – that was conceived as a counterweight to western dominance.This summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising US-China tensions, test the bloc’s ability to find common ground.Since its inception in 2009,Bricshas expanded as a forum for major emerging economies to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The group now rivals the US-dominated G7 forum of advanced economies, accounting for half of the global population.But its growth has also created new fractures and disunity – Iran was bombing Saudi Arabia and the UAE earlier this year, and Brics foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May.On Saturday, the bloc managed to unanimously agree on the wording of a joint declaration that reiterated a commitment to peaceful resolution of international disputes “through dialogue, consultation and diplomacy”.The “New Delhi declaration” ​called for “maximum restraint” in the Middle East, although it was worded so as not to call out member countries actively involved in conflicts.Jiang Shixue, the vice-president of the expert committee of the China thinktank Council for BRICs cooperation (China), said the 11 members “cannot speak with one voice on many issues”.“The only solution is to continuously strengthen political consensus,” he told the South China Morning Post.Beijing and Delhi have differing views on the role of the group.China has sought to expand Brics power as a counterweight to the US under Donald Trump’s leadership, which has launched global tariff and trade wars and retreated from multilateral institutions such as the UN, which afforded it international credibility.India has taken a more cautious approach, seeing Brics as a bridge between the west and the developing world.Saturday’s talks began with an address by Modi, who said Brics was “not against anyone”.Chietigj Bajpaee, a senior research fellow for South Asia in the Asia-Pacific programme at Chatham House, said this week that Delhi had found it hard to maintain its policy of “strategic hedging” during such a disruptive US presidency.“India’s position can appear out of sync in a forum whose membership includes countries with more overtly anti-western agendas, including China, Russia and Iran. And two other Brics countries, South Africa and Brazil, have suffered high-profile diplomatic disputes with the US,” he wrote.“The challenge for Delhi is that it wishes to promote this worldview in a way that is non-western but not explicitly anti-western.”Agence France-Pressecontributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsIndiaBricsXi JinpingChinaNarendra ModiAsia PacificSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Death toll from Philippines ferry fire rises to 35, as officials warn toll will grow | Philippines | The Guardian
description: The deadly fire had begun in the ferry’s cargo hold, then tore through the ship within seconds
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The deadly fire had begun in the ferry’s cargo hold, then tore through the ship within seconds
Content: A drone view shows emergency workers accessing the burnt M/V June Aster ferry, a day after a fire broke out on the vessel, off the coast of Palawan, Philippines.Photograph: Philippine Coast
