Guard/ReutersView image in fullscreenA drone view shows emergency workers accessing the burnt M/V June Aster ferry, a day after a fire broke out on the vessel, off the coast of Palawan, Philippines.Photograph: Philippine Coast Guard/ReutersPhilippinesDeath toll from Philippines ferry fire rises to 35, as officials warn toll will growThe deadly fire had begun in the ferry’s cargo hold, then tore through the ship within secondsAgence France-PresseSat 12 Sep 2026 00.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe bodies of passengers killed in aferry fire off the Philippinesarrived at a port near the resort town of Coron, Palawan, on Saturday morning, as the country’s coast guard warned the death toll of 35 would grow.Tents were being set up to receive 30 bodies brought from the M/V June Aster, which ran aground near the tourist hotspotafter a fire eruptedon Wednesday evening and tore through the vessel “in seconds”.Coast guard spokesperson Noemie Cayabyab told a Saturday press conference the remains would be turned over to police forensic investigators for “proper disposition and identification” before allowing local authorities to inform family members.“Currently, we are focused on the retrieval, and after that we will proceed with the investigation,” she said, confirming the bodies had been found in the ship’s economy accommodation area.Police investigators were seen arriving at the port shortly after the press conference ended.Asked how many bodies remained aboard the ship, she said authorities would provide an update later in the day.Cayabyab told AFP on Friday evening that the first transfer had been capped at 30 bodies because of the capacity of the patrol vessel transporting them and that additional cadavers remained on the ferry.Five others had been confirmed dead in the immediate wake of the fire.Photos released by the coast guard showed rows of body bags being placed into a small ship alongside men in hazmat suits. Thirty passengers and 13 crew have so far been rescued, while 54 people remain unaccounted for.On Friday, Cayabyab had told a radio station the fire had begun in the cargo hold, then tore through the ship within seconds.“From the time that they heard the loud explosion, the appearance of smoke, and then fire. It spread very quickly,” she said of survivors’ accounts.“Everything happened in seconds,” she said, adding that those who made it off the ship had not even had time to put on lifejackets.Myra Cabilan said she had flown to Coron to find her missing brother, 40-year-old Rammel Gonzaga, who had taken the ferry from Manila on a business trip with his brother-in-law.“His wife had just given birth a month ago. He was so happy he was given a daughter,” Cabilan said, fighting back tears.“At dawn, I still believed he survived. But he’s still missing. I have lost hope.”Hundreds of people desperate for news about the incident have taken to leaving comments on the Facebook page of a local mayor, searching for relatives, friends and even a dog.The ferry’s manifest listed 134 crew and passengers, but two had not boarded, according to the coast guard. The ferry was also carrying goods, an electric vehicle, a pickup truck, and motorcycles.The archipelago nationof 116 million has a long history of disasters involving the inter-island ferries that ply its seas.Many rely on cheap and poorly regulated boats and ships for transport between the country’s more than 7,000 islands, despite regular accidents.On Thursday, the company that owns the M/V June Aster, Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc, said it was fully cooperating with the investigation.Explore more on these topicsPhilippinesAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Do not call her a racist: anti-Pauline Hanson strategists tell campaigners character attacks won’t work in Victoria | One Nation | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: strategic rethink urges progressive activists to respectfully steer one-on-one conversations with One Nation supporters towards economic concerns
Author: Henry Belot
Headline: Exclusive: strategic rethink urges progressive activists to respectfully steer one-on-one conversations with One Nation supporters towards economic concerns
Content: The One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson. GetUp told campaigners Hanson’s ties to Gina Rinehart are ‘a problem’ but not what should be in focus.Photograph: Joel Carrett/EPAView image in fullscreenThe One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson. GetUp told campaigners Hanson’s ties to Gina Rinehart are ‘a problem’ but not what should be in focus.Photograph: Joel Carrett/EPAOne NationDo not call her a racist: anti-Pauline Hanson strategists tell campaigners character attacks won’t work in VictoriaExclusive:strategic rethink urges progressive activists to respectfully steer one-on-one conversations with One Nation supporters towards economic concernsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastHenry BelotSat 12 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 20.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe message from strategists was blunt: do not, however tempting, personally attackPauline Hansonor call her a racist.The request has been made to progressive campaigners and unionists who have been asked to start one-on-one conversations withOne Nationsupporters before the Victorian election in November.It is also indicative of a strategic rethink in response to One Nation’s sustained surge in public support and the party’s recent wins instate and federal byelectionsandin South Australia.Andrew Hastie accuses Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce of being ‘lying cowards’ over One Nation ‘traitor’ cartoonRead moreSeparate training sessions run by the peak body for unions in Victoria, the Trades Hall Council, and the progressive campaign group GetUp, have warned members they may be inadvertently pushing people to One Nation by not respectfully engaging with their legitimate economic concerns.“As best as you can, I know it’s hard, don’t make it personal,” a GetUp strategist told hundreds of members on a Thursday night Zoom call.“Going after Pauline Hanson personally and calling her a racist, or going after her character, although very tempting, just confirms what people already believe: that she is an outsider and the establishment is attacking her.”This is a change of approach for the progressive group, which spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on ads personally attacking Hanson and her deputy leader, Barnaby Joyce, during the Farrer byelection. The ads, which linked the pair to Donald Trump, had little impact. One Nationcomfortably won the seat.The reset, based on research conducted by the polling company Redbridge after the Farrer byelection, brought GetUp in line with advice from Trades Hall, which has been hosting training sessions for major unions in recent weeks.Oscar Kaspi-Crutchett, a senior researcher at Trades Hall, says people thinking about voting for One Nation shut down when they perceive personal attacks on the party’s leadership that do not acknowledge their legitimate concerns.“For many people, simply ignoring her racism is not going to be possible or desirable,” Kaspi-Crutchett said. “It’s what drives them to get involved in the fight against One Nation.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here“In these cases, we need to make it very clear that Hanson’s racism isn’t merely a character flaw but a sophisticated political device. It manufactures differences between groups which have none.”GetUp has also told campaigners to not personally attack Hanson’s billionaire benefactor.“Pauline Hanson is closely tied to Gina Rinehart, and it’s a problem, but it’s not what the research says should be in focus,” GetUp told campaigners.“It can be effective if it is raised organically by the person you’re speaking to but leading with it reads as a standard partisan attack, which triggers the same defensiveness as going after her character directly.”This advice marks another change for the group, which in the weeks after the Farrer byelection published ads describing Hanson as a“wannabe billionaire” flying around in “mummy Gina’s” private plane.Senior state and federal Labor sources, who declined to be named so they could speak freely, say these changes makes sense. They argue the group’s personal attacks on rightwing figures, including Peter Dutton during the 2016 and 2019 federal elections, were not helpful.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne Nation’s Warren Pickering admits to illegal drug use and says he is ‘no angel’ in extraordinary press conferenceRead moreGetUp’s decision to unveila banner behind Hanson during her National Press Clubaddress in June caused disquiet among Labor ranks, with some arguing it was unproductive. While the banner’s message focused on her record on wages, it also included cartoon images of cash flying around her.‘Listen to the beat, not the lyrics’Kaspi-Crutchett and his colleagues at Trades Hall are telling unionists to listen carefully for any hint of economic concerns that may be underpinning opinions about immigration, crime or culture wars.“Pauline Hanson’s greatest weaknesses and the policy areas where she is the most vulnerable are the ones where the Labor movement has the highest trust from the public: working conditions, entitlements, maternity leave,” he says.He says campaigners should resist the urge to fact-check conspiracy theories. Instead, conversations should be respectfully redirected to the economy.“Don’t listen to the lyrics, listen to the beat of what they are saying,” he says. “What is consistent is their dissatisfaction with the status quo so get them to tease out what that looks like and how it makes them feel.“There might be a spiel about Bill Gates but, eventually, you get to them saying ‘my kid can’t afford a house’.”In June, the head of Trades Hall Council, Luke Hilakari, rebuked 23 state Labor MPs and candidates for having“zero conversations” with their constituentsin the past two weeks, saying they needed to “work their ass off” to stop One Nation.Kaspi-Crutchett said one-on-one conversations are vital because the politicians that once persuaded people against voting for Hanson had “lost credibility with the people she is targeting”.“A nurse on the doorstep can do infinitely more than a legion of cabinet ministers and press secretaries.” Kaspi-Crutchett said.“The trust has been exhausted.”Explore more on these topicsOne NationPauline HansonAustralian politicsVictorian politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Labor has had 12 years to fix Victorian roads. Turning to ‘pothole populism’ now may be too late  | Victoria | The Guardian
description: Potholed roads are ‘devastating political advertising’ for the Victorian government – but Ben Carroll’s made them the focus of his campaign
Author: Benita Kolovos
Headline: Potholed roads are ‘devastating political advertising’ for the Victorian government – but Ben Carroll’s made them the focus of his campaign
Content: No matter where you’re driving in Victoria – rural road, regional freeway or inner-city street – you’re bound to encounter a pothole, writes Benita Kolovos.Photograph: James Ross/AAPView image in fullscreenNo matter where you’re driving in Victoria – rural road, regional freeway or inner-city street – you’re bound to encounter a pothole, writes Benita Kolovos.Photograph: James Ross/AAPVictoriaAnalysisLabor has had 12 years to fix Victorian roads. Turning to ‘pothole populism’ now may be too lateBenita KolovosPotholed roads are ‘devastating political advertising’ for the Victorian government – but Ben Carroll’s made them the focus of his campaignFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastSat 12 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 20.11 EDTShareAt a press conference to celebrate the sold-out NFL match played at Melbourne’s MCG on Friday, the Victorian premier,Ben Carroll, was heckled on one issue.“Fix the potholes,” a punter called out as they walked past the Victorian premier’s press conference.No matter where you’re driving in Victoria – be it a rural road, regional freeway or an inner-city street – you’re bound to encounter one. Then comes the split-second decision: swerve into another lane, or power through and hope your tyres survive the impact?Victoria’s historic work from home laws have unexpectedly stalled. Will they survive?Read moreFor regional Victorians it has been an issue for years. In 2024, the National party began collating images for its “Potholes for All Seasons” calendar, which was distributed to MPs at state parliament last year.But now potholes have become so omnipresent they could become the defining symbol of the Victorian election in November.At the Nepean byelection in May, the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, and her successful candidate, Anthony Marsh, made it a central issue of the campaign – going so far as to fill a pothole themselves, promptingan investigation by the transport department.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueThe headlines have kept coming. In July, the ABC reported thatseven cars were forced off the Calder Freeway near Gisbornedue to tyre damage from potholes. In August, the Herald Sun reported a dismal23 Victorian drivers had received compensationfrom the Transport Accident Commission for pothole damage over the last two years – despite thousands of complaints.AI-generated ads for the political lobby group Fix Victoriafeature potholes prominently. On Thursday, the group stood outside Parliament station handing out bumper stickers that read: “Not drunk, avoiding potholes”. At the same time, the Insurance Council of Australia chief executive Andrew Hall was telling reporters they had been “more claims for tyres and rim blowouts” in Victoria than other states, because of potholes.An auditor general reporttabled in state parliament on Wednesdayexamined more than 23,000km of Victorian roads and found almost half (48%) were rated in poor or very poor condition. It also found they were deteriorating faster than the government could repair them: the gap between the number of road defects recorded and those repaired doubled between January 2025 and June 2026.According to the auditor general, the Department ofTransporttold the government before the May budget it needed $3bn a year to maintain road pavement at existing levels while replacing ageing assets.But the government allocated only $1.04bn in the budget for 2026-27. That same financial year, it is forecast to spend $8.9bn on interest payments on state debt.Toby Ralph, a marketer and researcher who has worked on more than 50 elections worldwide, said potholes were “devastating political advertising” of the state’s poor financial situation.“They’re omnipresent, impossible to spin, and while motorists don’t study the state budget when they hit a pothole, they ask: with all the money being spent, why can’t you fix this?“Potholes are the symptom. The deeper problem is a government that needs to get its finances and priorities back in order.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSince becoming premier in July, Carroll has attempted a reset, promising to focus the government on the “basics”. He’s announced anadditional $300m to fix 500,000 potholesby the end of January, using money saved from delaying infrastructure projects and withhelp from prisoners.He’s committed to a review of TAC claims and promised to bring maintenance work back in-house, which is significant given the auditor general said most major repairs were conducted by four external contractors.The Coalition has pledged $5bn over four years to fix a million potholes – a 25% increase on current spending.Some senior Labor sources have described the party’s pothole plan as an attempt to “neutralise” the politically damaging issue, an approach questioned by Lissie Ratcliffe, chief of staff for Daniel Andrews when he was premier.“If you are stuck in the issues that your opponents are stronger and more trusted on, it is very difficult to win from there,” she said on the Socially Democratic podcast. She urged Carroll to “change the debate and get it on to a ground where, ideally, we’ve got a new idea or two and people think we’re the best people to deliver”.Others within the party have compared the strategy to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s“pothole populism”. The democratic socialist has made repairing potholes quickly part of his pitch to rebuild trust in government,telling reporters: “If you want someone to believe in the promise of a transformative vision … you have to first deliver on the thing that diminishes their faith on a daily basis.“If you are driving your car or you’re riding your bike and you hit the same pothole every single day, why would you trust city government in its ability to deliver something that you have never seen at that scale, when it can’t even do this?” Mandani said.But there’s a problem with that comparison. Mamdani is using potholes to prove his new style of government can deliver on its big, bold, progressive agenda. Carroll doesn’t have one. Instead, he’s pitching himself as fixing a problem his government has allowed to deteriorate over 12 years in office.Benita Kolovos is Guardian Australia’s Victorian state correspondentExplore more on these topicsVictoriaTransportBen CarrollVictorian politicsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: NSW government paid for homeless man to be sent back to New Zealand instead of offering housing | Housing | The Guardian
description: Local council and state government attempting to move on residents living in an encampment by the river in Wagga Wagga
Author: Cait Kelly
Headline: Local council and state government attempting to move on residents living in an encampment by the river in Wagga Wagga
Content: Mark Hudson in Wagga Wagga. Homes NSW repeatedly offered him a flight back to New Zealand.Photograph: suppliedView image in fullscreenMark Hudson in Wagga Wagga. Homes NSW repeatedly offered him a flight back to New Zealand.Photograph: suppliedHousingNSW government paid for homeless man to be sent back to New Zealand instead of offering housingLocal council and state government attempting to move on residents living in an encampment by the river in Wagga WaggaFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastCait KellyInequality reporterSat 12 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 20.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheNew South Walesgovernment paid for a homeless man in Wagga Wagga to be sent back to New Zealand instead of offering him temporary accommodation, in an attempt to move on residents living in an encampment by a river.The local council and state government have been attempting to clear out the encampment for several months after anewborn baby diedin May when its mother gave birth to twins in a tent.Residents of the encampment have faced increasing pressure to move on, including “compliance action” requests for them to leave or be fined up to $1,100. Advocates said at least four people have been fined about $110 for not moving on in time. The council has denied fining people “on the basis of where they are staying”.Mark Hudson, 53, said he has permanent residency in Australia and is therefore entitled to temporary accommodation. He arrived 18 years ago, but does not have a ​​​​​​​​​​Visa Entitlement Verification Online – to prove permanent residency. Despite this, Homes NSW repeatedly offered him a flight back to New Zealand, where he has not lived for over 18 years.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“They kept pressuring me,” Hudson said. “[The Homes NSW officer] offered it to me first, like six, seven times. She just kept on … ‘You want the flight? You want the flight?’”This week, they booked the flight to Sydney and then Auckland, at a cost to the taxpayer of $1,797. On Thursday the international flight was cancelled by the airline, and Hudson, who has a girlfriend in Wagga, and is about to take custody of his granddaughter, is still in Wagga. He also has a dog he does not want to leave.“They were chasing me all day yesterday to try and sort it out. They were like, we’ll sort the tickets out, we’ll arrange it again … But I’ve got my granddaughter now.”On Friday, after Guardian Australia contacted the NSW government, Hudson was offered accommodation, which he is expected to move into next week.“I didn’t want to leave Wilks [Park],” Hudson said. “I wanted to stay in Wagga. And it was just the approach was always bully tactics,” he said.A spokesperson for Homes NSW said it has been working with people facing housing insecurity in the area since April. It confirmed travel costs, including air fares, were one of the support options available.“Where a person is not eligible for social housing or other support services in New South Wales and requests assistance to return to their home country, Homes NSW may assist with that request as part of an individual support plan,” the spokesperson said.“Homes NSW have been working with Mark, a New Zealand citizen, who initiated discussions about returning to New Zealand where he has family.“If he has decided not to return to New Zealand, Homes NSW will continue to work with him to identify alternative accommodation, noting he is not eligible for social housing.”In April, a Guardian Australia investigation revealed that former international student, 32-year-old Nepali born Bikram Lama, Sydney’s “birdman”,died at central Sydney’s St James stationin December where he had been sleeping rough.His death exposed a gap in federal and state responses to homelessness for people who lose their visa status or are unable to prove permanent residency.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNSW residents need to prove permanent residency to access social housing, normally through Centrelink payments. If permanent residents have been in Australia for more than 10 years, they can receive six months’ worth of payments. Hudson was previously receiving Centrelink payments for six months, before being cut off. New Zealand citizens on special category visas are also entitled to emergency housing.Housing advocate Timothy Verhoef said it was a failure of the state government to offer Hudson a flight before offering him a home.“It has been a failure because they’ve paid $1,700 and nothing’s happened. It’s pushing the problem around.”Hudson has worked most of his life in Australia, as a truck driver and farm manager in Western Australia. He moved to Wagga to be closer to family in the area. He was not able to find work, so has been living in a tent by the river for almost two years, while getting help from family and eating at charities. Asked how he managed to survive, Hudson said “faith”.“You just rely on [public] showers and Vinnie’s to get through, and mates.“I would take temporary housing, but because I didn’t get on the plane, I guess they’ll hate me … I want to get some sort of housing first. Yeah, some sort of help.”Verhoef said the council, state government and local authorities had failed to provide genuine solutions for the people living along the river encampment.“The reality is that they haven’t worked together on anything substantial – they are just pushing a narrative to make it look like they are addressing the issue.”Explore more on these topicsHousingNew South WalesHomelessnessnewsShareReuse this content

title: Donald Trump says he would ‘love’ to see united Ireland | Ireland | The Guardian
description: US president says on visit to republic that unification will happen eventually so ‘may as well happen now’
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: US president says on visit to republic that unification will happen eventually so ‘may as well happen now’
Content: 1:35Protesters against Trump’s visit to Ireland react to ‘united Ireland’ comments – videoIrelandDonald Trump says he would ‘love’ to see united IrelandUS president says on visit to republic that unification will happen eventually so ‘may as well happen now’Rory CarrollIreland correspondentSat 12 Sep 2026 12.05 EDTFirst published on Sat 12 Sep 2026 09.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has said he would “love” to see a united Ireland and that it “may as well happen now”.The US president appeared to endorse the push for constitutional change on the island at the start of a two-day visit to Ireland on Saturday. The unexpected intervention prompted a swift rebuttal from the UK government and Northern Ireland’s unionist leaders.“I don’t want ⁠to cause any problems, ​but ‌I will ‌tell you, I’d love ‌to see it unified,” Trump told reporters at joint press conference with the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, in Dublin. “I think it would be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. You know what? The way I look at it, it’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.”The unification of NorthernIrelandwith the republic of Ireland would be “fantastic”, Trump said. “The UK will have something to say about it, obviously. But I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?”View image in fullscreenMicheál Martin welcomes Donald Trump to Farmleigh House, in Dublin, during his trip to the Republic of Ireland.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAThe intervention jolted his hosts and came two weeks after Andy Burnham saida referendum on unification was “off the table”, which angered Sinn Féin and other Irish nationalists.Speaking later on Saturday, Trump acknowledged that his comments on unification, made in response to a reporter’s question, would be controversial. “No matter what you say or how you say it, there’s no good answer,” he said. “I gave a nice answer, I think. We’ll worry about it tomorrow.” Unification, he added, would be a “very cool thing”.A Downing Street spokesperson said the prime minister still believed there was not the required support for unification to trigger a referendum, as set out in the Good Friday agreement.Gavin Robinson, the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) leader, said Northern Ireland’s constitutional future would be decided by its people, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington.“Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom because that is the settled democratic will of its people. I am confident Northern Ireland will continue to choose the UK and the security it offers. As unionists we are not interested in the destruction of our country by joining with the Irish republic.”View image in fullscreenSpectators watch as Air Force One flies Trump over the Irish Open in Doonbeg, County Clare.Photograph: Damien Eagers/PAColum Eastwood, an MP and former leader of the Social Democratic and Labour party (SDLP), and frequent critic of Trump, posted a clip of the president’s remarks on social media and wrote: “Always liked him.”The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, said: “President Trump is shooting from the hip as usual, just like he did with Greenland and Canada becoming the 51st state. This sort of loose talk about the future of democratic countries is deeply unhelpful and creates unnecessary tension.”Trump’s comments strayed from predecessors who sought to keep the White House neutral on Ireland’s constitutional future, but the off-the-cuff nature of the remarks suggested there was no change in US policy.Trump’s unofficial visit is centred on golf – he flew on Saturday afternoon to his resort in Doonbeg, County Clare, which is hosting the Irish Open – but started with a courtesy call in Dublin to Áras an Uachtaráin, the official residence and workplace ofthe Irish president, Catherine Connolly.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump and Catherine Connolly at her presidential residence in Phoenix Park, Dublin.Photograph: Tony Maxwell/PABefore her election to the ceremonial post last year,Connolly called Trump a bully and criticised his policiesin Gaza and Iran. Their brief encounter, behind closed doors, appeared to go smoothly despite a coded critique of White House policies.Connolly said in a statement afterwards that she “conveyed the strong view of the Irish people that the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted” and stressed the importance of the United Nations – an organisation Trump has disparaged. Trump said they had a wide-ranging discussion, including about energy and water, and that Connolly was “terrific”.Trump held a separate meeting with Martin at the Phoenix Park, where he told the press that Iran would seek peace after the US midterm elections and repeated his claim that his war had prevented Tehran obtaining a nuclear weapon.Asked about protests against his visit – a large crowd was gathering in central Dublin, 5 miles away, as well as at Doonbeg – the president said he had not seen any protests.View image in fullscreenDemonstrators protesting against Trump’s visit in Dublin.Photograph: Natalia Campos/ReutersAddressing guests as at the US ambassador’s residence, Trump assailed US Democrats as extremists and criticised Europe’s approach to immigration.He lauded US-Irish relations but reiterated a complaint about the American pharma giants in Ireland. “You took all our medical companies, we’ve got to get a couple of them back. You fleeced us but that’s OK.”Thousands of protesters marched through central Dublin and held a rally outside parliament. Speakers accused Trump of facilitating genocide in Gaza and led chants of “Donald Trump, can you hear? We don’t want you here.”View image in fullscreenA protest banner at a rally against Donald Trump in Dublin mocks his renaming of the Gulf of Mexico.Photograph: Rory Carroll/The GuardianOthers in the crowd accused the president of misogyny, sexual assault, racism and xenophobia. “Donald Trump is utterly immoral and he’s wrecking the world,” said Anne McGuinness, 70, who held a banner that said “unwelcome”.Emily Hamilton, whose daughter held a banner saying “Get rid of the evil orange”, said the Irish government should have shunned him. “We can’t stop him going to Doonbeg but we should not be welcoming him.”Mick Brennan, 70, said he and his wife Helen do not normally attend protests but made an exception for the US president. “We can’t stand that Trump fella, from his toes to his nose.”View image in fullscreenHelen and Mick Brennan hold a banner in Dublin to protest Donald Trump’s visit to Ireland.Photograph: Rory Carroll/The GuardianA smaller protest was held at Doonbeg. Trump is to stay overnight at his resort and present the Irish Open trophy to the winner on Sunday before returning to Washington.Explore more on these topicsIrelandDonald TrumpNorthern Irish politicsEuropeUS foreign policyNorthern IrelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump says he would ‘love’ to see unified Ireland and ‘it may as well happen now’ as he visits Dublin – as it happened | Ireland | The Guardian
description: US president is meeting politicians and business leaders – and playing golf – during two-day trip to Ireland
Author: Taz Ali
Headline: US president is meeting politicians and business leaders – and playing golf – during two-day trip to Ireland
Content: 06.11 EDTTrump: I'd love to see a unified IrelandTrump has weighed in on the question of Irish unity, saying he would“love to see it unified”and predicting that a unitedIrelandis “going to happen eventually”.He suggested it “may as well happen now” and appeared to cast Micheál Martin as the person to help make it happen.He said:double quotation markWell, I don’t want to cause any problems, but I will tell youI’d love to see it unified.I have friends on both sides, great people. They’re Irish people. How can they be bad, right?I’d love to see it unified. I think it would be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. It’s going to happen eventually.You know what? The way I look at it,it’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.We’re talking about it and you got the right man over here to get it moving.But, yeah, I think it would be a fantastic thing.Now the UK will have something to say about it, obviously. But I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?”Donald Trump during a meeting with Micheal Martin at Farmleigh House.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAShareUpdated at06.16 EDT

title: Sweden’s extremely close election could see far right enter government | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Latest poll shows 0.3-point gap between left and right blocs, with country’s reputation as global champion of human rights said to be at stake
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Latest poll shows 0.3-point gap between left and right blocs, with country’s reputation as global champion of human rights said to be at stake
Content: Posters for the far-right Sweden Democrats in Stockholm.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersView image in fullscreenPosters for the far-right Sweden Democrats in Stockholm.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersSwedenSweden’s extremely close election could see far right enter governmentLatest poll shows 0.3-point gap between left and right blocs, with country’s reputation as global champion of human rights said to be at stakeMiranda BryantNordic correspondentSat 12 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 11.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSweden goes to the polls on Sunday in an extremely close election that could see the far right enter government for the first time if the country’s rightwing parties can form a majority.Opinion polls show the centre-left opposition alliance ahead, with Magdalena ⁠Andersson of the Social Democrats the favourite to become prime minister again after four years in opposition, but her bloc’s lead has narrowed considerably in the final days of the campaign.View image in fullscreenMagdalena Andersson, the leader of the Social Democrats.Photograph: Simon Johnson/ReutersIn 2022, the current prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, the leader of the centre-right Moderates, broke a longstanding tabooto make a deal with the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD), so that his minority coalition could form a government.That agreement gave the SD outsized influence over government policy, especially on crime and immigration, and Kristersson has now gone further, promising ministerial posts for the SD if he is returned to power.The election comes days after Germany’s nativist Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) seized first place in a state election, and as Marine Le Pen leads the polls for next year’s presidential vote in France.Legal and civil rights experts have warned that such a result could further undermine Sweden’s long-held reputation as a global champion of human rights, which has significantly deteriorated under the current government.“What we have seen in the past four years is huge changes when it comes to policies on crime and immigration,” said John Stauffer, legalthe director at Civil Rights Defenders.View image in fullscreenSweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, talks to members of the media after a Moderate party rally.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters“That is also the concern moving forward into the next mandate period: that this government will continue with a clear aim to further decrease the number of people coming to Sweden, the number of people who can get protection, and also that as many people as possible with migrant backgrounds leave Sweden – either by force or voluntarily.”SD’s manifesto includes pledges to introduce “anti-Swedish sentiment in legislation on incitement against ethnic groups”, revoke permanent resident permits and further cut immigration.One of its slogans is a promise to “make Sweden Sweden again”.Despite recent changes – including the deportation of teenagers, lowering the age of criminal responsibility and sending 14-year-olds to adult prisons – many voters and politicians continued to seeSweden as a “champion of human rights and a champion of the rules-based world order where human rights is an important part”, Stauffer said.“But it is quite clear that the Sweden Democrats do not have that ambition. They don’t see Sweden as an important player on these issues on human rights. So there will be less focus on this and Sweden contributing to developing the judicial framework around human rights.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHow Sweden lost its soul – and stopped being Sweden | Martin GelinRead moreHe added: “It’s a fair guess that the negative trend will continue with SD in government, the view from abroad of Sweden will continue to deteriorate, less and less will [Sweden] be seen as a champion of human rights, but as any other country maybe. For some time Sweden has been seen as the exception.”In an attempt to win back voters, Andersson’s Social Democrats have also moved to the right on crime, immigration and integration, meaning that a win for the left is unlikely to mean a reform of current hardline policies, said Stauffer.“With a Social Democrats-led government, many of the things we see as problematic are not going to be rolled back. But maybe negative development will not continue in the same way,” he said.With polls so tight and record early voting expected, the performance of smaller parties could prove critical.View image in fullscreenThe Green party spokesperson, Amanda Lind, and the Sweden Democrats leader, Jimmie Åkesson, during an election debate in Stockholm on Thursday.Photograph: Anders Wiklund/EPAThe Liberals, who are tiny but part of the governing coalition and whose leader, Simona Mohamsson, has controversially cosied up to the SD’s leader, Jimmie Åkesson, in recent months, could be crucial for the right’s ability to form a coalition. And, on the left, turnout for the Centre party could also prove significant.Meanwhile, the Left party (Vänsterpartiet)has made some headway in the polls, which it hopes could be a sign of a surge. In Stockholm municipality, in particular, it is gaining ground on the Moderates and hopes to become the second biggest party.The SD had already won the immigration argument among mainstream Swedish political parties, said Bo Petersson, a political science professor at Malmö University, who argued that the election could become a test of whether the far-right party had any further appeal to Swedish voters. “The mainstream parties have taken the restrictive immigration politics and then there isn’t so much for SD to say ‘we are unique and stand for this’,” he said. “They have been a very clear part of the establishment.”Fredrik Furtenbach, a senior political correspondent for Sveriges Radio, Sweden’s public broadcaster, said that if the rightwing parties won, the SD was likely to get several ministerial posts which would be a “big breakthrough for them”.If the rightwing coalition lost, he expected there to be a post-election debate within the centre-right parties about “whether they allowed the Sweden Democrats to get too close”.The biggest issues among voters are healthcare, law and order, immigration and the economy.After heated television debates between leaders, the last of which was held on Friday night, election results are expected on Sunday night, but it could take weeks or even months of talks to form a government.The latest polls show an extremely tight race, with a Dagens Nyheter/Ipsos poll showing on Friday just 0.3 percentage points between the left and right blocs, which would leave Andersson’s left-leaning side with 175 seats and 174 for Kristersson’s right-leaning side.Explore more on these topicsSwedenEuropeThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: Firewall compromised: has Friedrich Merz blown ‘democracy’s last shot’? | Germany | The Guardian
description: Many fear chancellor is wrong man for the job at a time when Germany’s defences against far right are crumbling
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Many fear chancellor is wrong man for the job at a time when Germany’s defences against far right are crumbling
Content: Demonstrators at the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin on Monday to protest against the rise of the far-right AfD party.Photograph: T Seeliger/ hutterstockView image in fullscreenDemonstrators at the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin on Monday to protest against the rise of the far-right AfD party.Photograph: T Seeliger/ hutterstockGermanyFirewall compromised: has Friedrich Merz blown ‘democracy’s last shot’?Many fear chancellor is wrong man for the job at a time when Germany’s defences against far right are crumblingDeborah Colein BerlinSat 12 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA cataclysm. A 9.0 earthquake. A five-alarm fire. A bitter rejection ofGermany’s joyous reunification three decades ago, and a threat to the democratic postwar order.Sizing up the repercussions of last weekend’swinfor the far-rightAlternative für Deutschlandparty in the former communist state of Saxony-Anhalt, German commentators expressed a sense of doom, panic and helplessness in the political establishment.With nearly 44% of the vote, the AfD fell three seats short of an absolute majority. Its media savvy chief candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, is racing to find enough support from the other parties to prop up what would be the first rightwing extremist state government since the Nazi period.View image in fullscreenAfD co-leaders Alice Weidel (right) and Tino Chrupalla (left) with Saxony-Anhalt lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund.Photograph: Ebrahim Noroozi/APIt is still anyone’s guess whether he will succeed, leaving a corrosive uncertainty at the heart of Europe’s top economic power. Hanging in the balance is the fate of Friedrich Merz’s centre-right government, once called “democracy’s last shot” to prevent an extremist takeover in Germany.‘It breaks my heart’: far-right’s big election victory sparks dismay in German state capitalRead moreThe result in Saxony-Anhalt has put the conservative chancellor on the ropes, with further punishment for his Christian Democratic Union party (CDU) expected intwo more state polls later this month.“This is the worst defeat for the CDU in years – decades – and something has changed, not just in Saxony-Anhalt but in all ofGermany,” he said on Monday.Whether or not he survives politically until the next general election, due in 2029, will have dramatic repercussions for Germany and its European allies trying to beat back anti-democratic forces.Pivotal elections are duenext year in countries including France, Spain, Italy and Poland.Merz’s many critics say the 70-year-old former BlackRock executive is thewrong manat such a consequential crossroads, calling him aham-fistedandempathetically challengedleader who iserratic in his messaging.Only in office 16 months, the chancellor often seemed incapable of one of the basic tasks of leadership: making the case to voters that accepting bitter pills now could lead to a brighter future, said the political scientist Thomas Biebricher of Frankfurt’s Goethe University.View image in fullscreenFriedrich Merz: his future as chancellor is uncertain.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images“The prevailing impression at the moment is that, in terms of communication, he is unable to explain the many reforms – and the sacrifices they entail – to the public, and thereby win their acceptance,” Biebricher said, referring to planned cuts to the statutorypension and healthcare schemes.The former chancellorAngela Merkel, Merz’s longtime rival within the CDU, hascriticised him publiclyfor his hardline rhetoric on migration and integration but said she took no pleasure in the debacle given the stakes.“This is a turning point – a real turning point – in the history of the federal republic of Germany,” said Merkel, who left office of her own accord in 2021 after 16 years in power. “As a CDU member it breaks my heart.”View image in fullscreenMerz speaking to Angela Merkel at the CDU federal conference in Stuttgart in February.Photograph: Getty ImagesSpeaking at a digital affairs conference on Tuesday, she advised Merz to rethink his messaging in a changing political ecosystem in which emotions counted more than facts.Merkel, 72, noted that the CDU had pointed to data during the Saxony-Anhalt campaign showing that joblessness had fallen and household wealth had risen in the small, relatively poor state. “And then [Siegmund] says: ‘That may be so, but that’s not how it feels.’”The AfD formed in 2013, during Merkel’s tenure, as a Eurosceptic outfit opposed to bailouts for debt-mired countries. It grew increasingly radical during the 2015-2016refugee influx, when she left the borders open to more than a million asylum seekers fleeing war and hardship.Merz took office last year saying he would put the country back on track after the implosion of the previous government underOlaf Scholz. He promised a return to economic growth, a restoration of defence capabilities and urgent repairs to the creaking social welfare system.His recipe for confronting the far right – one of his key pledges – was competence in governing and solutions for Germans’ most urgent problems.Merz also promised a rejection of Merkel’s open-border policy in an attempt to rob the AfD of its signature issue. He hadinfamously accepted supportfrom the far-right party for a tough draft law on migration just before the February 2025 general election, before back-pedalling in the face of protests.View image in fullscreenAfD co-leader Alice Weidel walks past Merz at the Bundestag this week.Photograph: John MacDougall/AFP/Getty ImagesAs “irregular” arrivals of migrants havefallen sharplysince Merz took office, the AfD has successfully pivoted to a broader range of concerns about deindustrialisation, regional identity, affordability and crime to gain groundfar beyondits eastern heartland.The AfD, widely seen as more radical than comparable European parties, had been relegated to permanent opposition in Germany by the“firewall” strategyof shunning by the mainstream parties. But this policy is now widely seen to have failed, allowing the AfD to snipe from the sidelines about the slow pace of any positive change.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBiebricher said that for all Merz’s weaknesses, replacing him would not be a magic bullet for the mountain of challenges facing German security and prosperity.View image in fullscreenA forensic technician works near a Ukrainian aircraft at Leipzig airport, where a drone with an explosive device was found last month.Photograph: Hendrik Schmidt/DPA/APAs well as thethreat from Russia, he cited decrepit infrastructure, the demographic crunch on social welfare benefits, competition from China in once mighty industries such ascar manufacturing, and geopolitical upheaval weighing on supply chains and energy imports.“None of that simply goes away the moment you have someone who communicates better,” Biebrichertold public radio.View image in fullscreenVolkswagen employees during a rally against mass job cut plans in Zwickau in July.Photograph: Jens Schluter/AFP/Getty ImagesMerz’s centre-right CDU-CSU bloc, divided between conservatives and moderates, is nevertheless known for its internal discipline in times of crisis – if only out of fear of even graver consequences from drastic changes.The situation is seen as so grim that it has triggered paralysis, with neither the popular North Rhine-Westphalia state premier, Hendrik Wüst, or Bavaria’s ambitious leader, Markus Söder, keen at this stage to snatch the poisoned chalice.“Merz has now reached a stage where the crisis – which he himself constantly exacerbates – is stabilising him,” said the veteran political journalist Bernd Ulrich ofDie Zeit newspaper.“The CDU and the government (in coalition with the Social Democrats) as a whole are in such a dire state that, as far as anyone can tell, no one wants to take over his post.”Wüst, 51, leads a coalition with the Greens in Germany’s most populous state and faces a re-election battle next April. If he wins, the calls for Merz to make way for him may grow louder.Söder, who represents the bloc’s conservative wing, shares Merz’s view that it needs to echo the AfD’s harsh rhetoric on migration in order to win back support – a strategy political scientists havelong disparagedas counterproductive.1:24‘We should have learned more from history’: Germans react to AfD win – videoYet the dangers of keeping a revolt at bay by betting on a status quo voters so clearly reject are apparent.Much will depend on how bad the news is from the regional elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on 20 September. The AfD is polling well in both states, with clear momentum after Saxony-Anhalt, putting pressure on the CDU in particular.During a fiery clash with the AfD in parliament this week in which he laid out thethreat it poses to German democracy, Merz was reflective about how to steer the country – and himself – out of the current straits.He quoted from a letter he received from the rector of a theological university arguing how many opportunities still lay ahead for Germany and advising him not to give in to despair.Merz said he intended to take this to heart and stay on as chancellor using a new roadmap: “Admit mistakes, forgive, get back on your feet, shape the future.”Explore more on these topicsGermanyEuropeFriedrich MerzAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)The far rightAngela MerkelMigrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Saudi Arabia shuts down key oil pipeline, blaming drones from Iraq | Saudi Arabia | The Guardian
description: Riyadh has increased use of East-West pipeline since start of war on Iran to bypass closure of strait of Hormuz
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: Riyadh has increased use of East-West pipeline since start of war on Iran to bypass closure of strait of Hormuz
Content: A satellite image shows a fire-damaged facility on the East-West pipeline, south-east of Medina.Photograph: Planet Labs/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA satellite image shows a fire-damaged facility on the East-West pipeline, south-east of Medina.Photograph: Planet Labs/AFP/Getty ImagesSaudi ArabiaSaudi Arabia shuts down key oil pipeline, blaming drones from IraqRiyadh has increased use of East-West pipeline since start of war on Iran to bypass closure of strait of HormuzOliver Holmesand agenciesSat 12 Sep 2026 11.35 EDTFirst published on Sat 12 Sep 2026 01.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSaudi Arabia has shut down a critical oil pipeline, accusing militants in Iraq of launching drone attacks on the export route being used to bypass the lockdown of the strait of Hormuz.The world’s largest ⁠crude oil exporter has increased its use of the 745-mile (1,200km) pipeline running across the Arabian peninsula, which links Abqaiq, near the Gulf, to the port of Yanbu, on the Red Sea, since the US-Israeli war againstIranbegan.The Saudi foreign ministry condemned “the targeting of the East-West pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions by several drones coming fromIraq, which caused human injuries and damage”.An energy ministry official told the SPA news agency earlier that the pipeline was “stopped as a precaution”.Baghdad is under mounting pressure to prevent militant groups, including those backed by Saudi Arabia’s regional rival Iran, from launching attacks on Gulf countries from Iraqi soil.The US president, Donald Trump, said he believed Tehran was responsible for the aerial attack. “I ‌think they ‌are, probably they are,” Trump told reporters in ‌Dublin duringa visit to Ireland.On Saturday, Iraq’s government confirmed the attacks were launched from its territory and ordered an investigation. It condemned “the attacks targeting our brethren in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia”, and the office of the Iraqi prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, said the commander in charge of the southern province of Maysan had been dismissed.Satellite images from Copernicus Sentinel Data taken on Thursday showed black smoke billowing near Medina, along the general route of the East-West pipeline.View image in fullscreenBlack smoke over an area of the East-West pipeline south of Medina.Photograph: European Union/Copernicus Sentinel-3/ReutersAccording to the International Energy Agency, Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea port at the pipeline’s end have more than doubled since the war began.The news comes asYemen’s Houthi forces have captured the strategic island of Perimin the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the ​world’s vital shipping routes linking Europe and Asia.The rapid Houthi advance in Yemen: why it matters and what’s at stakeRead moreOil prices climbed past $100 (£74) a barrel this week, while average US diesel prices topped $6 for the first time on Friday – a potential headache for Trump before midterm elections in November.A failed attempt by the US and Israel to overthrow the Iranian regimethis year has destabilised the Gulf, and Iran and its proxies have now tightened their grip over two crucial shipping routes – the strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.Trump said ⁠on Saturday ⁠that ​everything would “work out ⁠just fine” when asked whether he ⁠could help ​move ‌traffic ‌through the strait ‌of Hormuz in light of fresh concerns about Saudi ‌Arabia.“Everything will work out ​just fine,” Trump said, speaking in Dublin ⁠after meeting ​the Irish president, ​Catherine Connolly.But Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, speaking on the sidelines of a developing nations Brics summit in India, said the Middle East did not need the US to be a “regional policeman”.Saudi Arabia has previously accused Tehran-backed Iraqi militias of targeting its oil infrastructure. It said the kingdom “reserves the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, its security, its facilities” and its people.Bahrain, Jordan and Qatar also condemned the attack on the Saudi pipeline, while the Gulf Cooperation Council denounced “a dangerous escalation and an unacceptable threat to the security of the kingdom”.Ed Miliband, the British ⁠foreign secretary, said ⁠on ⁠Saturday that he ​had spoken ⁠with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin ⁠Farhan ​Al ‌Saud, and ‌discussed the attacks.He added that ​the UK “stands firmly with ⁠Saudi Arabia and the ​internationally ​recognised government ​of ​Yemen against ‌these ​attacks”.Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels announced a maritime blockade in July against Saudi Arabia – which supports the Yemeni government – and attacked its oil tankers in the Red Sea.Aftertaking control of the Yemeni Red Sea coaston Friday, the Houthis said navigation through the Bab al-Mandab strait was “safe” for all but Saudi Arabia.Explore more on these topicsSaudi ArabiaMiddle East and north AfricaOilIranIraqHouthisStrait of HormuznewsShareReuse this content

title: IDF soldier filmed shooting Palestinian in leg amid West Bank settler standoff | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Incident is latest to raise questions over Israel’s ability or willingness to stop violent settlers in occupied territory
Author: Lorenzo Tondo
Headline: Incident is latest to raise questions over Israel’s ability or willingness to stop violent settlers in occupied territory
Content: A still from a video that shows a Palestinian man being shot in the leg.Photograph: Video Obtained by Reuters/ReutersView image in fullscreenA still from a video that shows a Palestinian man being shot in the leg.Photograph: Video Obtained by Reuters/ReutersWest BankIDF soldier filmed shooting Palestinian in leg amid West Bank settler standoffIncident is latest to raise questions over Israel’s ability or willingness to stop violent settlers in occupied territoryLorenzo Tondoin JerusalemSat 12 Sep 2026 09.44 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 11.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Israeli soldier has shot a Palestinian man, wounding him in the leg, as settlers confronted villagers by grazing livestock on Palestinian-owned land in the town of Faqqua in the occupiedWest Bank.Witnesses said a group of settlers had entered the area with their livestock, prompting residents to try to stop them. Israeli forces then intervened and, according to men at the scene, opened fire at residents. One of them shot Qassem Hussam, a Palestinian man in his mid-30s, wounding him in the leg.1:15Israeli forces shoot Palestinian man in the leg in West Bank village – videoReached by the Guardian, the IDF confirmed it had received a report of the incident and that the person who fired was one of its soldiers.“Earlier today [Saturday], a report was received regarding friction between Israeli civilians and Palestinians near the area of Faqqua,” the IDF said. “An IDF force that was at the scene fired into the air and toward a Palestinian.”Mohammed al-Sheikh, 34, who was standing next to Hussam, told the Guardian the confrontation began when villagers encountered Israeli settlers grazing livestock on Palestinian-owned land.“Then the Israeli soldiers came,” al-Sheikh said. “They started shooting. One soldier shot Hussam and he fell to the ground. We immediately went to help him and move him away. We couldn’t get an ambulance to the area, so we took him to hospital in a private car.”Hussam was taken to hospital in a light-to-moderate condition, according to thePalestineRed Crescent.The Israeli military said the incident was being reviewed by commanders and that its findings would be forwarded to the relevant authorities for examination. The IDF added that the military was investigating the soldier who shot the Palestinian man,apparently in breach of army protocol, according to the Times of Israel.Video of the incident shows a group of Israeli soldiers and settlers confronting unarmed Palestinian men before shots are fired.The incident is the latest to raise questions over the Israeli government’s ability or willingness to curb violent settlers in the occupied West Bank, where attacks have continued to increase.On 8 September, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, said he would “not stand by” as horrific suffering continued, writing in the Guardian that for too long the UK had been hesitant to act,“fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel”.Ed Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary, said the government would now take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety, and announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements.The dramatic shift in the UK’s position came after a summer of intense diplomacy against a backdrop of rising settler violence in the West Bank, which led 12 countries, including France and Canada, to announce sanctions.After Miliband described violent Jewish settler activity in the occupied West Bank as “ethnic cleansing” carried out with the tacit backing of the government of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, announced retaliatory measuresincluding the closure of the consulate and entry bans on several MPs.It marked the latest stage in a rapidly worsening dispute between the two countries, with diplomatic relations at their lowest point in years, even as violence in the West Bank has continued.Israeli forces also carried out raids across Jenin governorate on Saturday, arresting six people and injuring a 14-year-old boy, who suffered a broken hand, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa. Soldiers also raided several villages around Jenin, while forces entered at least five towns in Bethlehem governorate and set up a checkpoint at Za’atara.East of Ramallah, Israeli settlers attacked the outskirts of Burqa, throwing stones at homes and vehicles.On 4 September,two Palestinian teenagers were shot deadin al-Mughayyir after settlers entered the village under police and military escort and took dozens of sheep from a Palestinian home, residents and Israeli activists said.The victims were Khalil Abu Alia, 16, and Omar al-Nassan, 19. Three other pupils from their 470-strong school had already been killed by Israeli soldiers and settlers this year.According to the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), more than 1,111 Palestinians, including at least 243 children, have been killed in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since 7 October 2023.Explore more on these topicsWest BankIsraelPalestineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran’s Houthi allies capture strategic island on vital oil shipping route | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Rampant Yemeni fighters take control of island in narrow point of Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi is relying on for oil exports
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Rampant Yemeni fighters take control of island in narrow point of Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi is relying on for oil exports
Content: Houthi fighters on a march to mobilise more fighters against Saudi-backed government troops, in Sana'a on Thursday.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAView image in fullscreenHouthi fighters on a march to mobilise more fighters against Saudi-backed government troops, in Sana'a on Thursday.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAYemenIran’s Houthi allies capture strategic island on vital oil shipping routeRampant Yemeni fighters take control of island in narrow point of Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi is relying on for oil exportsWhy the rapid Houthi advance matters and what’s at stakePatrick WintourDiplomatic editorSat 12 Sep 2026 00.45 EDTFirst published on Fri 11 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYemen’s rampant Houthi forces have captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the ​world’s vital shipping routes.The Iran-aligned Houthis took control of the volcanic island after forces allied to the UN-backed, Aden-based government left in the latest of a dramatic series of reverses along Yemen’s west coast in recent days, includingthe loss of the port city of Mochaon Thursday.Saudi Arabia, which supports and bankrolls the official Yemen government, mounted air raids on Houthi positions in Mocha on Friday.The Bab al-Mandab strait links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal. Perim island, also known as Mayun, divides the waterway in two, close to its narrowest point. The United Arab Emirates, a former Saudi ally in the anti-Houthi coalition, had been building an airbase on the island before ending its active involvement in the conflict in January.Houthi advance mapSaudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab to export its crude sinceIranhas been targeting vessels in the strait of Hormuz. About 12% of the world’s goods are typically shipped through the strait.Saudi Arabia has now said it has shut down a crucial pipeline a day after it was attacked by drones, and Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels captured Perim.It said it had shut its East-West pipeline as “a precautionary measure”, blaming the attack on several drones that came from Iraq. In a statement carried by the state-run Saudi Press Agency, the kingdom said it would not respond to the attack to give the Iraqi government “an opportunity to take the necessary measures”.The pipeline, also known as the Petroline,runs for 1,201km (746 miles) from the Abqaiq oilfield in the kingdom’s east near Bahrain and Qatar, to the port city Yanbu at the Red Sea.Built in the 1980s, it has played an important role in Saudi Arabia’s ability to export oil after the disruption of the strait of Hormuz during the Iran war.Full Houthi control of shipping in the Bab al-Mandab strait, alongside Iranian control of the strait of Hormuz, would strengthen the chokeholds of anti-western forces over global energy shipments.Oilprices have risen to more than $100 a barrel as the fighting in Yemen has escalated.Iran hailed the Houthi advances in an official statement on Friday, its first extended comment on the renewed fighting inside Yemen. Iran and theHouthishave been allied since the Houthis rose to power inside Yemen in 2014.View image in fullscreenFighters loyal to the Houthis march during a rally to recruit more fighters, in Sana’a on Thursday.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesIn a statement the Houthis hailed the expulsion of “Saudi enemy” troops from six districts in the Taiz and Hodeidah regions, the capture of 4,500 sq miles, the targeting of “seven military divisions of the Saudi enemy’s forces” and the “killing, capture, and wounding” of hundreds of soldiers. It also claimed to have released hundreds of prisoners “held by the Saudi enemy’s mercenaries for years”.British diplomatic sources said they did not at present expect Donald Trump to sanction any US bombing of Houthi positions in Yemen, despite requests to do so from Saudi Arabia. The pace of the Houthi advance, and political divisions in the Yemen governorates not controlled by the Houthis, have left western capitals fearful that even the Yemen government capital, Aden, could fall to the Houthis. The UK effectively treated Yemen as a British protectorate until 1967.The Houthi offensive has cost more than 500 lives and displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday.View image in fullscreenPerim island seen in a 2021 satellite photograph.Photograph: Planet Labs Inc./APThe Houthi progress down the Red Sea coast from the port of Hodeidah also strengthens Iran’s hand in trying to reach an agreement with other Gulf states on future control of the strait of Hormuz, the central dispute between the US and Iran. Iran has reached an agreement on temporary approved routes with Oman, the country sharing the southern coast of the Hormuz strait. The proposed deal is supposed to be discussed at a meeting of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) foreign ministers in the Omani coastal city of Salalah on Monday.The deal, including a temporary approved route for shipping largely under Iranian control, would – if agreed by the GCC – put pressure on the US to lift its highly effective blockade of Iranian oil ports, which is severely damaging the Iranian economy.Map of Houthi-controlled areas of YemenThe US struck a surprise ceasefire deal with the Houthis in May 2025after the cost of a bombing campaign escalated, and Houthis gave private assurances that they would not attack US shipping in the Red Sea. The Houthi leadership this week continued to give similar assurances to all shipping except Saudi Arabian oil tankers.On 14 August Saudi Arabia assembled a 14-country international maritime naval coalition to protect freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab strait and the Gulf of Aden. The coalition, including Bahrain, Pakistan, Somalia, Djibouti, Turkey and Egypt, has so far been invisible, though Riyadh would argue that such a coalition of the willing takes time to assemble.Recriminations are under way over the fall of Mocha, with the role of Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, the leader of the National Resistance Forces that retreated from the city, under scrutiny. He said the retreat was necessary to regroup his forces.View image in fullscreenA view of the Bab al-Mandab strait from the Yemeni coast.Photograph: Khaled Ziad/AFP/Getty ImagesOn her Facebook page, the Yemeni 2011 Nobel peace prize winner, Tawakkol Karman, called on Yemen’s president, Rashad al-Alimi, to dismiss Saleh and to refer him for investigation and trial on charges of conspiracy and high treason.Amr al-Bidh, the foreign affairs representative of the separatist political organisation the Southern Transitional Council (STC), said he had warned western diplomats repeatedly of the need for a comprehensive national regional and international strategy to defeat the Houthis, adding occasional airstrikes were not enough.He accused the Saudis of strategic incompetence and of alienating the southern forces most needed to combat the Houthis.“The position is now very serious,” he said. “The Houthis’ presence in the strait means they will be able to control the waterways without needing to use sophisticated weapons that as a result they can now use elsewhere. The advance is also likely to give them a new income through control of ports along the west coast of the Red Sea.” The Houthis are already offering concessionary rates to draw traffic from ports controlled by the Yemeni government in the Gulf of Aden.The STC was the dominant political and military force in southern Yemen until this January, when Saudi Arabia bombed its troops, closed its political organisation down and detained as many as 20 of its leaders in Riyadh.A Saudi promise of a dialogue about the southern question made in January has never been kept, al-Bidh said, adding that Human Rights Watch warned in a March report that some pro-STC protests in Aden were being repressed with undue violence.“The betrayal of promises had left the southern population unwilling to leave their home territories to fight the Houthis in the north,” he said. “The Saudis for 10 years have been dependent on the people of the south to deter the Houthis, and the STC with as many as 80,000 troops at its disposal, has been the backbone of that force.”Saudi Arabia is facing a familiar dilemma: whether to reach a negotiated settlement with the Houthis on the future of Yemen or to try to push the highly stretched Houthi forces back.Although the Houthis operate independently of Tehran’s instructions, it is hugely to Iran’s advantage for them to be fighting Saudi Arabia, as the Saudis are more likely in turn to put pressure on Washington to relent over Iran.There is also concern in western capitals about the use of western weaponry by the Saudis in Yemen, and whether their activity complies with international humanitarian law, including whether the Saudi strikes can truly be seen as acts of self-defence.Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisUS-Israel war on IranIranOilSaudi ArabiaMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Nearly 50,000 Yemeni civilians flee as Houthis advance along Red Sea coast | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Global struggle for control of Bab al-Mandab strait threatens to turn Yemen’s on-off conflict into a forever war
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: Global struggle for control of Bab al-Mandab strait threatens to turn Yemen’s on-off conflict into a forever war
Content: Houthi rebels march during a mobilisation campaign in Sana’a on Thursday. The group’s advance and seizure of towns has come unexpectedly and fast.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenHouthi rebels march during a mobilisation campaign in Sana’a on Thursday. The group’s advance and seizure of towns has come unexpectedly and fast.Photograph: APYemenNearly 50,000 Yemeni civilians flee as Houthis advance along Red Sea coastGlobal struggle for control of Bab al-Mandab strait threatens to turn Yemen’s on-off conflict into a forever warViolence erupts in Yemen again: why it matters globally and how it is linked to the US-Iran warSaudi Arabia shuts down oil pipeline, blaming drones from IraqOliver HolmesSat 12 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 09.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNearly 50,000 people have fleda sudden advance by Houthi forces in western Yemen, with entire villages emptied and families trapped near frontline fighting with depleting food supplies, according to aid workers.Civilians in the Middle East’s poorest country have found themselves victims of a global struggle for control over one of the most important shipping routes in the world, which threatens to turn Yemen’s on-off conflict into a forever war.Ina lightning advance this week, the Iran-backed Houthi militants have seized a string of towns along the Red Sea coast from forces aligned with the US- and Saudi-backed Yemeni government. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed. Many fear a return to the full-scale civil war that killed 150,000 and brought many others to the brink of famine.Map of Yemen marking recent Houthi movementsThe UN International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Friday that 46,000 people had been displaced across the governates of Taiz and Hodeidah, where steep verdant mountain ridges give way to arid coastal plains. For many families, this was their second or even third time they had been forced out of their homes.Violence erupts in Yemen again: why it matters globally and how it is linked to the US-Iran warRead moreA significant number of people were observed to be leaving the city with their belongings. Fighting has cut key roads, while phone lines are down in some areas. “The scale of displacement is increasing rapidly,” said Joe Lowry, IOM’sMiddle East and north Africaspokesperson in Cairo.View image in fullscreenA heavily laden vehicle arrives in Sana’a as people flee frontline fighting.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAThe most urgent needs were emergency shelters, cash assistance, food, drinking water, household items, healthcare and protection services. “Civilians are bearing the brunt of renewed frontline warfare, airstrikes, shelling, and large-scale displacement,” Lowry said.“Many of those fleeing have arrived with very few belongings after leaving suddenly, due to shelling and frontline advances.”Lowry said aid workers were having to constantly reassess access, and adapt movements, as the situation changed. “It’s a highly fluid and uncertain situation marked by rapid territorial changes, population movements and growing concern among communities about further escalation,” he said.The Houthi advance has come unexpectedly and fast, particularlythe fall of the strategic port city of Mocha– widely regarded as the birthplace of the global coffee trade and the eponym​ for chocolate-flavoured coffee.View image in fullscreenResidents fled the strategic port city of Mocha after Houthi strikes which destroyed civilian infrastructure.Photograph: Al Joumhouriya TV/ReutersMohamed, 46, who left Mocha in the middle of the night, told Agence France-Presse there was an “apocalyptic” atmosphere in the city. Another man, Mujahid Tahami, who set off for the southern government-held city of Aden, said some families had fallen victim to “looting by gangs as they tried to flee”.Others reported that they had managed to flee in time, some on motorbikes, but other family members were not so lucky and were stuck.Yemen analysts have long criticised the US and its allies for taking a security-focused approach to the country that undervalues diplomacy and development. Washington launched a campaign of drone attacks against Sunni al-Qaida militants for much of the 21st century, but did not pay significant attention to the hardline Shia Houthi insurgency until its forces claimed the capital in 2014.View image in fullscreenHouthi soldiers stand guard next to a makeshift camp for internally displaced persons (IDPs), in Sana’a on Thursday.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPABy taking control of key areas this week, including islands off the coast, the anti-westHouthishope to gain a direct presence near the Bab al-Mandab strait, a 20-mile stretch of water and vital trade and energy route that connects Asia with Europe. ​The strait’s name is roughly translated as “the gate of tears” or “the gate of grief”, and its strong currents and winds made the passage between the Arabian peninsula and Africa’s east coast hazardous for centuries. Modern-day cargo ships have no physical issue passing through.​But if ​the Houthis were to close the natural chokepoint, the impact on the global economy could be disastrous. Ships would have to reroute around the southern tip of Africa, adding thousands of extra nautical miles. The fighting has already contributed to the price of oil rising above $100 a barrel after weeks when it was trading closer to $80.The fighting in Yemen, as well asHouthi missile strikes on Saudi Arabia, is the most significant violence in the country since the UN-brokered peace plan in 2022.The UN special envoy for Yemen, Hans Grundberg, told an emergency security council meeting on Thursday that the country faced “a new and more dangerous phase of war”.“This renewed war should alarm us all,” Grundberg said. “It effectively marks the end of the relative calm that Yemen has experienced for over four years since the UN-brokered truce. It not only threatens to plunge Yemen into a prolonged and expanding war, but also risks yet again dragging the country into the wider and unresolved regional confrontation, with global repercussions.”View image in fullscreen‘Civilians are bearing the brunt of renewed frontline warfare, airstrikes, shelling, and large-scale displacement,’ said Joe Lowry of the IOM.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAInstability in Yemen has been exploited by regional powers such as Saudi Arabia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates to fight proxy battles, and the failure to end the violence has led to the growth of powerful militias. The US-Israeli war on Iran has only heightened the tensions, with regional animosity at an all-time high.This has compounded one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. The most recent UN humanitarian report, released last month, warned that the country of 40 million was facing a deepening malnutrition crisis, with roughly half the population facing acute food insecurity nationwide.“Years of conflict, economic deterioration, displacement, climate-related shocks and regional tensions have steadily weakened livelihoods and household resilience,” the report warned. “At the same time, declining humanitarian funding and operational constraints are limiting the ability of aid organisations to provide assistance at the scale required.”On the Red Sea coast, those who escaped the latest wave of fighting had their lives, but were left in shock.“It’s a catastrophe, and the attacks are ongoing,” said Mohammed Khudairi, who fled the fighting to a displacement camp of wood-and-straw huts near the areas of Khokha. “We managed to leave, but others remain trapped there.”Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisInternally displaced peopleRefugeesMiddle East and north AfricaHumanitarian responseUnited NationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Portsmouth experiences second weekend of anti-immigration protests | Far right | The Guardian
description: Rightwing activists faced a heavy police presence and counter-demonstrations to their march against small boat crossings
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Rightwing activists faced a heavy police presence and counter-demonstrations to their march against small boat crossings
