Content: 1:02Anti-migrant rally and counter-protesters face off in Portsmouth – videoFar rightPortsmouth experiences second weekend of anti-immigration protestsRightwing activists faced a heavy police presence and counter-demonstrations  to their march against small boat crossingsSammy GecsoylerandRaphael BoydSat 12 Sep 2026 13.41 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 15.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo men and a teenage boy have been arrested inPortsmouthat a far-right protest against immigration.Far-right activists have gathered in Portsmouth for a second weekend after a small boat with 140 people seeking asylum on board was intercepted last Sunday while heading towards the city.They were greeted by counter-protesters as police warned they would not tolerate incitement of fear or violence.From black-clad agitators to an appeal for ‘Tommo’s Mum’: an unsettling week with the Patriot PlatformRead moreOne of the arrested, a 76-year-old man from Southampton, was detained on suspicion of concealing his identity at the Portsmouth protest. Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary had warned that protesters wearing face coverings could be arrested under powers in the Crime and Policing Act.A 33-year-old man from Portsmouth was also arrested on suspicion of obstructing a highway and a 16-year-old boy, also from Portsmouth, was arrested on suspicion of violent disorder in relation to scenes last Sunday.View image in fullscreenProtesters gather for a counter-demonstration in Portsmouth on Saturday.Photograph: James Veysey/ShutterstockDonna Jones, the police and crime commissioner for Hampshire and Isle of Wight, said that they “thankfully didn’t see repeated scenes of Sunday night with assaults on police officers and criminal damage to police vehicles and people’s property” and that “with the exception of a few people, it was peaceful and conducted in accordance with the new law calling for their faces to be uncovered”.Jones added: “The people of Portsmouth deserve to go about their business without fear and disruption.“While some may think it was arbitrary to use the new power directing people to remove face coverings, the police ensured it was implemented equally and impartially for everyone involved.“I will ensure this power is used proportionately in the future for both sides of the spectrum of protesters.”View image in fullscreenDemonstrators at an anti-immigration march in Portsmouth on Saturday.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAIn Portsmouth city centre, there was a large police presence where demonstrators assembled to march on Saturday.Some protesters held union flags while some wearing Portsmouth patriot branded clothing gathered outside All Saints Church on Commercial Road.A man with a megaphone got the crowd chanting “stop the boats”. He said the protest was against “illegal men invading the shores”.In the neighbouring car park, demonstrators holding Stand Up to Racism (SUTR) andRefugeesWelcome banners gathered. Signs included: “RNLI are heroes, no one is illegal” and “stop pretending your racism is patriotism”.Hundreds of people also gathered inGlasgowfor an anti-immigration rally and associated counter-protest.View image in fullscreenThe Pink Ladies event in Glasgow. The event passed off peacefully amid a heavy police presence and segregation of opposing protesters.Photograph: Iain Masterton/Alamy Live NewsThe Pink Ladies movement organised their event at Glasgow Green, prompting opposing groups, including SUTR, to arrange a counter-protest.The two groups were contained in separate areas on the eastern side of the park, with the People’s Palace and a heavy police presence between them.Ch Supt Stevie Dolan warned of a “strong response” if there was any violence after flashpoints at a previous protest in the same park in July.MSPs Alison Thewliss, a Scottish government minister, and Iris Duane were at the SUTR rally, with the Scottish Trades Union Congress general secretary Roz Foyer.View image in fullscreenPolice officers contain counter-protesters against a Pink Ladies rally beside Glasgow’s People’s Palace.Photograph: Steve Welsh/PAProminent figures on the Scottish right, such as Reform UK’s deputy leader in Scotland, Thomas Kerr, and the Reform councillor Audrey Dempsey, attended the Pink Ladies event.Saturday’s protests came after hundreds of far-right activists descended on Portsmouth last Sunday after a small boat crossing the Channel approached the city. The demonstrators tried to stop those onboard from being processed.Hampshire police said: “We will support those who want to express their views peacefully and lawfully, but we will not tolerate those whose only aim is to create fear and incite violence.”The opposing groups were allocated specific locations at which they could gather under protest conditions. Failure to comply with conditions could lead to arrest, police said. The anti-immigration protest marched to Guildhall Square and the counter-protest followed later on the same route.View image in fullscreenLifejackets at Eastney abandoned by people seeking asylum who made the crossing from France on 6 September.Photograph: Ollie Thompson/Solent News & Photo Agency/Solent NewsThe incident with the small boat last Sunday was thought to be the first time such a large vessel containing asylum seekers had been brought to Portsmouth and the first time that a significant group of anti-migrant protesters had tried to block newly arrived asylum seekers from being processed.Small boat crossings have fallen by more than 40% compared with the same period last year. Whilethe Home Office has disrupted the smugglers’ business model, their methods appear to have evolved by launching boats – such as the one that arrived last Sunday – from different parts of the French coast much farther from the UK, making the crossings more dangerous.Most small boat arrivals are rescued by Border Force and RNLI vessels on the English side of the Channel and brought ashore at Dover. RNLI volunteers and staff have faced abuse from protesters over their rescue work bringing some small boat migrants ashore.The first man charged over last weekend’s anti-migrant demonstration in Portsmouth appeared in court on Saturday.View image in fullscreenPolice officers at Eastney beach, Portsmouth, where hundreds of protesters gathered to meet a small boat arriving from France.Photograph: PADel Leon Somerville, 42, of Paulsgrove in Portsmouth, appeared before the city’s magistrates court charged with violent disorder and assaulting a police constable in the execution of their duty.Assistant chief constable Tony Rowlinson said Somerville’s arrest was the “first of what we fully anticipate to be a number of arrests” and hoped it would send a “clear warning” to those planning future disruption and disorder.The government condemned whatit described as the “thuggish behaviour” of the protesterslast Sunday. “We condemn the intimidating and thuggish behaviour we are seeing tonight,” a government spokesperson said. “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder.”Number of UK anti-migrant vigilante groups surges in last 18 monthsRead moreThe home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, met police on Thursday for reassurance they are ready to move quickly in dealing with “far-right groups” seeking to intimidate communities after last weekend’s events in Dover and Portsmouth. Official vehicles were damaged in Portsmouth anda small number of officers were injured, police said. In Dover,crowds of masked men blocked road access to the portin scenes that were condemned by politicians of all parties.Mahmood said: “These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents.“This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons.”Explore more on these topicsFar rightPortsmouthProtestImmigration and asylumRefugeesGlasgownewsShareReuse this content

title: Donations of £72m make Reform’s prospects both rosier and riskier | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Party can boost its campaign power with funds from billionaire backers, but it can also lose support from ordinary Britons
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Party can boost its campaign power with funds from billionaire backers, but it can also lose support from ordinary Britons
Content: ‘One of the downsides of the windfalls is the renewed focus they will place on Nigel Farage’s own finances.’Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘One of the downsides of the windfalls is the renewed focus they will place on Nigel Farage’s own finances.’Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianReform UKAnalysisDonations of £72m make Reform’s prospects both rosier and riskierPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentParty can boost its campaign power with funds from billionaire backers, but it can also lose support from ordinary BritonsSat 12 Sep 2026 12.06 EDTFirst published on Sat 12 Sep 2026 10.53 EDTShareAll things being equal, pretty much any political strategist would welcome a £72m war chest; a sum higher than thecombined spending of every major partyat the 2024 general election. But all things are not equal, and with such a huge amount comes risk.Reform UK has been vocal in its arguments thattwo sudden £36m windfallsfrom billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne merely “levels the playing field” with the bigger parties when it comes to funding.In one sense, this carries some weight. Of the £65m-ish spent in 2024 by the Labour, Conservative, Liberal Democrat, Green and Reform parties, less than a 10th was used by Nigel Farage’s party. Labour’s fighting fund was more than five times bigger.But these are unprecedented sums, donated at an unlikely time – an election is almost three years away even if Reform is convinced that Andy Burnham could seek his own personal mandate as early as next May.Number of UK anti-migrant vigilante groups surges in last 18 monthsRead moreThe donations give Reform huge scope to expand its electoral machine. They could fund the employment of a new staff member in every UK constituency until the election, though their impact is magnified by the fact that parties devote resources to a much smaller number of target seats.So, what is the downside? There are two. The first is that every time Farage presents Reform as the voice of ordinary Britons, his opponents can argue it is in reality the plaything of people who are wealthy and disconnected from everyday life to a degree almost unimaginable to most voters.Delo and Harborne are strikingly similar: cryptocurrency billionaires who are either based overseas – Harborne in Thailand, although he is electorally registered in the UK – or formerly so – Delo recently returned to the UK from Hong Kong.Opponents will also make much of the fact that Reform’s pledges to liberalise crypto rules in the UK appear likely to make both men even richer, though the party argues this was its stance before it attracted such donors.The second, and arguably bigger, concern for Reform is the renewed focus this places on Farage’s own finances, and the perceived cloud of sleaze which has in recent months become more dense around him and the party.As well as donating large sums to Reform previously, Harborne also gave £5m to Farage, a gift that Farage failed to declare on entering parliament, and which isbeing investigatedby the parliamentary standards watchdog as a potential breach of MPs’ rules.Farage only disclosed the gift whenthe Guardian revealedit in April, prompting not just the standards investigation and theslightly quixotic byelectionhe fought to supposedly clear his name, but a subsequent period when the Reform leader skipped his previous timetable of regular press conferences to avoid awkward questions.Things became even worse for Farage on the eve of Reform’s annual conference a week ago when undercover footage broadcast by Channel 4 News seeminglyshowed senior Reform officialstrying to avoid electoral laws on foreign donations, with Farage himself apparently informed.View image in fullscreenDan Jukes, left, stepped down after the Channel 4 News documentary was broadcast.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersThe party has denied any wrongdoing, but two key Farage aides – Dan Jukes, his de facto chief of staff, and James Orr, Reform’s head of policy – have been suspended, and policeare investigatingany potential wrongdoing.Optimistic Reform officials may argue privately that £72m could buy enough advertising to blitz any negative coverage, and it is notable how senior figures, such as the deputy leader, Richard Tice, insist the party is“at war” with traditional media.But it is more complex than that, especially under Westminster’s first-past-the-post electoral system. If a party hopes to win it must not only convince its base to turn out and vote, but not be so toxic so that other voters unite to stop it.Polls show increasing numbers of voters see Reform and its leader as not just undesirable but shifty, even dishonest, and they are willing to vote however is necessary to stop Farage entering No 10.Will another £72m in donations from extremely rich men make such perceptions worse? Very possibly. And is that something Reform could do without? Definitely.Explore more on these topicsReform UKNigel FarageParty fundingGeneral electionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Number of UK anti-migrant vigilante groups surges in last 18 months | The far right | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Many ‘use community protection as a cover for racist thuggery’, raising concerns about fresh disorder
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: Exclusive: Many ‘use community protection as a cover for racist thuggery’, raising concerns about fresh disorder
Content: A group of men organised via the anti-migrant Patriot Platform gather in Dover on 5 September.Photograph: Ay_audits/YoutubeView image in fullscreenA group of men organised via the anti-migrant Patriot Platform gather in Dover on 5 September.Photograph: Ay_audits/YoutubeThe far rightNumber of UK anti-migrant vigilante groups surges in last 18 monthsExclusive: Many ‘use community protection as a cover for racist thuggery’, raising concerns about fresh disorderPatrick GreenfieldandMichael GoodierSat 12 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 12.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least 28 anti-migrant vigilante groups have formed in the UK in the last 18 months, ranging from unauthorised street patrols claiming to protect women and children to groups harassing migrants in France and blocking ports.From Belfast to the south coast of England, the number of active groups has surged since the summer of 2025, according to analysis by the Guardian, amid widespread concerns over fresh disorder after black-clad vigilantes, many of them wearing balaclavas, blocked roads in Portsmouth and Dover last weekend.Often arguing that they are filling gaps left by the police or taking action on migration that the government is unable to, the groups range from small-scale community patrols near asylum-seeker accommodation to those attempting to stop migrants crossing the Channel from France.They include Scots Active, which conducts late-night patrols around Glasgow city centre claiming to protect the public from migrants, sometimes wearing balaclavas and stab-proof vests. It says its activities help ensure the safety of women and girls. It was one of two groups banned from TikTok earlier this year afterreportedly sharing footageclaiming to expose migrant hotels.graphicAnother is the British Security Project, a self-styled civilian safety group that has described itself as the “tip of the spear in mass deportation under a Rupert Lowe government”. It recruits “visible deterrent patrol” volunteers via its website and social media platforms, and responds to reports from the public about incidents claiming to involve migrants. It aims to “provide 124,000 security personnel to public spaces by 2035”, according to its Facebook page.When the Guardian contacted the group for comment, a spokesperson said it was neither vigilante nor anti-migrant. “The British Security Project is a developing non-profit community protection organisation committed to lawful, peaceful and accountable volunteer action,” they said. “It has no police or immigration-enforcement powers, does not permit people to be targeted because of their nationality or immigration status, and expressly prohibits vigilantism, intimidation, racism and unlawful discrimination.”Members of another group, Raise the Colours,made several trips to France in 2025 to try to stop migrants crossing the Channel in small boats. They filmed themselves claiming to have slashed dinghies on French beaches. France subsequently banned 10 members from the country.Members of far-right Patriot Platformblocked roads near Dover for several hourslast Saturday, disrupting traffic to and from the port. Kent police initially said they had received no warning, but later admitted officershad failed to act on calls made on Friday evening.On Sunday, about 200 black-clad men gathered in Portsmouth after 120 asylum seekers rescued from a dinghy were brought ashore there. They blocked roads and allegedly assaulted several police officers.0:57Riot police clash with far-right protesters in Portsmouth – videoThe home secretary, Shabana Mahmood,urged policeon Thursday to curb the activities of such groups, telling senior officers to make full use of their powers.The rise in vigilante groups is a recent phenomenon, overwhelmingly happening in the last year. Of the 31 active groups the Guardian was able to establish initiation dates for, 28 were set up since last summer, with a spike in August 2025 afterRaise the Colours’ flag operationand unrest at an asylum hotel in Epping. Setup dates were taken from online activity on Facebook and Instagram, domain name registrations and media reports.To classify as anti-migrant vigilantes, the Guardian considers that a group must have taken the law into its own hands in the name of opposing migrants or asylum seekers. Groups limited to more conventional protests and far-right political parties were not included.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenAnti-migrant demonstrators march in Epping, Essex, in September 2025.Photograph: Ian Davidson/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.In a campaign of intimidation last summer, a vigilante group called the Belfast Nightwatch First Division wasinvolved in targeting dark-skinned males in the city, challenging them to produce identification documents.Dr Julia Ebner, an expert on extremism at the University of Oxford, said the figures showed a rapid shift in the ways anti-migrant activists were mobilising which was particularly striking.“At the heart of most vigilante groups is the claim that the authorities are incapable or unwilling to protect a country’s citizens,” she said. “This is a dangerous dynamic, because when trust in authorities is undermined this can quickly translate into justifications of running their own policing operations or even violent campaigns – all supposedly for a good cause.“Another underlying narrative that is not new but has been amplified across social media is the idea that ‘our’ women and children are threatened by men of migrant backgrounds. There is also a performative aspect of vigilante movements: uniforms, patrols and security equipment can project authority and legitimacy even when the groups themselves are relatively small.View image in fullscreenPatriot Platform hold a silent vigil at the RNLI station in Poole from where a volunteer crewrescued about 140 migrants last weekend.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty Images“This can help far-right movements recruit new members and produce visually appealing social media content to increase their public profile and expand their followership.”Alex MacKinnon, a researcher at Hope Not Hate, said vigilantism had long been part of far-right activism, but that there had been a dramatic increase in extremists’ grassroots efforts in the last 18 months.“While vigilante groups typically purport to protect the wider community, the majority do not properly vet their members, resulting in several being exposed for their violent criminal histories,” he said.“Furthermore, they regularly engage in intimidatory behaviour, as seen in Patriot Platform’s Dover demonstration. Vigilante groups of this type often promote aggressive anti-migrant agendas, using ‘community protection’ as a cover for racist thuggery.”In response to the Guardian’s analysis, the National Police Chiefs’ Council said it was important for the public to report concerns about crime and safety.“Police officers are specially trained to respond to a wide range of incidents safely and lawfully,” a spokesperson said. “While we understand people may want to protect their communities, taking enforcement into your own hands can be dangerous, and could compromise a police investigation.”Explore more on these topicsThe far rightImmigration and asylumFar rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: Christopher Harborne matches £36m Reform donation of Ben Delo | Party funding | The Guardian
description: Party leader, Nigel Farage, ‘humbled’ by contributions from billionaires as Harborne addresses ‘media speculation’
Author: Geraldine McKelvie
Headline: Party leader, Nigel Farage, ‘humbled’ by contributions from billionaires as Harborne addresses ‘media speculation’
Content: From  left, Christopher Harborne, Nigel Farage and Ben Delo.Photograph: LPN/Getty Images/The Ben Delo FoundationView image in fullscreenFrom  left, Christopher Harborne, Nigel Farage and Ben Delo.Photograph: LPN/Getty Images/The Ben Delo FoundationParty fundingChristopher Harborne matches £36m Reform donation of Ben DeloParty leader, Nigel Farage, ‘humbled’ by contributions from billionaires as Harborne addresses ‘media speculation’Analysis: donations of £72m make Reform’s prospects both rosier and riskierGeraldine McKelvieSat 12 Sep 2026 11.09 EDTFirst published on Sat 12 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe cryptocurrency tycoon Christopher Harborne has given £36m to Reform UK, matching a donationfrom fellow billionaire Ben Delo.The pledges mean Reform has received a cash injection of £72m in just 24 hours. They are jointly the largest donations made to a UK political party and have intensified calls for restrictions on money received from individual donors.Reform’s leader,Nigel Farage, said he was “honoured and humbled” by the payments, which come as the party is facing intense scrutiny regarding its funding. Reform said it planned to use the money to hire about 400 campaign managers in target constituencies and was now on an “election footing”.The Metropolitan police is conductingan inquiry into Reform’s financesand Farage is facing a parliamentary standards investigation into a £5m gift from Harborne, made before he was first elected an MP in 2024. Reform UK and Farage have denied any wrongdoing.Harborne’s donation was announced on Saturday afternoon. The Guardian understands the money has already been received by Reform.Bridget Phillipson, the chair of the Labour party, said that Farage couldn’t “buy his way out of the sleaze and scandal he and Reform UK are drowning in – or the multiple police investigations that are ongoing into Reform’s dodgy finances”.View image in fullscreenNigel Farage on stage at Reform’s annual conference earlier this month.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPARachel Millward, the deputy leader of the Green party in England and Wales, accused the prime minister, Andy Burnham, of “flip flopping”on a cap on domestic donations. Burnham, who previously appeared supportive of a cap, has faced lobbying from trade unions who fear restrictions would inhibit their ability to donate to the Labour party.The Labour MP Stella Creasy tabled an amendment to the representation of the people bill, which is progressing through parliament and has its second reading in the Lords on Monday.Creasy proposed an annual cap of £100,000 on most domestic donations. Although it attracted the support of 60 MPs from various parties, it was not put to a vote.“The Labour party urgently needs to find a spine and support a tight cap on donations from individuals,” Millward said.Duncan Hames, ofTransparency International UK, said the donations made “an irrefutable case” for a cap, adding: “At this rate just two people could end up buying our democracy before the next election.”The campaign groupSpotlight on Corruptionsaid the donations could have a “huge and damaging impact” and accused the government of “ignoring the very high risk of the Americanisation of our politics”.Farage said that Delo and Harborne “know that we are the only party that can turn the country around and win the next general election – thanks to their generosity, we are now able to fight that election on a level playing field”.Harborne said: “There will be a lot of media speculation regarding this donation. So what do I expect in return for my donations? Nothing. No peerage, no policy change, just a party that is ready for government.“I have already accumulated enough wealth for the rest of my life. I am committed to putting that to work for Britain and humanity as a whole. I want the same as everyone else in Britain: for my children and grandchildren to have the chance to live happy and productive lives here and be rewarded for their hard work.“At the next general election, people will have to vote for the party that they think will best get that done and I’m making a donation very clearly to the party that I believe will do so.”Harborne is a citizen of the UK and Thailand, while Delo recently moved back to Britain from Hong Kong. As part of the new legislation, donations to political parties from Britons living abroad or those who have returned to the country within the past 12 months will be capped at £100,000 a year, with the rules backdated to March.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe protest group Climate Resistance have launched a poster campaign questioning Harborne’s links to Farage.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersThe Guardian asked Reform exactly how long each has been on the electoral roll. A spokesperson said: “All donations toReform UKcomply strictly with Electoral Commission rules and UK law. Both men are British citizens who are fully entitled to support political change in their own country, despite the establishment’s desperate attempts to silence opposition.”Their donations have amplified concerns about the influence of “mega donors” on British politics.Margaret Hodge, a Labour peer and former chair of the House of Commons public accounts committee, said she was “gobsmacked” to hear of Harborne’s donation and said it “reinforces the urgency of us dealing with the issue”. Hodge, who favours a cap, said there was now a “real danger” that British politics could be “captured by rich individuals”.“There has been a reluctance on Labour’s side to confront this danger because of the trade unions,” she said. “This highlights what a lot of us have been saying – you have to tackle the issue. We can’t leave it alone. Self-interest shouldn’t dominate.”From black-clad agitators to an appeal for ‘Tommo’s Mum’: an unsettling week with the Patriot PlatformRead moreMany senior Labour figures, including Hodge, believe union funds could be classified as a series of individual donations from members.“Union members could tick a box saying, ‘I wish to contribute [to the Labour party]’, so it becomes an individual donation, rather than a union [donation],” Hodge said, adding that she believed this would “strengthen democracy” and challenge the power of union leaders.However, this proposal is likely to be condemned by opposition parties and transparency campaigners.Shaun Bowler, who runs the campaign group Wake Up GB, has proposed financing political parties through a government funded civic voucher, in which voters could choose to allocate a small sum to the party of their choice.“The unions funded the Labour party to compete with Conservative funding,” he said. “If you take funding away from the Conservatives and everyone else, it’s a level playing field.”Explore more on these topicsParty fundingReform UKNigel FarageChristopher HarborneAndy BurnhamBridget PhillipsonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jeremy Thomas, British producer of The Last Emperor and Sexy Beast, dies aged 77 | Film industry | The Guardian
description: An outstanding figure in the UK film industry, Thomas was noted for collaborations with directors including Bernardo Bertolucci and David Cronenberg
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: An outstanding figure in the UK film industry, Thomas was noted for collaborations with directors including Bernardo Bertolucci and David Cronenberg
Content: Jeremy Thomas was the acclaimed producer behind a string of commercial and critical hits.Photograph: Anoush AbrarView image in fullscreenJeremy Thomas was the acclaimed producer behind a string of commercial and critical hits.Photograph: Anoush AbrarFilm industryJeremy Thomas, British producer of The Last Emperor and Sexy Beast, dies aged 77An outstanding figure in the UK film industry, Thomas was noted for collaborations with directors including Bernardo Bertolucci and David CronenbergAndrew PulverSat 12 Sep 2026 10.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 15.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJeremy Thomas, the distinguished British producer of films including Sexy Beast, High-Rise and the multi-Oscar-winning The Last Emperor, has died aged 77.A representative for Thomas said he died on Friday “peacefully, at his country home in Oxfordshire, surrounded by his family and loved ones”.Thomas, who started producing feature films in the early 1970s, was known for forging strong creative relationships with acclaimed auteurs, producing a string of films directed by the likes of Nicolas Roeg, David Cronenberg andBernardo Bertolucci.Jeremy Thomas: producer was cross between a kindly Cambridge don and the movie world’s cool uncleRead moreThe Last Emperor, directed by Bertolucci, was an early triumph for Thomas, winning nine Oscars including best picture. He went on to become a major figure in the British film-making establishment, including a spell as chair of the British Film Institute and winning a Bafta for outstanding British contribution to cinema.Thomas was held in universally high esteem by the rest of the film industry. Fellow producer Stephen Woolley told the Guardian: “He was a huge inspiration and a massively undervalued genius and necessary rebel in our industry. He sided with the subversives and movie anarchists and we loved him dearly. Jeremy showed with his first movie success The Shout that boundaries were there to be ignored or broken, and that movies are an international and all-embracing experience. Myself and my producing partner Elizabeth Karlsen look up to his guiding star still moving across the galaxy and inspiring film-makers from all nations and genders with his extraordinary body of stellar work.” Mike Downey, producer and former chair of the European film academy said: “Jeremy Thomas was one of the most significant producers of world cinema in the world. The list of the giants of cinema that he curated, encouraged, selflessly supported and believed in, often when others wouldn’t take the risk, was a tribute to his belief in film as an art above all else. Jeremy’s legacy is incalculable and he has left an indelible mark on cinema history.” Trainspotting producer Andrew Macdonaldsaid in a statement to Variety: “He was a hero for me. A rebel with taste.” Luca Guadagnino, director of A Bigger Splash and Queer said: “The canon of his work is unmatched, and some of the greatest movies of the past 50 years have been produced by him. And the level of the partnerships that he established in his career is incredible, from Nagisa Oshima to Bernardo Bertolucci.”Born in 1949, Thomas’s father, Ralph, was a prolific film director whose work included the popular Doctor in the House series starring Dirk Bogarde, and his uncle Gerald Thomas directed all 30 of the Carry On films. Thomas started out as an assistant editor, working on the Jimmy Cliff thriller The Harder They Come and Ken Loach’s Family Life, before gaining his first producer credit on Mad Dog Morgan in 1976, with Dennis Hopper as the 19th-century Australian outlaw of the title.Thomas was quickly into his stride, making Bad Timing, Insignificance and Eureka with Roeg, The Shout with Jerzy Skolimowski and Merry Christmas, Mr Lawrence with the Japanese master director Nagisa Oshima. The success of The Last Emperor, which Thomas had to finance independently, consolidated his status as a leading figure in British cinema, and he subsequently concentrated on prestige projects including The Sheltering Sky and Little Buddha (both with Bertolucci) and Naked Lunch (with Cronenberg).Thomas then suggested to Cronenberg he should direct JG Ballard’s Crash, and theresulting film was enormously controversial, resulting in local authority bans in several areas in the UK. Following this, Thomas’s films included riskier propositions, such as Sexy Beast, directed by Jonathan Glazer, an adaptation of Alexander Trocchi’s Young Adam, by David Mackenzie, and Terry Gilliam’s bizarre corpse comedy Tideland. Later highlights were Jim Jarmusch’s vampire fantasy Only Lovers Left Alive, another Ballard adaptation, High-Rise, directed by Ben Wheatley, and Tale of Tales and Dogman from the Italian director Matteo Garrone.In 2019 Thomas wasthe subject of a documentary by Mark Cousins, who accompanied him on his car drive from the UK to the Cannes film festival for another Garrone film, Pinocchio; it screened there in 2021. Thomas also directed one film himself: All the Little Animals, starring Christian Bale, which was released in 1999. His most recent film, Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo, directed by Takashi Miike, is due to premiere at the Toronto film festival on Monday.Explore more on these topicsFilm industryBFIKen LoachBernardo BertolucciFilm adaptationsDavid CronenbergnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI IPO will not happen in 2026 amid AI safety fears, Sam Altman says | US news | The Guardian
description: OpenAI’s decision comes after dire warnings about rapidly progressing technology and lawmakers’ calls for new rules
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: OpenAI’s decision comes after dire warnings about rapidly progressing technology and lawmakers’ calls for new rules
Content: OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, attends an event in Tokyo, Japan, on 3 February 2025.Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, attends an event in Tokyo, Japan, on 3 February 2025.Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersUS newsOpenAI IPO will not happen in 2026 amid AI safety fears, Sam Altman saysOpenAI’s decision comes after dire warnings about rapidly progressing technology and lawmakers’ calls for new rulesReutersSat 12 Sep 2026 19.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAIwill not go public in 2026,Sam Altmansaid in a Fortune interview published on Saturday, citing safety concerns overartificial intelligence.“I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don’t feel pressure on that,” Altman, OpenAI’s CEO,told Fortune.Growing numbers of US lawmakers ​arecalling for new rulesto govern AI systems after direwarningsfrom two researchers from OpenAI rival Anthropic that rapidly progressing artificial intelligence couldlead to the extinctionof the human race ‌in the not-too-distant future.The warnings follow cases of AI agentsgoing rogueto hack external systems and AI ​safety researchersquittingtheir companies concerned about the technology’s risks. Politicians, both Democrats and Republicans, have responded with alarm and calls for more action.‘We must slow the pace’: CEO of Anthropic calls for an AI slowdownRead moreThe New York Times in Junereportedthat the San Francisco-based OpenAI was considering whether to hold off on apotentiallytrillion-dollar IPO until next year. At the time, shares in Elon Musk’s SpaceX IPO were tumbling after a surge that sent that company’s valuation to $1.8tn.When asked by Fortune whether 2026 is off the table in favor of 2027, Altman said: “I would say not 2026. Yeah, we got a lot of stuff to do, like meeting this moment of what is going to be required for safety and alignment, and how the industry and governments can work together.”Altman also suggested that OpenAI and other leading AI companies may be close to announcing an agreement toslowAI development and work together to address safety risks, Fortune reported.Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, on Saturdayurged AI companiesto take a more deliberate approach to development.“We must slow the ‌pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote in an essay shared on social media.Altman later posted that he agreed with the sentiment.“I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Altman wrote in a response to Amodei’s post on the X platform. “This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had atOpenAIin recent weeks.”Safety concerns have not slowed down Anthropic’sown IPO plansso far. Anthropic is expected to begin marketing its initial public offering in mid-October at the earliest and complete the listing days before theUS midterm electionsin November, people familiar with the matter told Reuters this month.Explore more on these topicsUS newsOpenAISam AltmanAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingTechnology sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Fossilized 10,000-year-old mastodon tooth found by California scientist | California | The Guardian
description: Molar from large mammal that once lived in North America is in ‘immaculate condition’ after discovery in Bay Area
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Molar from large mammal that once lived in North America is in ‘immaculate condition’ after discovery in Bay Area
Content: The fossilized tooth of a Pacific mastodon on 10 June at Midpen’s headquarters in Los Altos, California.Photograph: Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District/APView image in fullscreenThe fossilized tooth of a Pacific mastodon on 10 June at Midpen’s headquarters in Los Altos, California.Photograph: Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District/APCaliforniaFossilized 10,000-year-old mastodon tooth found by California scientistMolar from large mammal that once lived in North America is in ‘immaculate condition’ after discovery in Bay AreaUwa Ede-OsifoSat 12 Sep 2026 16.34 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 16.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 10,000 year-old tooth in remarkable condition from an ancient Pacific mastodon, a large mammal that once inhabited North America, was recently discovered by aCaliforniascientist.Brigid Lynch, a geomorphologist, was working at a preserve in San Mateo county, when she stumbled across a peculiar rock.Paleontologists later confirmed it was not a stone, but an adult Pacific mastodon molar, according to a Wednesdaynews releasefrom the Midpeninsula regional open space district (Midpen).“The tooth itself is in immaculate condition. It’s the most complete mastodon molar from our area, and the most spectacular mastodon molar that I’ve ever seen. I had chills and shivers up and down my spine,” said paleontologist Wayne Thompson in a statement. “It’s another puzzle in the Ice Age saga that we can put into place.”One giant step: first known adult T rex footprints found in North DakotaRead moreThe pacific mastodon, related to modern-day elephants, were most prominent in the American west including what is nowCalifornia, Oregon, the northern Rocky Mountain region and parts of Mexico. The herbivore mammal, which dates back about 2.5m years ago in North America, went extinct more than 10,000 years ago due to the climate crisis’s effects on their habitat coupled with overhunting from humans.The fossilized tooth has been donated to Stanford University, where researchers at the school of sustainability will employ carbon dating to determine the molar’s exact age, according to Midpen.“Fossils are our only opportunity to see into past biodiversity,” said Christine Garcia, a curator and manager of the geoscience specimen collection at Stanford.“We can study fossils to better understand Earth’s past, past wildlife and the ecosystem they were a part of, and to help us make better predictions and better decisions about how to help our ecosystems and biodiversity thrive into the future.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines USGet the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSeveral ancient mastodon fossils have surfaced in recent years.In 2024, a New York state residentfounda mastodon jaw under the surface of their lawn. A year prior to that, a womanstumbled acrossa foot-long ancient mastodon tooth sticking out of the sand on a beach near California’s central coast.Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaFossilsWest CoastPalaeontologyExtinct wildlifenewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump asks Smithsonian to install ‘Colossus statue’ of George Washington with exhibit | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Trump, again trying to curate museum, says exhibit would stay until 2032 for 300th anniversary of Washington’s birth
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Trump, again trying to curate museum, says exhibit would stay until 2032 for 300th anniversary of Washington’s birth
Content: Exterior view of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History in Washington DC on 28 March 2025. At the right is the Infinity sculpture by José de Rivera.Photograph: Will Oliver/EPAView image in fullscreenExterior view of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History in Washington DC on 28 March 2025. At the right is the Infinity sculpture by José de Rivera.Photograph: Will Oliver/EPADonald TrumpTrump asks Smithsonian to install ‘Colossus statue’ of George Washington with exhibitTrump, again trying to curate museum, says exhibit would stay until 2032 for 300th anniversary of Washington’s birthEdward HelmoreSat 12 Sep 2026 15.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumpasked the Smithsonian Institution to install a 30ft “Colossus statue” of George Washington outside the National Museum of American History, and a special exhibit honoring the nation’s first president, in a social media post late on Friday.The president requested that the exhibit continue through February 2032, the 300th anniversary of Washington’s birth.“He is easily America’s Greatest Hero. Without him, our Country and our Freedoms wouldn’t exist,” Trumpposted on Truth Socialas he flew to his golf coursein Ireland.The statue of Washington would replace the current Infinity sculpture by New York artist José de Rivera, commissioned by the federal government and installed in 1967.Trump’s latest request underscores a perception that he sees himselfascurator-in-chiefofthenation’snational museum. His administrationissueda162-page reportin March 2025 accusing the museum of focusing too much on oppression, social justice and division rather than shared national achievements.‘Don’t I deserve a little grace?’: Lonnie Bunch on pressure from Trump and leaving the Smithsonian on his own termsRead moreIn July, Trumporderedthe interior department to display signs in front of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History that accuse the institution of inaccuracy.Theorderdeclared signs outside the National Museum of American History “shall notify visitors that the museum exhibits should be renovated consistent with the findings in the report”. Those signs have yet to appear.InFriday’s post, Trump complained that the Smithsonian currently doesn’t mention Washington’s fabled crossing of the Delaware River during the Revolutionary War, which he called “one of the greatest moments and turning points of the Revolution”.Nor, he said, was Washington’s victory at Trenton mentioned. “Stories of the Americans who fought and died for our Independence, deserve far more attention,” he wrote.Instead of a Center for Restorative History – arecently endedmuseum initiative to spotlight spotlights stories that have been excluded from the national historical narrative – Trump said the museum should have a “Center for American Heroes.”But it is not clear that Trump has the power to order the museum to make the change. The Smithsonian operates outside the executive branch and its leadership is overseen by a board of regents that includes JD Vance, Chief Justice John Roberts, a bipartisan group of lawmakers and a group of citizens.Last week, the Smithsonian’s secretary,Lonnie Bunch,announcedhe will step down by the end of the year, after seven years leading the institution.“We’re at a time when people are challenging that independence,” Bunchearlier toldthe Washington Post. “but I feel very strongly that it is as independent as we were before, and that I will continue to fight – for as long as I’m in this chair – for the independence of the Smithsonian.”The administration appears to be expanding its reach into arts and culture. For Constitution Day on 17 September, Trump asked the Smithsonian to install the 11ft statue of Washington featured at the recentFreedom 250 IndyCar racein the museum’s Flag Hall.Trump escalates Smithsonian attack with order for signs outside history museumRead moreThe board of the Kennedy Center,comprised largelyof Trump appointees, recently removed Blue, a sculpture by the late New York artist Joel Shapiro, which had been on the grounds of the center since 2019. There had been no public announcement or consultation ahead of its removal.Statues are a consistent theme in Trump’s many efforts toremakeWashington– including a proposal for a “Garden of Heroes” along the Potomac River to display statues of 250 prominent Americans – and he has installed a statue of Washington in the recently remodeled Rose Garden patio.But art in two dimensions is also included in the effort. Last month, the state departmentsaidit is contemplating selling a painting byKehinde Wileythat it removed from the US embassy in the Dominican Republic.The canvas, titled Young Artists after Siamesas 1960, features two young Dominican women standing, flanked by two seated male counterparts. It was commissioned from Wiley – who went onto paintBarack Obama’s official portrait – in 2013.Erin Scavino, the director ofArtin Embassies, called the painting “very woke”, adding that “it was by the gentleman who did Obama’s portrait, and it was aesthetically terrifying.”Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpWashington DCTrump administrationUS politicsArtExhibitionsMuseumsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former US detention officer charged with 20 counts of felony forgery | North Carolina | The Guardian
description: Michael Diehl allegedly forged magistrates’ signatures in North Carolina to allow enough time for ICE to take custody of prisoners
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Michael Diehl allegedly forged magistrates’ signatures in North Carolina to allow enough time for ICE to take custody of prisoners
Content: The Guilford county magistrate’s office notified the sheriff’s office about a potentially forged document.Photograph: Courtesy of the Guilford county sheriff's officeView image in fullscreenThe Guilford county magistrate’s office notified the sheriff’s office about a potentially forged document.Photograph: Courtesy of the Guilford county sheriff's officeNorth CarolinaFormer US detention officer charged with 20 counts of felony forgeryMichael Diehl allegedly forged magistrates’ signatures in North Carolina to allow enough time for ICE to take custody of prisonersKeely AougaSat 12 Sep 2026 14.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA former Guilford county detention officer in North Carolina faces forgery charges in connection to 20 alleged forgedImmigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)detainment documents, according to a Guilford county sheriff’s office (GCSO) news release.Guilford county’s sheriff, Danny H Rogers, reported that on Friday the Guilford county magistrate’s office notified the GCSO of a potentially forged court document submitted by GCSO detention officer Michael Diehl, 40.“The document, entitled ‘Order After Receipt of ICE Detainer and Administrative Warrant’, an AOC-CR-662 form, was associated with an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detainer issued for inmate Claudio Nepornuceno,” the statement read.Calls for investigation after video shows ICE officers using batons on protestersRead more“Upon review, the Magistrate’s Office and GCSO Detention staff determined that the document contained the allegedly forged signature of a different magistrate who didn’t process Nepornuceno’s initial arrest,” the statement added.UnderNorth Carolinalaw, when inmates are subject to an ICE detainer, they must see a magistrate with a copy of the ICE detainer. Afterwards, the magistrate can issue an AOC-CR-662 form, which allows the detention center to hold the inmate for up to 48 hours beyond the time they would otherwise be entitled to be released from custody. The 48-hour window allows ICE an opportunity to take custody of the inmate.However, the GCSO found that Nepornuceno was not presented before the magistrate with the detainer. Instead, the form containing the magistrate’s allegedly forged signature was submitted.A further investigation into the GCSO’s jail booking records identified 19 additional AOC-CR-662 forms associated with 19 additional inmates that contained allegedly forged signatures of magistrates.The investigation found that in each of these 20 cases, ICE had issued a detainer based on evidence that the inmate who was the subject of the detainer was in violation ofUS immigrationlaw.During the GCSO’s criminal investigation into the matter, Diehl’s employment with the sheriff’s office was terminated.And as a result of the investigation, Diehl was arrested and charged with 20 counts of felony common law forgery.He received a $5,000 secured bond and has since been released from custody.The investigation remains ongoing and additional charges may follow.The investigation into Diehl comes as the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown continues across the country.Since Trump’s inauguration, a record number of individuals – more than 70,000 – have been detained by ICE.Explore more on these topicsNorth CarolinaICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)US immigrationUS policingUS justice systemUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Mississippi police say more arrests to come in death of woman found hanging from tree | Mississippi | The Guardian
description: Officials still investigating death of Tasia Fortune, a Black woman, a day after man’s arrest in relation to killing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Officials still investigating death of Tasia Fortune, a Black woman, a day after man’s arrest in relation to killing
Content: Christy Spivey poses with a portrait of her late daughter, Tasia Fortune, on 8 September in Marion, Kentucky.Photograph: George Walker IV/APView image in fullscreenChristy Spivey poses with a portrait of her late daughter, Tasia Fortune, on 8 September in Marion, Kentucky.Photograph: George Walker IV/APMississippiMississippi police say more arrests to come in death of woman found hanging from treeOfficials still investigating death of Tasia Fortune, a Black woman, a day after man’s arrest in relation to killingAssociated PressSat 12 Sep 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMississippipolice said on Saturday they were still investigating the death of Tasia Fortune, a Black woman found hanging from a tree last month, a day after aman was arrestedin connection with the killing.Loved ones also painted a picture of Fortune as a mother, athlete and woman of faith who they hoped would not solely be remembered for her horrific death.Police sought and found Jarques Ratliff, 51, who is Black, and arrested him when they encountered him walking on the street, authorities said on Friday. Jackson’s police chief, RaShall Brackney, also said on Friday that additional arrests are expected in the case. Ratliff should appear in Jackson municipal court no later than Monday morning, said André de Gruy, Mississippi’s state defender.Brackney said Ratliff had an “association” with Fortune but would not elaborate on their relationship. She said police arrested Ratliff on a homicide charge and called that “an important development” in the investigation.“But it is not the conclusion. This case remains active, and additional arrests will be pending as our investigators continue to follow the evidence wherever it leads,” Brackney said on Friday. “We understand that this case has received media attention from across the globe, and across this community.”The state medical examiner’s office determined on Thursday evening that the death was a homicide, Brackney said, allowing police to execute the warrants they already had on hand.Police did not respond to calls and messages from the Associated Press on Saturday about potential updates to the investigation beyond confirming it was still going on.Ratliff also did not appear in Hinds county jail records on Saturday. It couldn’t immediately be determined if he had a lawyer, and a message was left for the public defender’s office. If represented by a public defender, it would be the Hinds county public defender, de Gruy said.Man arrested over death of Mississippi woman found hanging from a treeRead moreChristy Spivey, Fortune’s mother, said on Friday after police told her of the arrest: “I just started crying and told them, ‘Thank you, thank you, thank you.’”Spivey said police did not share a motive or whether DNA led them to the arrest. Spivey said she did not know the man who had been arrested, but she was asking her daughter’s friends if they knew him. Spivey described the family as “in disbelief” and “shock”.“We still don’t have a lot of answers,” Spivey said.Police discovered Fortune’s body hanging in the backyard of an abandoned home in Jackson on 3 August.Spivey said she was certain that her daughter, 29, would not have killed herself.“Absolutely not. Even if she could climb that tree, no, no, she would never, ever, ever,” Spivey said.An obituary about Fortune posted on the website of Tucker funeral home in Central City, Kentucky, in August stated that Fortune’s “path was not always easy, and there were highs and lows”. It also stated that she skipped her junior year of high school, was a star cross-country runner, and had a strong faith in God. Services were held last month inKentucky.“She leaves behind a powerful legacy of resilience, rooted deeply in her unwavering faith. Even in her darkest hours, she never stopped believing in her Savior,” the obituary stated.Fortune was also the mother of four children, but she rarely saw two of them, Spivey said. The last time Spivey saw her daughter was in late July for a planned family reunion in Kentucky that was canceled, but her daughter came to see her anyway.“When she was there, there was this pull, like a spiritual pull to her. I needed her. I guess God knew that was going to be it,” Spivey said.Spivey said she and Fortune’s father faced racism and violence as a mixed-race couple in Crittenden county, Kentucky, before Fortune was born.Fortune was taken from her parents and placed in foster care as a child. During her high school years, she moved around among group homes and eventually ran away to Mississippi. The obituary stated that she had lived in Jackson for 10 years.Spivey wasn’t sure where Fortune was living at the time of her death but said her daughter had been struggling with homelessness in recent years. Fortune had two sisters and was close with them. The father of one of her children was verbally and physically abusive to Fortune, Spivey said.Before she died, Fortune had talked about starting a cleaning business and was trying to get her life in order.“Say her name. Keep it going,” Spivey said. “Because I’m not going to stop until I get answers.”Explore more on these topicsMississippiUS crimeUS policingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tensions simmer on US-Canada border for two towns relying on each other | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: Canadians ‘angry’ at Trump for suggesting Canada should become 51st state, says mayor, as US businesses see sales fall amid trade war
Author: Rachel Leingang
Headline: Canadians ‘angry’ at Trump for suggesting Canada should become 51st state, says mayor, as US businesses see sales fall amid trade war
Content: The Gordie Howe international bridge that connects Windsor, Ontario, Canada and Detroit, Michigan.Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Gordie Howe international bridge that connects Windsor, Ontario, Canada and Detroit, Michigan.Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty ImagesTrump tariffsTensions simmer on US-Canada border for two towns relying on each otherCanadians ‘angry’ at Trump for suggesting Canada should become 51st state, says mayor, as US businesses see sales fall amid trade warRachel Leingangin International Falls, MinnesotaSat 12 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 12.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLike many Canadians, Tom Reid isn’t crossing the US-Canada border as often these days. But he needed a haircut.The woman who cuts his hair lives in International Falls, Minnesota – her “sister is married to my wife’s cousin”, he explained – and so Reid, whose duty free shop in Fort Frances, Ontario, has to travel to her.That’s how it goes for the residents of the two towns, divided by the Rainy River and an international border. They’re longtime friends and, in many cases, family. People cross the border frequently to shop, dine, go bowling, take their kids to sports and visit each other.But Trump’s trade war against the US’s northern neighbor, and his derogatory comments about their country, has Canadians – known for their politeness – angry.Furious, actually. They’re shopping less at US businesses, and, in anunusualshow of patriotism, encouraging consumers to “buy Canadian instead”.Reid is buying Canadian more and more, he said at the register in his shop, with the Canadian flag on the wall behind him. “I don’t have that much choice, eh?” he said.American business owners have seen declines in Canadian sales, while grappling with the uncertainty and costs associated with tariffs on their products. With tourist season winding down, and the leaves starting to change into yellows and oranges, the two towns are quieter.Canada’s retaliatory tariffswent into forcethis week, though no one who lived in the towns had seen that directly reflected in prices yet. It was the latest heated battle between the two countries in the last nearly two years.Canada’s retaliatory US tariffs take effect as trade dispute growsRead moreThe mayors of the two towns call each other friends, and signed a joint declaration in 2025 affirming that friendship after Trump retook the White House. The flags of Minnesota, Ontario, both towns, and both countries fly outside the town offices in Fort Frances. But there’s only so much – and really, nothing – that a local official can do to blunt the economic effects of slipshod tariffs put in place by one man, more than a thousand miles away in Washington.Hoping for the bestMost Canadians recognize this, according to Andrew Hallikas, the mayor of Fort Frances. They like Americans, and Fort Frances residents can relate to Minnesotans a lot: they share similar interests, in the outdoors and in community, he said. But they’re “irate” at Trump – for bullying their country, for going against an ally – and for suggesting Canada should become the 51st US state.“You cannot imagine how angry that makes us,” Hallikas said. “Please quote me on this. I cannot make this clear enough: we will never become the 51st state. We consider ourselves to probably be the best country in the world in which to live, and we’re quite content to remain that way, thank you very much.”For two towns that rely on each other, the tension of the trade war simmers underneath the surface. They all want it to end. They don’t know how, or when, it will.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Education Images/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesAs the Guardian interviewed the mayor of International Falls at a coffee shop on the town’s main drag, a Fort Frances resident interjected angrily to tell the mayor that Canadians are “so pissed off” at Trump for how he’s attacked their country and that International Falls needed Canadians to survive. Their town was suffering, and their businesses losing longtime customers from Canada, because of it, he said.“I’m originally from the Falls, but I’m an American living in Canada,” the man said. “I’m scared to put that American flag on my shirt, what he’s done.”Residents, and the leaders of the towns, are worried about how they will rebuild the relationship between their two countries if this continues for much longer. Businesses will find other suppliers. Shoppers will replace their favorites with homegrown options. The sense of nationalism hardens.“We just hope for the best at this point,” said the International Falls mayor, Drake Dill.Grant Hauschild, a Democratic Minnesota state senator who represents 65% of the state’s border with Canada, said he’s heard from businesses that have lost up to 30% of their revenue from Canadians. With people already struggling with inflation and high costs, he said a hit like that goes from “a concern to devastation”.“My hope is, of course, that the relationship goes back to normal once we pass these chaotic times,” Hauschild said. “I think that’s what really scares me most … Even if people want to go back to the way things were, they might have unfortunately kind of moved on – and moved beyond – the relationship.”Two towns, one communityTo cross the Rainy River into either side, people use a toll bridge, with the cost for an average car now $10. They present documents to customs agents on whichever side they’re entering, and answer questions about their purpose in town. People who cross regularly recognize the agents and ask after their families.The main parts of each respective town sit on either side of the crossing, with both towns initially growing around paper mills. Fort Frances’ mill has since closed; International Falls’ is still running. Fort Frances is larger than International Falls, and because Canada is more sparse, Fort Frances serves as a regional hub. Its hospital will soon be getting an MRI machine – a huge boon for its aging population.The shops on either side carry gifts from both countries, catering to tourists who fly in to fish, mostly for walleye, and largely on the Canadian side. In a Fort Frances store, kids books called “Little Minnesota” and “Little Canada” sat right beside each other on a shelf. In International Falls, shelves of souvenir cups carried designs for International Falls and Canada.View image in fullscreenFort Frances, Ontario, on 8 August 2021.Photograph: Jacob Boomsma/Getty Images/iStockphotoWhile Canadian flags line the shop windows and fly throughout downtown Fort Frances, Hallikas said this is not a reflection of increased patriotism, but just a border town welcoming visitors to their country. The two towns are “neighbors by geography, but we are friends by choice”, he said.“The bridge is over 100 years old, and we’ve been going back and forth it for over 100 years,” Hallikas said. “Before that, there was a ferry. But our friendship is still going to exist when Trump is long gone.”Dill, the International Falls mayor, owned a business and lived in Canada for 11 years. Many of his friends are Canadian. This fall, he will go up to an island in Canada to meet up with friends.“There’s no politics in that. There’s no thought of exchange rate, or trade war, or tariffs. It’s just – we’re friends,” he said. “But then you come home and you talk and you watch the news. … I would be really disappointed if it gets to a point where we can’t work through it, and there’s a fundamental change that will hurt International Falls significantly.”Residents on both sides have favorite products they grab whenever they cross. For Heather Johnson, executive director of the Fort Frances chamber of commerce, it’s Top the Tater, an iconic Minnesota chive and onion dip. She also checks prices on cheeses, and peruses the wider variety of pastas for sale in US stores. Johnson bowls weekly in a league in International Falls, made up of both Americans and Canadians.Leanne Guba, a Canadian who owns Hometown Hobby and Crafts in International Falls, crosses back into her home country once or twice a month, usually walking across the bridge, to buy ketchup chips, chocolate bars and Dad’s brand oatmeal chocolate chip cookies.American liquor is no longer on the shelves at government-run Ontario liquor stores, by order of Premier Doug Ford. The push to buy Canadian is “pretty well elbows-up”, Johnson said. “I’m drinking Canadian red wine now.”‘Mr T took care of that’Reid, the duty-free shop owner, said the tourist season was about average for him, with no noticeable decline in sales. He has seen some change in his customers.A couple of years ago, they’d come in with the signature red Maga (Make America Great Again) hats. Last year, not as many. This year, he didn’t see any red hats, and customers would tell him they didn’t vote for Trump. They’ll ask about the missing American bourbon from his shelves, and he’ll tell them, “Mr T took care of that”.View image in fullscreenThe Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, and Donald Trump at the White House on 7 October 2025.Photograph: Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press/APHe used to cross the border to go to a show, or the grocery store, or Menard’s, a hardware store, but not anymore. His daughter and her husband used to cross weekly for a date night and shopping, but no longer. People over here are “really upset” with Trump, he said. It has renewed his sense of Canadian pride, but “I’ve always had good pride”.Johnson, whose kids are now grown, said: “I’m glad that my kids grew up knowing both countries, and they know that there really isn’t a difference in people.”Across the border in International Falls, craft store owner Guba said she was seeing fewer Canadians, for several reasons. They’re dealing with rising costs, too, and the exchange rate is unfavorable. Some of it is politics, she said. Canadian regulars are coming less frequently.“They’re definitely being a little more picky about when they come over or being more careful about what they buy,” she said.The decline, while dealing with unpredictable tariffs on goods she brings in from overseas, has had an impact on her business. She’s adapted by seeking out new suppliers, bringing in new merchandise lines, and trying to reduce costs. She has a few companies she orders from in Canada – including a toy brand and a puzzle company – and expects the new tariffs will likely increase costs on those products.People are upset about the political dynamics, but they don’t tend to vent their political frustrations openly, she said. There may be the odd joke here and there, but not usually full-blown political debate. “We tend to try to stay friendly,” she said.The latest tourist season was “decent”, she said. “Overall, we’re still surviving … You can’t really control it.”‘We remain neutral’It’s tough to gauge the full impact of declining Canadian spending in the border town, though anecdotally, people are noticing it. The International Halls chamber of ommerce wouldn’t comment on the impact of the tariffs, or deteriorating relationship between the two countries, on the town.“We remain neutral on political matters so that we can best serve our diverse membership, which includes individuals and organizations with a wide range of views. Because of that, the Chamber does not have an official comment on the political issues surrounding the US-Canada relationship,” the chamber said in an email.Isaac Johnson, who owns the Coffee Landing café in International Falls and lives above it with his wife, said he still sees a lot of Canadians who come over to grab espresso and breakfast. He loves his Canadian customers, including the couple he watched meet up at the coffee shop from across the border. They later married.View image in fullscreenRainy River in International Falls Minnesota with a view across the river to Ontario Canada on28 July 2018Photograph: Don & Melinda Crawford/UIG/Getty Images/Collection Mix: Subjects RFThe locals are caught in the middle of political games, said Johnson, who tries to just focus on himself, his family, and his faith. But people do get emotional about it at times, and “if you definitely bring up politics, for sure,” he said – just as the man who confronted Dill, the mayor, did.The man, who didn’t share his name or want to have a longer conversation with a reporter, said he’s noticed far fewer Canadians around town, nothing like it used to be. He described Canadians as “very pissed off” and said snowbirds were selling their houses in the US. International Falls voters went for Trump in 2024.These broader issues, like the trade war, “pit us against each other”, Johnson said, noting that the man got mad at the mayor “over a guy that’s making billions off us all”.“I love the Canadians, I love Americans, and I love them coming over here and enjoying what we have here, and we can go and enjoy what they have,” Johnson said.Dill, the town’s mayor, said Canadians are “definitely” not coming to International Falls as much as they were, though he thinks it has more to do with the exchange rate. Still, he said later, “we need all the Canadian commerce we can get, and I would like to think they feel the same way”.Local officials are in a tough position. They have no control over the tariffs, though with their communities at the center of the impact, they are expected to answer questions and concerns over levies. They have no direct line to the Trump administration, if that would even make a difference. And their communities are suffering.Hope springs eternalHauschild, the Minnesota state senator, said he meets regularly with the Canadian consulate in St Paul, and reiterates his belief in a strong relationship with Canada. But as a state lawmaker, he has little to no control over any of it, beyond using his bully pulpit.Hallikas, the Fort Frances mayor, said most Canadians have “no rancor for individual Americans” and treat them kindly when they visit, largely avoiding talking about Trump or American politics. Americans will have to work to undo the damage Trump has done to the relationship between the two countries, and that will take time, even after the trade war simmers down or ends, he said.“But we’ll still be friends with the folks in Minnesota and International Falls,” Hallikas said.Dill said he doesn’t often run into the frustrations directed at him by the man in the coffee shop, though it happens. He doesn’t have any way he can directly fix the issue.“The US elected our current president and he has his own agenda and I don’t see that I can stop it,” he said. “I don’t want it to affect us locally. We’ll see. Hope springs eternal. I mean, I thought that everything was going along fine, but apparently it wasn’t.”The uncertainty of it all is “frustrating”, and he’s most curious about where it all lands, when a truce could be signed so that businesses can have a sense of comfort in planning for their futures. The two countries are engaged in a heated dispute – or a “donnybrook,” as they would say in Canada, noted Dill.He likened the current situation to two longtime best friends, who hunted and fished and vacationed together for years – until one of them said, you’ve been taking advantage of me for years.“That’s like driving a nail in a fence,” he said, “and then you pull it out, and even if the fence still stands, there’s a hole where the nail was.”Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsDonald TrumpTariffsInternational tradeCanadaAmericasGlobal economyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Iran’s Houthi allies capture strategic island on vital oil shipping route | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Rampant Yemeni fighters take control of island in narrow point of Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi is relying on for oil exports
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Rampant Yemeni fighters take control of island in narrow point of Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi is relying on for oil exports
Content: Houthi fighters on a march to mobilise more fighters against Saudi-backed government troops, in Sana'a on Thursday.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAView image in fullscreenHouthi fighters on a march to mobilise more fighters against Saudi-backed government troops, in Sana'a on Thursday.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAYemenIran’s Houthi allies capture strategic island on vital oil shipping routeRampant Yemeni fighters take control of island in narrow point of Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi is relying on for oil exportsWhy the rapid Houthi advance matters and what’s at stakePatrick WintourDiplomatic editorSat 12 Sep 2026 00.45 EDTFirst published on Fri 11 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYemen’s rampant Houthi forces have captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the ​world’s vital shipping routes.The Iran-aligned Houthis took control of the volcanic island after forces allied to the UN-backed, Aden-based government left in the latest of a dramatic series of reverses along Yemen’s west coast in recent days, includingthe loss of the port city of Mochaon Thursday.Saudi Arabia, which supports and bankrolls the official Yemen government, mounted air raids on Houthi positions in Mocha on Friday.The Bab al-Mandab strait links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal. Perim island, also known as Mayun, divides the waterway in two, close to its narrowest point. The United Arab Emirates, a former Saudi ally in the anti-Houthi coalition, had been building an airbase on the island before ending its active involvement in the conflict in January.Houthi advance mapSaudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab to export its crude sinceIranhas been targeting vessels in the strait of Hormuz. About 12% of the world’s goods are typically shipped through the strait.Saudi Arabia has now said it has shut down a crucial pipeline a day after it was attacked by drones, and Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels captured Perim.It said it had shut its East-West pipeline as “a precautionary measure”, blaming the attack on several drones that came from Iraq. In a statement carried by the state-run Saudi Press Agency, the kingdom said it would not respond to the attack to give the Iraqi government “an opportunity to take the necessary measures”.The pipeline, also known as the Petroline,runs for 1,201km (746 miles) from the Abqaiq oilfield in the kingdom’s east near Bahrain and Qatar, to the port city Yanbu at the Red Sea.Built in the 1980s, it has played an important role in Saudi Arabia’s ability to export oil after the disruption of the strait of Hormuz during the Iran war.Full Houthi control of shipping in the Bab al-Mandab strait, alongside Iranian control of the strait of Hormuz, would strengthen the chokeholds of anti-western forces over global energy shipments.Oilprices have risen to more than $100 a barrel as the fighting in Yemen has escalated.Iran hailed the Houthi advances in an official statement on Friday, its first extended comment on the renewed fighting inside Yemen. Iran and theHouthishave been allied since the Houthis rose to power inside Yemen in 2014.View image in fullscreenFighters loyal to the Houthis march during a rally to recruit more fighters, in Sana’a on Thursday.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesIn a statement the Houthis hailed the expulsion of “Saudi enemy” troops from six districts in the Taiz and Hodeidah regions, the capture of 4,500 sq miles, the targeting of “seven military divisions of the Saudi enemy’s forces” and the “killing, capture, and wounding” of hundreds of soldiers. It also claimed to have released hundreds of prisoners “held by the Saudi enemy’s mercenaries for years”.British diplomatic sources said they did not at present expect Donald Trump to sanction any US bombing of Houthi positions in Yemen, despite requests to do so from Saudi Arabia. The pace of the Houthi advance, and political divisions in the Yemen governorates not controlled by the Houthis, have left western capitals fearful that even the Yemen government capital, Aden, could fall to the Houthis. The UK effectively treated Yemen as a British protectorate until 1967.The Houthi offensive has cost more than 500 lives and displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday.View image in fullscreenPerim island seen in a 2021 satellite photograph.Photograph: Planet Labs Inc./APThe Houthi progress down the Red Sea coast from the port of Hodeidah also strengthens Iran’s hand in trying to reach an agreement with other Gulf states on future control of the strait of Hormuz, the central dispute between the US and Iran. Iran has reached an agreement on temporary approved routes with Oman, the country sharing the southern coast of the Hormuz strait. The proposed deal is supposed to be discussed at a meeting of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) foreign ministers in the Omani coastal city of Salalah on Monday.The deal, including a temporary approved route for shipping largely under Iranian control, would – if agreed by the GCC – put pressure on the US to lift its highly effective blockade of Iranian oil ports, which is severely damaging the Iranian economy.Map of Houthi-controlled areas of YemenThe US struck a surprise ceasefire deal with the Houthis in May 2025after the cost of a bombing campaign escalated, and Houthis gave private assurances that they would not attack US shipping in the Red Sea. The Houthi leadership this week continued to give similar assurances to all shipping except Saudi Arabian oil tankers.On 14 August Saudi Arabia assembled a 14-country international maritime naval coalition to protect freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab strait and the Gulf of Aden. The coalition, including Bahrain, Pakistan, Somalia, Djibouti, Turkey and Egypt, has so far been invisible, though Riyadh would argue that such a coalition of the willing takes time to assemble.Recriminations are under way over the fall of Mocha, with the role of Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, the leader of the National Resistance Forces that retreated from the city, under scrutiny.
