He said the retreat was necessary to regroup his forces.View image in fullscreenA view of the Bab al-Mandab strait from the Yemeni coast.Photograph: Khaled Ziad/AFP/Getty ImagesOn her Facebook page, the Yemeni 2011 Nobel peace prize winner, Tawakkol Karman, called on Yemen’s president, Rashad al-Alimi, to dismiss Saleh and to refer him for investigation and trial on charges of conspiracy and high treason.Amr al-Bidh, the foreign affairs representative of the separatist political organisation the Southern Transitional Council (STC), said he had warned western diplomats repeatedly of the need for a comprehensive national regional and international strategy to defeat the Houthis, adding occasional airstrikes were not enough.He accused the Saudis of strategic incompetence and of alienating the southern forces most needed to combat the Houthis.“The position is now very serious,” he said. “The Houthis’ presence in the strait means they will be able to control the waterways without needing to use sophisticated weapons that as a result they can now use elsewhere. The advance is also likely to give them a new income through control of ports along the west coast of the Red Sea.” The Houthis are already offering concessionary rates to draw traffic from ports controlled by the Yemeni government in the Gulf of Aden.The STC was the dominant political and military force in southern Yemen until this January, when Saudi Arabia bombed its troops, closed its political organisation down and detained as many as 20 of its leaders in Riyadh.A Saudi promise of a dialogue about the southern question made in January has never been kept, al-Bidh said, adding that Human Rights Watch warned in a March report that some pro-STC protests in Aden were being repressed with undue violence.“The betrayal of promises had left the southern population unwilling to leave their home territories to fight the Houthis in the north,” he said. “The Saudis for 10 years have been dependent on the people of the south to deter the Houthis, and the STC with as many as 80,000 troops at its disposal, has been the backbone of that force.”Saudi Arabia is facing a familiar dilemma: whether to reach a negotiated settlement with the Houthis on the future of Yemen or to try to push the highly stretched Houthi forces back.Although the Houthis operate independently of Tehran’s instructions, it is hugely to Iran’s advantage for them to be fighting Saudi Arabia, as the Saudis are more likely in turn to put pressure on Washington to relent over Iran.There is also concern in western capitals about the use of western weaponry by the Saudis in Yemen, and whether their activity complies with international humanitarian law, including whether the Saudi strikes can truly be seen as acts of self-defence.Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisUS-Israel war on IranIranOilSaudi ArabiaMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘There’s a weird market failure in media’: David Brooks on how his new podcast will tackle the big questions | Podcasting | The Guardian
description: The former New York Times columnist is taking a step away from politics to focus on moral and humanistic concerns the media rarely cover
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: The former New York Times columnist is taking a step away from politics to focus on moral and humanistic concerns the media rarely cover
Content: David Brooks hosts The Atlantic’s new video podcast ‘The Permanent Questions’.Photograph: Rebecca DavisView image in fullscreenDavid Brooks hosts The Atlantic’s new video podcast ‘The Permanent Questions’.Photograph: Rebecca DavisPodcastingInterview‘There’s a weird market failure in media’: David Brooks on how his new podcast will tackle the big questionsJeremy Barrin WashingtonThe former New York Times columnist is taking a step away from politics to focus on moral and humanistic concerns the media rarely coverSat 12 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDavid Brooks knows there are plenty of podcasts out there. But as the veteran commentator prepares to launch his own, he believes there is still space for someone to tackle the big moral questions facing us all.Brooks, who left theNew York Timesin February after 22 years and joined the Atlantic magazine full-time as a staff writer, hopes to fill that market gap with a new video podcast called The Permanent Questions, funded in part by Yale University, that will air weekly starting on Sunday.Here he talks about the dehumanization of culture, the need to discuss morals, why he left the Times and why we need more pro-Trump voices in the mainstream media.This interview has been edited for clarity and conciseness.What inspired you to host this video podcast?I’ve thought this for a long time that there’s a weird market failure in media – that we have a ton of podcasts about politics, tech, business, health, sports, but not enough about the big humanistic questions that get covered in a liberal arts education.And I think that’s part of a wider dehumanization of our culture that all the things that sort of ennoble the human spirit, we are doing less of it, like reading, religious services, conversation, friendship, that sort of stuff.I wanted to do it mostly because, personally, I had great teachers in college and they really changed my life, and I wanted to have that kind of conversation again. I thought it’d be fun. Other people would want to have these kinds of conversations. So that was a selfish reason. But then socially, I just think at a time of great technological advance, doing something very humanistic, having conversations like the one we just taped, which was: “Do humans have souls?” I think they do, and the guy I interviewed thinks they don’t, so we just had an argument. But I needed this, and I think the culture needs to ask the big questions again.While you are most well-known for your lengthy career as a political columnist for the Times, you have said that you plan to move away from politics as your primary focus. Do you anticipate that the podcast will therefore stay away from the Trump administration?Yeah, I will probably steer clear of the Trump presidency except for as it shows up in the wider cultural thing. So if you look at the pieces I’ve written for the Atlantic, the big pieces are like, “How the Ivy League broke America” and “Was the nuclear family a mistake?” Those are all sort of sociological and cultural pieces, and so we’ll do a lot of that kind of stuff. And then my books are all in that avenue too. So I think we’ll probably steer clear of Trump just because there’s no shortage of Trump commentary in the world.Do you think there’s basically an oversaturation of political podcasts these days?I’ve long believed that American culture as a whole is overpoliticized and undermoralized, which is to say that we follow every little political scandal, whether we’re going to remember it in two days or not. And so the big questions of life, like: how do you sit with someone who’s just lost a child or a spouse? … somehow those are weirdly underaddressed. I thought the podcast world was saturated 10 years ago – that is clearly proven to be wrong. And so I don’t know if I would say it’s saturated, but it’s well-supplied with political podcasts.How did you come to the decision to leave the Times?I am of the generation that thinks, ‘Well, you go to the New York Times, there’s no place else. That’s it. That’s your terminus point.’ And so I never even considered leaving the Times. But once I gave myself permission – basically I got called by the president of Yale University who asked me to take on the project and that sort of opened the door, and I thought there are a number of reasons, but I’ve been there 22 years. I got another 10 years probably [of] a full-time career. And if I end it with just having been at the same job for 32 years, I’ll be a little disappointed in myself.Are there new skills you have had to learn to host a video podcast rather than writing a column?The big one is reading prompter and talking into camera. I’ve always spoken from notes and it turns out when you speak from notes on a podcast, it looks kind of impersonal. So I’ve got to learn to read the prompter without sounding like a robot, and so far I have not achieved that. And for the other part, it’s just having a conversation. I think the art form is being friendly and confrontational at the same time. And I’ve noticed this in the last year or two that podcast hosts, especially [New York Times video podcast hosts] Ezra Klein and Ross Douthat, they were getting more challenging of the guests. It wasn’t just an interview any more. It was: we will have an argument, and I think that’s made them all better. And so I’m not naturally a super-confrontational guy, but I’m trying to learn how to be confrontational. Also, I notice when I listen to other podcasters, they have to really listen hard. They have to be able to respond to what the person says rather than just going to the next question on the sheet, and that’s a skill.Douthat, your former Times colleague on the opinion side,recently left the publication to join CBS Newsas a 60 Minutes correspondent. Are you hopeful for his transition to television?I’m hopeful. I think he’s a great podcast host, so if he does that kind of interview and they let him … Ross and I are friends, obviously, but I actually haven’t spoken to him since he left the Times. I think the big shift there is moving from – the Times’ audience is a certain thing, and the CBS audience, I imagine, is a somewhat different thing. And so making that shift, I think that’ll be interesting.Do you think newspapers, particularly on their opinion pages, have struggled to find voices that can represent the full range of political perspectives, particularly on the conservative side?When I was hired at the Times, Gail Collins, who hired me, said, “We think you’re as conservative as our readers can stand.” And it was a good line, and there’s some truth to that. You have to be kind of conservative, but kind of able to write to the Times audience. And it helped in my case that I was not a Southern Baptist from Texas, but a New York Jew from the Lower East Side. So culturally, I was already right there.I’ll say this about media generally: I think we all know we need to hire more pro-Trump voices, but to be a journalist, you have to cross a certain professionalism threshold, like knowing how to do the basic job – the craft. And a lot of people who are on the pro-Trump side reject that whole epistemology, if you want to put it that way. They reject the whole idea of doing journalism the way I was taught to do journalism. They’re much more like, ‘Screw you, and the whole epistemological train you walked in on.’ I think it’s been hard for organizations to find someone who is a) pro-Trump, and b) just an outstanding journalist. There are such people – I think the Times has a contributing writer,Chris Caldwell, who used to be with me at the Weekly Standard. I think he clearly checks both boxes. But I think in general, it’s proven hard to find people in that, maybe because people who have more Trump views or have more working-class views, they’ve thought, ‘Ah, journalism, not for me. That’s enemy territory.’If you have no Trump voices, you’re basically telling 40% of America, “Your voices aren’t worth hearing.” … I think it’s just bad for the country if “the media” seems to be either you’re part of the coastal elite, or you’re Candace Owens and Tucker Carlson. There’s got to be ground in the middle there.Explore more on these topicsPodcastingUS politicsNew York TimesinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Elena Rybakina beats Aryna Sabalenka to seal dramatic US Open title triumph   | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Elena Rybakina battled to a 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 victory over Aryna Sabalenka to succeed her rival as the US Open champion
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Elena Rybakina battled to a 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 victory over Aryna Sabalenka to succeed her rival as the US Open champion
Content: Elena Rybakina shows off the trophy in New York after beating rival Aryna SabalenkaPhotograph: Robert Deutsch/Imagn Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenElena Rybakina shows off the trophy in New York after beating rival Aryna SabalenkaPhotograph: Robert Deutsch/Imagn Images/ReutersUS Open Tennis 2026Elena Rybakina beats Aryna Sabalenka to seal dramatic US Open title triumphRybakina wins 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 despite first-serve problemsOvercomes top seed and two-time defending championTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsSat 12 Sep 2026 19.02 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 21.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEven after she had won grand slam titles and conquered all surfaces, Elena Rybakina has always been considered lesser than the greatest players of her era. She has long been one of the most devastating shotmakers in the world, but there were always a couple more consistent and mentally tougher players above her.She leaves New York, finally, as the undisputed best tennis player on the planet, the new standard bearer of the women’s game, after following up her snatching of the No 1 ranking fromAryna Sabalenkaby succeeding her as the US Open champion. As she has done throughout this unforgettable week, the Kazakhstani showed her toughness in another spectacular tussle with her great rival, nervelessly closing out a 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 victory over Sabalenka, the top seed and two-time defending champion.Elena Rybakina beats Aryna Sabalenka to win US Open for first time – as it happenedRead moreBefore the final, Rybakina had not always played her best tennis this year in New York, but the past two weeks stand as the greatest mental performance of her career. She has had to overcome an achilles injury that sidelined her for a week before the tournament and left her uncertain if she would even compete. There was also the immense pressure of trying to clinch the world No 1 ranking. Then four consecutive grand slam or Olympic champions laid in wait for her during the second week of the tournament. She cleared every hurdle without hesitation.Her trials throughout the past fortnight imbued her with the confidence to play such a composed match against her biggest rival to close out the tournament. Here, the 27-year-old began the match with her serve, the most important shot in her arsenal, completely misfiring, yet she still showed off the breadth of her game by completely overpowering Sabalenka from the baseline. When the Belarusian fought her way back into the match and forced a final set, Rybakina was unfazed. She saved her best serving for the most important stretch, flitting through her service games early in set three and putting pressure on Sabalenka to keep up. Sabalenka, like so many players over the past year, simply could not.View image in fullscreenElena Rybakina struggled to make first serves in the opening set but otherwise her game was in good shape.Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPARybakina has become known and loved for her understated reactions to such monumental achievements, but after shouting in jubilation following her semi-final win over Coco Gauff, here she triumphantly raised both hands into the air upon firing down her 12th ace of the match to seal the victory. It meant everything. “It’s still so difficult to process what happened,” she said. “Too much achievements these few weeks. I’m super happy, very proud of all the work. Yeah, it’s just amazing. Difficult to find words, but super happy.”In addition to taking Sabalenka’s No 1 ranking, Rybakina has now also taken the status as the best hard-court player in the world. She now holds the three biggest hard-court titles: the Australian Open, the US Open and the WTA Finals. She joins figures such as Lindsay Davenport, Jennifer Capriati, Ash Barty, Angelique Kerber and Virginia Wade as three-time grand slam champions. Having previously won Wimbledon in 2022 and the 2026 Australian Open, Rybakina is suddenly a French Open away from completing the career grand slam.Sabalenka’s run to the final was an impressive feat considering how disastrous her past few months have been on the tour, but there was no consoling her after this defeat. Although she showed good sportsmanship in all of her interactions with Rybakina, including initiating a warm hug at the net, Sabalenka tossed her racket and then slumped into a seat in her courtside player box. When a cameraperson approached her, they were quickly told to “fuck off”.View image in fullscreenAryna Sabalenka had lost the No 1 ranking and now her US Open title to Elena Rybakina.Photograph: Eduardo Muñoz/ReutersSabalenka has reached eight consecutive grand slam finals on hard courts, an astounding feat, but any competitor in her shoes would be upset by the number of titles she has been able to win from those positions. Sabalenka is now 4-6 in grand slam finals and just hasn’t been able to produce her best tennis when it matters most. Most painfully of all, her opportunity to three-peat at the US Open has come and gone: “It’s really tough to control your emotions when you lose in the final of the grand slam and when you were trying to go for three-peat,” Sabalenka said of her on-court emotions. “So I just wanted to let it go, because if I would hold it inside, right now or here or there on the court, I wouldn’t be able to say a word or I would just go not really nice over there. So I just wanted to let all of that aggression and disappointment go outside.”This was a historic encounter. Since the Australian Open became a hard court tournament in 1988, this is just the second time that the same two players contested both finals in the same year. It is also the third time that the top two players in the world have competed in a grand slam final with the ranking switching hands. No matter the terrain or stakes, though, these two champions inspire a high level of tennis from each other. Their three major finals have each produced dramatic, high quality three-set matches.However, for a long time Sabalenka was clearly the superior player in this rivalry, even if Rybakina could beat her on any given day. This year the terms of engagement have truly shifted with Rybakina winning their last two grand slam finals in addition to defeating Sabalenka in the championship match of the WTA Finals. It is now up to Sabalenka to return to the practice court and figure out a way past the new leader of her sport.Afterwards, as Sabalenka discussed the end of her reign at No 1, she was informed that her time on top of the WTA rankings had lasted for 99 consecutive weeks, the sixth longest consecutive run at No 1 in history: “Well, that’s amazing. Let’s see if Elena can beat me in that,” she said, laughing. Then she added: “If she continues to play like that? Then, yeah, I’m in trouble.”Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisTennisUS sportsAryna SabalenkanewsShareReuse this content

title: USA survive Spain scare to set up Olympic final rematch with France at Fiba World Cup | Fiba Women's Basketball World Cup 2026 | The Guardian
description: USA survive a major scare from Spain to reach a fifth straight World Cup final, where they will face France in a rematch of the 2024 Olympic final
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: USA survive a major scare from Spain to reach a fifth straight World Cup final, where they will face France in a rematch of the 2024 Olympic final
Content: Angel Reese reacts during the USA’s 76-66 semi-final win over Spain at the Fiba Women’s Basketball World Cup in Berlin on Saturday.Photograph: Christina Pahnke/sampics/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAngel Reese reacts during the USA’s 76-66 semi-final win over Spain at the Fiba Women’s Basketball World Cup in Berlin on Saturday.Photograph: Christina Pahnke/sampics/Getty ImagesFiba Women's Basketball World Cup 2026USA survive Spain scare to set up Olympic final rematch with France at Fiba World CupFour-time defending champions beat Spain 76-66Stewart scores 16 as USA pull away in fourthAmericans to face France in rematch of Paris finalGuardian sportand agenciesSat 12 Sep 2026 16.08 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 17.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe United States advanced to the Fiba Women’sBasketballWorld Cup final for the fifth consecutive time, pulling away in the fourth quarter to beat Spain 76-66 on Saturday in Berlin.Breanna Stewart scored 16 points and Kahleah Copper added 13 for the four-time defending champions, who were tied at 58 entering the fourth quarter before finally taking control. Jackie Young added 12 points.“I think it’s two great teams going to go head-to-head,” Copper said. “You know I’m excited for the matchup. I’m excited for us to be able to compete.”Spain led 13-4 midway through the first quarter and trailed only 39-36 at halftime. María Conde and Iyana Martín hit three-pointers early in the third as Spain erased the deficit, while Martín’s two free throws with 53 seconds left sent the game into the fourth tied at 58.Copper and Young scored to open the fourth before Stewart helped the US create separation. The Americans stretched their lead to eight with just over six minutes remaining before Young’s steal and layup made it 76-64 with 1:42 left.Conde and Martín scored 17 points apiece for Spain, who held the Americans to 40% shooting. The US made only three of 18 three-point attempts, while Caitlin Clark finished with one point and missed all three of her shots from beyond the arc.View image in fullscreenCaitlin Clark and her USA teammates celebrate after beating Spain 76-66 to reach the Fiba Women’s Basketball World Cup final in Berlin.Photograph: Annegret Hilse/ReutersUS coach Kara Lawson was happy with the defense in the fourth quarter when the team held Spain to only eight points.“I thought defensively, it was the best we had played, from guarding the ball to guarding the ball screen to boxing out and limiting to one shot,” Lawson said. “Every phase of defense, we were precise and we were locked in, so when we get all that going together, we feel like we can create some separation.”To Aliyah Boston, who was playing in the World Cup for the first time, the game had an NCAA Final Four feel to it.“When you’re in a tournament like this, it doesn’t always have to be pretty. You just have to come out with the win,” she said. “For us, it’s about not hanging our heads. I think we did a great job with our rotations. Everyone came in, gave energy, gave great minutes, scored the ball. It’s about making sure that when your name is called, you’re ready to go.”The victory extended the Americans’ World Cup winning streak to 35 games. The US, unbeaten at the tournament since a semi-final loss to Russia in 2006, will face France in Sunday’s final after the French defeated host Germany 86-64.The hotly anticipated final will be a rematch of the 2024 Olympic gold medal game, where the USescaped with a 67-66 victoryafter France’s Gabby Williams stepped on the three-point line on a potential tying shot at the buzzer.“I think it’s two great teams going to go head-to-head,” said Kahleah Copper, who had 13 points in the win against Spain. “You know I’m excited for the matchup. I’m excited for us to be able to compete.”Explore more on these topicsFiba Women's Basketball World Cup 2026USA women's basketball teamBasketballUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Guimarães and Saka fire Arsenal to win at Sunderland after Raya spot-kick save | Premier League | The Guardian
description: A stoppage-time penalty from Bukayo Saka sealed Arsenal’s 2-0 victory against Sunderland, who missed a spot-kick to take the lead in the second half
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: A stoppage-time penalty from Bukayo Saka sealed Arsenal’s 2-0 victory against Sunderland, who missed a spot-kick to take the lead in the second half
Content: Bruno Guimarães shows his delight after giving Arsenal the lead in the second half.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAView image in fullscreenBruno Guimarães shows his delight after giving Arsenal the lead in the second half.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAPremier LeagueGuimarães and Saka fire Arsenal to win at Sunderland after Raya spot-kick saveLouise Taylorat the Stadium of LightSat 12 Sep 2026 17.14 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 19.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the final whistle blew Bruno Guimarães wore a mischievous smile, Enzo Le Fée was a study in dejection and Arsenal’s immaculate start to the season remained unblemished.Sunderland 0-2 Arsenal: Guimarães and Saka sink Black Cats in Premier League – liveRead moreTwo minutes after David Raya had rather majestically saved Le Fée’s second-half penalty, Guimarães delighted his new north London public and plenty of old friends in Newcastle by sending a shot curving past Robin Roefs from the edge of the area.Mikel Arteta’s champions were en route to another win in a campaign that has now produced six victories in six games in all competitions, including the Community Shield. No one, though, should be deceived by the emphasis lent to the scoreline by Bukayo Saka’s stoppage-time penalty; this was most definitely the toughest test this term for Arsenal.IfSunderlandcan keep playing like this, Régis Le Bris and his players should have real cause for optimism – even if they could have done without Reinildo’s late sending-off for felling Saka when conceding that penalty and collecting a second yellow card.His penalty miss aside,chapeauxoff to Le Fee, who has deservedly made Zinedine Zidane’s provisional France squad for the forthcoming Nations League matches. Sunderland’s attacking playmaker knew another good performance here could only enhance his chances of moving from longlist to shortlist and he did not take long to draw a foul and win a dangerous free-kick.View image in fullscreenPlayers tussle in the Sunderland penalty area during a even first half.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersArsenal’s former captain Granit Xhaka delighted in curling the meanest of dead balls in Dan Ballard’s direction but the home central defender, a one-time Gunners youth captain, could not quite connect.There had been a similar reprieve for Le Bris’s rearguard when Saka failed to make the most of Declan Rice’s fine early delivery. Yet, bar a Gabriel Magalhães shot from distance that whizzed just wide of Roefs’s goal, a Kai Havertz shot on the turn saved smartly and a low 20-yard effort that Le Fée dragged fractionally wide of an upright, that was pretty much it in terms of first-half goalmouth action.Mikel Arteta’s side were taking their time to establish a settled passing rhythm. If Sunderland’s superb organisation hardly assisted the visiting cause, Arsenal looked a little fazed whenever the outstanding Nordi Mukiele – surely another candidate for the France squad – advanced from right-back.Ezri Konsa, meanwhile, did not appear to be either relishing or winning his extremely physical contest with Le Bris’s ever-combative centre-forward, Brian Brobbey. If a packed Stadium of Light enjoyed that little subplot, the roof was nearly lifted off by the roar of approval that greeted Reinildo’s full-blooded early challenge on Martin Ødegaard.View image in fullscreenMikel Arteta is booked by John Brooks for leaving his technical area.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersOne constant was Arteta’s excursions outside his technical area and eventually the referee, John Brooks, responded by jogging over to the touchline and waving a yellow card in the Arsenal manager’s face. While that booking was hardly unmerited, it seemed a shame that Brooks turned a blind eye to some persistent shirt-pulling from both sides at corners.With the match even at the interval, Arteta replaced Myles Lewis-Skelly and the hobbling Ben White with Guimarães and Jurriën Timber. The Brazilian’s past as Newcastle’s captain ensured Guimarães’s every touch was booed, while Sunderland started the new half strongly, with Brobbey continuing to bully Konsa.A penalty area encounter with Ballard at a throw proved no more welcome and when Konsa grappled the defender to the ground, Brooks – much to Arteta’s chagrin – had no hesitation in pointing to the spot.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenBruno Guimarães, who had been jeered by Sunderland fans for being a former Newcastle player, taunts them after scoring.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersLe Fée attempted to squeeze his kick just inside an upright but Raya, excellent throughout, guessed correctly and tipped the ball quite brilliantly on to the woodwork. Talk about a sliding-doors moment. Two minutes later and very much against the run of play, Arsenal broke from another Sunderland throw and Guimarães did the rest.Mikel Arteta says penalty given to Sunderland ‘unacceptable at this level’Read moreWith no option but to take risks, Le Bris switched to 4-4-2 and also introduced Malick Fofana, newly signed from Lyon, and he quickly created chaos in Arsenal’s box.Although it took Roefs, who saved superbly from Saka, and Ballard, responsible for a vital header off the line, to keep Le Bris’s side in the game, while Timber had a headed “goal” disallowed for offside, Arteta had reason to look slightly nervous as Mukiele volleyed Le Fée’s corner over the bar.By now Xhaka, booked for sliding into Guimarães, was enjoying himself in midfield and from one of his corners Mukiele again went close.A comeback beckoned but Saka had different ideas as Arsenal issued a reminder that they will not surrender their title lightly.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueSunderlandArsenalmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Missouri coach blasts Kansas over slavery references after Border War win | College football | The Guardian
description: Eli Drinkwitz said he was ‘embarrassed’ by Kansas invoking the rivalry’s roots in the violent pre-Civil War struggle over slavery after Missouri’s 38-21 win
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Eli Drinkwitz said he was ‘embarrassed’ by Kansas invoking the rivalry’s roots in the violent pre-Civil War struggle over slavery after Missouri’s 38-21 win
Content: Naeshaun Montgomery celebrates after scoring a touchdown during Missouri’s 38-21 win over Kansas in Lawrence on Friday night.Photograph: Jay Biggerstaff/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNaeshaun Montgomery celebrates after scoring a touchdown during Missouri’s 38-21 win over Kansas in Lawrence on Friday night.Photograph: Jay Biggerstaff/Getty ImagesCollege footballMissouri coach blasts Kansas over slavery references after Border War winTigers beat Kansas 38-21 in historic Border WarRivalry has roots in pre-Civil War slavery conflictDrinkwitz says buildup left him ‘embarrassed’AgenciesSat 12 Sep 2026 12.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe latest edition of the Border War between Missouri and Kansas turned out to be a mere skirmish for a half.Robert Woodyard Jr produced back-to-back turnovers soon after the break, and Austin Simmons and the potent Tigers offense turned them into touchdowns, helping No 23 Missouri break open a tie game and roll to a 38-21 victory Friday night.The wild world of LSU: from tigers on the field to wooing ex-NFL playersRead moreJamal Roberts ran for 125 yards and a touchdown, and Donovan Olugbode and Cayden Lee caught TD passes, as the Tigers (2-0) beat their biggest rival for the fifth straight time in their first trip across the state line since 29 October 2005.“The things that we gave them were undisciplined penalties, special teams were not good tonight in any form or facet, but we overcame it,” Tigers coach Eli Drinkwitz said, “and that’s what you have to do on the road.”That’s not all Drinkwitz had to say, though He took umbrage with the way Kansas leaned into the historic nature of the rivalry, which began as an armed conflict over the issue of slavery along the state line in the years leading up to the Civil War.“I’m just glad the whole right-versus-wrong crap got settled on the football field,” Drinkwitz said. “I get there’s a past to it but why are we stirring that bullcrap up? It’s 9/11. We need more unity. I was embarrassed for them. That’s why I tried to embarrass them.”The Tigers threw to the end zone in the final seconds, trying to get one last score, before running out the clock.“There was a lot of juice in the stadium,” Jayhawks coach Lance Leipold said. “Just some things happened – a couple of things you just can’t do if you play ranked teams and want to beat them.”View image in fullscreenMissouri head coach Eli Drinkwitz argues with an official during the Tigers’ 38-21 win over Kansas on Friday night in Lawrence.Photograph: Jay Biggerstaff/Getty ImagesThe game was tied 14-all early in the second half when Woodyard fell on Kansas quarterback Isaiah Marshall’s fumble, and Simmons quickly found Olugbode for the go-ahead touchdown. On the Jayhawks’ next offensive play, Woodyard faded into the secondary and was there to pick off Marshall’s pass, setting up Xai’Shaun Edwards’ touchdown run.Marshall finished with 168 yards passing, two touchdowns and two interceptions for the Jayhawks (1-1), who haven’t beaten Missouri since 29 November 2008. The sophomore quarterback also carried 20 times but managed just 23 yards.Kansas actually jumped on the Tigers early, just as it did last season in Columbia, when a series that went on hiatus after the Tigers’ departure for the SEC finally resumed after more than a decade. This time around, the Jayhawks capitalized on Missouri miscues: four false start penalties in the first half alone, blown blocking assignments and two blocked field-goal attempts.On the second block, the Jayhawks’ Austin Alexander scooped up the ball and ran 88 yards for the first points of the game.Roberts, once more taking center stage for the Tigers with All-American Ahmad Hardy rehabbing after a gunshot wound earlier this year, quickly provided an answer, jetting over the right side for a 64-yard touchdown run. It was the longest of his career, eclipsing a 63-yarder that Roberts scored with 1:49 to go to clinch last year’s 42-31 victory over the Jayhawks.The teams traded touchdowns late in the first half, sending the 122nd edition of the Border War to the break tied 14-all.But two big plays by Woodyards and the Missouri defense tilted the game in their favor, and after Marshall found Nahzae Cox to get Kansas to 28-21 late in the third quarter, the Tigers’ Blake Craig added a field goal to help them regain control.“Energy never changed, honestly. The mentality always stayed the same,” Simmons said. “We were just trying to win at all costs.”Explore more on these topicsCollege footballCollege sportsUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Solheim Cup: Hull and Woad flop for Europe as Kupcho pulls USA level | Solheim Cup | The Guardian
description: USA win three fourballs matches to make score 8-8 against Europe and leave the Solheim Cup finely poised heading into the final day
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: USA win three fourballs matches to make score 8-8 against Europe and leave the Solheim Cup finely poised heading into the final day
Content: Charley Hull (left) has struggled for Europe, who are level at 8-8 with USA in the Solheim Cup.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APView image in fullscreenCharley Hull (left) has struggled for Europe, who are level at 8-8 with USA in the Solheim Cup.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APSolheim CupSolheim Cup: Hull and Woad flop for Europe as Kupcho pulls USA levelScores level at 8-8 after dramatic day twoAnna Nordqvist pairing of star duo fails to pay offEwan Murrayat Bernardus GolfSat 12 Sep 2026 14.25 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 17.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has been the great anomaly of this Solheim Cup. Europe keeping perfect pace with the United States is an impressive achievement even without factoring in the meagre points contribution from Charley Hull and Lottie Woad. European hopes of reclaiming thetrophy lost to the United States two years agosurely depend heavily on their star turns finding singles form.The heroics of Jennifer Kupcho in fading light dashed Europe’s ambitions of taking a lead. It is 8-8 as things stand. A 12-match shootout remains.Solheim Cup golf 2026: Europe take charge against USA after day two foursomes – liveRead moreAnna Nordqvist’s deployment of Hull and Woad as a pairing on Saturday morning has to be considered odd. The duo had claimed half a point from two previous outings. Hull does not look particularly suited to foursomes. Woad is aSolheim Cupdebutant. Nordqvist, it appeared, focused heavily on the status of both players inside the world’s top 10. The tactic backfired; Alison Lee and Lauren Coughlin thumped the English pair, 6&5. Undeterred, Nordqvist sent Hull and Woad back out. This time it was Yealimi Noh and Andrea Lee who emerged victorious.“I don’t think people understand these are the best players in the world,” said Nordqvist when asked whether Saturday afternoon selection was wise. “I think they played [against] the strongest pairings in each session. Lottie herself made six birdies yesterday in the afternoon. So they’re playing solid and I wouldn’t be surprised if we get a little bit of blue on that board this afternoon.”View image in fullscreenA 90-foot birdie from Jennifer Kupcho (left) at the 17th hole pulled her and Lindy Duncan (right) level.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APThe Swede’s hopes proved in vain. Troubles on the greens undermined the performance of Hull and Woad as the Americans prevailed on the final green. The Europeans gave the regular impression they would rather be elsewhere. A high point came on the 17th, where Woad’s brave putt from 15ft kept the match alive. At the final tee, Hull pulled a fairway wood into water.Nordqvist’s decision-making created history, with Hull and Woad the first to play four sessions together in the same Solheim Cup. Nordqvist’s faith has failed to find reward. In fairness, in Noh the Europeans in question faced the player of this event. She has been exceptional.Hull and Woad said they knew they would play every session, which raises questions over how nimble their captain is. “It was pretty frustrating,” said Hull of the fourball loss. Woad added: “It doesn’t matter who wins the points. I would happily lose my matches if we win.”This is indeed a team business. After back-to-back tied sessions, Europe forged ahead on Saturday morning. The superb Maja Stark and Linn Grant saw off Allisen Corpuz and the world No 1, Nelly Korda. Angela Stanford, the US captain, stood down Korda after lunch.View image in fullscreenThe world No 1 Nelly Korda did not compete in the afternoon fourballs.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APLeona Maguire and Esther Henseleit enjoyed a successful reunion as they defeated the US pair of Kupcho and Rose Zhang. The European rookies Mimi Rhodes and Nastasia Nadaud were again outstanding as they claimed a point from Auston Kim and Andrea Lee. Alison Lee and Coughlin returned the sole US reward of the foursomes.Coughlin will be the only US player to feature in all five sessions. Stanford explained that was not determined before the event. Coughlin and Megan Khang tasted fourball defeat to Stark and Grant. “Maja played out of her mind,” Coughlin said.Noh and Andrea Lee confirmed victory over Hull and Woad on the last green. Kim and Zhang were 3&2 winners over Maguire and Nadaud. In seeking to tie the fourball session, Europe needed Carlota Ciganda and Céline Boutier to hold off Kupcho and Lindy Duncan.Europe were two up after 14. A three from Duncan on the 15th narrowed the deficit, but the Europeans looked like they would do enough to cling on. Enter Kupcho, who converted in extraordinary circumstances from 90ft and off the green at the 17th. She followed it up with a birdie from 30ft at the last. From moments like these, Solheim Cups are won. No wonder Ciganda and Boutier looked distraught.A background cause for concern for the US arrived from Angel Yin. The 27-year-old had been a serious doubt to feature due to illness that significantly disrupted her season. That Yin did not play on Saturday was no great shock, but the sight of her pounding balls for a lengthy time on the driving range as competitive action unfolded elsewhere implied she is struggling for form.Yin and the US need six points from the 12 remaining to hold on to the trophy. Six and a half is the European requirement. Momentum is suddenly with the visitors.Explore more on these topicsSolheim CupUS sportsGolfnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lando Norris shocks himself by pipping Kimi Antonelli to F1 Spanish GP pole | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Lando Norris beat Kimi Antonelli by one hundredth of a second as Max Verstappen qualified third on the tough Madring track
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Lando Norris beat Kimi Antonelli by one hundredth of a second as Max Verstappen qualified third on the tough Madring track
Content: Lando Norris punches the air after claiming pole position for the Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid.Photograph: Bernat Armangué/APView image in fullscreenLando Norris punches the air after claiming pole position for the Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid.Photograph: Bernat Armangué/APFormula One 2026Lando Norris shocks himself by pipping Kimi Antonelli to F1 Spanish GP poleBriton beats Antonelli by one hundredth of a secondVerstappen qualifies third on tough Madring trackGiles Richardsat the MadringSat 12 Sep 2026 11.32 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 16.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProving that timing is all, not least in making a statement,Lando Norriskept his very best to last for a moment that must be considered close to Formula One perfection. His pole position at the sport’s newest circuit, the Madring, for the Spanish Grand Prix was so immense it left him shocked. Not least in that he had not threatened the top of the timesheets at any point over the weekend until the final lap of the final session, and then he was masterly.On a circuit that has proved punishingly unforgiving with some major crashes, keeping it clean was vital, but for the top spot, absolute commitment and inch-perfect execution was the differentiator in threading the needle inside the looming walls of this high-speed challenge.Formula One 2026: Norris pips Antonelli to Spanish Grand Prix pole by 0.011sec – liveRead moreNorris had it nailed from nowhere, admitting it had all come together in one of those almost unworldly moments drivers occasionally experience, of instinct, touch, speed and judgment combining to remarkable effect.It had to be to beat the championship leader, Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli, who had showed his own flair and commitment, into second by one hundredth of a second, with Red Bull’s Max Verstappen in third.Quick GuideSpanish F1 qualifyingShow1Lando Norris🇬🇧McLaren1:31.8242Kimi Antonelli🇮🇹Mercedes1:31.8353Max Verstappen🇳🇱Red Bull1:31.9644Lewis Hamilton🇬🇧Ferrari1:32.0135Charles Leclerc🇲🇨Ferrari1:32.0196George Russell🇬🇧Mercedes1:32.1497Oscar Piastri🇦🇺McLaren1:32.2948Liam Lawson🇳🇿Red Bull1:32.3169Franco Colapinto🇦🇷Alpine1:32.90310Arvid Lindblad🇬🇧Racing Bulls1:33.041Eliminated in Q211Nico Hülkenberg🇩🇪Audi1:33.22312Gabriel Bortoleto🇧🇷Audi1:33.38813Esteban Ocon🇫🇷Haas1:33.66714Pierre Gasly🇫🇷Alpine1:33.75315Yuki Tsunoda🇯🇵Racing Bulls1:34.08416Alexander Albon🇹🇭Williams1:35.532Eliminated in Q1†17Carlos Sainz🇪🇸Williams1:35.31218Fernando Alonso🇪🇸Aston Martin1:35.38819Sergio Pérez🇲🇽Cadillac1:35.91320Valtteri Bottas🇫🇮Cadillac1:38.011No timeOliver Bearman🇬🇧HaasLance Stroll🇨🇦Aston Martin†Three-place penalty for impeding BottasWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“I’m a little bit surprised to be here now, but it was probably one of the best laps I’ve done in my career,” said Norris. “One of those laps where everything just came together. I had a good idea of what I wanted to do, but it was whether my brain let me do it on the last lap, and pretty much everything worked perfectly.“One of those laps where you look at the lap time at the end, and you are like: ‘Oh shit, that was pretty good.’ For the last corner, I thought I was in the wall and the boys were going to have to repair the car tonight.”Norris did just kiss up against the wall with his left rear on the final corner. The achievement was put in perspective by theMcLarenteam principal, Andrea Stella, an engineer not given to hyperbole at the best of times. “That’s a bit of masterpiece,” he said. “In the final corner he made a mistake of three-tenths. So he was on a just incredible lap. Definitely one of the best of his life until the last corner. He just realised what’s available in the car.”That is was at such a challenging circuit made it all the more special, more so given how competitive the opposition were. Antonelli, Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton, who finished fourth, had all been in the mix after the first runs in Q3, but it was Norris who found the edge.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli (left) will start second on the grid in Madrid, with Lando Norris (centre) on pole and Max Verstappen third.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersAfter his outstanding victory from 19th on the grid at the last round in Monza, Antonelli leads Russell by 66 points in the championship. Hamilton is 76 points back in third place and Norris 96 adrift.The pole may prove to be absolutely vital for him. The Madring is described as a street circuit, but it is made up of public roads and purpose-built track. It does, however, conform to street-circuit norms of being narrow and unforgiving.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe layout produces high speeds, but there have been real concerns from drivers that overtaking will be extremely difficult, especially with braking zones angled into corners, which makes passing enormously tricky. Leading cars will simply take to the middle of the track ensuring a move is unfeasible, making a procession on Sunday a real risk and track position, which Norris has, crucial.Strategy will be key, as will calls made under flags both yellow and red, with the latter almost certain to play a part given the likelihood of stoppages to deal with the results of any driver errors or mechanical failures. It will also be informed by what is a high-grip, but also high-degradation, surface.View image in fullscreenThe Madring circuit in Madrid is known for being an unforgiving track.Photograph: Albert Gea/ReutersThe session was also a suitably tense, dramatic show and notable for proceeding without incident despite there being some major crashes over the weekend. The 3.365-mile circuit had been designed to be fast and a spectacle, but it is an enormously challenging and, as some have intimated, dangerous test. Quite how unforgiving was once more demonstrated in final practice when the red flags were brought out after Hamilton went into the wall as he locked up and hit the barriers nose-first at the final corner.Britain’s Oliver Bearman also took a massive hit, having spun and slewed side-on into the concrete barriers at turn 10, wiping out the left side of his car. He was unhurt, but the damage was so bad his Haas team were unable to rebuild the car in time for qualifying.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportLando NorrisMcLarennewsShareReuse this content

title: What can halt Fifa’s authoritarian turn under Infantino? Change from the outside | Soccer | The Guardian
description: The World Cup and its aftermath made clear that Fifa needs independent oversight by governments and NGOs dedicated to preserving the people’s game
Author: Jules Boykoff
Headline: The World Cup and its aftermath made clear that Fifa needs independent oversight by governments and NGOs dedicated to preserving the people’s game
Content: Gianni Infantino’s ties to Donald Trump have drawn scrutiny from Fifa member associations around the globe.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino’s ties to Donald Trump have drawn scrutiny from Fifa member associations around the globe.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersSoccerWhat can halt Fifa’s authoritarian turn under Infantino? Change from the outsideJules BoykoffThe World Cup and its aftermath made clear that Fifa needs independent oversight by governments and NGOs dedicated to preserving the people’s gameSat 12 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTShareThe 2026 World Cup was a whirling swirl of scintillating soccer that prompted much-needed conversations about the vitality of diaspora, the fortitude of the underdog, the power of sport. In a world fractured along myriad cultural axes floating in an entertainment system dominated by on-demand content, the tournament provided a moment, perhaps unlike any other event, that brought together people from different backgrounds to simultaneously experience something meaningful.After the tournament concluded, Fifa president Gianni Infantino dropped a political pipebomb into the after-party,proposing to privatizethe World Cup by injecting $20bn in private capital, with an assist from JP Morgan and Thrive Capital, the investment vehicle orchestrated by Joshua Kushner, brother to Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law.Turns out, Infantino hadn’t just been sucking up to Trump the whole time – from hand-delivering the confectedFifa peace prizeto obliging him with thered card reversalheard ’round the world – ostensibly to ensure the World Cup money spigot remained winched wide open. Apparently, Infantino was also studying Trump’s nepotism-flecked smash-and-grab techniques. Not unlike the Trump administrationnixingenergy-project grants for states “based solely” on whether they supported him in the 2024 presidential election, football associations thatbackedInfantino’s private-equity scheme would get more money while those that disagreed would receive less. And just as Trump and the rightwing media ecosystem havedestabilizedthe very notion of truth in US political discourse, Fifa subverted the notion of fairness when it nullified the red card for a US player.But something deeper and even more important is going on. Amid therising tide of authoritarianismaround the world, includingin the USunder Trump, Fifa under Infantino has itself become increasingly dictatorial. Although Fifaclaimsit acts “in full respect” of its self-trumpeted “democratic and governance principles”, and that its president’s private-equity fever dream was “about the democratization of football worldwide”, the reality is that Fifa emulates the dictatorships before whom Infantino so readily genuflects. Many within the governing body learned about the privatization gambitthrough the newsrather than proper consultation (just as they had heard ofInfantino’s decisionto hand Trump the peace prize). Although Fifa statutes limit presidents to “no more than three terms of office”, and Infantino was first elected in 2016 and then re-elected – unopposed by acclamation – in 2019 and 2023, he hasdeclaredthat he could run again in 2027. Infantino is infamous for besmirching journalists and avoiding press conferences. Tough questions are signs of reporters “spreading hate”. For him, information is meant to flow unidirectionally, cascading from on high.More than 100,000 people add names to complaint against Gianni InfantinoRead moreWhat can be done? Yes, it’s past time to “give Fifa’s boss the boot”, as a US Soccer vice-president put it. But despite Infantino’s spectacular miscalculations and dictatorial shifts, those who have the power to “boot” him have instead made him the frontrunner in next year’s election. Although soccer’s regional governing bodies in Europe (Uefa), Asia (AFC), as well as North, Central America and the Caribbean (Concacaf) have publicly rebuked Infantino, with Europe eventhreateningto boycott international competitions, fissures have emerged:Mexico,Qatarand several Asian national associations have broken ranks to signal support for the beleaguered Infantino. The Confederation of African Football (CAF), which represents 54 countries, “unanimously reconfirmed its support” for Infantino, who needs only 106 votes to survive his re-election bid next March. Dislodging Infantino is an uphill fight.That’s because Fifa’s patronage system is a powerful sedative for dissent: it distributes millions to football associations around the globe under a system of clientelism grounded in fidelity and orchestrated with scant public oversight. This is soccer symbiosis awash in cash and lacking accountability.Even though Fifa’s proposed privatization could have hurt players, fans and clubs alike, plenty of federations were ready to support it. Sure, private equity has an ignominious record of acquiring holdings with social value, stripping them for parts and leaving a husk of what once was. Exhibit A:sports media. Exhibit B:hospitals. Making football into Exhibit C would not only have risked destroying the world’s most popular sport. It would have been a crime against collective joy. Nevertheless, administrators around the world were happy to back the gambit. This is a testament to the power of that patronage system, built up over decades by successive presidents, from João Havelange to Sepp Blatter to Gianni Infantino.The top candidates to replace Infantino are freighted with cumbersome baggage. Victor Montagliani rose to become head of Concacaf and a Fifa Council vice-president despitecontroversial handlingsof scandals and partnerships. Another possibility, Fifa Council member Nasser Al-Khelaifi of Qatar,statedthat he had “no ambition, no intention and no interest in the Fifa role”. Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, top man at the Asian Football Confederation,already lostto Infantino back in 2016 and has long beendoggedby allegations of human-rights violations in Bahrain, which he denies. Lise Klaveness, who heads the Norwegian FA, would bring principle and panache to the presidency – and she hasa strong recordof standing up to Infantino – but she is essentially unelectable in an organizationdrenched in sexism.Let’s be clear: change at Fifa must come from outside the organization. For too long, Fifa has monitored itself. The 2026 World Cup and its aftermath demonstrate unequivocally that Fifa requires independent oversight, toothy regulation carried out by governments and NGOs dedicated to preserving the people’s game as a social good.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionToward that end,FairSquare, the London-based nonprofit human-rights organization on whose advisory board I serve, recently launched a “Reboot Fifa” campaign todeclareInfantino ineligible for the March election and to createthe biggest-ever class-action complaintagainst Infantino for openly violating Fifa’s own governingstatuteson political neutrality by consistently cozying up to Trump.Donninga red Maga-style cap with “45—47” and “USA” emblazoned on it at a Board of Peace meeting cannot be considered “Fifa remain[ing] neutralin matters of politics”.Infantino’s clumsy overstepping has galvanized calls for reform and created a chance to reject authoritarianism creep.Fixing the Fifa greed zombie requires a vibrant pushback on all fronts. We must support Jamie Raskin who, as the ranking member on the House judiciary committee, hasdemandedFifa furnish all its documented contact with Trump, members of his administration and the Trump Organization. Switzerland’s parliament shouldreconsiderFifa’s tax-free status under Swiss law. We should rally behind soccer A-listers like England international Lucy Bronze and former France star Mikaël Silvestre who areinsistingthat “Change is necessary” and that “enough is enough”. If not now, then when?Explore more on these topicsFootballFootball politicsFifaGianni InfantinoDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: De Zerbi says Spurs have ‘mental block’ after wait for league win continues | Tottenham Hotspur | The Guardian
description: The Spurs manager said after the 0-0 draw with Everton: ‘[It is] a mental block because four games, no wins, no goals scored … it is tough for the players’
Author: David Hytner
Headline: The Spurs manager said after the 0-0 draw with Everton: ‘[It is] a mental block because four games, no wins, no goals scored … it is tough for the players’
Content: Roberto De Zerbi said injuries during the pre-season tour to New Zealand and Australia have contributed to Spurs’ slow start.Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenRoberto De Zerbi said injuries during the pre-season tour to New Zealand and Australia have contributed to Spurs’ slow start.Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/ReutersTottenham HotspurDe Zerbi says Spurs have ‘mental block’ after wait for league win continues‘No wins, no goals scored … it is tough for the players’Spurs in 17th place after 0-0 draw against EvertonDavid Hytnerat Tottenham Hotspur StadiumSat 12 Sep 2026 16.36 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRoberto De Zerbi says his Tottenham players continue to lack physical fitness and must “unblock” themselves in psychological terms after they drew their latest Premier League blank in ahome 0-0 with Everton. It is now four games in the competition since the start of the season without a goal for Spurs; they sit 17th in the table with two points and were booed off by frustrated fans.De Zerbi gave a number of explanations for Spurs’ slow start, chief among them the injuries that a clutch of players sustained on the long-haul pre-season tour to New Zealand and Australia. He lamented the impact of the World Cup on the return dates of certain players and mentioned how Sávio and Omar Marmoush had signed late in the transfer window.Tottenham waiting for first league goal of season after draw against EvertonRead moreDe Zerbi talked up a positive opening 30 minutes from his players againstEvertonbut accepted they ran out of steam and that there was a psychological problem.“There is a word in Italian –sbloccarsi– that literally translates as if we unblock ourselves,” De Zerbi said. “[It is] a mental block because four games, no wins, no goals scored … it is tough for the players. The team is extremely strong, we can score goals and we can win games. And then we have to respect the history of the players in their careers. Forget Dominic Solanke and Marmoush – the other players … they didn’t score many, many goals in their careers and we have to find these goals. I think we can do so with the quality of our play.”De Zerbi warmed to a familiar theme when he went back tothe pre-season tour. “I said we started this season late for many, many reasons; too late,” he said. “Many players at the World Cup, many injuries, many problems in Australia. Micky van de Ven suffered an injury in Australia. Domi Solanke the same. James Maddison the same. Mateus Fernandes suffered an injury in Australia. He lost 15 days and it’s not so quick. Sávio and Marmoush, they came 10 days ago. I started to work with this [whole] group not last Thursday but two Thursdays ago. So, I think we have not the right physical condition yet.Quick GuidePlay our football trivia game, On the ballShowThe Guardian'sdaily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues?Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“We played very well in the first 30 minutes and then maybe the energy, maybe the fact we didn’t score … maybe we lost in some players a little confidence. We have to be not positive but realistic.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“If we extend that part of the game to 60, 70, 80 and 90 minutes, in my opinion, we are going to win many games. We have to improve in the last third of the pitch, for sure. The last decision, the last pass and we have to shoot more times, especially when we have space and time. But I can’t say nothing bad about the players.”Explore more on these topicsTottenham HotspurRoberto De ZerbiEvertonPremier LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Hull stun Chelsea with Mohamed Belloumi double before João Pedro rescues a point  | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Mohamed Belloumi scored twice to extend Hull’s fine start in the Premier League with a 2-2 draw at Chelsea
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Mohamed Belloumi scored twice to extend Hull’s fine start in the Premier League with a 2-2 draw at Chelsea
Content: Mohamed Belloumi scored twice to help Hull earn a point at Chelsea.Photograph: Daniel Hambury/Focus Images Ltd/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMohamed Belloumi scored twice to help Hull earn a point at Chelsea.Photograph: Daniel Hambury/Focus Images Ltd/ShutterstockPremier LeagueHull stun Chelsea with Mohamed Belloumi double before João Pedro rescues a pointJacob Steinbergat Stamford BridgeSat 12 Sep 2026 12.10 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 16.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe chants from the away end about winning the league were sung in jest, but Hull continue to show they are here to stay. Sergej Jakirovic’s dogged, intelligent side are third in thePremier Leagueafter extending their unbeaten start to four games and can even count themselves unfortunate not to have beaten another of the Big Six after pushing Chelsea to the limit in an absorbing battle at a frustrated Stamford Bridge.Hull were 2-1 up at half-time and they had the chances to snatch the points during the second half. It took two big saves from Emiliano Martínez to prevent an upset, but this was not a good day for theChelseagoalkeeper or his new teammates. He was one of several at fault when Hull, having dusted themselves down after conceding from Morgan Rogers early on, went ahead through Mohamed Belloumi’s quickfire double. The ease with which Chelsea’s advantage was handed over left the normally calm and considered Xabi Alonso accusing his side of being “soft” without the ball.Tottenham Hotspur v Everton: Premier League – liveRead moreAlonso craves the comfort of a forgettable win. Chelsea have been exhilarating in attack, but they cannot defend. They are conceding two goals per game and the basketball nature of Alonso’s approach has created chaos rather than control. “It’s all entertaining, but I hope that one day you say it was a boring game and we win,” he said. “It will take time. When we get the lead you still need to be competing and not to give the chance so easily for them to come back.“Especially in the first goal, we can do much better. It was too soft to give them hope because until then we were controlling, we were creating chances, but that changed the mood. We will get better, but it’s having an impact on our performances.”It is ridiculous that Rogers, Cole Palmer and João Pedro are having to do so much in attack. Chelsea led after seven minutes, surging forward when they left four players forward at a Hull corner. João Pedro’s pass reached Rogers and the £117m signing from Aston Villa drove past Regan Slater before beating Konstantinos Tzolaki at his near post with a low, hard and early shot from the left.View image in fullscreenJoão Pedro fires home Chelsea’s equaliser in the second half.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAChelsea should have pushed on after becoming the first side to breach Hull since their promotion. Pedro Neto tested Tzolakis from the right, but the hosts became vague and complacent. This was the first time they have dominated possession in a league game this season and the result was not convincing. Hull limited them to an xG of 0.89, highlighting Chelsea’s issues against low blocks, and were clinical when they attacked.The soft defending Alonso referenced for the equaliser started with Malo Gusto failing to deal with a long punt from Tzolakis in the 28th minute. Ryan Giles outmuscled the right-back and hooked a cross to the far post. Jorrel Hato misread the Hull left-back’s delivery, leaving Belloumi to rap a shot past Martínez.Chelsea are without a win against promoted sides in five home games. They do not smell danger, while Alonso’s decision to leave Maxence Lacroix out at centre-back and shift from a back three to a 4-2-3-1 system backfired. Hull had so much space on the flanks. They pushed again and Belloumi’s flick found Lewie Coyle, who ran off Rogers but saw his shot cleared off the line by Levi Colwill.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrustrated Liverpool fail to take chances as Fulham claim deserved first pointRead more“The dynamic in terms of conceding, I don’t like it,” Alonso said. “Open play, set-pieces, long balls, this toughness, this competitive sense, we can do better.”There was no response from Chelsea after Colwill turned Coyle’s shot wide. A corner came in from the left, Martínez flapped and Semi Ajayi’s header hit the bar. The ball came to Belloumi, whose shot flew in thanks to a deflection.Alonso reacted at half-time, Hato making way for Pep Chavarría at left-back. Reece James drew a save from Tzolakis with a free-kick but Hull carried a threat on the break. They almost extended their lead when Martínez spilled a shot from Slater.Martínez redeemed himself, blocking the rebound from McBurnie, and Chelsea soon levelled. Palmer, otherwise quiet, surprised Hull with a direct run. The No 10 drove down the left and picked out João Pedro, who lashed a shot into the roof of the net.Hull refused to lie down. Ajayi, Giles and John Egan were outstanding at the back and the visitors maintained their shape when losing Nobel Mendy after a nasty collision with João Pedro.Jakirovic made bold substitutions. Alonso threw Danny Welbeck on. Palmer scooped over from 20 yards and Tzolakis thwarted Rogers, but Hull had the best chance. Giles crossed again and Mohamed-Ali Cho shot straight at Martínez from close range.Hull settled for a point. Jakirovic quashed talk of qualifying for Europe, insisting that survival remains the aim. The Bosnian has everyone pulling in the same direction. Before the start of the season he told his staff he would give them seven days off if Hull took eight points from their first five games. Mission completed with a game to spare.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueChelseaHull Citymatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Frustrated Liverpool lack any spark as Fulham claim deserved first point | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Liverpool struggled to create any chances as they were held to a 0-0 Premier League draw with Fulham at Anfield
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Liverpool struggled to create any chances as they were held to a 0-0 Premier League draw with Fulham at Anfield
Content: Bernd Leno makes a save to keep Fulham’s clean sheet intact at Anfield.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenBernd Leno makes a save to keep Fulham’s clean sheet intact at Anfield.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAPremier LeagueFrustrated Liverpool lack any spark as Fulham claim deserved first pointAndy Hunterat AnfieldSat 12 Sep 2026 12.06 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 16.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleÁlvaro Arbeloa was often the obstacle to Andoni Iraola’s international ambitions back in the days when both were vying for a right-back role with Spain. On his return to Anfield, and under the watchful eye of former manager Rafael Benítez, Arbeloa thwarted Iraola once again to claim his firstPremier Leaguepoint as Fulham head coach against an ineffective Liverpool.Fulham belied their lowly position and run of three league defeats to take a merited point from a Liverpool team that was a pale imitation of the one thatbeat Atlético Madridin the Champions League on Wednesday. Iraola fielded a front four that cost almost £400m but the most impressive forward on display was the Fulham academy graduate Josh King. The draw was Liverpool’s third in four league games under their new head coach and the seventh in 12 Premier League matches at Anfield in 2026. Progress can be painfully slow at times.Hull stun Chelsea with Mohamed Belloumi double before João Pedro rescues a pointRead more“It is the first game we’ve had problems creating chances and making the difference offensively,” Iraola said. “It is easy for me to say the players were tired (after Atlético). There was a lack of freshness and, we cannot hide it, it was the worst turnaround in terms of 60-70 hours. But this is going to happen in the season and we have to adapt. Sometimes you need a set play or a moment of brilliance to win these kind of games but we were not as good offensively as other games.”Liverpool were sluggish and sloppy – Florian Wirtz and Kostas Tsimikas put simple passes straight out of play in the first half, setting the tone for a disjointed performance – while Fulham bypassed the central midfield pairing of Dominik Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch repeatedly. The visitors’ confidence and composure on the ball, along with their defensive organisation, was hugely impressive considering the start to the season under the former Real Madrid interim coach andLiverpooldefender. With more conviction in front of goal, Arbeloa’s side could have capitalised on Liverpool’s malaise.Bradley Barcola created an early, difficult chance for Alexander Isak that the striker swept wide of the far post. Victor Muñoz went closer still with a glancing header from a Szoboszlai corner. Bernd Leno, theFulhamgoalkeeper, reacted superbly to claw the ball away. But that was the sum total of Liverpool’s first-half enterprise.Fulham were gifted a glorious opportunity when Alisson played a ridiculous pass to Gravenberch, who was under pressure from Sander Berge. Berge’s challenge fell to King, who was sent flying by the Liverpool goalkeeper but the referee, Thomas Bramall, played a good advantage as Gonzalo García received the loose ball. García had time to pick his spot but Jérémy Jacquet blocked his shot in front of the goalline.View image in fullscreenJérémy Jacquet clears the ball off the line to deny Fulham the lead.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAThe visitors prospered down their left and Oscar Bobb missed another good opening when, unmarked and 18 yards out, he miscontrolled Alex Iwobi’s pinpoint delivery. Jacquet came to Liverpool’s rescue once again seconds later when preventing García breaking through with an excellent challenge.Liverpool were deserving of a few home truths during the break – chiefly, you would have been lambasted for this last season under Arne Slot – and performed with more intensity in the second half. But not with any more threat. The introductions of Cody Gakpo, Alexis Mac Allister and Milos Kerkez brought modest improvement but Fulham continued to contain the hosts comfortably. The new signing David Affengruber had a fine debut and Calvin Bassey was commanding against Isak.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe visitors remained dangerous on the counterattack and Alisson pushed away a King effort that was heading for the top corner. King’s replacement, Rodrigo Muniz, let a decent chance run away from him inside the area and the substitute Kevin dragged a shot wide from 18 yards. Isak finally escaped Bassey’s attentions in stoppage time but his flicked header from a Szoboszlai corner sailed wide.Arbeloa said: “When you are not winning games it’s not so easy for your players to believe in your ideas. But they believe in the way we have been working and I showed them the things that we were doing so well. We were more balanced and controlled the transitions well. I’m happy with the point but more with the performance of my players and the character, the personality and the ambition they showed in this stadium.”Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueLiverpoolFulhammatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: European football: Dortmund win again but Freiburg top after Gladbach rout | European club football | The Guardian
description: Borussia Dortmund beat Paderborn 3-0 but Freiburg topped the Bundesliga on goal difference after thumping Borussia Mönchengladbach 5-0
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Borussia Dortmund beat Paderborn 3-0 but Freiburg topped the Bundesliga on goal difference after thumping Borussia Mönchengladbach 5-0
Content: The ball hits the back of the net for Felix Nmecha’s second goal as Borussia Dortmund beat Paderborn 3-0.Photograph: Christopher Neundorf/EPAView image in fullscreenThe ball hits the back of the net for Felix Nmecha’s second goal as Borussia Dortmund beat Paderborn 3-0.Photograph: Christopher Neundorf/EPAEuropean club footballEuropean football: Dortmund win again but Freiburg top after Gladbach routMilan come from behind in 2-2 draw with LazioKylian Mbappé strikes twice as Real Madrid cruiseAgence France-PresseSat 12 Sep 2026 17.17 EDTFirst published on Sat 12 Sep 2026 13.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFelix Nmecha scored twice and Fábio Silva grabbed another asBorussia Dortmundwon 3-0 at home to promotedPaderbornto continue their perfect start in the Bundesliga. Dortmund’s win made it three from three in the league this campaign, their best start in 11 seasons, dating back to Thomas Tuchel’s time.Starting up front alongside Serhou Guirassy for the first time this season, Silva converted a clever pass from the Guinean to give the hosts the lead after five minutes. Guirassy had two goals disallowed for offside in the first half but Dortmund were rarely troubled by the toothless visitors, who are yet to score since returning to the top flight.Nmecha came off the bench to score twice, wrapping up victory for the hosts with a stunning late bicycle kick.Dortmund captain Nico Schlotterbeck made his first appearance since picking up an ankle injury at the World Cup and told Sky Germany he kept his comeback under wraps. “We just hadn’t communicated that much yet because I didn’t want to,” Schlotterbeck said, adding “I missed it terribly. It was a serious injury but I’m glad to be back now.”Freiburgthumped a poorBorussia Mönchengladbach5-0 at home to climb to the top. Yannik Engelhardt and Igor Matanovic netted twice each and Maximilian Eggestein added a late fifth as the hosts sent Gladbach, who finished with 10 men, to the foot of the table.View image in fullscreenFreiburg’s Matthias Ginter (centre) congratulates Igor Matanovic on the opening goal against Borussia Mönchengladbach.Photograph: Philipp von Ditfurth/DPA/APA 2-2 home draw withBayer LeverkusenendedAugsburg’s short stint as leaders. Augsburg were top after the last matchday for the first time in their history but were held by Leverkusen despite a double from Michael Gregoritsch.Eintracht Frankfurtwon their first match of the campaign with a 3-1 victory at neighbouringMainz, with Can Uzun’s double either side of a Jonathan Burkardt goal. Frankfurt’s goalkeeper Noah Atubolu kept his remarkable penalty-saving record alive when he stopped a first-half effort from Nadiem Amiri. Atubolu’s save was his sixth in a row, extending his own Bundesliga record.West Ham loanee Niclas Füllkrug kept his excellent run of form since returning to the Bundesliga going, scoring the equaliser forWerder Bremenin a 1-1 draw atCologne. Thijs Dallinga missed a penalty after eight minutes but teammate Linton Maina put Cologne ahead moments later.Füllkrug’s goal came in the 69th minute and is his third in four games since returning to Germany. He only found the net three times in 29 matches for West Ham and scored just once in 20 games on loan atMilanlast season.Elsewhere,Hoffenheimwon 2-1 at home againstStuttgartthanks to a double from Adam Hlozek. On Sunday,Bayern Munichtravel to promotedElversberg– who have a 100% record – whileRB LeipzighostHamburg.In Spain, Kylian Mbappé scored twice ⁠asRealMadridenjoyed a 4-1 victory overRayo Vallecano⁠in La Liga ⁠at ​the Santiago Bernabéu. Goals from Álvaro Carreras and Jude ⁠Bellingham made the result comfortable for José Mourinho’s side.View image in fullscreenKylian Mbappé celebrates scoring Real’s fourth against Rayo Vallecano.Photograph: Manu Fernández/APA 14th-minute ⁠penalty from Mbappé was followed three minutes ​later by ‌a simple finish ‌from Carreras, with Mbappé turned provider ‌this time. A relaxed Real found little resistance from Rayo thereafter and, 11 minutes before half time, Vinícius Júnior raced down the left to set up ‌Bellingham for a neat finish into the corner.Six minutes into the ​second half, Sergio Camello pulled a goal back for Rayo following sloppyReal Madridplay. Despite whistles from the ⁠home crowd, Real kept Rayo at ​bay, ​before closing out the ​game with a 90th-minute goal ​from ‌Mbappé.The result ​moved ​Real on to 12 points, level with leadersBarcelona, who have a game in hand. Barça are atLevanteon Sunday afternoon.Alavésmissed the chance to go top overnight with a 2-1 defeat atRacing Santander.In Italy, Diego Moreira scored twice asMilancame from two goals down to hold early season Serie A pacesettersLazio2-2 in Rome on Saturday. Moreira came off the bench at half-time and hauled Milan level after Matteo Cancellieri and Tijjani Noslin had given the hosts the lead at the interval.Despite losing their 100% record having started the season with three wins, Gennaro Gattuso’s side move to the top of the table. Ruben Amorim’s Milan are fourth on eight points, after also drawing last weekend at Juventus.View image in fullscreenMilan’s Diego Moreira celebrates scoring in his side’s 2-2 draw with Lazio.Photograph: Riccardo Antimiani/EPACancellieri opened his account for the campaign after 10 minutes when he connected with a Mattia Zaccagni cross. A dominant Lazio had good chances to pull further clear before Noslin doubled their lead after 39 minutes with a close-range finish.Amorim attempted to stem the tide by making three substitutions at half-time, bringing on playmaker Christian Pulisic and Moreira. His changes bore fruit after 65 minutes as Moreira volleyed home to halve the deficit. Less than two minutes later, the former Strasbourg player equalised with a fierce strike from outside the box, but neither side could find a late winner.Atalantaslumped to a 2-1 defeat at home toCagliari, with Sead Kolasinac handling the ball in the box to concede a second-half penalty that gave the visitors the win.Cagliaritook the lead in the 19th ⁠minute when 19-year-old forward Paul Mendy rattled in the opener off the underside of the crossbar, ​but Gianluca Scamacca levelled for the home side ​four minutes before the break.Mendy had the ​ball in the net again early in the second half only for the goal to be ruled out ​for a narrow offside, but ‌they took the lead ​again after Kolasinac was penalised, ​Daniel Maldini firing home from the spot to secure the three points.The result moved Cagliari up to fourth in the table with nine points from their four games, whileAtalantaare in ninth spot on six points.
