Earlier, hostsGenoa, who have yet to win this season, were held 1-1 by newly promotedFrosinone, who have seven points.ChampionsInterhostUdineseon Monday, withRomaheading toTorinoandComoat home toParma. Inter and Roma have both won each of their first three matches.Explore more on these topicsEuropean club footballBundesligaLa LigaRacing SantanderAlavesBorussia DortmundPaderbornnewsShareReuse this content

title: Farke’s blueprint for revitalised Leeds continues upward trajectory | Leeds United | The Guardian
description: Daniel Farke is embracing bravery and is encouraging ambition after leading a remarkable turnaround in Leeds’s fortunes
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: Daniel Farke is embracing bravery and is encouraging ambition after leading a remarkable turnaround in Leeds’s fortunes
Content: Leeds are unbeaten in the Premier League after last Saturday’s draw at Brighton.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersView image in fullscreenLeeds are unbeaten in the Premier League after last Saturday’s draw at Brighton.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersLeeds UnitedFarke’s blueprint for revitalised Leeds continues upward trajectoryLeeds manager embraces bravery and is encouraging ambition after leading a remarkable turnaround in fortunesLouise TaylorSat 12 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEleven years have passed since Daniel Farke mounted a magnificent palomino horse and rode round the perimeter of the pitch at Lippstadt, waving farewell to a capacity crowd. It seemed a fun way for the lower-tier German club’s centre-forward turned manager and sporting director to say goodbye. Yet few in the stands knew Farke was scared of horses and hauled himself into the saddle only out of politeness towards his chair, who had arranged this special surprise.“I couldn’t deny him,” he said. “But it cured my fear – it was enjoyable.”These days the Leeds manager is demanding similar bravery, as well as instant adaptability, from his players. “We want to be hard to predict,” said Farke as he prepared to welcome his compatriot Matthias Jaissle’s rapid counterattacking Newcastle team to Elland Road on Monday night. “We have different approaches. For example, if a team has two very good centre-backs who dominate aerially it makes sense to build with more low passes.“It’s always in our DNA that we want to be on the ball and, in the buildup, we always want to be brave. Also it’s possible to break the [opposition] pressing by playing good football out from the back.”View image in fullscreenDaniel Farke says ‘anything is possible’ for Leeds this season ahead of match with Newcastle on Monday.Photograph: Matthew Childs/Action Images/ReutersNot that Leeds are averse to taking the direct route. This season only Hull and Nottingham Forest have played a higher percentage of their passes long than a Leeds XI invariably spearheaded by the formidable Dominic Calvert-Lewin. As Farke says: “We very often have a physical target player up front that we can be a bit more direct into.”If such tactical variety is designed to keep rivals guessing, a fusion of alternative styles also befits a coach who admires the contrasting approaches of his close friends Pep Guardiola and Jürgen Klopp.Adaptability almost certainly saved his job last season. From 4 October to 29 November Leeds played seven Premier League games, losing six. They have since completed 28 league fixtures, losing five, while reachingan FA Cup semi-final.Farke is negotiating from a position of strength as he discusses extending a contract that has less than a year to run. “Daniel’s done great,” the Leeds managing director, Robbie Evans, said this week. “We want him to be here long term and we’re working on it.”View image in fullscreenDaniel Farke’s half-time changes against Manchester City in November transformed Leeds’s fortunes.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAEverything changed on 29 November.Leeds lost 3-2at Manchester City but Farke’s half-time switch to a back three, allied to Calvert-Lewin’s introduction, provided him with a timely lifeline. The changes enabled the visitors, trailing 2-0, to level in a transformative second-half performance spoiled only by Phil Foden’s stoppage-time winner.It marked the start of an upward trajectory that has continued this season as Leeds, alternating between three and four at the back, have remained unbeaten, like Newcastle.A watershed perhaps came when England’s James Trafford arrived this summer from City for £40m – a record fee for a British goalkeeper. Given Newcastle had tried to buy Trafford on three occasions his signing represents something of a coup for Leeds. Throw in the abundance of diggers, hard hats and hi-vis vests on view at Elland Road as the stadium is expanded from a capacity of just under 38,000 to 53,000 and the sense of a club on the up is almost palpable.“Something’s going well here,” Trafford said after signing. “They [the owners, 49er Enterprises] want to take the club back to where it has been historically and I think everyone here believes that is going to happen.“With the energy, physicality and quality in this team anything is possible this season. The spirit is incredible. It’s really, really good and that can take you a long way.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf such harmony can be attributed to Farke’s “no dickheads” policy when it comes to potential signings and the midfielder Ethan Ampadu’s impressive embrace of the captaincy, astute recruitment is steadily raising the team’s calibre.The Bosnia and Herzegovina centre-half Tarik Muharemovic is proving an outstanding defender and a fine distributor. The £34m buy from Sassuolo is emblematic of the amalgam of robust athleticism and technical ability that increasingly characterises a Leeds team further enhanced by Harry Wilson’s arrival from Fulham.View image in fullscreenTarik Muharemovic scored for Leeds against Chelsea in the Carabao Cup and has already proved to be an astute summer signing.Photograph: Adam Davy/PANot that Farke is getting carried away. After seeing Trafford’s deputy, Michael Zetterer, overwhelmed as a rotatedLeeds lost 6-3 at Chelseain the Carabao Cup on Wednesday he was not in the mood for excuses.“Let’s be honest, it was a nightmare debut,” Farke said on Thursday. “You feel a bit for him, but sometimes in life you have the worst possible start. He will have pressure next time, but he’s a good goalkeeper. They live a privileged life and he’s playing for a big club.”On Monday, he will offer Jaissle a somewhat warmer greeting. They share a friendship with Klopp and Thomas Tuchel, but the Newcastle manager’s recent posting in Jeddah with Al-Ahli helped ensure that, until now, their paths have not crossed.“He’s made a bright start,” Farke said. “Newcastle are very dangerous, especially counterattacking and it will be difficult. But we want to be on top of their challenge. We want as many points as possible.”Explore more on these topicsLeeds UnitedNewcastle UnitedfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Febrile Manchester derby awaits amid growing rift between United fans and club | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: City heading to a fortress but home supporters will protest before kick-off over club’s drive against ticket touts
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: City heading to a fortress but home supporters will protest before kick-off over club’s drive against ticket touts
Content: Michael Carrick’s side have a strong home record in 2026 – but divisions have opened up at Old Trafford between supporters and the club.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenMichael Carrick’s side have a strong home record in 2026 – but divisions have opened up at Old Trafford between supporters and the club.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAManchester UnitedFebrile Manchester derby awaits amid growing rift between United fans and clubCity heading to a fortress but home supporters will protest before kick-off over club’s drive against ticket toutsJamie JacksonSat 12 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 15.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester United’s nine victories from 10 Premier League games at Old Trafford in 2026 cast their stadium as a fortress Manchester City aim to ransack on Sunday, to join Leeds in departing with three points during this calendar year.Michael Carrick has overseen the division’s highest home points-per-game return in that span: 2.7, ahead of Arsenal’s 2.27 (from 12 matches) and Manchester City’s 2.25 (11); and his side have scored the most goals: 26, to City’s 23, and the champions’ 20.Kobbie Mainoo moves from outsider to main man after summer of hurtRead moreWhen Enzo Maresca’s side motor across town, the 199th edition of a local squabble that draws a riveted global audience will be as febrile as ever – on and off the pitch.A United fan group, the 1958, has called for a “peaceful protest” before kick-off, starting at a pub near the stadium, against what it believes is disproportionate action in the club’s drive to eradicate ticket touting. United said on Friday that 685 accounts had been subject to a ban and 464 supporters had received a reduced sanction or final warning.Then, when the whistle blows, United will attempt to end City’s perfect start of four victories in all competitions, improve a disappointing return of four points from three league games and repeat the opening result of Carrick’s second interim tenure, achieved in January four days after his appointment: a 2-0 downing of Pep Guardiola’s visitors in which Bryan Mbeumo and Patrick Dorgu were on target.A 2-1 defeat by Leeds on 13 April is the sole blemish on United’s league record at Old Trafford since. The sequence shows how impressive Carrick’s stewardship has been and last month’s 5-2 hammering of Ipswich came in his first home game as the permanent manager.View image in fullscreenBruno Fernandes has been integral to Manchester United’s recent success at Old Trafford.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoScan the results of his 10 away league games and you find four wins (at Arsenal, Everton, Chelsea and Brighton), four draws (West Ham, Bournemouth, Sunderland and Everton) and two defeats (Newcastle and Hull): 16 points from 30, compared with 27 from 30 when United play in front of their crowd.A major factor behind the home record is easy to identify: Bruno Fernandes. In the 10 Old Trafford games the 31-year-old has provided 10 assists and scored five times. Without the captain Carrick’s team would surely struggle, as his hat-trick against Ipswich underlined.Mbeumo and Matheus Cunha have been key support acts, scoring four goals each (Cunha also has two assists), and Benjamin Sesko has impressed with five goals at an average of one every 70.8 minutes.United’s rearguard is the achilles heel: 13 goals conceded in the 10 home matches (Arsenal have allowed seven, City nine) is hardly parsimonious, so on Sunday the visitors will hope to prosper by hogging the ball, stymieing the opportunity for fast breaks that Mbeumo, Fernandes, Cunha and Sesko thrive on, and going at pace at the creaky defence.City did not do this enough in Tuesday’s 2-0 Champions League victory at Porto, perhaps because Elliot Anderson was stood down, and perhaps, too, because Maresca’s nascent team are in the work-in-progress phase.View image in fullscreenElliot Anderson has settled quickly at Manchester City after his £116m move from Nottingham Forest.Photograph: Dave Thompson/APAnderson has looked a natural schemer since his £116m transfer from Nottingham Forest, running contests. In last Saturday’s 1-0 win over Coventry his display was Rodri-esque: a big call, but no exaggeration as the 23-year-old sprayed passes around, snuffed out danger, demanded to be found when under pressure and showed a spurt of speed to escape traffic.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnited have their ownmidfield lieutenant: Kobbie Mainoo, who has started nine of the 10 home league games under Carrick, scoring once and assisting once. The match he missed? The Leeds reverse, which is surely no coincidence because the 21-year-old’s ability to mould time and space is priceless in the hurly-burly of the 100mph Premier League – as his masterclass versus Ipswich reiterated.Harry Maguire calls the lad from Stockport United “midfield monster” so in the showdown between Mainoo and Anderson we may witness the derby’s defining battle – and the future of England’s engine room.A United victory would send those of the red persuasion home happy, bragging rights secured in the workplace and local hostelries. But an underlying discontent will remain: at the longstanding grievance regarding the Glazers’ ownership that has haemorrhaged resources and saddled the club with a near £1.3bn debt, and at the recent initiative designed to eliminate the black market resale of tickets.It is a worthy act but the accusation from fans is of a draconian approach. In July United began contacting supporters who used six or more devices to access accounts linked to the club or to forward tickets, on the basis this suggested the potential buying of seats to resell. Those in question were asked why multiple accounts were accessed, to identify the differing devices used, and for photo ID to prove validity.A joint statement by six fan groups complained “of longstanding supporters who have followed Manchester United for decades, often across multiple generations of the same family, being treated as suspects”.The dispute continues. On Tuesday the 1958 said: “Supporters are now facing serious sanctions which can remove their right to attend matches. We believe nobody should face such action without being told clearly what they are accused of and being shown the evidence used to justify it. If there is clear, substantive evidence of serious wrongdoing or organised ticket touting, show it. No loyal supporter should be treated as guilty without being given a fair opportunity to understand and challenge the case against them.”United said that in addition to the sanctions and warnings, they had identified 1,617 accounts that required further review owing to “unusual activity”.So before the derby will be the latest protest against the latest issue that shows the fracture between proud institution and proud fanbase. Against this backdrop Carrick hopes to extend United’s proud home record – which viewed through the prism of the disconnect between club and supporters is particularly impressive.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMichael CarrickFootball ticket pricesFootball politicsManchester CityfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Emery takes responsibility as Forest strike late at winless Aston Villa | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Aston Villa ended their goal drought in the Premier League but fell to a late Igor Jesus strike as Nottingham Forest won 2-1 at Villa Park
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: Aston Villa ended their goal drought in the Premier League but fell to a late Igor Jesus strike as Nottingham Forest won 2-1 at Villa Park
Content: Igor Jesus scored his first Premier League goal of the season to seal victory.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenIgor Jesus scored his first Premier League goal of the season to seal victory.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersPremier LeagueEmery takes responsibility as Forest strike late at winless Aston VillaBen Fisherat Villa ParkSat 12 Sep 2026 12.09 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 16.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis summer there were a couple of significant pieces of the puzzle for Oliver Glasner to put into place atNottingham Forest. The first was a mobile striker to lead the line and the other was a right wing-back to fit his favoured 3-4-3 system. Enter Liam Delap and Daniel Muñoz, both of whom had a big say in Forest’s first win under Glasner, though the match-winner was one of the old brigade in Igor Jesus.Delap registered his first Forest goal in style, a powerful shot from 25 yards and Muñoz was involved in the slick move that culminated in Igor Jesus reading Morgan Gibbs-White’s exquisite backheel to down Aston Villa, who remain winless in thePremier League.Tottenham Hotspur v Everton: Premier League – liveRead moreThat the winner came down Villa’s left made things even more painful from their perspective. For the final 12 minutes, including six in stoppage time, John McGinn was operating as an emergency left-back after Ian Maatsen’s injury reduced them to 10 men. By the 63rd minute, after sending on Johan Manzambi and Ibrahim Mbaye for their Villa debuts, Unai Emery had used all five substitutions; Pau Torres was forced off with a hamstring problem midway through the first half that could sideline him for a month and Tammy Abraham and Alysson, who pulled Villa level, arrived at the interval. Abraham replaced Nicolas Jackson, who Emery felt was at risk of a second yellow card.Those changes left Villa unable to replace Maatsen after the full-back was cynically fouled by James McAtee, whom Emery felt should have been sent off for the challenge. Emery said the video assistant referee, Timothy Wood, should have flagged the incident to the referee, Andy Madley. “It’s a clear tackle behind the player and, for me, it should be a red card,” he said. “But it’s not an excuse for how we played the second half. We played so poorly and this is my responsibility.”View image in fullscreenUnai Emery, the Aston Villa head coach, is without a win in the Premier League this season.Photograph: Tony O Brien/ReutersFor the second successive season, Villa are winless in their opening four league matches and for so long it seemed they would again fail to score. Alysson’s header from McGinn’s dainty cross after a short corner meant they were spared ruminating on the moment Matz Sels twice denied Victor Lindelöf. In between Sels repelling Lindelöf with his feet and taking his side-foot shot to the face, Murillo smacked an attempted clearance against his own post. Lindelöf has scored one goal in almost six years, his last in November 2023.Villa were rattled by Forest seizing the lead 45 seconds into the second half. Murillo dispossessed Emiliano Buendía, snapping into a challenge after Boubacar Kamara’s flick and then Delap jinked clear of Ross Barkley. Delap’s next couple of touches took the ball out of his feet, dribbling diagonally across the pitch before sending an unerring right-foot shot into the Villa net.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrustrated Liverpool fail to take chances as Fulham claim deserved first pointRead moreEmery sent on Mbaye and Manzambi in place of Buendía and Barkley but their arrivals did not bring instant success. Instead Delap thought he had doubled his and Forest’s tally, only for the offside flag and a VAR check to deny him. A few moments earlier Tyrone Mings, a first-half substitute for the injured Torres, made a desperate block to thwart Dan Ndoye after superb holdup play by Delap.Forest, without key defenders Nikola Milenkovic and Jair Cunha through injury, had been readying Igor Jesus when Villa scored, but the striker still arrived to replace Ndoye, who, after a first-half collision with Maatsen, was left with what Glasner described as “a nose like a boxer in the 12th round”. At that point, Villa Park was primed for a grandstand finale, but Forest also roused. Zion Suzuki was twice called into action, his best save clambering down to his right to keep out a Xaver Schlager header, but then Igor Jesus popped up with the winner.View image in fullscreenLiam Delap (right) opened his account for Nottingham Forest with a 46th-minute strike.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersMuñoz exchanged passes with Gibbs-White, who eliminated three Villa defenders with a sumptuous flick before Igor Jesus coolly passed the ball past Suzuki to maintain Glasner’s pristine record against Emery. Glasner has not lost in eight meetings against Emery, winning six and drawing two.“I spoke to him before the game and it’s still 5-2 for him, five European trophies to two,” said Forest’s head coach. “So I said to myself: ‘Oliver Glasner, stay humble.’ And this is how I will stay. The players deserve all the credit, because they did so well, and our fans deserve credit because they supported us, and so now we all go back and will have a lovely Saturday evening.”Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueAston VillaNottingham Forestmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Flemming and Ipswich floor 10-man Crystal Palace with 90th-minute winner | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Zian Flemming’s first goal for Ipswich snatched a dramatic 3-2 victory at 10-man Crystal Palace for their second Premier League win of the season
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Zian Flemming’s first goal for Ipswich snatched a dramatic 3-2 victory at 10-man Crystal Palace for their second Premier League win of the season
Content: Ipswich's Zian Flemming is pumped up after scoring their late winner at Selhurst Park.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenIpswich's Zian Flemming is pumped up after scoring their late winner at Selhurst Park.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersPremier LeagueFlemming and Ipswich floor 10-man Crystal Palace with 90th-minute winnerEd Aaronsat Selhurst ParkSat 12 Sep 2026 12.16 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 16.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis victory has been a long time coming for Gary O’Neil. The Millwall supporter from Beckenham, whose son plays for Crystal Palace’s academy, had picked up a solitary point on his previous five trips to this part of south London as a manager. So it was no wonder that he celebrated Zian Flemming’s winning goal in the 90th minute with the same gusto as the travelling Ipswich supporters.On a topsy-turvy afternoon Palace took the lead before Emersonn and Leif Davis cancelled out Anan Khalaili’s first goal for Palace after Axel Disasi’s red card. Jørgen Strand Larsen equalised with 15 minutes remaining but Khalaili had his head in his hands after missing an open goal minutes later and it was to prove crucial as Flemming – the last of the 14 new players signed by Ipswich in the summer in a record spend of £190m for a promoted side – scrambled home the winner after Davis hit the crossbar with a looping header.Liverpool v Fulham, Chelsea v Hull City, and more: football clockwatch – liveRead moreIpswich managed 22 points when they were in thePremier Leaguetwo years ago, but look far better equipped to survive this time around. “I don’t care where I win, as long as I win,” said O’Neill of ending his Selhurst Park run without a victory. “It’s been the best four months of my career, playing or managing. I’ve loved it, every minute of it. The playing group just gives everything. We’ll lose some, but we’ll give everything when we lose.”The chances of either side keeping a clean sheet looked slim given Palace have not managed one in the Premier League since April and Ipswich have conceded 58 goals since their last in December 2024 – a run of 23 matches. Palace badly missed their captain, Dean Henderson, who was absent due to injury, and Pierre Sage may regret showing his ruthless streak by dropping Jaydee Canvot for what he described as “a sporting decision” after being unhappy with his performances in training.While 18-year-old Honest Ahanor did well on his debut, Walter Benítez was at fault for Flemming’s winner that means Palace have lost their opening two home games of a Premier League season for the first time since 2018 and conceded more goals than any other team in the division.“I need more from him and I’m sure he is able to give that,” said Sage of Canvot’s omission from the matchday squad. “I don’t care about my authority. I want the players at 100% of what they are able to do. And when they give less, I have to shake them.”View image in fullscreenLeif Davis nods home Ipswich’s second.Photograph: David Klein/ReutersLike Palace, Ipswich had conceded eight goals from their opening three matches and it was easy to see why. Kjell Scherpen was extremely fortunate to get away with a misplaced pass that went straight to Adam Wharton but Palace’s stand-in captain scuffed his shot with the goal gaping.The hosts were ahead three minutes later when Ipswich lost the ball cheaply in midfield and Daichi Kamada set up Khalaili to drill home his first Palace goal via a deflection off Davis. Strand Larsen would have left Ipswich with a mountain to climb if he had finished off another chance soon after. But O’Neil was given hope when Davis whipped over a cross for Emersonn to equalise. Palace’s defenders appeared to stop for a split second because they thought the left-back was offside in the buildup.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThings went from bad to worse for Palace when Disasi charged recklessly into a challenge on Jack Clarke and caught him just below the knee with his studs raised. The referee, Chris Kavanagh, had no choice but to send him off.Sage opted to withdraw Palace’s chief creative spark Yéremy Pino and replace him with another defender, Takehiro Tomiyasu. That only encouraged Ipswich to push forward, although their second goal owed more to luck than anything else. Dara O’Shea’s cross came off Emersonn’s shoulder and the ball somehow diverted straight to Davis to nod home just before the break.Sage still looked less than impressed when he emerged for the second half. Palace’s 10 men roused themselves and Quinten Timber twice went close before Strand Larsen found the breakthrough. Kamada was the architect with a clever pass that allowed the Norway striker to hold off the challenge of Issa Diop and beat Scherpen. But it was Flemming who had the last laugh after coming off the bench as he reacted quicker than Benítez when a header from Davis came off the woodwork to leave O’Neil and Ipswich’s fans celebrating a landmark win.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueCrystal PalaceIpswich Townmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Mikel Arteta says penalty given to Sunderland ‘unacceptable at this level’ | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: Mikel Arteta’s delight at Arsenal’s latest win was tempered by his fury with the referee John Brooks for giving Sunderland a penalty
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: Mikel Arteta’s delight at Arsenal’s latest win was tempered by his fury with the referee John Brooks for giving Sunderland a penalty
Content: Arsenal players react after referee John Brooks awarded Sunderland a penalty .Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenArsenal players react after referee John Brooks awarded Sunderland a penalty .Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersArsenalMikel Arteta says penalty given to Sunderland ‘unacceptable at this level’Arsenal manager angry: ‘This can never be a penalty’‘It’s a judo roll from the opponent. Ezri does nothing’Louise Taylorat the Stadium of LightSat 12 Sep 2026 18.47 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 18.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMikel Arteta’s delight at Arsenal’s latest win was tempered by his fury with the referee John Brooks as the championstriumphed 2-0 at Sunderlandon Saturday night.Before Bruno Guimarães gave Arsenal the lead in a tight match that Régis Le Bris’s team were arguably unlucky to lose, David Raya made a brilliant save to deny Enzo Le Fée from the penalty spot. Arteta, however, did not believe that Ezri Konsa had hauled Dan Ballard to the ground, instead blaming theSunderlandman for pulling down his opponent.Guimarães and Saka fire Arsenal to win at Sunderland after Raya spot-kick saveRead more“We had to overcome a really tough opponent in a difficult place,” said Arsenal’s manager. “Sunderland can suffocate you and they decided to be really physical and very direct and we also had to overcome a situation that, in my opinion was unacceptable at this level.“I’m very worried and sad because this can never be a penalty. It’s a judo roll from the opponent. Ezri does nothing. We have to take responsibility to protect the game. Today the game was unprotected and it could have cost us the win and our momentum. I’m really sad. It should never have happened.”Arteta, who was booked in the first half for persistently stepping out of his technical area, hailed Guimarães’s goal as “beautiful” after watching Bukayo Saka scored a second goal from the penalty spot in stoppage time, when Sunderland’s Reinildo was sent off for a second bookable offence.Le Bris was left with mixed feelings. “I’m proud and disappointed, these are the two words that are in my mind at the minute,” said Sunderland’s manager. “I’m proud because I think we showed that we are really close to achieving something big against one of the best teams in Europe right now. After the first half we were a bit reserved with the ball I think, but our second half was excellent.“We got the momentum, created chances and it was a big save from Raya from the penalty. I think it was very good goalkeeping rather than a poor penalty. Raya was absolutely impressive today.“We stayed in the game and we created other chances but we didn’t score and that was the difference today.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQuick GuidePlay our football trivia game, On the ballShowThe Guardian'sdaily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues?Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“We had intensity and togetherness and we were brave as well at times with the ball. We were flexible tactically because this Arsenal team creates chances. Today we found a solution to stop them and we created chances as well so it shows that we are getting better. It’s not enough yet but we are close.”Explore more on these topicsArsenalMikel ArtetaSunderlandRefereesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Keely Hodgkinson has to settle for silver as Audrey Werro takes Ultimate gold | Athletics | The Guardian
description: Audrey Werro won the 800m and the $150,000 prize, 0.38 ahead of Keely Hodgkinson, at the Ultimate Championships in Budapest
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Audrey Werro won the 800m and the $150,000 prize, 0.38 ahead of Keely Hodgkinson, at the Ultimate Championships in Budapest
Content: Keely Hodgkinson (left) overtakes Femke Broeders-Bol (centre) but Audrey Werro (right) takes gold in the women's 800m at the Ultimate Championships.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenKeely Hodgkinson (left) overtakes Femke Broeders-Bol (centre) but Audrey Werro (right) takes gold in the women's 800m at the Ultimate Championships.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAAthleticsKeely Hodgkinson has to settle for silver as Audrey Werro takes Ultimate goldSwiss wins $150,000 with dominant display in 800mGeorgia Hunter Bell second to Kazimierska in 1500mSean Inglein BudapestSat 12 Sep 2026 16.50 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 19.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis season has witnessed an extraordinary arms race between three of the greatest female 800m runners in history. But, as so often over the summer months, it concluded with the sight of Audrey Werro going nuclear.There were some in the press seats who wondered whether the brilliant 22-year-old Swiss might be tired and vulnerable, whether Britain’s Olympic champion,Keely Hodgkinson, or the fast-rising Dutch star Femke Broeders-Bol could take advantage. But at these Ultimate Championships in Budapest, Werro proved again she was 2026’s ultimate performer as she took the $150,000 first prize with another dominant display.Brave new world: Ultimate Championship brings glowing javelins and $10m prize fund to track and fieldRead moreWerro’s formula is simple but devastatingly effective. Run the first 200m in a shade over 27sec to take the lead, control the race like a puppet master, and then apply the squeeze in the last 300m. As things stand, no one has an answer.She applied it perfectly here, to win in 1min 55.88sec, with Hodgkinson second in 1:56.26 and Broeders-Bol a further half a second back in third.Werro’s statistics during the outdoor season are extraordinary. Sincelosing to Hodgkinson at the world indoor championships, Werro has won all 14 events she has entered, run four of the 10 fastest times in history, and tookgold at the European championships. Indeed, the only time she has failed to cross the line first was when she was tripped up in the semi-finals in Birmingham.After this latest win she described her season as “really crazy” and suggested she would use her first prize to improve her training. God help her rivals if that is truly the case.The scary thing for Hodgkinson and Broeders-Bol? Werro is 22, and only started full-time training this year after finishing her studies. Jarmila Kratochvilova’s 43-year-old world record is already within striking distance. Would anyone be surprised if she found the 0.43 needed to topple it in 2027?However, it would be foolish to write off Hodgkinson, who confirmed that she had torn a hamstring during the European championships, which meant she was unable to do the speed work needed to compete with Werro.“I think, on the outside, people might think I’d be disappointed with that, but I’m actually quite proud of how I approached that,” said Hodgkinson. “I didn’t even know I was going to be here. It was very much touch and go. I was really going at it with rehab.“It’s been a bit of a frustrating season, but I think overall I’ve finished second in the world, and I can’t really be too hard on myself with that,” she added. “And congrats to Audrey, as well. Incredible season, absolutely incredible, dominant. Yeah, I look forward to racing her again next season.”That comment was a measure of Hodgkinson’s class after a frustrating year, which started with a world indoor 800m record and a world indoor title. But she has not been able to show the same form after badly scarring her knees in a fall in Eugene in July, and then tearing her hamstring last month.“I felt good,” said Hodgkinson. “I think with the injury I had to prepare a bit like Tokyo last year. I had to just take my foot off speed and focus more on strength.”Earlier in the evening Hodgkinson’s training partner Georgia Hunter Bell also finished second behind Klaudia Kazimierska after a thrilling 1500m.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen Kazimierska kicked for home with 200m remaining, Hunter Bell was the only athlete to immediately respond. It led to a thrilling duel along the final straight, with the Pole having just enough to win in 3:57.55, with Hunter Bell 0.15sec back in second.It left Hunter Bell $75,000 richer and she was delighted with her performance, after what she felt was a flat display in the Diamond League final last weekend. “I thought it was a great race,” she said. “I’m really happy with that. I felt really comfortable the whole race. I chose to go on the rail because last week I ran 15 extra meters by running wide, and that really took the sting out of my kick at the end.”View image in fullscreenGeorgia Hunter Bell, (left) congratulatesKlaudia Kazimierska, after winning the women’s 1500m final.Photograph: Dénes Erdős/APWhen it comes to the cash, Hunter Bell has certainly earned it this year, having won gold at the world indoors, Commonwealth Games and European championships. “I mean, the money is interesting,” she said. “I’m not really thinking about that in the home straight. I’m just thinking about trying to get to the line first.“But I’ve run 20 races this year. I’ve shown up to absolutely everything that I can, and done myself proud. I had 14 wins, three out of four majors won, one runner-up. I’m not going to sniff at 75k.”One of the performances of the night came in the women’s 100m as the world champion, Melissa Jefferson-Wooden, ran a scorching 10.62sec to take victory. It was the fastest time in the world this year, too quick for the Olympic 100m gold medallist, Julien Alfred, who was second in 10.74, with another US star, Sha’Carri Richardson, third in 10.76. Britain’s Amy Hunt was last in 11.09.Explore more on these topicsAthleticsKeely HodgkinsonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Championship roundup: Boro win seven-goal thriller; Burnley lose again | Championship | The Guardian
description: Ashley Phillips was the unlikely late matchwinner as Middlesbrough edged a seven-goal thriller, beating Norwich 4-3 at the Riverside Stadium
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ashley Phillips was the unlikely late matchwinner as Middlesbrough edged a seven-goal thriller, beating Norwich 4-3 at the Riverside Stadium
Content: Ashley Phillips races away after scoring Middlesbrough’s late winner against Norwich.Photograph: Bruce Rollinson/PAView image in fullscreenAshley Phillips races away after scoring Middlesbrough’s late winner against Norwich.Photograph: Bruce Rollinson/PAChampionshipChampionship roundup: Boro win seven-goal thriller; Burnley lose againAdded-time winner from Phillips sinks NorwichSaints hit four; Burnley beaten 3-1 at SwanseaPress AssociationSat 12 Sep 2026 12.47 EDTFirst published on Sat 12 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAshley Phillips was the unlikely late matchwinner asMiddlesbroughedged a seven-goal thriller, beatingNorwich4-3 at Riverside Stadium.Norwich looking for a third win on the bounce, made the perfect start with 50 seconds on the clock when striker Mohamed Touré hammered in, but within seven minutes Boro had gone ahead. Sebastian Berhalter powered in his first Middlesbrough goal to level, before winger Amario Cozier-Duberry had the Riverside crowd bouncing with a tidy finish.Norwich fell further behind when Berhalter added his second in the 36th minute, but then fought back when Jovon Makama’s predatory finish 20 minutes from time was followed by an equaliser from fellow substitute Jacob Wright.However, defender Phillips – with his first league career goal – popped up in the area with the killer blow to secure a third straight home win for Middlesbrough.Quick GuideLeague One roundup: Leicester ease pressure on Martin with much-needed win at StockportShowThe beleagueredLeicestermanager, Russell Martin, saw his side claim a much-needed win in a League One thriller againstStockport. The Foxes held on for a 4-3 victory at Edgeley Park, their second of the league season, after a double from Emil Riis and one from Johan Lundstram had put Leicester three goals in front. Jack Diamond had cancelled out Liam Cullen’s early opener for Leicester, and two goals in four minutes from Oliver Norwood and Kyle Wootton put the pressure right on the visitors, but they did not buckle.Sheffield Wednesday, the leaders, dropped points at home as they were held to a goalless draw byWigan, while it was the same score for second-placedHuddersfieldatMansfielddespite the Stags having Owen Dodgson sent off only moments after he came on at half-time.Bradfordsit only one point off the top thanks to George Pratt, whose first EFL goal earned a 1-0 win to endNotts County’s unbeaten start to the campaign.ManagerlessWycombeclaimed their first victory of the season, triumphing 3-2 atLeyton Orient. Tom Hounsell, who took the interim reins after Michael Duff’s dismissal this week, saw the new signing Jayden Wareham make it two goals in two matches before Jack Grimmer’s own goal pulled Orient level. Fred Onyedinma put Wanderers back ahead just before half-time and Dan Harvie doubled the lead moments after the break, but Jaze Kabia quickly reduced the deficit again.Cambridgeare up to fourth after goals from Liam Bennett and Kelland Watts enabled them to come from behind to beatReading2-1, while two very late strikes from Louie Sibley and Gatlin O’Donkor earnedOxforda 3-0 success againstBurton.Plymouthwere also 3-0 winners, Olivier Irow, Ronan Curtis and Aribim Pepple scoring againstBarnsley, while bottom-placedDoncasterlost again, Myles Hippolyte scoring in a 1-0 victory forAFC Wimbledon. An entertaining encounter betweenBlackpoolandBromleyended 2-2, and Chris Conn-Clarke levelled late on forPeterboroughin a 1-1 draw withMK Dons.Press AssociationWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Cyle Larin scored twice asSouthamptonhammeredBristol City4-1 at St Mary’s. Larin scored in either half, with late goals from Kuryu Matsuki and Finn Azaz after Lorent Tolaj had pulled one back for the visitors. Southampton are formidable opposition at St Mary’s and have not lost on their own patch since January.Swanseamoved back into the automatic promotion places as they piled more misery on the newBurnleymanager Nicky Hayen, whose side slumped to the bottom of the table with a 3-1 defeat. The victory took Vitor Matos’ side level on points with West Ham at the top. ForBurnley, it was a fourth defeat in seven league games and they are still awaiting their first win.View image in fullscreenNicky Hayen reacts as his Burnley side sink to the bottom of the Championship.Photograph: Steven Paston/PABoth goals they conceded in the first half were avoidable and had their shooting been more precise they could have been at least on level terms. The former Leicester and England striker Jamie Vardy came on with half an hour left, and had the ball in the Swansea net nine minutes later only for the goal to be ruled out for offside.Hayen layer described next weekend’s home match with Derby as a “must-win game”, adding: “I mentioned a few weeks ago that we had to survive until the international break, where we can finally work properly on the training pitch.“But surviving means taking points and winning games, which we haven’t managed to do enough. What we desperately need is one victory to reward the performance and rebuild confidence. I’ll keep working exactly as I always do. I treat every game as if it were my last, because that keeps you sharp and injects energy into the squad and tomorrow I will put that energy back into the group.”Chris Davies said hisBirminghamside are heading in the right direction after they fought back to win 2-1 atDerby. Davies saw his players dig in through more than 13 minutes of added time to secure a second league win of the season. Derby had gone ahead against the run of play in the 40th minute through Bobby Clark. Birmingham’s response was instant with Carlos Vicente heading in at the back post from Liam Millar’s cross. They scored again in the 64th minute when Paik Seung-ho headed in a corner for his first goal since December.View image in fullscreenGoalkeeper James Beadle laps up Birmingham’s win at Pride Park.Photograph: Lee Keuneke/PADavies said: “We’ve looked a completely different team to last season, not only stylistically but just the strength and mental strength. It pains me to say it but we would have lost that game last season.”Steven Schumacher hailedBoltongoalkeeper Gavin Bazunu’s “outstanding” display after a 1-0 victory overCardiff. Substitute Thierry Gale headed in a last-minute winner to earn Bolton only a second win since returning to theChampionshipas last season’s League One playoff champions. Bazunu contributed 10 saves, including a stunning second-half stop to deny Yousef Salech’s close-range header.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQuick GuideLeague Two roundup: Charlie Lakin scores twice as Barnet beat Accrington and go topShowBarnettook over at the top of League Two after they beatAccrington2-1 andBristol Roverslost 2-0 toGrimsby. Charlie Lakin’s double enabled Barnet to come from behind after Charlie Caton’s first-half opener, with Devon Matthews seeing red for Stanley. Rovers were also reduced to 10 men, but Tommy Leigh’s dismissal came when they were already 2-0 down after goals for Kieran Green and Geza David Turi.Yorkare a point back after a 4-0 thumping of 10-manSwindon, in-form Alex Newby scoring twice, andCheltenhamalso sit on 11 points thanks to a 3-1 win overCrawley. Dylan Morgan opened the scoring early on for Crawley, but two goals for Charlie McCann and one for Andreas Weimann turned the tables.A topsy-turvy clash betweenRotherhamandSalfordended 3-3, with the Ammies going from two up to 3-2 down and having Abraham Odoh sent off but Macaulay Langstaff equalised from the penalty spot.Port Valeare off the bottom thanks to George Byers’ penalty in a 1-0 win overExeterand are replaced byRochdale, who drew 0-0 withWalsall.ShrewsburyandGillinghamwere 2-0 winners againstNorthamptonandTranmere, respectively, whileChesterfielddefeatedOldham2-1.ColchesterandCreweplayed out a 1-1 draw, as didNewportandFleetwood.Press AssociationWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Dapo Afolayan’s double helpedBlackburnsecure a much-needed 3-1 win overMillwallat a discontented Ewood Park. The game had not kicked off before the first “Venky’s out’’ chants could be heard but Afolayan, who turned 29 on Friday, gave the home fans something to cheer with a deft improvised flick to open the scoring in the 41st minute.Although Lydon Dykes’ penalty levelled matters six minutes after the restart, Afolayan’s thumping strike around the hour mark restored the lead. Blackburn managed the closing stages well and substitute Andri Gudjohnsen made the game safe in stoppage time with a breakaway goal to end a four-game winless run.Jack McGlynn orchestratedStoke’sfirst away win since January with a deserved 2-1 success atWatford. A 1-1 draw at Cardiff in midweek had ended a sequence of nine consecutive defeats away from Staffordshire, and Stoke were good value for their first win in 11 road trips – and their third success in four league games. McGlynn opened the scoring on half-time with Eric Bocat doubling the lead 13 minutes into the second half. Amin Nabizada’s reply came too late forWatford.Watford’s manager, Alessio Dionisi, said: “My players are tired: it’s normal when you play every three days for 10 matches, and we are a good team when we have them all available, but I know our situation. If we stick together and we believe in the future, I’m sure the future will be better.”Callum Styles earnedWest Broma point as they came from behind to draw 1-1 againstQPRat The Hawthorns.QPRled through a Chris Mepham own goal in the 38th minute which came completely against the run of play. That lead lasted just three minutes as Styles equalised to extend West Brom’s unbeaten home record to 11 games, while Rangers have yet to lose on their travels this season.Freddie Draper came off the bench to net a late winner in a hard-fought 1-0 win forLincolnaway atPreston. Draper headed in Andrei Coubis’ long throw in the 81st minute. Lincoln are now unbeaten in their last four league games, while Preston’s nightmare start continues, with three points from the first 21 available.Lincoln’s joint head coach Tom Shaw praised his side for perfecting “the real ugly side of football … we’re very proud of how we play. We’ve recruited, nurtured and developed a set of players that have got incredible character. We pride ourselves on those horrible, ugly things.”Charltonmaintained their unbeaten home record this season with a 0-0 draw againstPortsmouth. The game may have lacked goals, but it was not devoid of entertainment, particularly in an open second half.Explore more on these topicsChampionshipBolton WanderersCardiff CityBirmingham CityDerby CountyWest Bromwich AlbionQPRnewsShareReuse this content

title: Elena Rybakina beats Aryna Sabalenka to win US Open for first time – as it happened | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: The new No 1 underlined her status as the best player in the world by ending the two-time defending champion’s reign with a 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 victory
Author: Katy Murrells
Headline: The new No 1 underlined her status as the best player in the world by ending the two-time defending champion’s reign with a 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 victory
Content: 2h ago19.38 EDTSo congratulations to Rybakina, who played a superb match, maintaining her focus to get over the line having secured the world No 1 ranking for the first time a few days ago, and maintaining her composure to play a near-perfect third set against Sabalenka after losing the second. Rybakina just didn’t let Sabalenka settle, pushing the departing No 1 back with her power – and it’s not often we say that. I don’t think it was nerves from Sabalenka, I think Rybakina was just too good. When Rybakina’s playing at her peak, no one can live with her right now on a hard court, so it’s back to the drawing board for Sabalenka, as she reflects on a first season since 2022 without a slam title and how she can come back stronger. After all, that’s what rivalries are all about, pushing each other to continually improve. Many thanks for reading today and do join us again tomorrow for Alexander Zverev v Ben Shelton. title: Ben Shelton faces date with destiny against Zverev in US Open final | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: World No 4 will become the first Black American man to win the singles title at Flushing Meadow since Arthur Ashe if he can beat Zverez for the first time
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: World No 4 will become the first Black American man to win the singles title at Flushing Meadow since Arthur Ashe if he can beat Zverez for the first time
Content: Ben Shelton has defeated Carlos Alcaraz and Frances Tiafoe on the way to the US Open final.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAView image in fullscreenBen Shelton has defeated Carlos Alcaraz and Frances Tiafoe on the way to the US Open final.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAUS Open Tennis 2026Ben Shelton faces date with destiny against Zverev in US Open finalWorld No 4 will become the first Black American man to win the singles title at Flushing Meadow since Arthur Ashe if he can beat German for the first timeTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowSat 12 Sep 2026 15.32 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs Ben Shelton lapped up the explosion of joy and adoration from a full Arthur Ashe Stadium after reaching a grand slam final for the first time, one of his first thoughts was of his paternal grandmother, Regina, who died this year. Shelton credited his grandmother with ensuring that his father, Bryan, made it as a top professional, becoming one of a small group of Black men on the tour. “My dad lost his mom earlier this year and she’s the reason he was able to play tennis,” he said. “Without her, there’s no Ben Shelton standing here today. So this one is for her.”Shelton stands on the verge of history. On Sunday, he will attempt to become the first Black American man to win the US Open singles title since Arthur Ashe in 1968, a feat he will attempt inside the stadium named after Ashe. Shelton would also be the first Black man to win any grand slam singles title since Yannick Noah at Roland Garros in 1983, and the third overall. He is also aiming to become the first American man to win a major singles title since Andy Roddick won the US Open in 2003.Five-set tennis is under attack. Killing it would be a colossal unforced error | Andrew LawrenceRead moreThe final step, however, will be the most difficult. Tennis is a game of match-ups and Shelton has had an especially difficult time against Alexander Zverev,the Roland Garros championand the top seed in the absence of Jannik Sinner. After winning the first set they played, at Cincinnati in 2024, Shelton has lost 10 sets in a row to Zverev, compiling a 0-5 record against the German on hard courts, grass and clay.Zverev is well suited for left-handed opponents due to the strength of his two-handed backhand, which allows him to counter the effects of their swinging serve out wide from the left advantage side as well as their crosscourt forehand from the same position.There are plenty of reasons, however, for Shelton to be hopeful that things will be different in New York. He will remind himself of the fact that they have never faced each other in a grand slam tournament, where the American so often elevates his game, and particularly that the theme of this tournament has been breaking new ground in difficult match-ups.“Problem-solving has been the name of the game here,” he said. “I was 0-1 against Stef [Stefanos Tsitsipas], 0-3 against Carlos [Alcaraz], Foe [Frances Tiafoe] beat me the last time we played on this court. It’s been a lot of uphill battle, so I think I’m fully ready for the challenge to problem-solve.”His father and coach, Bryan, stressed how well his son, who is 7-2 in finals, competes with a title on the line: “He’s got an amazing record on Sundays. Don’t want to jinx him here, but if you look at his record throughout his career, he’s played well on Sundays.View image in fullscreenBen Shelton has failed to beat Alexander Zverev in their previous five meetings.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPA“So that’s where he wants to be. He feels like he’s going to play his best tennis at the end of the week, or end of the two weeks. So glad he has a chance at the US Open.”One of the most striking aspects of Shelton’s emergence has been his relentless improvement. His path took him through the college route where he started as an unremarkable prospect. When he first emerged on the ATP Tour, the strengths he showed with his enormous serve, athleticism and the variation he could play with were counterbalanced by glaring weaknesses in his backhand, return and consistency from the baseline. They were all still present on his explosive first full season on the tour in 2023, which he began with a run to the quarter-finals of the Australian Open on his first trip outside the United States. He reached the semi-finals of the US Open that year, yet despite progressing only one round further this year, Shelton is a different player now.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe has made such drastic improvements to his backhand, return of serve and consistency, which is what has allowed him to perform at such a high level during this tournament.Against Alcaraz, he returned well and was the far more stable player from the baseline. In hiswin over Tiafoe, he saved one of the best backhand days of his career for one of the biggest matches.“I still feel so many categories that I think I have a long way to go, but I’ve made improvements and changes in some of the most important categories to be able to compete at the top,” he said. “Return of serve, stability from the baseline, even my serve, the way that I go about putting together my service games has improved, and my ability to focus for long periods of time are all areas that have come together and have helped me play at the level I’m playing. But the pursuit and hunger to get better, to find ways that I can improve, it’s just a part of who I am and something that will never change.”Late on Friday night, as Shelton left the court and only just began to digest his achievement, a smile spread widely across his father’s face. “To do it here at the US Open and be playing on the final day, this kid, it’s kind of surreal,” he said. “I didn’t think he was going to even get into this sport and then to be where he’s at right now, I mean, it’s just hard to believe, hard to believe and just super, super grateful.”Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisTennisAlexander ZverevUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: This week’s soccer questions: were we wrong about Man City and does the Ballon d’Or ignore Americans? | Soccer | The Guardian
description: We look at Enzo Maresca’s takeover in Guardiola’s shadow, shifting dynamics in women’s soccer and Raphinha’s incredible form at Barcelona
Author: Graham Ruthven
Headline: We look at Enzo Maresca’s takeover in Guardiola’s shadow, shifting dynamics in women’s soccer and Raphinha’s incredible form at Barcelona
Content: Enzo Maresca has won his first three Premier League games plus his Champions League opener with Manchester City.Photograph: José Coelho/EPAView image in fullscreenEnzo Maresca has won his first three Premier League games plus his Champions League opener with Manchester City.Photograph: José Coelho/EPASoccerThis week’s soccer questions: were we wrong about Man City and does the Ballon d’Or ignore Americans?We look at Enzo Maresca’s takeover in Guardiola’s shadow, shifting dynamics in women’s soccer and Raphinha’s incredible form at BarcelonaGraham RuthvenSat 12 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWere predictions of Manchester City’s post-Pep drop-off overstated?Squint hard enough and Manchester City still look like Manchester City. They’re still playing the same possession-hungry soccer. Erling Haaland is stillscoringgoals. They even have a new manager with vaguely the same appearance and oeuvre as their old manager. An AI Pep Guardiola in the dugout.Of course, nothing is truly the same at City this season. How could it be? This is a club that was moulded in the image of Guardiola over a full decade. Everything was geared towards the Catalan coach whose manic intensity energized everything at the Etihad Stadium. Take that energy away and many assumed the lights would turn off.So far, though, Enzo Maresca’sManchester Cityhave played some bright soccer, winning their first three Premier League matches of the season and starting their Champions League campaign with a comfortable 2-0 away win over Porto on Tuesday. If a post-Pep drop-off is coming, it hasn’t hit City yet.This isn’t to say there hasn’t been vulnerability. Maresca is still integrating a number of summer signings. It will take time for Elliot Anderson, Ayyoub Bouaddi and Enzo Fernández to settle into City’s reshaped midfield unit. As if life after Guardiola wasn’t stark enough, Manchester City are also attempting to move on from Rodri, the central pillar who supported so much within their team.The scale of turnover at the Etihad this summer was huge. Bernardo Silva and John Stones departed, too. Eleven senior squad members in total left, and yet Manchester City have already shown enough tosuggestthey will once again compete for the biggest prizes this season. Predictions of their demise may have been premature.Why does the Ballon d’Or Féminin continue to ignore the USA’s best players?View image in fullscreenGotham midfielder Rose Lavelle was the only American player to make the shortlist for this year’s Ballon d’Or Féminin.Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPAThirty candidates for the 2026 Ballon d’Or Féminin and just one American – Rose Lavelle. Nobody expected to see any star-spangled representation on the men’s shortlist (as good as Malik Tillman was at the World Cup), but the sight of just one American name on theshortlistfor the women’s award was jarring considering the country’s standing as a women’s soccer superpower.Americans have been overlooked for the most prestigious individual prize in soccer before. Last year, Emily Fox was the highest-ranking US player in the final voting, finishing 25th. Lindsey Heaps (26th) was the only other American in the top 30. The year before that, when the US women’s national team won gold at the Paris Olympics, there wasn’t an American in the top three.None of this is to say Americans should be rewarded by right. The women’s soccer landscape has shifted dramatically in recent times with many of the sport’s best players now operating in Europe. Long gone are the days when the NWSL (and the various iterations before it) sat unchallenged at the top of the women’s soccer food chain.This shifting power dynamic could be a factor in why the Ballon d’Or Féminin has a habit of overlooking Americans. This is, after all, a European award. After decades of American dominance of the women’s game, is this Europe getting a small form of revenge? Is the Ballon d’Or Féminin shortlist deliberate rage bait?Trinity Rodman could have been nominated. Ashley Sanchez, fresh from setting the NWSL single-season scoring record for an American, might have been listed. Otherwise, it’s a bit difficult to make a case that many others were overlooked. It wasn’t a vintage year for Americans at the elite level. That, rather than any sort of agenda, may be the true explanation for their Ballon d’Or Féminin omission.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHas Raphinha found his best position as Barcelona’s new No 9?Conventional wisdom saidBarcelonaneeded a new No 9 this summer. Hansi Flick’s Barca, however, are anything but conventional and they may be stronger than ever after the departures of Robert Lewandowski and Ferran Torres. The Spanish champions never needed a new center-forward when they had Raphinha.Five games into the season, the Brazilian has already notched eight goals. Against Feyenoord on Wednesday, heled the linefor a Barcelona team who are destroying opponents at will, producing one of the Champions League’s first highlight-reel moments of the season by sending two defenders sliding off the Camp Nou pitch with a feint and finish.Champions League review: Irish heroics, rejected resignations and Mourinho’s returnRead moreRaphinha has made a habit of proving his doubters wrong. Some of those doubters have come from within his own club, who attempted to sell the former Leeds United winger before Flick turned him into one of the game’s most productive wide attackers. Raphinha’s latest evolution looks to have elevated him to an even higher level.Far from being a “false nine”, Raphinha is moving as if he’s played his entire career through the middle. His penalty box instincts are sharp. His ability to link play is smooth. The 29-year-old has made the shift to playing center forward appear so easy thatBarcelona’s public pursuit of Julián Álvareznow looks a waste of time.Gabriel Jesus arrived on deadline day to give Barca at least one out-and-out striker in their squad. The former Arsenal and Manchester City forward will be a useful option if he can avoid the injury issues that have plagued his career to date. His goal against Feyenoord showed what he can offer. It was nothing, however, compared to what Raphinha is doing.Explore more on these topicsFootballEuropean club footballManchester CityUSA women's football teamUS sportsEnzo MarescaBarcelonafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI IPO will not happen in 2026 amid AI safety fears, Sam Altman says | US news | The Guardian
description: OpenAI’s decision comes after dire warnings about rapidly progressing technology and lawmakers’ calls for new rules
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: OpenAI’s decision comes after dire warnings about rapidly progressing technology and lawmakers’ calls for new rules
Content: OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, attends an event in Tokyo, Japan, on 3 February 2025.Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, attends an event in Tokyo, Japan, on 3 February 2025.Photograph: Kim Kyung-Hoon/ReutersUS newsOpenAI IPO will not happen in 2026 amid AI safety fears, Sam Altman saysOpenAI’s decision comes after dire warnings about rapidly progressing technology and lawmakers’ calls for new rulesReutersSat 12 Sep 2026 19.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAIwill not go public in 2026,Sam Altmansaid in a Fortune interview published on Saturday, citing safety concerns overartificial intelligence.“I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don’t feel pressure on that,” Altman, OpenAI’s CEO,told Fortune.Growing numbers of US lawmakers ​arecalling for new rulesto govern AI systems after direwarningsfrom two researchers from OpenAI rival Anthropic that rapidly progressing artificial intelligence couldlead to the extinctionof the human race ‌in the not-too-distant future.The warnings follow cases of AI agentsgoing rogueto hack external systems and AI ​safety researchersquittingtheir companies concerned about the technology’s risks. Politicians, both Democrats and Republicans, have responded with alarm and calls for more action.‘We must slow the pace’: CEO of Anthropic calls for an AI slowdownRead moreThe New York Times in Junereportedthat the San Francisco-based OpenAI was considering whether to hold off on apotentiallytrillion-dollar IPO until next year. At the time, shares in Elon Musk’s SpaceX IPO were tumbling after a surge that sent that company’s valuation to $1.8tn.When asked by Fortune whether 2026 is off the table in favor of 2027, Altman said: “I would say not 2026. Yeah, we got a lot of stuff to do, like meeting this moment of what is going to be required for safety and alignment, and how the industry and governments can work together.”Altman also suggested that OpenAI and other leading AI companies may be close to announcing an agreement toslowAI development and work together to address safety risks, Fortune reported.Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, on Saturdayurged AI companiesto take a more deliberate approach to development.“We must slow the ‌pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote in an essay shared on social media.Altman later posted that he agreed with the sentiment.“I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Altman wrote in a response to Amodei’s post on the X platform. “This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had atOpenAIin recent weeks.”Safety concerns have not slowed down Anthropic’sown IPO plansso far. Anthropic is expected to begin marketing its initial public offering in mid-October at the earliest and complete the listing days before theUS midterm electionsin November, people familiar with the matter told Reuters this month.Explore more on these topicsUS newsOpenAISam AltmanAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingTechnology sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We must slow the pace’: CEO of Anthropic calls for an AI slowdown | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: In a social media post, Dario Amodei proposed a plan including third-party evaluations of AI systems
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: In a social media post, Dario Amodei proposed a plan including third-party evaluations of AI systems
Content: Dario Amodei said that AI development, if left unchecked, ‘could outrun our ability to understand and control’ it.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/ReutersView image in fullscreenDario Amodei said that AI development, if left unchecked, ‘could outrun our ability to understand and control’ it.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)‘We must slow the pace’: CEO of Anthropic calls for an AI slowdownIn a social media post, Dario Amodei proposed a plan including third-party evaluations of AI systemsEdward HelmoreSat 12 Sep 2026 11.46 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 16.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe CEO of the artificial intelligence companyAnthropicissued a new appeal on Saturday for theAIindustry to “slow down” and offered a three-part plan for doing so, saying that his company would “unilaterally” commit to the first of the steps.In apost on social media,Dario Amodei shared a link to an essay titled We Must Pace the Frontier in which he laid out how Anthropic would provide “third-party evaluators with permanent, employee-level access to our systems, so that they can verify adherence to our safety measures, report on incidents, and assess models’ alignment during training”.The move comes after a former Anthropic researcher warned on Wednesday that AI could precipitate human extinction by 2030. Researcher Jacob Coxon said in a series ofpoststhat he had quit his job because Anthropic and his previous employer, OpenAI, were ignoring or mishandling their response to the threat AI posed.“Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon wrote. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade … No other human activity poses this level of danger.”Anthropic researchers say AI could cause human extinction by 2030Read moreAn Anthropic spokesperson saidin a statement to the Guardianthat the company had “always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks” and it was building “models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry”.“I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,”Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI,postedon social media. “Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same. We’ll have more to share soon.”Other tech figures echoed this, including Elon Musk, whosimply posted, “Dario is right.” The OpenAI researcher Aidan McLaughlin alsocalledthe post “excellent” and said he agreed “with basically every word”.Earlier this year, Amodeipublished a lengthy essaytitled The Adolescence of Technology that addressed some of fears surrounding the accelerating technology.In his latest essay, he said that “carefully wielded, AI can be the latest in a long line of technological miracles that have uplifted and ennobled humanity.“But like many technologies before it, AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious … A race to the bottom, spurred by commercial incentives, can make these risks more acute,” he wrote.But, Amodei continued, “over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence – not just investing in risk prevention, but pacing the rate of capabilities advancement so that risk prevention has time to keep up.“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” he added in bold type.Amodei also wrote that over the summer he’d seen AI “advancing drastically faster”, a dynamic called recursive self-improvement.“Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all,” he said.The executive also addressed the recent Hugging Face incident, in which a swarm of AI agents created by OpenAI acted as a “fanatically devoted collectiveconducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAmodei wrote that simply dismissing the Hugging Face incursions because theOpenAIswarms appeared to have no malicious intent was not sufficient.“It’s easy to dismiss this incident because no one was hurt and the economic damage was minimal, but in my opinion, a swarm that possessed greater capabilities but a similar level of misalignment could have caused catastrophic damage,” he wrote.Anthropic details bad actors’ efforts to misuse its AI for bioweaponsRead moreClément Delangue, the CEO of Hugging Face,wrote in responseto Amodei’s Saturday letter that “it’s now clear that alignment is critical and won’t be solved behind the closed doors of a handful of frontier labs”. Delangue said Hugging Face had asked to be part of Anthropic’s “embedded evaluators” program.He added: “Let’s make AI safer by making it more transparent!”The three-step plan Amodei proposes includes building AI “at a balanced rate that aims to ensure its safety” by “ensuring companies take adequate time to align and safeguard their models, and for third party evaluators to confirm this”.The second step he proposes is to require industry-wide coordination, and the third is to ensure global coordination. “The steps do not need to be taken strictly in order, and some of them may be much harder to achieve than others,” he wrote.Amodei said he continues “to believe that AI can enormously improve the quality of human life”. But he warned that “the measures I propose to advance the frontier at a safe pace will not be easy. But I believe we owe it to humanity to try.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)AnthropicOpenAIElon MuskSam AltmanComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Immature playground boasting’: Mathematicians uneasy at OpenAI’s latest scalp | Mathematics | The Guardian
description: As OpenAI model cracks Millennium Prize Problem that puzzled experts for decades, many feel shocked at pace of change
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: As OpenAI model cracks Millennium Prize Problem that puzzled experts for decades, many feel shocked at pace of change
Content: For many mathematicians, it is the weeks, months and years spent circling a problem that appeals.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenFor many mathematicians, it is the weeks, months and years spent circling a problem that appeals.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersMathematics‘Immature playground boasting’: Mathematicians uneasy at OpenAI’s latest scalpAs OpenAI model cracks Millennium Prize Problem that puzzled experts for decades, many feel shocked at pace of changeIan SampleScience editorSat 12 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 08.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a week that left mathematicians reeling. Hot on the heels of aflurry of casesof artificial intelligencefurthering the field, OpenAI declared a major scalp: its latest AI model had cracked a Millennium Prize Problem, a puzzle with a $1m reward that had defied human brains for decades.The achievement bore little resemblance to how mathematical problems normally fall. A near-trillion dollar private company had unleashed 10,000 agents – AI systems that carry out tasks autonomously – on the problem. The bill was estimated at $15m.The trajectory towards AI capable of superhuman maths has long been clear, but tonail such a substantial problemso swiftly sent shock waves through the field. Mathematicians are asking what will be left for them if works in progress are hoovered up and claimed by others, and how they should train the next generation when even fiendish assignments can be solved at the press of a button.“I feel slightly shell-shocked,” said Prof Colva Roney-Dougal, the head of pure mathematics at the University of St Andrews. At a recent public lecture, she said she believed that AI was unlikely to do anything remarkable soon. “Three months later, I’m totally wrong,” she says. “We’re all just waiting to see what happens. It’s coming so fast.”Prof David Silvester, a mathematician at the University of Manchester, said the field felt “very unstable” given the pace of change. “All the open maths problems could fall with enough resources,” he said. “This is irreversible. This is not going to change.”Prof James Robinson, a mathematician at the University of Warwick, said hard problems were the fuel of mathematics, driving creative approaches across successive generations. “It’s frustrating to see these big tech companies burning this fuel up just so that they can show off about how great their latest model is,” he said. “It seems like immature playground boasting writ large, underpinned by billions of dollars and the potential for significant environmental damage in an age when climate change is probably the biggest challenge we face.”One reason Silvester went into maths was the rush that comes from cracking a problem. For many mathematicians it is the weeks, months and years spent circling a problem, breaking it down, trying one approach after another, and never quitting that appeals. “Without that, the subject seems completely different to me,” Silvester said.Mathematicians already devote considerable time to verifying each other’s proofs. It was this kind of review that found a gap in Andrew Wiles’s work onFermat’s Last Theoremin 1993, prompting a year of further effort to fix the flaw. Silvester suspects mathematicians might find themselves poring over ever more proofs dashed out by AI. “It’s more like becoming an accountant, you’re auditing, you’re checking,” he said.There are knock-on effects throughout the field. Mathematicians are recruited on the strength of their published papers, but problems they have been working on for months might now be solved by AI in days. “There’s a real sense of ‘I could spend the next month thinking about something and somebody else does it by pushing a button’,” says Roney-Dougal. “That’s horrible, and I think it’s going to be horrible for a few years.”It’s also a headache for teaching undergraduates.Universitiesroutinely set students problems and quizzes to work through at home. That kind of coursework is now dead. “There’s no point in doing it because we can’t vouch for its authenticity,” says Silvester. Lecturers are now having to tell students not to use AI for some problems, while ensuring they can use it for others: after all, AI-assisted maths is the future.For all the upheaval, Prof Alexander Paseau, who studies the philosophy of mathematics at the University of Oxford, believes maths will not lose much of its appeal. “The challenge still remains, even if AI is eventually better than humans at research,” he said. “You’ll still want to be able to understand the mathematics yourself. And we’ll still enjoy it and appreciate its beauty: the sheer enjoyment and the beauty of a mathematical proof will always be there. AI is not going to take any of that away.”A lot of AI maths does not solve problems from scratch, but builds on work by humans, he added. TheOpenAIbreakthrough, for example, relied heavily on work by the Madrid-based mathematicians Diego Córdoba and Luis Martinez-Zoroa.OpenAI’s work described asolution to the Navier-Stokes problemwhich involves equations that predict how fluids, and even the weather, behave. It is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems published by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000. The company’s announcement on Tuesday has led to further concerns in the community. OpenAI set its latest model to work after hearing rumours that two Millennium Problems had been solved by mathematicians. Prof Tristan Buckmaster at New York University and Levent Alpöge at Anthropic were doing related work on Navier-Stokes and had used OpenAI’s products in the process. They suspected OpenAI’s model had learned from their work-in-progress. After an investigation, OpenAIdenied this was the case.Some mathematicians are still wary, however. “The big story now in mathematics is that nobody wants to share anything,” Buckmaster told the Guardian. “Mathematics is different today than it was only a few days ago.
