title: Deepfakes are wrecking influencers’ credibility, one fake ad at a time | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Influencers aren’t just battling competitors for brand deals. They’re now battling AI versions of themselves
Author: Arielle Pardes
Headline: Influencers aren’t just battling competitors for brand deals. They’re now battling AI versions of themselves
Content: ‘It’s so violating. [They look] just like me, but the upside-down version.’Illustration: Guardian Design/TiktokView image in fullscreen‘It’s so violating. [They look] just like me, but the upside-down version.’Illustration: Guardian Design/TiktokGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.ReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)Deepfakes are wrecking influencers’ credibility, one fake ad at a timeInfluencers aren’t just battling competitors for brand deals. They’re now battling AI versions of themselvesSupported byAbout this contentArielle PardesSat 12 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarlier this year, Emily Schuman, the creator of the lifestyle blog Cupcakes and Cashmere, saw a photo of herself she didn’t recognize onInstagram. In a sponsored ad, Schuman, who has more than 500,000 Instagram followers, is holding up a vial of GLP-1 drugs, advertising the telehealth company Gala. There was just one problem: Schuman had never heard of Gala and had nothing to do with the ad.The ad was based on a digitally altered version of a selfie Schuman had taken in her car and posted on Instagram years earlier. Once her followers got wind, they flooded her inbox with questions about the sponsorship as it didn’t seem consistent with Schuman’s personal brand. Soon after, Schuman discovered this was just the beginning. There was also an Instagram post where an AI version of her with darker hair appears to apply foundation to promote a makeup brand called Meroda Cosmetics, andTikTokposts with generated images of her promoting the blood testing company Superpower.“It’s so violating,” she said. The videos and images look “just like me, but the upside down version”.Neither Gala nor Meroda responded to requests for comment. Superpower CEO Max Marchione said the TikTok post wasn’t a real ad, but instead came from a scammer his company later reported. “Whilst scamming isn’t new, AI has made this much worse,” he said.As generative AI makes it easier to create text, code and media, it has also supercharged the creation of deepfakes, the synthetic photos and videos that can be nearly indistinguishable from reality. Influencers are some of the easiest people to impersonate due to the sheer amount of videos and images AI can learn from. The vulnerability represents a new workplace threat: influencers aren’t just competing for brand deals with other creators, but also fighting to preserve the credibility of their own likeness – the very asset that generates their income.“Their brand is their business,” said Alice Marwick, the director of research at the Data & Society Research Institute, who published a recent paper on the rise of AI impersonation scams. “If their brand takes a hit, so does everything in their business life.”On social media, impersonation schemes run a large spectrum, from deepfaked Elon Musk promoting a fraudulent cryptocurrency, to brands quietly scraping an influencer’s image to manufacture ads. Global consumers may have lost as much as $3.7bn due to deepfake scams in 2026, according toan investigationfrom the VPN-maker Surfshark’s research team. The investigation found that social media impersonations on social media accounted for about half of all losses.Easy targets for deepfakesCelebrities and influencers are often the easiest to impersonate because they “have hundreds of hours of footage and thousands of pictures of them online. So you can feed that into a model and produce a fairly convincing deepfake,” said Marwick. Taylor Swift, Oprah Winfrey, Kim Kardashian, Gwyneth Paltrow and Tom Hanks have all been deepfaked by AI to promote various products online.But big celebrities aren’t alone. On Instagram, beauty influencer Arielle Lorre was deepfaked to promote a skincare brand. Fashion creator Jessi Caparella discovered altered images of herself on Pinterest redirecting traffic to affiliate clothing links. And deepfaked videos of OnlyFans creator Elaina St James were used to trick fans into sending money to fraudulent accounts. While the financial impact of these impersonation schemes is hard to pinpoint, creators say that deepfakes dilute their value, cost them the trust of their followers, and can be time-consuming to fight: even when one deepfake post is reported and removed, another one pops up in its place.With AI, “impersonation is much easier and much more convincing … [so] scams can be operated at a much larger scale,” said Marwick. “It’s often really believable. And with every new frontier model, they get better and better.”One reason for the rise of deepfakes may be a growing use of AI-generated marketing content in general. AI-generated or “virtual” influencers accounted for $1.37bn, or about 4% of all brand spending in 2026, according toresearchfrom marketing consultancy Digital Applied. Virtual influencers may not have the same authenticity as real people, but they are much cheaper, always available, and infinitely customizable, which makes them attractive for some brand campaigns.While the ad industry has always blurred the line between real and fake with airbrushing, CGI and other digital editing tools, the rise of AI has allowed brands to generate content from nothing with minimal production costs. And for some brands, that means crossing the line into deepfakes.Influencers are doing whatever they can to fight the issue. Molly Tranchin, a fashion influencer known as FashionVeggie with more than 500,000 followers on Instagram, recently filed alawsuitagainst the underwear brand Eby. According to the lawsuit, Tranchin had a contract to create three marketing videos for Eby in exchange for a fee. Eby was entitled to one round of “reasonable edits” for Tranchin to revise. The lawsuit claims that instead of posting the videos Tranchin submitted – in which she posed “modestly covering her chest and breasts with her arms” – the brand instead posted a deepfake video of Tranchin in a different pose, “exposing her breasts and nipples through one of Eby’s sheer bras”.Tranchin has since dropped the lawsuit over a lack of jurisdiction and plans to refile it in a different court, according to court documents filed last month.Eby spokesperson Clara Spahr said the company couldn’t comment on the pending litigation but will address the claims through the legal process.The fight for their likenessTranchin, whose lawsuit is ongoing, has the benefit of knowing exactly who to hold accountable for the deepfakes. Other creators are not as lucky.When Schuman discovered the deepfaked ads using her likeness, she and her manager immediately reported them toMeta. She said many of her followers, who brought these ads to her attention, also reported them. But it took weeks of badgering before Meta removed the GLP-1 ad. The makeup ad still remains in circulation on Instagram, despite many attempts from Schuman to get it taken down.Both Meta and TikTok explicitly prohibit using artificial intelligence or digital manipulation to replicate a person’s identity. But the reality is that these platforms’ personalization algorithms may inadvertently grease the wheels for these schemes.Meta, for example, allows advertisers to use hyper-targeted audience slicing, meaning bad actors can quietly launch fraudulent ads, create new accounts if one gets flagged, and scale their reach rapidly. In response to complaints about rampant scams on its platforms, Meta introducednew toolsthis year, including stronger advertiser verification policies and an AI detection tool to prevent “celeb-bait”, or the impersonation of celebrities. But experts say these tools do not go far enough, and that the company lacks incentive to clean up its own ad ecosystem. Meta did not respond to multiple requests for comment.“The reality is that platforms make a lot of money off scams,” Marwick said.Meta made about $16bn from ads promoting scams or banned goods, accounting for about 10% of its revenue in 2024, according to a2025 investigationfrom Reuters. That investigation also quoted an internal presentation from Meta’s safety team, which estimated that its platforms were “involved in a third of all successful scams in the US”.Not only do deepfakes hurt brand deals for individual influencers, but they also challenge the entire influencer marketing ecosystem. They disrupt the already delicate premise that a real person trusts a product or brand, and therefore their followers should do the same.Schuman said she is deciding whether or not she needs to retain legal counsel to help her fight off the deepfakes as they keep popping up. Besides reporting the offending posts and threatening legal action, influencers don’t have much recourse.“That’s money and time lost,” Schuman said about hiring a lawyer. But the alternative is a hit to her reputation. “So it’s a lose-lose from all ways of looking at it.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ReworkedSocial mediaMetaTikTokInstagramDigital mediaDeepfakefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Why is Trump’s $5,000 offer to voters ‘like a woman’? Ask Fox News | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Host Jesse Watters says Trump’s offer to Americans if Republicans retain Congress is ‘an enticement’, not a bribe
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Host Jesse Watters says Trump’s offer to Americans if Republicans retain Congress is ‘an enticement’, not a bribe
Content: ‘The president himself, meanwhile, doesn’t seem keen to elaborate on his cunning plan to win friends and influence voters.’Photograph: Callaghan O’Hare/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The president himself, meanwhile, doesn’t seem keen to elaborate on his cunning plan to win friends and influence voters.’Photograph: Callaghan O’Hare/ReutersOpinionDonald TrumpWhy is Trump’s $5,000 offer to voters ‘like a woman’? Ask Fox NewsArwa MahdawiHost Jesse Watters says Trump’s offer to Americans if Republicans retain Congress is ‘an enticement’, not a bribeSat 12 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTShareIthink I finally understand why Fox News pays Jesse Watters the big bucks. The network star, famous for hot takeslikemen shouldn’t “eat soup in public”, has an incredible talent for inserting misogyny into absolutely any news story.Take, for example, Donald Trump’s ludicrousannouncementon Wednesday night that he will give every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the US Congress in November’s midterm election. That’s a story about apparent bribery, right? A story about fiscal recklessness and empty promises. A story about how the president, whose popularity is plummeting, is so out of ideas that he’s resorted (yet again) to dangling cash in front of voters.Actually, says Watters, it’s none of the above; it’s just Trump behaving like a woman.“That $5,000 check, Dana, that’s not a bribe,” Watters told Fox anchor Dana Perino onThursday. “We’re calling it an enticement … It’s like a woman. Sometimes a woman can entice you, OK? Maybe – it doesn’t mean you’re going home with her, but it keeps you interested. It keeps you intrigued and wanting more. That’s what this is about.”Perhaps the Fox News host isn’t completely wrong. After all, I am a woman and I am about to entice you tolook upthe story about how Watters courted his much younger second wife. It’s very intriguing.But back to thisdefinitely-not-a-bribe$5,000 payment which the president calls a Trump “dividend”. I wouldn’t start spending it now, if I were you. The president, like his right-hand manElon Musk, has a habit of making grandiose promises he doesn’t keep. Remember theDoge dividendsfloated last February? Those haven’t materialized. Nor have the tariff dividends that Trump made so much noise about. “People that are against Tariffs are FOOLS!” Trump said in aTruth Socialpost last year. “We are taking in Trillions of Dollars and … A dividend of at least $2000 a person (not including high income people!) will be paid to everyone.” Almost a year after that post, nobody has received a tariff dividend. However, ithas been estimatedby the Joint Economic Committee – Minority that the average American family will pay more than $2,500 in tariff costs this year.I feel pretty confident saying there is a 0.00001% chance that anyone is going to get a $5,000 Republican celebration check. But let’s just play along for a minute and pretend that Trump isn’t afabulist. Let’s pretend that the president is a serious man who makes thoughtful policy proposals, rather than an opportunist who says whatever inane thing happens to pop into his brain in the moment. Isn’t it a bit reckless to be giving all this money away, a total that exceeds $1tn, when the US national debtrecently surpassed$40tn for the first time? As Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, said in a statement, that debt “doesn’t exist solely on the government’s ledgers”, it is shouldered by everyone. “The more we borrow, the more we exacerbate inflation, squeeze out other priorities in the budget, and leave ourselves vulnerable to emergencies at home and turmoil abroad.”Don’t worry about all that, says the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick. “It’s not tax money,” Lutnick told NBC News onThursday. The Trump administration is going to earn that money from various moneymaking endeavours like the Trump Platinum Card, which allows wealthy people to pay up to $5m to extend their US visas. JD Vance, meanwhile, has suggested that the money might come from US tariff revenues, even though economists have pointed out the $125bn in tariff revenues wouldn’t come close tocovering the costs.The president himself, meanwhile, doesn’t seem keen to elaborate on his cunning plan to win friends and influence voters. When the ABC reporter Rachel Scott asked him about the rationale behind the $5,000 checks on Thursday night, he said it was a reward to Americans for putting up with Joe Biden. After Scott tried to ask a follow-up question, Trumplunged at herand said: “Your network … you’re the worst.” Which is very on-brand for the president. He can’t seem to handle being asked tough questions by anyone, but gets particularly nasty when those questions areposed by a woman.While Trump doesn’t want to get into the details of his dividend, the proposal reflects how the president is looking at some very unconventional ways to sway the midterms. He may not end up issuing people celebration checks, but he has alreadygutted election security programsand attempted to limit voting access. The real story here isn’t $5,000 cheques, it’s the fact that America’s self-styled king seems intent on meddling with the election, and no meaningful checks and balances are stopping him.Ectopic pregnancy deaths in the US have nearly doubledA ProPublica analysis found almost 200 women died after an ectopic pregnancy from 2020 to 2025. That’s compared to about 100 in the previous six years. To nobody’s surprise, mortality is worse in states with strict abortion bans. “While they cautioned that abortion bans alone can’t explain the national rise, maternal health experts said any examination of the spike should include the documented delays in care caused by the laws, including for ectopic pregnancies,”ProPublica notes.Sudanese refugees are being forced into sex workSudan’s civil war, which started in 2023, has created the world’s worst displacement crisis. Now, many of the women who fled to Egypt arebeing sexually exploited.What’s happened to Pete Hegseth’s testosterone screening guidance?The Pentagon published a guidance document on 2 September outlining a new mandatory testosterone screening process to create a “High-T military”. However, the very next day it was withdrawn from the public domain forreasons that remain unclear.Maybe someone in the Pentagon came to their senses.Secret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealedNaza, ahighly-fetednew film from the Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, reveals the secret systems used in mass killings of civilians in Gaza. “Several interviewees worked in a secret intelligence unit that reports directly to the office of Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu,”the Guardian writes. “[O]ne said their mission was to ‘thwart peace’.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhy does the hard right shrug off domestic abusers in their midst?The short answer is because they are misogynists who cynically weaponize women’s rights to advance their agenda. But do readZoe Williams, who has a longer and more eloquent answer, following on from the attack on a female protester at theReform UK conference.The Republican convention showed an image of Hasan Piker in his underwearThey seem to think showing photos of a buff podcaster in his underwear demonstrates that the left are scary “radicals”.The rise of hairy young womenPhoebe Bridgers’unshaven legsat her Venice film festival debut sparked a flurry of headlines. But,says Leah Harper, Bridgers’ “au naturel look may signal that attitudes are changing – particularly among younger generations”.Emma Bonino, feminist Italian politician, dies aged 78Boninogot involved in politics after she had an abortion (then illegal) at age 26 and said she decided that “never, never, never again should anyone have to suffer this humiliation”. She handed herself in to the police as an act of protest, leading a campaign to eventually legalize abortion in 1978.Princess Diana’s ‘revenge dress’ is going up for auctionDiana famously wore the fitted black dress on the same night that Charles admitted to his infidelity on TV in 1994. It will be auctionedoff in December.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionFox NewsUS midterm elections 2026FoxcommentShareReuse this content

title: What can halt Fifa’s authoritarian turn under Infantino? Change from the outside | Soccer | The Guardian
description: The World Cup and its aftermath made clear that Fifa needs independent oversight by governments and NGOs dedicated to preserving the people’s game
Author: Jules Boykoff
Headline: The World Cup and its aftermath made clear that Fifa needs independent oversight by governments and NGOs dedicated to preserving the people’s game
Content: Gianni Infantino’s ties to Donald Trump have drawn scrutiny from Fifa member associations around the globe.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino’s ties to Donald Trump have drawn scrutiny from Fifa member associations around the globe.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersSoccerWhat can halt Fifa’s authoritarian turn under Infantino? Change from the outsideJules BoykoffThe World Cup and its aftermath made clear that Fifa needs independent oversight by governments and NGOs dedicated to preserving the people’s gameSat 12 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTShareThe 2026 World Cup was a whirling swirl of scintillating soccer that prompted much-needed conversations about the vitality of diaspora, the fortitude of the underdog, the power of sport. In a world fractured along myriad cultural axes floating in an entertainment system dominated by on-demand content, the tournament provided a moment, perhaps unlike any other event, that brought together people from different backgrounds to simultaneously experience something meaningful.After the tournament concluded, Fifa president Gianni Infantino dropped a political pipebomb into the after-party,proposing to privatizethe World Cup by injecting $20bn in private capital, with an assist from JP Morgan and Thrive Capital, the investment vehicle orchestrated by Joshua Kushner, brother to Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law.Turns out, Infantino hadn’t just been sucking up to Trump the whole time – from hand-delivering the confectedFifa peace prizeto obliging him with thered card reversalheard ’round the world – ostensibly to ensure the World Cup money spigot remained winched wide open. Apparently, Infantino was also studying Trump’s nepotism-flecked smash-and-grab techniques. Not unlike the Trump administrationnixingenergy-project grants for states “based solely” on whether they supported him in the 2024 presidential election, football associations thatbackedInfantino’s private-equity scheme would get more money while those that disagreed would receive less. And just as Trump and the rightwing media ecosystem havedestabilizedthe very notion of truth in US political discourse, Fifa subverted the notion of fairness when it nullified the red card for a US player.But something deeper and even more important is going on. Amid therising tide of authoritarianismaround the world, includingin the USunder Trump, Fifa under Infantino has itself become increasingly dictatorial. Although Fifaclaimsit acts “in full respect” of its self-trumpeted “democratic and governance principles”, and that its president’s private-equity fever dream was “about the democratization of football worldwide”, the reality is that Fifa emulates the dictatorships before whom Infantino so readily genuflects. Many within the governing body learned about the privatization gambitthrough the newsrather than proper consultation (just as they had heard ofInfantino’s decisionto hand Trump the peace prize). Although Fifa statutes limit presidents to “no more than three terms of office”, and Infantino was first elected in 2016 and then re-elected – unopposed by acclamation – in 2019 and 2023, he hasdeclaredthat he could run again in 2027. Infantino is infamous for besmirching journalists and avoiding press conferences. Tough questions are signs of reporters “spreading hate”. For him, information is meant to flow unidirectionally, cascading from on high.More than 100,000 people add names to complaint against Gianni InfantinoRead moreWhat can be done? Yes, it’s past time to “give Fifa’s boss the boot”, as a US Soccer vice-president put it. But despite Infantino’s spectacular miscalculations and dictatorial shifts, those who have the power to “boot” him have instead made him the frontrunner in next year’s election. Although soccer’s regional governing bodies in Europe (Uefa), Asia (AFC), as well as North, Central America and the Caribbean (Concacaf) have publicly rebuked Infantino, with Europe eventhreateningto boycott international competitions, fissures have emerged:Mexico,Qatarand several Asian national associations have broken ranks to signal support for the beleaguered Infantino. The Confederation of African Football (CAF), which represents 54 countries, “unanimously reconfirmed its support” for Infantino, who needs only 106 votes to survive his re-election bid next March. Dislodging Infantino is an uphill fight.That’s because Fifa’s patronage system is a powerful sedative for dissent: it distributes millions to football associations around the globe under a system of clientelism grounded in fidelity and orchestrated with scant public oversight. This is soccer symbiosis awash in cash and lacking accountability.Even though Fifa’s proposed privatization could have hurt players, fans and clubs alike, plenty of federations were ready to support it. Sure, private equity has an ignominious record of acquiring holdings with social value, stripping them for parts and leaving a husk of what once was. Exhibit A:sports media. Exhibit B:hospitals. Making football into Exhibit C would not only have risked destroying the world’s most popular sport. It would have been a crime against collective joy. Nevertheless, administrators around the world were happy to back the gambit. This is a testament to the power of that patronage system, built up over decades by successive presidents, from João Havelange to Sepp Blatter to Gianni Infantino.The top candidates to replace Infantino are freighted with cumbersome baggage. Victor Montagliani rose to become head of Concacaf and a Fifa Council vice-president despitecontroversial handlingsof scandals and partnerships. Another possibility, Fifa Council member Nasser Al-Khelaifi of Qatar,statedthat he had “no ambition, no intention and no interest in the Fifa role”. Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, top man at the Asian Football Confederation,already lostto Infantino back in 2016 and has long beendoggedby allegations of human-rights violations in Bahrain, which he denies. Lise Klaveness, who heads the Norwegian FA, would bring principle and panache to the presidency – and she hasa strong recordof standing up to Infantino – but she is essentially unelectable in an organizationdrenched in sexism.Let’s be clear: change at Fifa must come from outside the organization. For too long, Fifa has monitored itself. The 2026 World Cup and its aftermath demonstrate unequivocally that Fifa requires independent oversight, toothy regulation carried out by governments and NGOs dedicated to preserving the people’s game as a social good.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionToward that end,FairSquare, the London-based nonprofit human-rights organization on whose advisory board I serve, recently launched a “Reboot Fifa” campaign todeclareInfantino ineligible for the March election and to createthe biggest-ever class-action complaintagainst Infantino for openly violating Fifa’s own governingstatuteson political neutrality by consistently cozying up to Trump.Donninga red Maga-style cap with “45—47” and “USA” emblazoned on it at a Board of Peace meeting cannot be considered “Fifa remain[ing] neutralin matters of politics”.Infantino’s clumsy overstepping has galvanized calls for reform and created a chance to reject authoritarianism creep.Fixing the Fifa greed zombie requires a vibrant pushback on all fronts. We must support Jamie Raskin who, as the ranking member on the House judiciary committee, hasdemandedFifa furnish all its documented contact with Trump, members of his administration and the Trump Organization. Switzerland’s parliament shouldreconsiderFifa’s tax-free status under Swiss law. We should rally behind soccer A-listers like England international Lucy Bronze and former France star Mikaël Silvestre who areinsistingthat “Change is necessary” and that “enough is enough”. If not now, then when?Explore more on these topicsFootballFootball politicsFifaGianni InfantinoDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: The far right is becoming normalised in Germany – and winning. Australia should take heed | Charlotte Feakins | The Guardian
description: One Nation and the AfD may not look the same, but they are singing from the same song sheet - and both have had recent electoral success
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: One Nation and the AfD may not look the same, but they are singing from the same song sheet - and both have had recent electoral success
Content: A participant displays a placard with the lettering 'No AfD' in front of the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin on 7 September 2026.Photograph: John MacDougall/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA participant displays a placard with the lettering 'No AfD' in front of the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin on 7 September 2026.Photograph: John MacDougall/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionOne NationThe far right is becoming normalised in Germany – and winning. Australia should take heedCharlotte FeakinsOne Nation and the AfD may not look the same, but they are singing from the same song sheet - and both have had recent electoral successFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastSat 12 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 19.59 EDTShareTherecent winfor the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in Germany is shocking, except it’s not shocking. The writing has been on the wall for quite some time.Last Sunday, the far-right, pro-Russian and anti-immigration AfD won almost 44% of the vote in theelectionin Saxony-Anhalt, a largely rural state in the former East Germany, more than doubling its previous result and finishing far ahead of the Christian Democrats.Why is the far-right AfD’s state victory significant and what might happen next in German politics?Read moreIt sits within a troubling global trend. In 2025, nearly one in four countries worldwide experienced democraticbacksliding, with Europe and North America home to six of the 10 countries newly identified as autocratising, including Italy, the UK and the US.Despite the cultural and historical differences, Australia is not immune. We cannot afford to be complacent.This time last year, I travelled to Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, a predominantly rural region in Germany’s north-east, to examine the culture of the far right and its counter-responses as part of my research. Like Saxony-Anhalt, it’s an area where the AfD has significant support. My colleagues and I spent days walking the streets of towns and cities, including Rostock and Greifswald, as well as attending an anti-fascist music festival. We wanted to understand how extremism was encountered and expressed in everyday life. But what we found, or more precisely did not find, surprised us.View image in fullscreen‘Antifa’ graffiti in Rostock, Germany, 2025.Photograph: Charlotte FeakinsFor a politics so extreme and increasingly popular, visual expressions of the far right were remarkably scarce. We encountered graffitied walls and hundreds of activist stickers on street signs, lamp-posts and electricity boxes. Of these, only one or two were associated with the far right. The counter-movement dominated the streetscape. Its stickers and graffiti were vibrant, loud and sharp, with a clear intent and recurring “anti-fascist” message. Yet a subtler pattern was emerging. The far right was made visible not through its own stickers or graffiti, but in the intolerance directed towards the counter-movement: freshly placed anti-fascist and pro-refugee stickers were being actively defaced.View image in fullscreenA ‘Refugees Welcome’ sticker defaced, Greifswald, Germany, 2025.Photograph: Charlotte FeakinsLooking back now, that landscape feels strangely prescient. As far-right ideas move beyond the fringe and enter mainstream political discourse, they become harder to detect, let alone recognise as extreme – an insidious process that gradually reshapes what is considered “normal”.In Australia, we tend to imagine the far right as young white men dressed in black and wearing balaclavas, marching through the streets, performing Nazi salutes or standing in front of historic buildings holding banners. These deliberate acts of spectacle are designed to attract attention, provoke and intimidate. They are easy to identify and condemn, appearing separate from the political mainstream.But far-right politics does not only appear wearing a balaclava. Increasingly, it does not look extreme at all. Across Europe, far-right politicians are neat, polished and smooth-talking. They are unnervinglynormal. Their messages are often simple and repeatable, circulating like memes through algorithm-driven news feeds, amplified by increasingly powerfulactorsin the tech and media sectors and, in some cases, legitimised at the ballot box.While One Nation politicians area long way fromthe smooth-talking politicians we see in the AfD, the minor party’s recent successes in byelections inFarrerandSecret Harbourshould make us take notice.View image in fullscreenAfD’s Tino Chrupalla (L), Ulrich Siegmund and Alice Weidel. ‘At a time when the future feels increasingly uncertain, far-right politics offers something simple and seductive: certainty, belonging and the promise of a return to an imagined past.’Photograph: Maja Hitij/Getty ImagesAfD andOne Nationmay not look or even sound the same, but they are singing from the same song sheet. Their histories, politics and contexts are different, but both draw on exclusion, national restoration, grievance and distrust. Their growing electoral success raises a critical question: why are these ideas finding a more receptive audience now?Across the world authoritarians want to tell us what a ‘good life’ looks like. Here’s how liberals must respond | Alexandre LefebvreRead morePart of the answer may lie in how the future is imagined. Climate disruption is intensifying amid economic insecurity, war and displacement. AI is transforming how we work, communicate and understand what is real, while immense wealth and technological power are increasingly concentrated in the hands of a few. These are real, present-day challenges, and the anxiety surrounding them is being amplified through social media feeds in which extreme, frightening and divisive versions of events can dominate. At a time when the future feels increasingly uncertain, rightwing populist politics offers something simple and seductive: certainty, belonging and the promise of a return to an imagined past.As these pressures compound, their impacts radiate through our economies, communities and politics. Instead of looking sideways for someone to blame, we need to think more critically: to question where power is held, who benefits from the decisions being made, and who is being asked to bear their consequences. Otherwise, legitimate fears about the future can too easily be used to turn people against each other.Dr Charlotte Feakins is a heritage researcher and lecturer at the University of Sydney and co-convener of anupcoming symposiumon why the humanities matter in uncertain timesExplore more on these topicsOne NationOpinionAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)GermanyAustralian politicsEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: As Australia faces an AI-generated future, a human rights act is needed more than ever | Julianne Schultz | The Guardian
description: Without laws requiring transparency or a right of review, our human rights will be rationed away by algorithmic and automated decision-making tools
Author: Julianne Schultz
Headline: Without laws requiring transparency or a right of review, our human rights will be rationed away by algorithmic and automated decision-making tools
Content: The federal government has been warned about ‘catastrophic’ outcomes from its algorithmic aged care funding tool.Photograph: Alistair Berg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe federal government has been warned about ‘catastrophic’ outcomes from its algorithmic aged care funding tool.Photograph: Alistair Berg/Getty ImagesOpinionHuman Rights ActAs Australia faces an AI-generated future, a human rights act is needed more than everJulianne SchultzWithout laws requiring transparency or a right of review, our human rights will be rationed away by algorithmic and automated decision-making toolsSat 12 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 19.34 EDTShareAs we hurtle towards a post-human future, the absence of a human rights act in Australia will put us all at ever greater risk.Human rights, which the Australian parliament has never managed to properly legislate despite overwhelming public support, risks becoming a dimly remembered artefact of another age at precisely the moment we need it most.Artificial – authoritarian – intelligence, automated decision-making, independent assessment tools and algorithms willshape the lives we liveand the public support we receive.‘Catastrophic’ fears: health staff made lists of concerning cases days after Australia’s aged care funding tool launchRead moreBut human rights arenot adequately legislatedin Canberra – despite the recommendation of aparliamentary committee, ahuge petitionand campaign and effective laws in Victoria, Queensland and ACT. Now rights can easily be lost in an environment shaped by opaque algorithms and computers that say no.The government has been patting itself on the back with its proposed digital duty of care – “my feed my way”, as the prime minister announced with uncharacteristic pithiness. It aims to introduce limits on the algorithms perfected by the global surveillance giants and give Australians the right to help shape the information they receive (but not its accuracy).Meanwhile, the government is racing to use similar tools tothat determine how much support people receive for essential services when they need them most.Kate Chaney’s private member’sbill is the only sign of pushback.Hundreds of thousands of public servantshave been trainedon how to use artificial intelligence. Yetthe information commissionerfound that few departments declared their use of AI.GovAI is set to become something more than an announcement. Every department and agency was required to appoint a chief AI officer by July.Come December, the privacy statements of every department – and company – that uses AI to make decisions that impact human beingswill have to be updatedto note this.But who reads privacy statements before clicking consent?The law falls short of therobodebt royal commissionrecommendations. It does not require companies and departments to reveal how the process works, the business rules and algorithms, or provide a right to human review of automated decisions.The provision of care to older Australians is currently the biggest canary in this mine.After only 10 months, it is clear that the department of ageing’s automated integrated assessment tool (IAT) – used to determine eligibility and access to services – is failing. Contrary to all best practise recommendations or the scarifying experience of robodebt, it has no human oversight or override options.AsMelissa Davey reported, within days of the tool’s adoption, alarm bells began to ring.State health officials recognised that it was potentially catastrophic; spreadsheets of inappropriate decisions were compiled in every state. “Misaligned IAT outcomes”, they were called in NSW. In the words of the head of WA Health: “Without a pathway for discretion, a small but vulnerable group of older people might experience catastrophic outcomes while waiting for algorithmically determined access to services.”Beyond the human pain and suffering, this matters a great deal for the states and territories. It istheir hospital bedsthat become the only option for elderly people who cannot get adequate care at home, or access to a residential care bed.The equivalent of whole hospitals are filled with people who should be receiving more appropriate care elsewhere.For years we watched and listened to the horror stories of aged care as they were revealed to the royal commission. Before the commission finally reported, the pandemic exacerbated the problem as residential facilities became “no-go zones”, leaving the elderly marooned, their loved ones tapping on windows and staff fearful.The human rights of thousands of people were gravely infringed.Those designing the new Aged Care Act, which came into effect last November, took this seriously. The beginning of the act is a testament to the fundamental right to be treated with dignity, respect and independence.In residential care homes all over Australia, the statement of the human rights of the elder person was tacked up on notice boards for those who could still read – and their loved ones – to note.What was not so prominent was the inability of those residents to take legal action if their rights were breached. There was a complaints mechanism, but these werenot fully legally enforceable rights.The human right of the aged to care were again to be rationed – by algorithms, queues for assessments, caps on the number of places and access to providers, by regulations that made delivering services at home or in facilities onerous.At the time, it was only the super-observant departmental officials in the states and some advocacy groups who realised access was also being rationed by an algorithm that could not be overridden by a human being.The contrast between the frontend of the Aged Care Act and its backend implementation could not have been sharper. The beginning of the act describes the rights of older Australians to receive care and be treated with dignity and respect. But the implementation is about transactions: minutes of care, checklists of tasks, organisational obligations.“The plumbing of the reforms is undermining the poetry of the act,” the former inspector general of aged care Natalie Siegel-Browntold the National Press Club.Instead of life, it is the human rights of the elderly, that toparaphrase TS Eliot, are being “measured out … with coffee spoons”.Julianne Schultz is the author of The Idea of AustraliaExplore more on these topicsHuman Rights ActOpinionAged careAI (artificial intelligence)Australian lawcommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: Comedians should not be hot | Amy Annette | The Guardian
description: People making a living from being funny should be exempt from the beauty rules the rest of society plays by, says comedian Amy Annette
Author: Amy Annette
Headline: People making a living from being funny should be exempt from the beauty rules the rest of society plays by, says comedian Amy Annette
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onComedyThe hill I will die on: Comedians should not be hotAmy AnnettePeople making a living from being funny should be exempt from the beauty rules the rest of society plays bySat 12 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 06.12 EDTShareIt’s a fact that being funny is an evolutionary trait, developed by the unattractive to entice the very good-looking to mate with them. Yes, that is a fact, and no I won’t look it up. And therefore it is not OK for attractive people to also be funny. And I don’t think that I’m going too far when I say that comedians being hot is a crime against nature.I use the word “hot” intentionally. Beauty is ineffable. It can be found anywhere and in anyone. Hotness is different. It’s playing the game of society’s beauty norms and winning. Although, by spendinganytime playing, you have lost (like golf). I’m not ugly, but I’ll never be hot. I simply don’t have it in me. The effort! The commitment! The other day I went to a wedding and thought to myself: “I really like this couple, maybe I’ll shave above the knee.” A hot person would have probably already been professionally hairless, and, if not would have booked in a wax ASAP.Many US comedians these days are celebrity-level hot. Hot by normal people standards, not just by comedy’s traditionally low bar. I think I know why. If you are a woman with any visibility, there will inevitably be a response online to your looks. If you are in any way not meeting normative beauty standards, it will be pointed out to you. A lot. If you can attain hotness, you may think that you become more bulletproof – that you will be judged on your jokes and not your looks. That’s what I think has happened with comedians such as Nikki Glaser, whodid an incredible job of hostingthe Golden Globes, but did so looking as polished as any A-list actor.It wasn’t always like this. I grew up looking up to Wanda Sykes, Rosie O’Donnell, Dawn French and Jo Brand. Now to be clear, these are attractive people –no onewore a velvet tabard dress/top in the early 00s like Dawn French, and no one ever will – but they weren’t trying to be hot. They talked about beauty standards and they often addressed how they differed from the norms, but they never felt the need to meet them.Of course, when I say “hot comedians”, really I mean “hot female comedians” – because there is obviously more pressure on women to be hot. There is still room for the schlubby, basketball-shorted Adam Sandler everyman comedian. But for the new generations of comedians, it seems that similar pressures are now affecting men.Matt Rife angrily refuted claimshe’d had plastic surgery recently, claiming that he just can’t help being gorgeous. “If anything,” he said, “as a comedian, it actually made shit harder.” I agree, if by “shit harder” he means “much, much easier”.No good can come of this new standard. I’m not saying all comedians need to be ugly, but I am worried we’re getting to a point where all comedians need to be hot. Please. No. Think of us, the happily hairy thighed, and let us be as non-hot as we like.Amy Annette is a comedianskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Bayeux tapestrymania has gripped Britain. But what does it say about our own age of war and upheaval?  | Charlotte Higgins | The Guardian
description: The tapestry is drawing crowds to the British Museum – and each person who sees it will draw a different meaning from this epic, vivid artwork, says the Guardian’s chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins
Author: Charlotte Higgins
Headline: The tapestry is drawing crowds to the British Museum – and each person who sees it will draw a different meaning from this epic, vivid artwork, says the Guardian’s chief culture writer Charlotte Higgins
Content: Bayeux tapestry-themed merchandise at the British Museum in London, September 2026.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenBayeux tapestry-themed merchandise at the British Museum in London, September 2026.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersOpinionBayeux tapestryBayeux tapestrymania has gripped Britain. But what does it say about our own age of war and upheaval?Charlotte HigginsThe tapestry is drawing crowds to the British Museum – and each person who sees it will draw a different meaning from this epic, vivid artworkSat 12 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 12.50 EDTShareIhave seen theBayeux tapestryfour times since childhood, and loved it on each viewing, for the sheer miracle of its survival and the glorious vividness of its detail. But the fourth time, earlier this week, was different – how could it not be?Tapestrymania has taken hold in London. The textile has been proffered as a diplomatic symbol, the occasion for crowned heads and presidents to mingle and speechify. And, assuming you agree that it was embroidered in England by Englishwomen’s hands (since many scholars argue it waslikely stitched in Canterburyrather than Bayeux, Normandy – the tapestry’s home),it is charged with the potency of return, rather than simply of arrival.If you want to see the Bayeux tapestryat the British Museum, be alert for the next ticket release in October, be resigned to sitting in along digital queueand be ready to hand over £33. Or, perhaps more realistically, be prepared for disappointment. Viewing times are restricted to protect its delicate fibres from damage, so they can’t simply be extended beyond normal hours. Demand will outstrip supply.We see celebrated artworks through the lens of our own historical moment, our own biography. Encountering the tapestry again this week, in a time of war, it seemed impossible to observe the violence of the battles it depicts without a cold dread: the decapitated trunks, the horses clashing and tumbling, the looters stripping the killed of their arms and armour. But what really struck me was how legible the artwork is. Across nearly 1,000 years, its narrative clarity is such that, in its temporary gallery, you barely need to glance up at the British Museum’s animated interpretation. All it asks of you is to look, and the story will lay itself out generously before you.The Bayeux tapestry: a stupefying, thrilling, horrifying masterpiece that shakes the earthRead moreView image in fullscreenPeople queueing to see the Bayeux tapestry at the British Museum in London, 10 September 2026.Photograph: James Manning/PAAs a child, on a school trip to Bayeux, I was encouraged to see the tapestry as a cartoon strip. That makes sense, of course, to a child, and cartoonists of recent times have often used the tapestry to riff on.In his coverfor the post D-day, 15 July 1944 edition of the New Yorker, Rea Irvin lovingly parodied the tapestry, putting “George Rex” on his throne instead ofEdward the Confessorand depicting landing vessels stuffed with GIs, rather than wooden ships filled with Norman troops. It was irresistible in its neat reversal: Normandy invaded from England rather than vice versa.Now, though, I’d rather see it as a visual poem. An epic of conquest. In the wake of that other recent cultural sensation,Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, you do not need to be a classics nerd like me (and Mary Beard and I will make apodcaston the tapestry through a classical lens soon) to spot the resonances with ancient epic. The voyaging, the misadventures, the landing on an unfamiliar shore to be met by hostile inhabitants – and then the battle.One of the most satisfying elements of the tapestry is its pacing, which also has the feel of epic. The relatively slow buildup, with the scenes of Harold and his English setting out across the sea with falcons on their wrists, and tunics pulled up as they wade out to their boats. The drama of Harold’s capture in northernFrance, his retrieval by William of Normandy, and Harold’s rescue of men sinking into the quicksand at Mont Saint-Michel. The fateful (but unspecified) oath Harold swears to William. The death of Edward back in Westminster, his weeping wife and Harold’s acclamation as king of England. Finally, the clash of armies and Harold’s death.View image in fullscreenA detail of the 70m-long Bayeux tapestry, September 2026.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersBut – also like an ancient epic – it has its moments of strangeness and humour. The main scenes on the textile are bordered by images of fantastic beasts, but also scenes of everyday life – of people ploughing and scattering seed. A reminder of existences that grind on despite the machinations of kings. It reminds me of how imagery works in ancient epic, where similes do a comparable job of pulling the reader out of the main action into a world of nature and ordinary people doing ordinary things.Above all, the tapestry resonates with theAeneid, the origin myth of the Roman empire by the poet Virgil (who died in 19BC), the story of which would certainly have been available to the learned elites of 11th-century northern Europe. Like the Aeneid, the tapestry offers adventures at sea, a decisive battle, a new ruler, all heralded by the arrival of a comet signifying a great reversal. Even the feasting scene – William and his men devouring skewers of meat before the battle – has an epic feel.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is, then, an English epic: an origin myth for Norman power in England, a story that everyone, or nearly everyone, educated in the UK knows: 1066, Harold with an arrow in his eye, William the Conqueror. Like the Aeneid, it has surface-level propaganda stitched into it. Quite likely commissioned by William’s half-brother, Odo, in the 1070s, its business is to show viewers the inevitability of the crown’s acquisition by this new Norman king. And, since it began to be part of the British imagination from its rediscovery in the 18th century, it has been so successful at imparting that narrative that hardly anyone hasheard of Edgar Ætheling, the figure who had a stronger claim on the English throne than either Harold or William, and is completely absent from the tapestry.But there is another reason for its extraordinary modern persistence than its sheer narrative force, economy and clarity. Despite its “official” status, an object created at the behest of conquering Normans, it is an incredibly open, and surprisingly even-handed, work of art. It has none of the posturing that blatant propaganda contains. Harold and William are portrayed as equals, with Harold accorded significant moments of valour and virtue – it is far from puffing up William solely as a new but better Julius Caesar who managed to conquer England, unlike Caesar, as his biographer, William of Poitiers, had it. The Latin text of the tapestry is clear but laconic. When we are told that “Harold swears an oath to William”, we are not told the nature of this oath (to support William in his claim to Edward’s crown? But who knows).The textile is an object whose story is completed by its viewer, which is why it is such a rich and generative artefact. Sometimes that “completion” has been for ill:the Nazissaw it strongly in relation to theories of racial superiority, fascinated by the Normans’ Nordic origins.And what now? TheBayeux tapestry, back (perhaps!) in England after as much as (perhaps!) 900 years, is just beginning a period of intense and excited scrutiny by a thrilled public. What will be read into those ancient threads? What will we take from it? Whatever emerges, it will almost certainly reveal more about us, now, in the 21st century, than the time in which it was made. The narrative of the tapestry is wonderfully clear. But the story it is telling us is ours to compose.Charlotte Higgins is the Guardian’s chief culture writerExplore more on these topicsBayeux tapestryOpinionBritish MuseumArtFranceEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Call it the Miliband doctrine. Let’s hope the new Israeli settlement boycott is just the start | Steve Bloomfield | The Guardian
description: This week’s bold move suggests that Britain will once again have an ‘ethical dimension’ to its foreign policy. That’s good for the world, says former Observer international editor Steve Bloomfield
Author: Steve Bloomfield
Headline: This week’s bold move suggests that Britain will once again have an ‘ethical dimension’ to its foreign policy. That’s good for the world, says former Observer international editor Steve Bloomfield
Content: Illustration: Nate Kitch/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Nate Kitch/The GuardianOpinionEd MilibandCall it the Miliband doctrine. Let’s hope the new Israeli settlement boycott is just the startSteve BloomfieldThis week’s move suggests that, even in the age of Trump, Britain will once again have an ‘ethical dimension’ to its foreign policy. That’s good for the worldSat 12 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 09.29 EDTShareAlmost 30 years ago, the Labour titanRobin Cookannounced his arrival at the Foreign Office by laying out what would become described as an“ethical foreign policy”. The UK, he said, “must support the demands of other peoples for the democratic rights on which we insist for ourselves”. Human rights would be “at the heart of our foreign policy”.In the 25 years since Cook was demoted, Britain has had a further 14 foreign secretaries – including seven in the past six years – few of whom can claim to have placed progressive ideals at the heart of their actions.Ed Miliband’s speech on Tuesdayoutlining the UK’s decision to impose economic sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank – and unveiling the international coalition he has built to support it – suggests that Cook may finally have a successor.Describing what is happening in theWest Bankas “ethnic cleansing” carried out by “settler terrorists”, Miliband used language that Palestinians have longed to hear from a British foreign secretary. Vital, too, was his official recognition that the occupation of the West Bank is “unlawful”.Britain was not acting alone. Miliband and diplomats at the Foreign Office have carefully formed a 12-nation coalition, including France and Canada, that spoke with one voice. A cautious European Union, partly blocked by a handful of Benjamin Netanyahu allies, could not have taken such action; while US membership of the G7 – regardless of Donald Trump – would have always made that avenue impossible too.The consequences of the sanctions forIsraelcould be profound, although much will depend on the implementation. The most far-reaching proposal announced by Miliband was the targeting of those who “finance … illegal settlements”. That could mean every single Israeli bank. For those banks it will pose a crucial question: do you want to do business with the settlements or the UK? It could pose a question for Israeli citizens too: do you want your credit card to work in the settlements or when you’re on holiday in London?Ahead of elections at the end of next month there is growing awareness in Israel of the lack of western allies the country can now rely upon. Supportis ebbing away in the US too. More Americansnow sympathise with the Palestinians than the Israelis,while more than half now back a Palestinian state.Even centrist Democrats are beginning to suggest the US position could change. In the wake of Miliband’s announcement, Hillary Clinton, the former secretary of state, on Thursday called for a“crackdown on settler violence”and said the US should “take a very tough position” if Netanyahu is re-elected.Beyond Israel, the past few days have shown that Britain now has a government that understands that the world has changed since Trump’s re-election. Since the second world war, the US has been Britain’s most important diplomatic partner. For many of those in Whitehall, adjusting to the realisation that Washington is no longer the first phone call when trying to come up with a diplomatic solution has not been straightforward.It is enormously promising that the Foreign Office could not only pull together a strong coalition but also lead it. This time the phone calls to Washington came at the end, once the policy had been agreed –Andy Burnhambriefing Trump, and Miliband talking through the details with his secretary of state, Marco Rubio.Alongside the E3 of Britain, France and Germany, which has taken the lead on forming a rival western policy on Ukraine, it is clear we’re moving into a new era of ad hoc diplomatic groups that may be just as effective as their more formal predecessors.Traditional alliances, from the G7 to Nato, are falling apart – destroyed from the inside by a US president who is opposed to multilateralism, liberal democracy and the rule of law. For the first year of Trump’s second term in office, the “rest of the west” was inert: some leaders simply refused to believe that the US was no longer an ally, while others fully understood the challenge but hadn’t worked out how to meet it.But since the start of 2026, the debate has been over, thanks to the publication of Trump’s incendiary national security strategy and his relentless desire to annex Greenland, threatening a Nato ally with invasion. AsMark Carney laid out in Davos, there has been a “rupture” in the international rules-based order and it is vital that the middle powers come together.The big question for Burnham and Miliband is whether they can build on this start and turn Britain into a progressive international force. How they deal with three key issues will be indicative. The easiest – but most expensive – will be aid. Both have expressed a desire to reverse Keir Starmer’s 40% cut to the international aid and development budget, a decision that managed to be both immoral and self-defeating. If this can be done, the UK may regain some of the soft power it so carelessly threw away.They will face a bigger challenge in Ukraine, where the E3-led “coalition of the willing” has so far had little impact on the only two men who count, Trump and the Russian president, Vladimir Putin. While the US president so far appears unwilling to waste any political capital in saving Netanyahu, he seems more disposed to come to the aid of his counterpart in Moscow.Finally, there is another war that Miliband should be striving to end: the long-running conflict in Sudan. Just as with Israel, it will involve standing up to a close ally in the Middle East, in this case the United Arab Emirates (UAE). For the past few years, the UAE has been funding and arming the Rapid Support Forces, a militia group that now controls large swathes of the country and has been accused by a UN report of committing atrocities that bear the“hallmarks of genocide”.The bravery that the government has displayed on Israel has been, so far, sadly missing on Sudan. The UK has consistently failed to criticise the UAE, merely urging nameless “external actors” to stop“supplying, funding and fuelling the war”. Another coalition of the willing exists here, too, the E4+, which includes France, Germany and Norway. But they need to move beyond statements expressing “deep concern” if anything is going to change.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThese ad hoc alliances may not last. By next spring, Emmanuel Macron will no longer be in the Élysée palace, possibly replaced by a far-right president. Friedrich Merz is fighting for his political survival in Germany too, where again the biggest threat is a far-right party aligned with Trump. It is vital that Miliband makes use of these alliances while he can.Placing values at the heart of foreign policy is fraught with political risk. Within days of Cook’s speech in May 1997, it emerged that the UK was planning to sell more Hawk jets to an Indonesian regime that was attacking its own civilians in East Timor. “Ethical foreign policy” became a joke, rather than a doctrine.But it’s worth noting that Cook didn’t actually use the phrase he was credited with. Instead he said the UK’s foreign policy “must have an ethical dimension”, a caveat that showed an understanding that human rights cannot always trump realpolitik.During his four years in office, that ethical dimension could be seen in the banning of landmines, an annual human rights report and the Nato-led military action to stop ethnic cleansing in Kosovo.Miliband, too, is no wide-eyed idealist. There were those who would have wanted him to go further – for instance, by declaring that there has been a genocide inGaza. He has also come to the conclusion that however dangerous Trump is, the UK must be careful about how – and when – it stands up to him.But the past few days have shown that foreign policy with an ethical dimension is not only possible but can make a difference. There will be many people around the world, from Gaza to Darfur, who hope it continues.Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer and a previous winner of the Orwell prizeDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
