title: Woman Unknown wins Venice film festival as NAZA takes special jury prize | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: May el-Toukhy becomes eighth female director to take Golden Lion as Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love and Guardian-produced exposé of Israel’s Gaza killings also awarded
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: May el-Toukhy becomes eighth female director to take Golden Lion as Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love and Guardian-produced exposé of Israel’s Gaza killings also awarded
Content: Mathilde Arcel holds the Volpi Cup for best actress beside her Woman Unknown director, May el-Toukhy, who won the Golden Lion for best film.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersView image in fullscreenMathilde Arcel holds the Volpi Cup for best actress beside her Woman Unknown director, May el-Toukhy, who won the Golden Lion for best film.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersVenice film festivalWoman Unknown wins Venice film festival as NAZA takes special jury prizeMay el-Toukhy becomes eighth female director to take Golden Lion as Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love and Guardian-produced exposé of Israel’s Gaza killings also awardedBold and bravura choices as Venice celebrates A Woman Unknown, Possible Love – and NAZAPhilip OltermannEuropean culture editorSat 12 Sep 2026 17.17 EDTFirst published on Sat 12 Sep 2026 16.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMay el-Toukhy’s Woman Unknown has scooped the Golden Lion at theVenice film festival, at an awards ceremony that also saw the Gaza documentary NAZA win the jury prize.Set in the immediate aftermath of Danish liberation from Nazi occupation, the Egyptian-Danish director’s film tells the story of a young housemaid, Marie (Mathilde Arcel), who is about to marry her widowed employer but anxious about him discovering a shameful secret in her past: during the war, Marie had an intimate relationship with a German soldier.The Guardian’s film critic hailed Woman Unknown as“elegantly appointed” in his review, likening it to Alfred Hitchcock’s Rebecca.Arcel also won the festival’s best actress prize, the Volpi Cup, which puzzled some critics: usually,Venicedoesn’t award more than one prize to a film. Speaking to the press after the ceremony, the jury president, Maggie Gyllenhaal, said they were able to make an exception because the jury’s vote for the Danish actor was unanimous. “She is going to blow our socks off,” she said.View image in fullscreenMaggie Gyllenhaal (left), president of the 2026 Venice jury, and the festival’s president, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, hand the Golden Lion to May el-Toukhy.Photograph: Yara Nardi/ReutersIn an emotional acceptance speech, El-Toukhy thanked Gyllenhaal for addressing the underrepresentation of female film-makers at the start of the festival. Woman Unknown was the only film in competition to be solely directed by a woman.“This film has been incredibly challenging to make financially, logistically, emotionally,” El-Toukhy said. “And what kept me going was the urgent need to illuminate the unknown women of our common history, to make them known. And especially tonight, I feel like I succeeded in doing just that.”View image in fullscreenLee Chang-dong (right) is presented with the grand jury prize for Possible Love by veteran Hong Kong film-maker and jury member Johnnie To.Photograph: Scott A Garfitt/APThe runner-up grand jury prize went to the Korean directorLee Chang-dong’s Possible Love, a simmering tale of an unhappy married couple befriended by a documentary maker and her wealthy husband, which drew rave reviews.The special jury prize, Venice’s equivalent of a bronze medal, went toYuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary NAZA, about Israel’s AI-powered mass killing of civilians in Gaza.The film, which was produced by the Guardian, is based on testimony from24 Israeli military insiders who are interviewed anonymouslyat night on rooftops in Tel Aviv. It takes its title from an acronym used by the intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza.View image in fullscreenNAZA directors Rachel Szor, left, and Yuval Abraham with the special jury award.Photograph: Yara Nardi/Reuters“It’s honestly not very easy to stand here, thinking of all the Israeli politicians and journalists who are now attacking this film and denying it without even seeing it,” Abraham said when accepting his prize. “So much is being done not to look at reality.”The day after NAZA’s premiere, the Israeli military “categorically denied” the allegations made in the film.‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligenceRead moreThe Russian director Ilya Khrzhanovsky won the Silver Lion for best director forthe visually stunning DAU, a biopic of the Nobel prize-winning quantum physicist Lev Landau, who was pressured into working on the Soviet Union’s nuclear weapons programme.The inclusion of Khrzhanovsky’s film in the Venice lineup wascriticised by the Ukrainian governmentin the run-up to the festival, over its lead actor Teodor Currentzis’s refusal to condemn the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and for having received funding from a Russian businessman who was later sanctioned by the US and Ukraine.View image in fullscreenIlya Khrzhanovsky with his Silver Lion best director award for DAU.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersDAU was filmed in Kharkiv between 2008 and 2011, before the start of the conflict. At a press conference on the Lido, Khrzhanovsky said: “The only thing I can wish for is peace and success for the Ukrainian government to succeed in the best possible way, to save the country and to win this war.”John Malkovich took home the Volpi Cup for best actor, for his role as an erratic veteran CIA agent whose cancer diagnosis leads him to question the morality of his profession, inMartin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe 72-year-old US actor was not present in Venice and accepted his award via a video link. “I am humbled to be chosen for this award, which has been given to so many wonderful actors over the past 83 iterations of the Venice film festival,” Malkovich said.Full list of winnersGolden Lion for best film: Woman Unknown, directed by May el-ToukhyGrand jury prize: Possible Love, directed by Lee Chang-dongSilver Lion for best director: Ilya Khrzhanovsky for DAUSpecial jury prize: NAZA, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel SzorBest screenplay: Un bon petit soldat (A Good Little Soldier), Stéphane Brizé, Coralie Amédéo, Olivier GorceVolpi Cup for best actress: Mathilde Arcel in Woman UnknownVolpi Cup for best actor:John Malkovichin Wild Horse NineMarcello Mastroianni award for best young actor: Malou Khebizi in15/18 A Place to HealArmani Beauty audience award: Eu contez (I Matter), directed by Alina ȘerbanLuigi De Laurentiis award for debut film: La maison du vent (House of the Wind), directed by Auguste Bernard Kouemo YanghuExplore more on these topicsVenice film festivalGazaNAZAJohn MalkovichFestivalsWorld cinemaAwards and prizesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Naomi Klein: ‘Extreme wealth has a deranging effect. It turns you into a supremacist’ | Society books | The Guardian
description: She’s tackled neoliberalism and the digital world, now the writer and activist is taking on tech billionaires. She explains how the super-rich are capitalising on climate and financial chaos in pursuit of power
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: She’s tackled neoliberalism and the digital world, now the writer and activist is taking on tech billionaires. She explains how the super-rich are capitalising on climate and financial chaos in pursuit of power
Content: Naomi Klein.Photograph: Tanya GoehringView image in fullscreenNaomi Klein.Photograph: Tanya GoehringSociety booksInterviewNaomi Klein: ‘Extreme wealth has a deranging effect. It turns you into a supremacist’Zoe WilliamsShe’s tackled neoliberalism and the digital world, now the writer and activist is taking on tech billionaires. She explainshow the super-rich are capitalising on climate and financial chaos in pursuit of powerSat 12 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNaomi Klein’s new book starts on a mountaintop with two “faithful men gathering an audience to share their vision”. It’s a vision of a paradise city, gated at every entrance, no need for weapons there, everyone in it rich. One of the men has tears in his eyes as he describes its beauty. The opening scene of End Times Fascism, co-written with Astra Taylor, is not a metaphor, however. The men are Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. The year is 2026, the mountain is Davos. The paradise city will be calledNew Gaza.The World Economic Forum get-together inDavos, Switzerland, has always had a twin purpose – to provide a platform for the super-rich to describe all the good they are doing on poverty and climate, and to give us a glimpse into their enviable lives. This year what we witnessed was, quite brazenly, the world’s richest men gathering to discuss the real estate possibilities of a mass grave.At that same Davos, Donald Trump announced hisBoard of Peacefor the reconstruction of Gaza – it has delivered nothing substantial in the seven months since, but more significantly, Klein says, “we’re being hit with so many extraordinary events that it’s hard to hold on to what a big deal it is: they have announced a privatised United Nations”.“I think we understand that wealth compounds, right? Certainly rich people understand that wealth compounds,” Klein continues, speaking to me from her peaceful, roomy study in British Columbia. “But I don’t feel like we spend a lot of time really thinking about the implications of what it means for that much wealth to be compounded, and what that does psychologically. Part of the new shamelessness we’re seeing is just what happens when this amount of financial, mediagenic, technological and military weaponry is concentrated in the hands of this very small, unaccountable group of people. They stop trying to seduce us in any way.”Klein looks calm and curious as she delivers this message. She has a ready laugh. But then, she had the same unruffled, buoyant delivery when I interviewed her on stage in Manchester for Doppelgänger, her 2023 book in which she described how the digital world is destroying our connection to reality, and one another. In 1999, when her breakthrough work No Logo was published, she seemed exhilaratingly certain, at 29, that neoliberalism was bringing harm that we couldn’t yet even see the extent of, and nonetheless appeared centred and happy in the world. Somehow she manages to maintain this attitude, even though the news she delivers is always so convincingly, unbelievably bad.End Times Fascism describes the world we’re in, where the components of authoritarianism are modelled everywhere you look: anarcho-libertarian economics in Argentina, the destruction of a free press in Russia, the erosion of democratic institutions in Hungary (until Viktor Orbán was deposed), “anti-immigrant neofascism” in Italy, the weaponisation of trans identity by Jair Bolsonaro in Brazil, Islamophobia in Modi’s India. But this is fascism with a difference. Its proponents are actively willing an apocalypse, or a wave of interconnected apocalypses brought forth by climate change and financial chaos, to hasten us towards a post-democratic world in which only a rich few survive to prosper.double quotation markThese are trends I’ve been following for a long time, the privatised enclave born of shock, of disaster, I saw when I was reporting from IraqThis book started as anarticle in the Guardian, “which went totally viral,” Klein says. “Astra and I knew there was a lot more reporting to do, but on a personal level, did we want to spend the next year in the minds of these people, in these cultures? Then Astra said, ‘I’m down the rabbit hole, I’m gonna be listening to these guys anyway. So I may as well feel like I’m doing something about it.’ This is the reason it’s the first book I’ve co-written. When you go to dark, scary places, it’s nice to bring a friend.” Astra Taylor is also a writer, activist and documentary maker, and founded theDebt Collective, a fascinating experiment in building structured, quasi-unionised solidarity around personal debt, with the long term goals of abolishing student tuition fees, nationalising healthcare and building tenant power.In the book, Klein and Taylor introduce us to the religious fundamentalists, Christian Zionists and Christian Nationalists in the US, readying themselves for the second coming. Describing a “bunkered state”, the authors connect climate-related disasters, a rabid anti-immigrant standing army in the form of ICE and a politics built on false promises and misinformation to depict a febrile, riven society that doesn’t know what to believe. But the truly terrifying bit is the bridging section, on tech billionaires. The super-rich have apocalypse fantasies of their own, built not on faith or ideology but on a calm and rational evaluation of how best to maintain their position; they would genuinely rather reign in hell than share in heaven. And they have all the money to make sure they get there.“These are trends I’ve been following for a long time,” Klein says. “The privatised enclave born of shock, of disaster, I saw when I was reporting from Iraq. There’s the image of the Green Zone, this Emerald City run by the US in the middle of Baghdad, built by Halliburton and all of these private contractors, with the power to appoint a viceroy. In the final parts of The Shock Doctrine [2007], I talk about how these contractors migrated [from Iraq] to Hurricane Katrina, and the idea that these climate disasters are their next growth frontier. Reporters started calling New Orleans ‘Baghdad on the Bayou’. The gang’s all here, there’s Halliburton, there’s Bechtel, there’s Blackwater.”But, and she cannot stress this enough, as useful as it is to know the recent history of these trends, you should not take comfort from the idea that you’ve seen it all before. “I have found the image of a spiral really useful, in terms of how to make sense of the fact that our era is both familiar and different,” Klein says. “The thing about a spiral is that you’re going round, but you’re not going to the same place. If the spiral is pointing down, it’s deeper, it’s tighter, it’s carrying more velocity, it’s carrying more force, it’s carrying more heat, it’s carrying more violence.” The image is at once poetic and extremely sobering. She proffers a brief morale boost, like someone handing you a slice of orange on your way into a war zone. “You can flip a spiral – it goes outwards, it’s the spiral of the universe.”At the moment we’re in now, when crises and disasters hit so frequently that we’re in a constant state of disorientation and shock, the status quo isn’t static, it’s always getting worse. “There’s this impulse to read history,” Klein says. “We’ve seen it again and again. After 9/11, people were suddenly reading history books about Afghanistan and Iraq, Chomsky, trying to find their bearings. We saw it again during the pandemic, people were reading about the plagues of the past. But there’s a trap in believing that everything has happened before, that there is not a compounding effect of history. After Donald Trump was re-elected, I’ll be honest with you, Shock Doctrine sales went crazy. People were saying, ‘It’s exactly like you said,’ and I was thinking, ‘I don’t think it is’.”double quotation markMusk’s satellites  are crawling through the sky, and he wants more. Who said he could? Who gave him that right?’The neoliberal age – for brevity let’s call it the period between the end of the cold war and Covid – was “capitalism lying on the couch in its underwear, going ‘what are you gonna do, leave me?’ In the cold war, a little competition went a long way – after the collapse of the Soviet Union, that competition is lost, capitalism stopped trying.” But there was a vulnerability to being super-rich in those days, because whether you’d come by your wealth through privatisation politics in the US or Europe, or by hastier, more kleptocratic means in ex-communist states, it was plainly public wealth that you’d captured. “So they would stage these seduction rituals, whether it was at Davos or Aspen, or atTed, or theClinton Global Initiative. They’d say, ‘We are going to cure the sick, and we are going to fund your schools in this new and exciting way, don’t worry about us. Don’t be afraid of our wealth. This is actually a new way of redistributing for the public good.’”I distinctly remember that world: huge conferences like the Skoll foundation awards, where journalists would be wined and dined while watching immensely rich people hand out £20,000 prizes to grassroots clean water initiatives in Kenya. To be fair, in the era before and directly after the financial crash, there were plenty of dissenting voices about capitalist benevolence solving intractable problems like inequality. Many people, Klein at their vanguard, pointed out that it smelled like a scam. But while we were having that discussion, the wealth agenda moved on.In the run-up to the 2024 presidential election, at the Faena Hotel in Miami, Peter Thiel hosted panel discussions titled “the enemy”, naming sustainable development goals, “precautionary principles” and “social responsibility” as those foes, rounded off with an “apocalypse ball”-themed fancy dress party . Some of the costumes, Klein and Taylor write, were “a doctor of eugenics’’; a “Haitian chef with a bloodied cat toy hanging out of his apron [a reference to the Springfield immigrant pet‑eating hoax, which spread in 2024, repeated by both Trump and JD Vance]; a couple wearing pagers as a ha-ha reference to Israel’s murderous attack in Lebanon.”View image in fullscreenNaomi Klein and Astra Taylor.Photograph: naomiklein.substack.comThiel has been explicitly anti-democracy for years, writing in 2009, “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.” But other tech billionaires have had a complete volte face. “Jeff Bezos renamed a stadium in Seattle the Climate Pledge Arena, and gave out Earth prizes,” Klein points out. Elon Musk invested in electric cars and once saw himself as a saviour figure. “Any time anyone was in trouble, Musk would rush in to save them, ‘I shall save Puerto Rico’, ‘I shall save the children stuck down the mine’. It’s fun to be a superhero, right? But if you’re going to be a superhero, you should be worshipped. And people stopped worshiping them.” Now, the climate pledges are gone, replaced by a performed nihilism around averting climate crisis, coupled with a determination to build ever more data centres. “We’re not dealing with stupid people who don’t understand climate change,” Klein says. “We’re dealing with people who know very clearly what it means to wire together35 gas turbines in Memphis.” (It means gargantuan energy and water use, as well as the destruction of air and sound quality in the vicinity, all for Musk to power Grok, hisintermittently Nazi large language model.)The speed with which previously Democrat-leaning billionaires fell in behind Trump in 2024 was jaw-dropping. “I don’t think that Mark Zuckerberg’s phase of seeming to care deeply about democracy and climate change was real,” Klein says. “He reincarnates as whatever is good for his business. Figures like Thiel and Musk, where there is real ideology there, are easier to understand than figures like Bezos and Zuckerberg, where it really does feel like there’s notherethere, they’re just uninteresting guys that ended up massively rich.” She’s passingly interested in what combination of events created these men, many of whom were forged in the dotcom boom, when they were worshipped as gods, pictured on the cover of Time magazine in gold thrones. There’s an element of ego rage, that we just aren’t grateful enough. Ultimately, though, “we end the book concluding that wealth has its own deranging effects. It almost inevitably turns you into a supremacist because humans are creatures of story and you need a story to rationalise, why you? Why do you have so much in a time of so much want and need? And the only possible story that’s available is that there’s something about you that justifies it.”There’s a new goading quality to the talking points of the super-rich – explicit eugenicism and Islamophobia, raw delight in the prospect of AI wiping out our jobs. It almost feels as though they’re daring us to rebel, just so that they can prove that rebellion is fruitless.On that, though, Klein would disagree. It is not beyond our collective means to build a wealth disarmament movement, or a tech disarmament movement. She points to the Pearson brothers, KeShaun and Justin, fighting Musk’s Colossus 2 data centre in Memphis: “the way they so consciously root their struggle in the history of the civil rights movement, and the environmental justice movement in Memphis, going back to the formerly enslaved people who built Boxtown. This is where MLK was murdered, assassinated after marching with the sanitation workers in Memphis.” KeShaun Pearson leads Memphis Community Against Pollution, which has had major wins against oil pipelines, the industrial release of carcinogenic chemicals, and is now mobilising against data centres. Justin is running for Congress.In End Times Fascism, Klein and Taylor raise Walter Benjamin’s concept “jetztzeit”, literally “now time”, a moment so pregnant with the spirit, the urgency of revolution that it marshals the energy of all movements that went before it. Again, it’s poetic, but it’s also literal, observable. If we want to oppose this new fascist strain, we really have to get a move on. “I don’t tend to use this language, I try to be measured, but I think I’ve earned the right to escalate,” she says. “The moment we’re in, people are really mad and however mad you are, it’s not enough. Because there is something so profound about no longer believing in the future, about seeing no value in our shared home, in the natural world. They’re traitors to creation.”Klein doesn’t want for reasons to fight. “I’ve made a choice to live very close to nature in a pretty wild part of British Columbia,” she says. “On a dark night, it’s a blanket of stars. And now we see so many of what I call Elon’s space bugs [Starlink satellites] just crawling through the sky. He wants to increase that a hundredfold. Who said he could? Who gave him that right? That’s a place where I find my anger. I get really angry about the stars. I get really angry about the orcas. I get really angry about Gaza. Other people will find their anger somewhere else. We have to find our places of deepest love and fight like hell.”End Times Fascism by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor is published by Allen Lane on15 September.To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: Apocalypse: this end-of-days survival show is an absolute slam dunk  | Television | The Guardian
description: Geeks, toffs and biceps go to war in a wild survival experiment that answers that eternal question: if society collapsed, could you cope? This is going to be huge!
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: Geeks, toffs and biceps go to war in a wild survival experiment that answers that eternal question: if society collapsed, could you cope? This is going to be huge!
Content: Bertie looking at Scott in Apocalypse.Photograph: channel 4View image in fullscreenBertie looking at Scott in Apocalypse.Photograph: channel 4The watcherTelevisionApocalypse: this end-of-days survival show is an absolute slam dunkGeeks, toffs and biceps go to war in a wild survival experiment that answers that eternal question: if society collapsed, could you cope? This is going to be huge!Rhik SamadderSat 12 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHave you ever wondered how Cormac McCarthy’s wasteland novelThe Roadcould be made into a reality show? No? Well someone who works in TV has, so here we are. Who knows if they experienced a follow-up thought: that the instinct to package the end of the world as entertainment might be the most dystopian aspect of the whole enterprise, but hey. Apocalypse (Sunday 13 September, 9pm, Channel 4) launches this week, and people are buzzing!It’s a slam dunk for a show, because we’ve all run the thought experiment. If society collapsed, how would you get food and find shelter? Would you hunker down or forge alliances? To what depravities might you stoop without the rule of law? Apocalypse puts this empty talk to the test. Seven strangers are dropped at the edge of an abandoned town. They have no access to phones, light, electricity or infrastructure. They do have access to boarded-up supermarkets, desolate buildings, broken vehicles. How soon until they eat each other?I’d have loved to see this done with ordinary Joes off the street, like the first series of Big Brother. But we live in a different time, and so each of the volunteers is a “type”. There is inevitably a content creator, a Paralympian, a theatre director and an event emcee, who sounds plummier than nana’s crumble. There is useful testosterone to be found in the form of a diesel mechanic, and a square-bodied Australian hunter with a Crocodile Dundee accent thicker than his biceps. (I think he’s a cattle farmer, though it’s possible he works in Kettle Pharma.)Naturally, tensions spill over. When the team find live chickens near an abandoned trailer and a can of Spam, they become hysterical with joy. Crocodile Dundee, despairing of their sweetshop mentality, rations everyone to a quarter of a tomato a day. The geeks start muttering about a revolt. Starving and fractious, one positive is at least they’re not alone. On the downside, they’re not alone. Within hours of the contestants realising they are not the only team in the town, tribalism starts to do its thing.When the Spam is stolen, a full-scale battle is declared, and teams tool up with baseball bats. Resource scarcity does this. Some contestants go three or four days without eating. Even before things get that bad, anxiety is abnormally high. “It’s been 45 minutes, and tanks are running low,” gasps Kiera, a psychologist and self-identified princess. She is attempting to prise the boards off a food mart within one hour of arriving in the town, and I’ve never related to anything harder.The showHuntedhad us all imagining how we would go on the lam, evading the attention of the surveillance state. Apocalypse picks up the baton, imagining a world with no state whatsoever. It’s an omnipresent dread, thanks to climate crisis, global instability and AI-induced job despair. There have been countless wilderness survival shows, but none in an urban setting. This feels close to home.Here’s my hot take: I reckon most people think that when the apocalypse comes, they will secretly be good at it. They imagine finding high ground, teaming up with a doctor, foraging nuts from Tesco. Maybe they’ll repopulate the Earth with Dannii Minogue or something. Pure fantasy. As one mate cruelly framed my chances: “Your glasses will break on the first day, and then you’ll be screwed.” Joke’s on him; I never thought I’d be good. I panic when my phone drops to 4G. If the end of days comes, I will simply vomit and turn to the wall, well before my spectacles betray me.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionApocalypse will probably be huge. I found watching it depressing, because the mirror it holds up is not a flattering one. Loudmouths take charge, people steal and lie, dehumanise each other, thirst for violence. I’m sure the production has guardrails against how far they’ll go, and what they’ll show – I know the chickens’ chances don’t look good – but that’s not even the point. It’s a bleak view of us, the only certainty being that human nature will out. Maybe we’re all selfish when we’re lying in a hole in the ground. Cormac McCarthy would dig it.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe watcherReality TVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I love a bit of mischief!’ Liza Tarbuck on why she’s swapping her Radio 2 mic for a potter’s wheel | Television | The Guardian
description: Her riotous weekly show had an army of devoted fans. Now Tarbuck has joined the ranks of star presenters leaving the BBC – and she’s getting her hands dirty
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: Her riotous weekly show had an army of devoted fans. Now Tarbuck has joined the ranks of star presenters leaving the BBC – and she’s getting her hands dirty
Content: ‘It’s the stuff of dreams!’ Liza Tarbuck doing her Radio 2 show.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreen‘It’s the stuff of dreams!’ Liza Tarbuck doing her Radio 2 show.Photograph: BBCTelevisionInterview‘I love a bit of mischief!’ Liza Tarbuck on why she’s swapping her Radio 2 mic for a potter’s wheelMichael HoganHer riotous weekly show had an army of devoted fans. Now Tarbuck has joined the ranks of star presenters leaving the BBC – and she’s getting her hands dirtySat 12 Sep 2026 04.22 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 16.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAtragedy. A national disaster. A loss to the cultural landscape that should be discussed in parliament. These were just a few listener reactions when Liza Tarbuck left herRadio 2show earlier this year. “I was bereft about it, too,” sighs Tarbuck. “I miss angsting over the playlist. I miss the texts and emails. For two hours every weekend, we were a proper gang.”Tarbuck hosted her Saturday evening show for 14 years, building it into the funniest show on British radio. Her riotous mix of freewheeling chat and hand-picked tunes (the music could span nine decadesin the same show) drew an audience of 2 million, and received more messages from listeners – 50 per minute – than any other programme on the station.Allow TikTok content?This article includes content provided byTikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueIt became a cult phenomenon thanks to its running jokes, hilarious crowd-sourced stories and Tarbuck’s anarchic links to the 7pm news bulletin (“Smell that fromage! We interrupt this fun to bring you some miserable news”). “I love a bit of mischief,” she chuckles. “It’s like nectar to me.”She called it “by appointment radio” and it was, attracting a loyal fanbase – including many fellow broadcasters. Regular listeners were dubbed “the hivemind” or “the murmuration”.The final edition aired in January but her departure wasn’t confirmed until March, when Tarbuck posted a heartfelt, hand-written farewell message on Instagram. “I think you’ve guessed,” she wrote. “Some fool left a door open and I sneaked out. A French exit. Together we made two hours of radio feel like a private members’ club. That’s the stuff of dreams. Thank you for letting me in, it’s been a privilege.” Many devotees were distraught. They still take to social media each Saturday to compare it to missing a friend.View image in fullscreenTarbuck as Siobhan in The Change.Photograph: Channel 4Mystery swirled around her departure. Over a video call overlooking her verdant London garden (“My top tip is pots with drip trays”), Tarbuck cheerfully shrugs this off. “Lots of people, very kindly, thought I was ill or my parents were ill, but that wasn’t the case,” she says. “I was at Radio 2 on and off for 36 years in total. I realised it was time to go. The messages I received were deeply moving.”She joined a talent exodus from the station in recent years, following the likes of Ken Bruce, Zoe Ball and Simon Mayo, as well as the late Paul O’Grady, out of the Broadcasting House door. “The talent leaving Radio 2 tells its own story,” she says. “It’s no wonder people get upset by it. Listeners have allowed us into their home, which is a precious thing and should never be taken for granted. That’s why the audience take it personally.”She laments the loss of such stalwart names and maverick talents. “TheBBCneeds high standards and a certain level of curation because it’s a world leader. Ever since we were all sat in front of Bill & Ben or Blue Peter, it was the place to be. But you can’t live off that reputation for ever. You have to keep it being the place to be. You do that by pushing the boundaries and not worrying about what commercial radio is doing. Let them do it. It doesn’t matter.”Fans retain hope for a triumphant return to the airwaves. “Maybe there will be a comeback in some form,” she says. “I genuinely don’t know. I couldn’t do a show that didn’t have music flowing through it, and the difficulty is how to pay the artists. But I’m figuring that out.” So the murmuration should keep the faith? “Always. We’re all still out here, flying in some line of formation.”View image in fullscreenTarbuck (right) with Emma Wray in Watching.Photograph: Cinematic/AlamyThe 61-year-old actor and broadcaster – daughter of comedian Jimmy – has enjoyed an eccentrically eclectic career. After making her name in long-running ITV sitcom Watching, she took the lead in Linda Green, Paul Abbott’s BBC comedy-drama. More recently, she appeared inBridget Christie’s menopause comedy The Change and played Anne Hathaway in Ben Elton’s Shakespeare sitcom Upstart Crow.She has presented everything from The Big Breakfast to Britain’s Top Dog. Tarbuck even won Taskmaster while wearing asurprisingly convincing false beard. “It was eight years ago but people still stop me to talk about the beard and the BMXing,” she laughs.Now she is returning to TV to present The Great Celebrity Pottery Throw Down. This fresh twist on Channel 4’s ceramic contest sees six celebrities roll up their sleeves, brave the wheel and battle the clay. Across five weeks, the contestants – comedians Lucy Beaumont, Richard Herring and Fatiha El-Ghorri, former footballer Paul Merson, actor Layton Williams and presenter Denise van Outen – make everything from raku animals to garden gnomes.View image in fullscreen‘It’s inspiring!’ … Tarbuck with judges Keith Brymer Jones and Rich Miller on The Great Celebrity Pottery Throw Down.Photograph: Patch Dolan/Channel 4In the process, they blossom under the expert eye of judges Keith Brymer Jones and Rich Miller. “Keith is fabulous,” says Tarbuck fondly. “A really good laugh. But trust me, Rich is the one slyly holding it all together. They’re both open-hearted and emotionally intelligent, which is a lovely quality in men of a certain age. That makes it a safe space and brings people’s barriers down. Celebrities aside – what a horrible label – they’re just humans. Keith said to me early on: ‘Just watch the clay work as therapy,’ and it really did.”El-Ghorri makes a cathartic cancer confession. Beaumont and Williams find pottery helps with their recent ADHD diagnoses. Merson plans to continue the hobby beyond the series because it helps him stay in the moment – which he needs as a recovering addict. He believes ceramics classes should be offered in rehab. “Mr Merson’s got a great slant on things,” says Tarbuck. “He’s a blokey bloke but he’s done so much work on himself. He’s great company and very intelligent. Although he’d hate me saying that.”Her favourite contestant, however, was Beaumont. “I just love Lucy, she’s so ‘other’,” laughs Tarbuck. “She has an unbelievable brain, but bless her, she had a nightmare. Every time she emerged from the drying room, her hair would be full of fine clay dust. She was furious but in a hilarious way.”There’s a dramatic droppage (“I was terrified that I’d break something but thankfully it wasn’t me”) and some trademark blubbing from Brymer Jones. “‘Keith the Weep’ set me off once,” admits Tarbuck. “Somebody really needed praise at that time and, seeing how it was received, that’s what made me go. It was tangibly moving.”Over the heartwarming series, these rookie potters display real progression. “Growth definitely happens,” nods Tarbuck. “It’s inspiring TV. I enjoy [sister show] The Great British Sewing Bee because I leave that programme thinking I can make a jacket. I have a go and end up with a wrap skirt. That’s happened three times.”She’s more of a ceramic collector than a maker herself, Tarbuck confesses, but she relishes crafting. “I’m quite handy. I paint. I garden. I’m into beading and mosaic. I think it comes from having an airy-fairy job where there’s nothing tangible at the end. As an antidote to acting and presenting, you make something you can put your hands on and go: ‘Look what I did today!’ It helps me stay sane and grounded.”It’s a treat to have Tarbuck back on our screens and she’s quietly plotting more projects. “I’ve got a good idea for a Time Team type of show. Roaming the British isles, having a dig around. History is entrancing. You’ve got to keep the creative possibilities bubbling. I do something nice and mundane like walking the dog [she has a Portuguese podengo called Ringo] and all sorts of ideas start percolating. All I can do is keep pushing them out there and some will stick.”Meanwhile, the murmuration should watch this space. “I’m interested in the immediacy of YouTube,” she says. “I don’t know much about Patreon but I’m assured that would be a good platform if I were to do a radio show. But it’s not just about radio – it’s about variety. You can sit and wait for an acting job to come in, but I don’t know how much good that does you. Sometimes you have to branch out and be brave. Why limit yourself?”The Great Celebrity Pottery Throw Down starts on 13 September on Channel 4Explore more on these topicsTelevisionRadio 2Channel 4The Great Pottery Throw DownBBCTelevision industryRadio industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From Practical Magic 2 to Saturday Night Live UK: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead | Culture | The Guardian
description: Bullock and Kidman try to put a second spell on you in the fantasy comedy sequel, while the topical sketch show returns after a well-regarded debut
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Bullock and Kidman try to put a second spell on you in the fantasy comedy sequel, while the topical sketch show returns after a well-regarded debut
Content: Every witch way … Nicole Kidman as Gillian Owens in Practical Magic 2.Photograph: Jaap Buitendijk/© 2026 Warner Bros. Ent. All Rights ReservedView image in fullscreenEvery witch way … Nicole Kidman as Gillian Owens in Practical Magic 2.Photograph: Jaap Buitendijk/© 2026 Warner Bros. Ent. All Rights ReservedGoing out, staying inCultureFrom Practical Magic 2 to Saturday Night Live UK: your complete entertainment guide to the week aheadBullock and Kidman try to put a second spell on you in the fantasy comedy sequel, while the topical sketch show returns after a well-regarded debutSat 12 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleContents1Going out: Cinema2Going out: Gigs3Going out: Art4Going out: Stage5Staying in: Streaming6Staying in: Games7Staying in: Albums8Staying in: Brain foodView image in fullscreenGoing out:CinemaPractical Magic 2Out nowThe beloved fantasy romance from the 1990s returns with Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman reprising their roles as the Owens sisters. The story picks up 25 years later, with more family secrets and curses in the offing, plus a trip to the UK. Sure to be spellbinding stuff.Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore?Out 18 September for one night onlyCaptured during their 2025 tour, this music documentary blends footage from the live shows with archive material and new narration from Jarvis Cocker, to trace the band’s rise from outsider status in Sheffield to global fame, via megahits such as Common People and lesser-known fan favourites. Directed by Garth Jennings.PressureOut nowAndrew Scott heads up an all-star cast in a drama exploring the second world war from a slightly quirky angle: the weather forecast. Don’t laugh: it was a crucial piece of the puzzle in the 72 hours leading up to D-day, with Britain’s chief meteorological officer James Stagg unexpectedly finding himself the man of the moment.Everybody Digs Bill EvansOut nowA winner at the Berlin festival, Grant Gee’s biopic explores the aftermath of the death of bass player Scott LaFaro, and the impact the tragedy has on jazz pianist Bill Evans, who is torn between New York and suburbia as he attempts to navigate his profound grief. Starring Anders Danielsen Lie, Bill Pullman and Laurie Metcalf.Catherine BrayGoing out:GigsView image in fullscreenLast days of disco … Saint Etienne call it quits.Saint EtienneBirmingham,12 September; Manchester,15 September; Bristol,16 September; London,18 September; tour continues to 26 SeptemberThe beloved indie dance-pop trio head out on their final tour after more than 30 years. So expect songs such as the bangersome Glad from last year’s album International to rub shoulders with their 90s classics.Michael CraggCBSO/YamadaSymphony Hall, Birmingham,17 SeptemberThe dynamic Japanese conductor has embarked on one of classical music’s great endurance tests: a complete cycle of Gustav Mahler’s symphonies. Symphony No 2 promises to be a truly monumental season-opener – and also marks the CBSO Chorus’s 1,000th performance.Flora WillsonChris CheekLondon,15 September; Leeds,16 September; Aberdeen,17 September; Cambridge,18 SeptemberThe album Dear Paul by this versatile saxophonist was dedicated to Paul Motian, his old employer and one of jazz’s most creative percussionists. These gigs with fine Swiss drummer Florian Arbenz, a true Motian inheritor, will confirm just why.John FordhamWu LyfDublin,15 September; London,17 September; Brighton,18 SeptemberReleased in April, A Wave That Will Never Break marked the return of the enigmatic Manchester experimentalists after their 2012 split. It luxuriates in what they call “heavy pop” so remember your earplugs.MCGoing out:ArtView image in fullscreenIt’s grate … a work by Laura Porter from her exhibition Holding.Photograph: Courtesy of Laura PorterLaura PorterIrving Gallery, Oxford,to 10 OctoberThis north Devon-based artist is seriously into recycling, taking discarded old clothes, breaking them down and turning them into a mouldable, papier mache-style pulp and twisting them into wobbly geometric shapes.Liz LarnerCamdenArtCentre, London,to 17 JanuaryIt’s the debut UK institutional show by this influential American sculptor and ceramicist, filled with rocky, prehistoric-looking references to cosmic matter, ancient mythology and the grizzly politics of resource extraction.Gabriel OrozcoWhite Cube Bermondsey, London,16 Septemberto 8 NovemberMexico’s leading conceptualist returns to London for another show of minimal, ephemeral geometric installation work, this time dealing with the idea that objects can act as historical records.Celebrating Julia Carter Preston, CeramicistVarious venues, Liverpool,to 28 FebruaryLiverpool is rolling out the red carpet for home-town ceramics hero Julia Carter Preston (1926-2012) with five galleries across the city hosting displays of her work at the same time, including shows at the Bluecoat and Walker Art Gallery.Eddy FrankelGoing out:StageView image in fullscreenGeneration gain … Phil Wang.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianPhil WangStockton,12 September; Leeds,13 September; Tunbridge Wells,16 September; Northampton,17 September; Guildford,18 September; touring to 23 MayThanks to hit podcasts, presenting gigs and film cameos, a small cohort of millennial standups have finally ascended to the mainstream comedy firmament. Foremost among them is 36-year-old Wang, who returns to muse on ageing and his generation in new show Uh Oh.Rachel AroestiJasmin Vardimon: LullabyJV Home, Ashford,18& 19 September; touring to 13 FebruaryThe work that got choreographer Jasmin Vardimon noticed 23 years ago was a dance-theatre piece called Lullaby, set on a hospital ward. Two decades later, she’s revisiting and reinventing it for today’s world.Lyndsey WinshipGolden BoyAlmeida theatre, London, to 31 OctoberDirector Sam Yates has assembled a knockout cast for his revival of Clifford Odets’s classic American play. Josh O’Connor stars as a gifted violinist, drawn into the brutal world of professional boxing in depression-era New York.Miriam GillinsonTill The Stars Come DownNottingham Playhouse, to 26 SeptemberBeth Steel’s heartfelt and exquisitely observed comedy was an Olivier-nominated smash in the West End. It’s set in Mansfield, where a family gather for a wedding.MGskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStaying in:StreamingView image in fullscreenSure shot … Maria Sten in Neagley.Photograph: Amazon Prime VideoNeagleyPrime Video,16 SeptemberThe Alan Ritchson-led TV adaptation of Lee Child’s Jack Reacher novels has been a huge hit with critics and viewers, making a spin-off a no-brainer. This new series revolves around Maria Sten’s titular protege and private investigator.Saturday Night Live UKSky One & Now,12 September, 10pmA new prime minister means plenty of fresh material for the British iteration of the US sketch behemoth, but let’s hope the show doesn’t change too drastically: series one’s subtle edginess and stubborn idiosyncrasy was a recipe for surprising, naysayer-silencing success.ApocalypseChannel 4,13 September, 9pmChannel 4 be Channel 4-ing with its latest discomfiting social experiment. A group of civilians are left in an abandoned town to test how they cope with the kind of end-of-civilisation situation (no running water, no heating, no electricity) that could in reality be merely a couple of cyber-attacks away.Monster: The Lizzie Borden StoryNetflix,17 SeptemberRyan Murphy and Ian Brennan’s queasily contentious anthology series has previously dramatised the lives of some of America’s most notorious killers. This time round, however, the focus is on a more ambiguous figure in Borden, who was ultimately acquitted of the 1892 murders of her father and stepmother.RAStaying in:GamesView image in fullscreenSlash and burn … Wolverine.Illustration: Sony Interactive EntertainmentMarvel’s WolverinePS5;out15 SeptemberThe creators of the brilliant Marvel’s Spider-Man games take on an altogether more brutal hero in this pummelling slash-’em-up. Evil billionaire Bolivar Trask is kidnapping mutants and only you and your claws can stop him.Fire Emblem: Fortune’s WeaveNintendo Switch 2;out17 SeptemberIn the vast, fantastical Dagdan empire, warriors gather to fight in a tournament where the winner is granted one wish – but dark forces are gathering on the horizon and the fate of young contender Cai is in your hands. Expect an epic narrative adventure with fiendish tactical combat.Keith StuartStaying in:AlbumsView image in fullscreenA certain romance … Bloc Party.Photograph: Charlie PryorBloc Party – Anatomy of a Brief RomanceOut nowFollowing a further lineup reshuffle in 2023 – new bassist Harry Deacon makes his debut here – art-rockers Bloc Party return with their seventh album. Produced by Trevor Horn, songs such as Love Bombs and Coming on Strong are full of frontman Kele Okereke’s tightly wound energy.This Is Lorelei – The Singer in My BandOut nowAs one half of art-rock misfits Water from Your Eyes, Nate Amos, AKA This Is Lorelei, often deals in shape-shifting abstraction. On The Singer in My Band, however, he swaps that for twangy guitar riffs, crumpled Elliott Smith-esque singalongs and a surprising amount of sunshine.Standing on the Corner – IIOut nowFormed in Brooklyn more than a decade ago, Standing on the Corner, who have previously worked with Solange, are a multidisciplinary collective led by Gio Escobar. On the frazzled II they blend psychedelia, rock, no-wave rap, R&B and post-hardcore into a heavy sonic soup.Sylvan Esso – Ow ∞Out nowHaving built their own studio, the American electropop duo of Amelia Randall Meath and Nick Sanborn set about improvising, writing five to 10 songs a day. The result is this obscurely titled fifth album, which features the pogoing Hot Slob and the blown-out bop Sledge.MCStaying in:Brain foodView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Bob HolmesAcross the HorizonPodcastMusician Bob Holmes hosts this soothing series analysing the world of ambient country music. He and his guests, including guitarist Hayden Pedigo, discuss how Americana can conjure imaginative worlds.RobWordsYouTubeYouTuber and linguist RobWords produces fascinating video essays on the many quirks of the English language. Highlights include the hidden logic behind typographical symbols, the literal meanings of body parts and sarcastic punctuation.People Fixing the World: The Pictures That Help and HealBBC World Service,15 September, 8.06amJournalist Myra Anubi’s documentary on the creatives producing visual aids for disabled people is a hopeful insight into how technology can be harnessed for good. She hears from one app user who believes they saved his life.Ammar KaliaExplore more on these topicsCultureGoing out, staying inDanceTheatreTelevisionArtGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

Young album, but a late-period Neil Young album nonetheless.”Alexis PetridisRead the full reviewPick of the restHaruomi Hosono: Yours SincerelyGhostly International; out nowView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Ghostly International/PASummed up in a sentenceCreative and captivating, the septuagenarian beloved by Harry Styles brings a hint of mischief to his innocently charming songs.What our reviewer said“His 23rd solo album is wilful, playful, unpredictable and utterly beguiling. Rooted in the Japanese concept of omoiyari, roughly translated as compassion, these songs are big-hearted, focusing on warmth and positivity.”Stevie ChickRead the full reviewGretchen Parlato: The Wise OnesEdition; out nowSummed up in a sentenceWith guests including Robert Glasper, Parlato turns her immaculate phrasing to soft funk, dancefloor numbers and interpretations of Stevie Wonder and Tears for Fears.What our reviewer said“Perhaps aimed at a wider marketplace than its more improvisational and intimate predecessors Flor and Lean In, and not without a humdrum moment or two, The Wise Ones nonetheless confirms that Parlato’s inimitable character never lets her slip into the generic.”John FordhamRead the full reviewLucas Debargue: Gershwin VariationsSony; out nowSummed up in a sentenceAlongside supple and distinctive accounts of Rhapsody in Blue and the Piano Concerto and Preludes, the French pianist showcases his jazz chops in reinterpretations of Gershwin’s timeless songs.What our reviewer said“His 12 virtuoso etudes on Gershwin songs, impeccable compositions in their own right, view familiar tunes through unfamiliar lenses. Embraceable You, for example, is reinvented as a sultry rumba, while Fascinating Rhythm is a cheeky Parisian waltz.”Clive PagetRead the full reviewNow touring …Angine de PoitrineLe Poisson Rouge, New York; touring nowView image in fullscreenAngine de Poitrine.Photograph: José Sena Goulão/EPASummed up in a sentenceThe brilliantly strange experimental band’s live show is a must-see spectacle powered by glorious noise and wild flair.What our reviewer said“The songs had not especially changed from how they sound on their albums and in studios. The ability to finally see the duo’s superb musicianship up close carried the show – as did the reminders that they are still human.”Alexander AbnosRead the full reviewFurther reading‘We’re not Lady Gaga and Elton John’: unmasking Angine de Poitrine, the year’s buzziest, dottiest bandExplore more on these topicsCultureThe week in reviewsTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guide #260: From Oasis to K-pop, music is going mad for the big-screen documentary | Culture | The Guardian
description: A new wave of concert films and career retrospectives is drawing fans to cinemas – but why now?
Author: Gwilym Mumford
Headline: A new wave of concert films and career retrospectives is drawing fans to cinemas – but why now?
Content: Stirring … Liam (left) and Noel Gallagher in Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger.Photograph: Simon EmmettView image in fullscreenStirring … Liam (left) and Noel Gallagher in Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger.Photograph: Simon EmmettThe Guide newsletterCultureThe Guide #260: From Oasis to K-pop, music is going mad for the big-screen documentaryA new wave of concert films and career retrospectives is drawing fans to cinemas – but why now?Don’t get The Guide delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereGwilym MumfordSat 12 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a moment towards the end ofDon’t Look Back in Anger, the newly released documentary capturing Oasis’s 2025 reunion tour, that helps explain why those planet-conquering gigs happened in the first place. Liam and Noel Gallagher are sitting down together for the rarest of paired interviews – the first since the 2009 scrap that broke up the band and created such a huge appetite for their return. Had Oasis’s story ended with that backstage fight in Paris, both Gallaghers note, their legacy would have been one of astonishing success curtailed by “chaos”. Instead, those reunion gigs, as well as proving wildly lucrative, have allowed them to add a triumphant coda to that messy ending. “It feels like a weight has been lifted,” a surprisingly contemplative Liam says.That maybe makes Don’t Look Back in Anger sound more navel-gazing than this entertaining and often very funny film is – as you might expect of any doc that features a sweary rumination from Noel on Liam’s ability to balance a tambourine on his head (“If I did that I’d look an utter cunt, but somehow he does it and it’s the greatest thing I’ve ever seen”). Still, for all the droll quippery and bucket-hatted euphoria, there is something poignant and self-reflective at the film’s heart: hatchets are buried, departed friends are toasted and legacies are contemplated. What you leave behind was clearly on the minds of the brothers Gallagher throughout the tour and film.And there’s no better way of shoring up your legacy, if you’re a musician or band tiptoeing toward heritage status, than having a documentary made about you. As last year’s record-breakingBecoming Led Zeppelinproved, these are platinum-status times for the music doc and its close cousin the concert film (Don’t Look Back in Anger, with its extensive use of archive footage, is a mix of both). Go to the cinema most weeks and there will be at least one screening – by my count there have been more than 30 this year alone, ranging from gleaming high-definition gigs by K-pop superstars you’ve only just heard of (Enhypen, Stray Kids, Ateez), to archive-rich career retrospectives of acts entering their autumn years (from Megadeth toJames) and immaculate restorations of fuzzily remembered gigs from artists no longer with us (Soul to Soul,EPiC: Elvis Presley in Concert). And that’s not including the many, many straight-to-streaming music docs and concert films, or scripted films – such as the box office-toppingMichael Jackson biopicor the Green Day-authored coming-of-age comedyNimrods– that serve the same reputation-burnishing purpose.View image in fullscreenMad for it … Oasis fans in Don’t Look Back in Anger.Photograph: Oasis: Don’t Look Back in AngerEver since DA Pennebaker trained his camera on a Bob Dylan in 1967’sDon’t Look Back, the value of a well-made music doc has been obvious, but the current climate is particularly welcoming for the genre. Live footage has never been easier to capture or archive footage simpler to upload and digitise. And with the number of people going to the cinema still significantly down since the pandemic, there’s an enthusiasm among exhibitors to show films that lure in fandoms, particularly younger ones, that cinemas might otherwise not reach.With studios and streamers lining up to take on these projects, artists, or artists’ estates, can demand a share of control over the finished product, particularly if they’re the ones with the rights to archive material and the songs themselves. (Though, intriguingly,Oasisdon’t seem to have demanded editorial control over Don’t Look Back in Anger; had they done so, you imagine they might have nixed the extended footage of one fan wearing a kit of the Gallagher brothers’ hated Manchester United.)Looking at the sea of concert films and music documentaries released in the last year, a generational divide of sorts jumps out between the former and the latter. Younger artists, without much of a history to trumpet, are largely the subjects of concert films, where the kineticism of their live shows can be shown off, enticing fans who didn’t catch the actual gig to start saving up for that next tour. Older artists with extensive archives and a long, winding narrative to draw from are more likely to be profiled in documentaries, or documentary-concert film hybrids, where they make their case for a place in pop’s pantheon.Don’t Look Back in Anger goes further than many of its peers, though, by suggesting the band’s music has grown beyond their control, becoming part of some sort of wider folk memory. “You want to be writing songs that people take and stick into their lives and go ‘It’s mine now’,” Liam says, and the documentary goes out of its way to show that transference, spending as much time with Oasis fans, from Argentinian football ultras to Korean oyster-divers, as it does with the Gallaghers. Perhaps its most stirring moment comes during the gigs in Manchester’s Heaton Park, where instead of paid-up fans, the cameras follow those clambering over fences for a communal ticketless sing-along of Bring It on Down, as if the musichas passed from possession of the band to the wider public.That framing may sound self-aggrandising, but we are shown compelling evidence: just witness the footage of Don’t Look Back in Anger (the song) beingspontaneously sungat the vigil for the 2017 Manchester Arena bombing. In another scene, a priest uses the Gallaghers’ reunion to highlight the importance of forgiveness – playing to the cameras, perhaps, but there’s a distinctly religious quality to some of the footage here: the ecstatic wailing of fans, the mass devotional sing-alongs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPerhaps that’s the power of music – or a slickly produced documentary, at least: to make our ephemeral rock stars immortal.To read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive The Guide in your inbox every FridayExplore more on these topicsCultureThe Guide newsletterOasisLiam GallagherNoel GallagherDocumentary filmsPop and rocknewslettersShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: surprise smash hit show Saturday Night Live UK is back! | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Jeff Goldblum is the first guest host and new faces join the comedy cast. Plus, another magnificent farewell to the Proms! Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Jeff Goldblum is the first guest host and new faces join the comedy cast. Plus, another magnificent farewell to the Proms! Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: New faces … Freddie Meredith joins Saturday Night Live UK.Photograph: Sky UK/Eva PentelView image in fullscreenNew faces … Freddie Meredith joins Saturday Night Live UK.Photograph: Sky UK/Eva PentelTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: surprise smash hit show Saturday Night Live UK is back!Jeff Goldblum is the first guest host and new faces join the comedy cast. Plus, another magnificent farewell to the Proms! Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Priya Elan,Jack Seale,Graeme VirtueandEllen E JonesSat 12 Sep 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 01.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSaturday Night Live UK10pm, Sky OneEarlier this year, pretty much everybody expected this US late-night import to fail. But it turned out to be such a hoot (mostly thanks to Jack Shep’s golden Princess Diana impression) that its return is a welcome relief to autumn nights. The comedy names that made it such a success are back – along with newbie Freddie Meredith – and they’re joined by the first celebrity host, Jeff Goldblum.HRLast Night of the Proms7.10pm, BBC TwoThe biggest night of the Proms and a bittersweet end to the season. Katie Derham and Nick Mohammed host the classical bonanza, ranging from Bernstein’s dazzling Overture to Candide to Holst’s buoyant Jupiter and hits from Guys and Dolls. As per tradition, Land of Hope and Glory et al marks the big end and can be seen on BBC One from 9pm.HRThe Celebrity Inner Circle8.15pm, BBC OneWith Britain’s Got Talent not returning until next year, Amanda Holden’s reign of Saturday night telly continues with season two of this QI-meets-The Traitors quiz show. Six contestants including a standup and a “retired granny” are paired with celebrities, as they outsmart each other until one of them goes home with £18k.Priya ElanThe Box8.15pm, ITV1Gary Lineker’s bafflingly contrived celebrity gameshow continues, randomly. After a witless debating task at the Oxford Union, Brighton beach at least offers the appearance of physical peril as the contestants swim in the murky sea. But if you can identify the point of any of what’s going on, you ought to win a cash prize.Jack SealeBeck9pm, BBC FourAnother chewy case for venerable cop Martin Beck (Peter Haber) and the Stockholm homicide squad. Their attempts to solve the gang-related murder of a 17-year-old girl are disrupted by a shotgun-wielding vigilante with street justice on his mind.Graeme VirtueChaka Khan: Radio 2 in the Park 202610pm, BBC TwoYou can catch highlights of the vintage pop festival at 9pm, featuring Lulu, Texas and Emeli Sandé. Then stick around for this full set from the queen of funk, Chaka Khan, with all the hits to sing along to, from Ain’t Nobody to I Feel For You and, of course, I’m Every Woman.HRFilm choiceIn the Grey, out now, Prime VideoView image in fullscreenDirty work … In the Grey on Prime Video.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyThere’s a conspicuous absence of cockneys in this new action thriller – but otherwise it’s your typical Guy Ritchie joint, elevated by the presence of Jake Gyllenhaal as Bronco Beauregard, one half of a glorified, globe-trotting debt-collecting duo with Henry Cavill as his more reticent other half, Sid. Eiza González is on – effectively – Miss Moneypenny duties as Rachel Wild, a lawyer who employs Bronco and Sid to do her dirty work (ie all the cool stunts), on account of their absolute willingness to operate in the legal-moral grey zone of the title.Ellen E JonesThe History of Sound, 7.50am, 2.50pm, Sky Cinema PremiereFeted young actors Paul Mescal and Josh O’Connor have teamed up for this melancholy romance about music and missed connection. Mescal plays Lionel, a gifted musician who meets a more scholarly academic, David (O’Connor), while studying at the New England Conservatory of Music, in the midst of the first world war. Reunited after armistice, the two travel around rural Maine together, recording their folk music on the new-fangled “wax cylinders” and – ultimately, fleetingly – falling in love. Director Oliver Hermanus’s previous work includes Living, the Bill Nighy-starring re-imagining of Kurosawa’s 50s classic Ikiru, and this is a similar symphony of longing and decade-spanning desire.EEJThe Red Shoes, 9.50am, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenSpectacular sissonnes … The Red Shoes on BBC Two.Photograph: The Archers/AllstarIf you’ve never seen Powell and Pressburger’s 1948 meta-dance-thriller, you’ve never seen the colour red. It’s that serious. Loosely based on Hans Christian Andersen’s gruesome fairytale, it revolves round aspiring ballerina Victoria Page (a resplendent Moira Shearer) and her toxic relationship with the world-renowned impresario Boris Lermontov (Anton Walbrook). Boris forces her to choose between her art and her love for composer Julian Craster (Marius Goring). But the story is near-irrelevant when the cinematography and choreography are this spectacular.EEJLive sportSolheim Cup Golf, 6am, Sky Sports Main EventDay two of the women’s competition.Premiership Rugby: Harlequins v Northampton Saints, 4.30pm, TNT Sports 2At Twickenham Stoop.Athletics: The Ultimate Championships, 5pm, BBC TwoDay two, with the women’s javelin.Premier Leage Football: Tottenham v Everton, 5pm, Sky Sports Main EventFollowed by Sunderland v Arsenal at 6.30pm on TNT Sports 1.Tennis: US Open, 8pm, Sky Sports Main EventThe women’s final.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Scottish Ballet: Emergence review – riveting visions of gods and insects | Dance | The Guardian
description: The world premiere of Julia Cheng’s Entress and a bold return for Crystal Pite’s Emergence both explore collective power
Author: Róisín O'Brien
Headline: The world premiere of Julia Cheng’s Entress and a bold return for Crystal Pite’s Emergence both explore collective power
Content: Sensorial force … Rishan Benjamin (left) and Kayla-Maree Tarantolo in Entress.Photograph: Andy RossView image in fullscreenSensorial force … Rishan Benjamin (left) and Kayla-Maree Tarantolo in Entress.Photograph: Andy RossGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.DanceReviewScottish Ballet: Emergence review – riveting visions of gods and insectsTheatre Royal, GlasgowThe premiere of Julia Cheng’s Entress and a bold return for Crystal Pite’s Emergence both explore collective powerRóisín O'BrienSat 12 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is a significant moment for a choreographer to create work for a large ballet company for the first time. This is the thread that joins these two Scottish Ballet performances: the world premiere of Entress by Julia Cheng and a restaging of Crystal Pite’s Emergence, choreographed for the National Ballet of Canada in 2009 and first performed by Scottish Balletat the Edinburgh international festival in 2016.Coming from a varied dance background that includes hip-hop andwaacking, Cheng received Olivier nominations for her choreography for Cabaret and Fiddler on the Roof. She brings an assured patience to the myth-like Entress (from an old Scottish word meaning “right to enter”); scenes exploring groupthink, purging and transformation are allowed time to develop.Yann Seabra’s smartly designed set comprises a scratched black floor that rises halfway up the stage and a floating white sheet that hangs from the ceiling, a soft, open chrysalis. Nüwa (Rishan Benjamin), the Chinese goddess who created humanity, hovers aloft on the raised platform edge, distant from the darkly clad, crouched ensemble.View image in fullscreenA soft, open chrysalis … Julia Cheng’s Entress, designed by Yann Seabra.Photograph: Andy RossStanding alone is the nameless protagonist, the compellingly emotive Kayla-Maree Tarantolo. A pariah figure, she pulses and rebels against her group, who fly past and through her in scenes of increasing strain. Cheng is less focused on the dancers’ technique (though it’s there in nimble partnering and complex hand-patterns), and more on the sensorial force their collective impression makes.Under a capacious score by Isobel Waller-Bridge, flitting between tinkling keys and brooding strings, percussionist Beibei Wang brings momentum and palpable sonic texture. There’s a visual simplicity to the overall arc of Entress, even if the specific events of the story are sometimes hazy. Nonetheless, it’s an absorbing vision from Cheng.View image in fullscreenComplex machinations … Emergence by Crystal Pite.Photograph: Andy RossSeeing the dancers for Emergence creep through a large black eyelet at the back of the stage is a rare instance when a contemporary dance viewer can get genuinely giddy. Pite’s ability to craft physical complexity without losing thematic substance is unmatched.In this scuttling, twitching ballet, we see a mostly segregated hive; the female dancers dominate on their pointe shoes, whispering counts as their wooden blocks deliberately pound the dancefloor, adding to the cacophony of insect-like sounds in Owen Belton’s score. The men, each with black ink traced down their arms, hunch down then fearlessly slide across the floor in elastic contortions. There’s an order here – a frenzied, alien, and deathly beautiful order – but its complex machinations gleefully resist easy interpretation. It’s a bold entry from near the beginning of this choreographer’s astounding oeuvre.AtTheatre Royal, Glasgow, until 12 September.
