title: Kent is having a champagne moment: ‘English wine has gone from a joke to world-class’ | Wine holidays | The Guardian
description: French champagne house Taittinger is helping produce a premium fizz in the Garden of England – and now visitors can visit the beautiful winery and sample it
Author: Phoebe Taplin
Headline: French champagne house Taittinger is helping produce a premium fizz in the Garden of England – and now visitors can visit the beautiful winery and sample it
Content: The Domaine Evremond vineyard sits within an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, just outside Chilham in Kent.View image in fullscreenThe Domaine Evremond vineyard sits within an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, just outside Chilham in Kent.Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Wine holidaysKent is having a champagne moment: ‘English wine has gone from a joke to world-class’French champagne house Taittinger is helping produce a premium fizz in the Garden of England – and now visitors can visit the beautiful winery and sample itPhoebe TaplinSat 12 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe grapes are turning purple on tall green vines, which stretch down towards the distant flint-and-limestone tower of Chilham church. These rows of Pinot Meunier, destined for English sparkling wine, are 51% owned by French champagne house Taittinger. “England is now the most exciting wine region,” says host and sales executive Hilary Sharp as she leads me aroundDomaine Evremondvineyard, which opened its visitor centre last year to coincide with the launch of its first wine.In his 2023 bookVines in a Cold Climate, drinks writer Henry Jeffreys charts the rise of English wine “from a joke to world-class in 30 years”. The book opens with an alcohol-fuelled scene of vine-planting at Domaine Evremond in May 2017: unseasonably cold, rainy, muddy, with rambling anecdotes from anglophile Pierre-Emmanuel Taittinger about “English women encountered in his misspent youth”. The vineyard is named for the exiled French aristocratCharles de Saint-Évremond, a symbol of hedonistic Anglo-French cooperation. The bon vivant introduced champagne to England and party-loving Charles II made him governor of Duck Island in St James’s Park.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian GraphicsWe stroll past a Land Rover, parked up by a windbreak of crab apple trees. Harriet opens the back to reveal a tray of glasses with a chilled bottle ofDomaine Evremond’s Edition I, and we’re soon sipping creamy, citrussy fizz with a view of vines. It tastes great to me, but I’m no expert.Wine critic Jancis Robinson gave it a “distinguished” 16/20 and Jeffreys, in hisSubstack, Drinking Culture, describes “bright green apple fruit with a reassuring bass note of croissant and Marmite”. King Charles III toasted French president Emmanuel Macron with this wine at a state banquet last summer.double quotation markThe vineyard is named for the exiled French aristocrat Charles de Saint-Évremond, the bon vivant who introduced champagne to EnglandTaittinger’s vineyard director, Christelle Rinville, supervises the vines at Domaine Evremond, regularly taking Le Shuttle from Champagne and enthusing about flinty Kentish subsoils. One of the companies that dug through chalk to make the Channel tunnel excavated Evremond’s 25-metre-deep cellars, where 1.5 million bottles can stay cool around the UK’s first subterranean winery.View image in fullscreenDomaine Evremond’s new winery buildingAn elegant umbrella-shaded terrace outside the chalk-cliff walls of the winery has long rustic tables with vases of wildflowers. Visitors can sample the wine (£12.50 a glass, £55 a bottle) from Wednesday to Sunday and there areyear-round tours and tastings. Sitting here under blue skies, among banks of yarrow, knapweed, vetch and wild carrot scorched by the relentless sun, it doesn’t feel very English.Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent. The unirrigated vines (unlike many other crops) seem to be thriving, and the harvest will be up to three weeks early. Jeffreys writes: “Currently the climate in south-east England is similar to that of Champagne in the 1970s.” Optimal latitudes for wine are supposed to be 30 to 50 degrees, with Champagne at the northerly end of the range. Chilham sits at 51 degrees north.double quotation markAn orchard of plums is drooping under the weight of purple fruit. In the hedges, honey-scented wild clematis tangles with wine-dark blackberriesThe vineyard is ahalf-hour walk through fieldsfrom the village, with its cafes, pubs and railway station, where only the front four carriages fit next to the short platform. Bearded butter-yellow cobs of sweetcorn are bursting out of pale green husks beside the path. I loop back to Chilham throughPerry Wood. Just beyond the vines, I can see an old oasthouse through branches laden with rosy gala apples. The land was bought in 2015 from the fruit-growing Gaskain family, whose managing director, Mark Gaskain, oversees day-to-day operations in the vineyards as well as producing about 70 million apples a year.Further on, an orchard of plums is drooping under the weight of purple fruit and crates are stacked up ready for harvest. In the hedges, sprawling hops and honey-scented wild clematis tangle with reddening rosehips and sweet, wine-dark blackberries. Sparrows snack on early-ripened hawthorn under arching beech and sweet chestnut trees, ancient ivy-wreathed hedge maples and squirrel-haunted hazels. Huge clumps of mistletoe hang from towering poplars.View image in fullscreenChilham Castle’s gardens were landscaped by Capability Brown and now include a vineyard.Photograph: Goddard New Era/AlamyCottage gardens are heady with late summer roses, scented lavender, aromatic catnip. I wander past wisteria-clad walls and a row of mud-built house martin nests with late fledglings still cheeping under half-timbered eaves while gathering swallows twitter on the wires.Deputy church warden Lynda Twaite shows me round the flint-walledSt Mary’s, pointing out memorials and a battered old school table, graffitied by 18th-century kids. The pilgrim route to Canterbury runs through the lime- and yew-shadowed churchyard. Across the square, I peer through the gates at creeper-covered Jacobean Chilham Castle. Itsgardens, landscaped by Capability Brown, now include a new vineyard.double quotation markKent has 120 commercially-active vineyards, with last year’s harvest producing more than five million bottles.Before heading to theWoolpack Innfor the night, I take an evening stroll by the River Stour, with a view of weatherboarded Chilham Mill framed by willowherb and ripe elderberries. The river sparkles in the sun and turquoise damselflies hover among loosestrife and waterlilies.The Woolpack’s garden has a Mediterranean feel, with pink hydrangeas, agapanthus and a 600-year-old olive tree. The brick-walled bar has a curving window seat, weathered oak beams and is stuffed with prints and plants and quirky lighting. After a multimillion-pound renovation a couple of years ago, suites and bedrooms upstairs are named after Kentish vineyards, while the big rooms in Rose Cottage, across the lane, come with their own private gardens.View image in fullscreenThe Woolpack Inn’s ‘Woolly cheeseboard ’is served on a slice of tree trunk.Photograph: Phoebe Taplin/The GuardianI sit in the leafy shade with a “Woolly cheeseboard” on a slice of tree trunk. As much cheese-based installation as meal, its applewood-smoked and creamy goat are artfully arranged among crackers, olives, nuts, dried fruit, chutneys and tangy homemade pickles. To go with it, there are pints of Shepherd Neame’s toffee-appley Master Brew from down the road in Faversham, or glasses of the local cuvée at cellar door prices.The best UK vineyards to visit this summer – and what to drink at themRead moreDomaine Evremond helped found theWine Garden of England, a collaboration of Kent vineyards. August 2026 also saw the launch of a new tourism initiative, theKentish Wine Way, encouraging people to visit “England’s largest and most awarded wine region”. The county has 120 commercially active vineyards and more than 25% of Britain’s vines by area, with last year’s harvest producing more than five million bottles. From the train window next day, after hours of walking through wooded hills and burdened orchards, several vineyards roll past, glowing in the evening sunlight.Accommodation was provided bythe Woolpack Inn(doubles from£140 B&B) and some transport bySoutheastern(advance tickets from London St Pancras from £16 each way)Five more Kent vineyards to visitBalfour WineryView image in fullscreenBalfourproduced the first English wine to win a gold medal and a trophy at theInternational Wine Challengefor its 2004 Brut Rosé. Most days, you can pick up a map at the Cellar Door and wander free around the vineyards, orchards, wildflower meadows and ancient oakwoods – or book a range ofexperiences(from £15pp for a self-tutored tasting). There’s a freeshuttle busto Balfour from Marden train station Friday to Sunday (45 mins from London or Canterbury), andcar-free visitors get 20% offthe year-round tours and tastings.Biddenden VineyardsFive miles fromSissinghurst Castle Garden, the vineyard atBiddendenis the oldest in Kent. Drinks journalist Henry Jeffreys writes that the Barnes family are “apple growers who moved into grapes in 1969 when Joyce Barnes … heard a segment about English viticulture on Radio 4’s Woman’s Hour and decided to plant some vines”. You can still buy all kinds of fancy apple juice and cider here, as well as a range of experiences. Most run from May to September (from £15 for a self-guided tour and tasting flight) with a new behind-the-scenes production tour and tasting added this year for the colder months (£30).Chapel DownView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Tim WinterChapel Down, near Tenterden, is England’s largest wine producer, with bottles in numerous supermarkets, made using fruit from more than 700 acres of vineyards across south-east England. A half-hour taxi ride from Ashford International, it offers various tours and tastings, including a cheese and wine pairing (£70).Simpsons’ Wine EstateRuth and Charles Simpson started making wine in Languedoc in 2002 and, since 2012, in Kent, which they call “one of the most dynamic wine-producing regions of the world”.Bookable sessionsinclude tastings (from £25) on a glass-walled mezzanine floor in the winery with velvet sofas and an optional helter-skelter slide to get back down after sampling their still and sparkling wines.WestwellView image in fullscreenOn the edge of the Kent Downs,Westwellis close to Charing station and a short walk from the Pilgrims’ Way. The vineyard is known for its experimental approaches, including wild yeasts, small-scale production and cloudy, naturally sparklingPet Nats. Alongside regular tours, there are Friday pizza nights and seasonal supper clubs. Tour and tasting £28.Explore more on these topicsWine holidaysKent holidaysFood and drinkEngland holidaysUnited Kingdom holidaysShort breaksWeekend breaksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Wonderfully rich and nutty’: the best supermarket mature cheddar, tasted and rated | Cheese | The Guardian
description: These days, there’s a bewildering array of mature cheddar out there, but the good stuff can be hard to find. Which blocks have that tangy farmhouse flavour and which are better left on the supermarket shelf?• The best vegan cheese, tasted and rated
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: These days, there’s a bewildering array of mature cheddar out there, but the good stuff can be hard to find. Which blocks have that tangy farmhouse flavour and which are better left on the supermarket shelf?• The best vegan cheese, tasted and rated
Content: Say cheese: we put mature cheddars to the taste test, to find which block comes out on top.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.View image in fullscreenSay cheese: we put mature cheddars to the taste test, to find which block comes out on top.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterCheeseReview‘Wonderfully rich and nutty’: the best supermarket mature cheddar, tasted and ratedThese days, there’s a bewildering array of mature cheddar out there, but the good stuff can be hard to find. Which blocks have that tangy farmhouse flavour and which are better left on the supermarket shelf?The best vegan cheese, tasted and ratedTom HuntSat 12 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs a West Country lad from the Somerset borders, I believe cheddar should come from Cheddar. The village boastsEngland’s largest limestone gorge, at three miles long and almost 400ft deep, and the stable low temperatures, high humidity and unique microbiome of its caves are perfect for maturing this famous cheese.But good cheddar can be hard to find, not least because it’s a British kitchen staple that’s often sold as a loss-leader and produced by industrial creameries. The resulting generic block of cheese is pleasant enough, but if you want something with a complex flavour profile, crunchy calcium lactate crystals and a creamy texture, you’re going to have to put in some legwork.Today’s test group are all labelled mature and mostly carry a strength rating of four, though I’ve awarded my own strength scoring as they vary greatly and there’s a huge range in quality, texture and flavour. Every big supermarket tends to have a wall of different cheddars, so try as many as you can to find your fit.The best supermarket mature cheddarBest overall:M&S British mature cheddarView image in fullscreen£4.25 for 550g at Ocado (77p/100g)★★★☆☆A large, utilitarian block of creamy cheddar made at Taw Valley Creamery in Devon. Rich and sharp, with a clear, lactic-sour twang. Full of umami, with a buttery texture and some crystallisation. Strength rating of four.Best bargain:Sainsbury’s West Country farmhouse mature cheddarView image in fullscreen£2.95 for 400g at Sainsbury’s (74p/100g)★★★☆☆A protected designation of origin cheese made in Somerset using traditional methods and British milk. Produced by Barber’s dairy, the oldest cheddar maker in the world, this wonderfully savoury cheese is rich and nutty with a crumbly yet creamy texture. Strength: four.And the rest …Godminster the Mighty Middlewick Witch mature cheddarView image in fullscreen£3.80 for 200g at Ocado (£1.90/100g)★★★★☆A small but punchy and crystalline block of mature cheddar made by Godminster in Somerset. There’s a real depth of flavour and sweet umami notes, and it’s also tangy and crunchy with calcium crystals. Strength rating five, and my best splurge.Valley Spire British mature cheddarView image in fullscreen£2.45 for 400g at Lidl (61p/100g), in store only★★★☆☆A creamy block that’s sharp and lively on the nose, with a pungent undertone and very creamy mouthfeel. Good flavour development, too – all buttery, savoury and umami-rich. Lives up to its strength rating of four.Aldi Specially Selected West Country mature cheddarView image in fullscreen£2.99 for 350g at Aldi (85p/100g), in store only★★★☆☆A classic, crumbly yet buttery block studded with calcium crystals, and also made by Barber’s. Matured for up to 12 months, this has an intensely flavoured, tangy, salty and cow-y flavour. Strength: four.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTesco Finest mature cheddarView image in fullscreen£4 for 350g at Tesco (£1.14/100g)★★☆☆☆A large, family-friendly, sweet and creamy block of Cornish cheddar made by Davidstow Creamery. Mild but still flavourful, with lactic sweetness and a little tang. Strength: two.Davidstow Cornwall classic 12 months mature cheddarView image in fullscreen£3.75 for 350g at Morrisons (£1.07/100g)£3.80 for 350g at Ocado (£1.09/100g)★★☆☆☆A creamy block from Britain’s largest cheese factory. Made with 100% Cornish milk and matured for at least 12 months. Not too strong (strength three) with a milky, lactic sharpness and a rounded sweetness. Some crystallisation.Cathedral City mature cheddarView image in fullscreen£3.24 for 550g at Asda (59p/100g)£5.45 for 550g at Tesco (99p/100g)★★☆☆☆A family-friendly, creamy and smooth Cornish cheddar made by Davidstow Creamery with West Country milk. Sweet, acidic, grassy and with a smooth, buttery texture. Strength: three.Morrisons British mature cheddarView image in fullscreen£2.95 for 400g at Morrisons (74p/100g)★☆☆☆☆A sweet, slightly rubbery cheddar made with British milk. It has a slightly chemical aroma (packaging leakage, perhaps?), and is very creamy, more like a younger cheddar, but with a lactic sweet milk and hay umaminess. Strength: three.Asda British mature cheddarView image in fullscreen£2.74 for 250g at Asda (£1.10/100g)★☆☆☆☆A small block of creamy cheddar with little provenance other than that it’s made at an “award-winning” British creamery, albeit without naming it. A touch sour, very buttery and soft. Strength: three.For more, read our roundup of thebest vegan cheeseand thebest supermarket fetaExplore more on these topicsCheeseThe FilterFoodBritish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Meera Sodha’s vegetarian recipe for mushroom claypot rice | Vegetables | The Guardian
description: I’m taking a break to replenish my creative reserves. Until then, I leave you with this champion champignon number
Author: Meera Sodha
Headline: I’m taking a break to replenish my creative reserves. Until then, I leave you with this champion champignon number
Content: Meera Sodha’s mushroom claypot rice.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.View image in fullscreenMeera Sodha’s mushroom claypot rice.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Mandy Thompson.Meera Sodha recipesVegetablesMeera Sodha’s vegetarian recipe for mushroom claypot riceI’m taking a break to replenish my creative reserves. Until then, I leave you with this champion champignon numberMeera SodhaSat 12 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the nine years that I’ve been writing this column, I’ve had two babies,a breakdownand very little time away from writing a weekly recipe. I love this column, and creating recipes for you makes me feel like the luckiest duck alive, but I don’t believe that anyone can be endlessly creative without occasionally filling up their own cup. So, I’m taking six months out to travel, replenish and see what treasures I can find for us out there in the big wide world. Treasures such as this gentle claypot rice, which is based on the magical one atDongnae in Bristol. Until then, so long.Mushroom claypot riceYou’ll need a casserole pot with a tight-fitting lid. Weighing the stock will ensure just the right amount of liquid to rice, so use digital scales, if possible.Prep10 minSoak30 minCook1 hrServes4400g white short-grain rice, or sushi rice60g (4 tbsp) light soy sauce60g (4 tbsp) Shaoxing wine30g (2 tbsp) mirin15g white-wine vinegarFine sea salt400g mixed enoki, shiitake, king oyster and oyster mushrooms4 tbsp neutral oil– I use rapeseed2 tbsp toasted sesame oil10 spring onions(100g), whites and greens trimmed, finely sliced and washed1½cm x 1½cm piece fresh ginger, peeled and finely minced2 large garlic cloves, peeled and minced4 eggs(medium or large ones)Put the rice in a large bowl, cover with cold water, then swish with your hands until the water turns cloudy. Pour away the water, then repeat five more times, until the water is clear-ish. Leave the rice to soak in cold water for 30 minutes, then drain.Meanwhile, weigh out the soy sauce, Shaoxing wine, mirin and vinegar into a jug, add 380ml water and half a teaspoon of salt, and mix well.Tear the oyster mushrooms into 2cm-thick strips and chop the shiitake into ½cm-thick slices. Put three tablespoons of neutral oil in your widest frying pan on a medium to high heat. When bubbles form around a wooden spoon, add half the mixed mushrooms, or as many as will fit without (really) overlapping, and leave for three to four minutes without touching them. Turn over the mushrooms and cook for another three to four minutes, or until beautifully bronzed all over. Transfer the mushrooms to a plate, season with a big pinch of salt, then repeat with the remaining mushrooms; add a drizzle of more oil, if need be.Put the last tablespoon of neutral oil and the sesame oil in a casserole pot on a medium heat. When it’s hot, add the spring onions, ginger and garlic, and fry for two minutes, until the onions are Kermit-green and the garlic smells good. Add half the fried mushrooms, mix, then add the drained rice and mix again.Add the stock and bring to a boil. Scatter the remaining mushrooms evenly over the top and pop on the lid. Turn down to a simmer and leave the rice to cook for 15 minutes. Take off the heat and, with the lid on, leave to rest for 10 minutes.In the meantime, soft-boil the eggs (for a soft, slightly jammy egg, I cook medium eggs for six and a half minutes), then peel them.Divide the mushroom rice between four bowls, use the back of a spoon to make a dent in the middle of each portion and serve with two soft-boiled egg halves (or a raw egg yolk, to be stirred in before eating).Explore more on these topicsVegetablesMeera Sodha recipesFoodRiceEggsMain courseKorean food and drinkAutumn food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content
